The analysis of both tide gauges provided a basis for characterising the tidal regime across the study region. For simplicity, however, a single representative water-level forcing was applied across all study sites, as described in Table 3.2 and Section 1.4. This provides a consistent basis for comparing habitat responses between sites, although it does not capture all local differences in tidal amplitude, phase and water-level variability.
It it important to highlight that the use of the four dominant constituents also represents a deliberate simplification of the observed water-level regime. Seasonal and interannual variability, including variations associated with the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), can influence inundation patterns and sediment dynamics. The duration and timing of these variations may affect vegetation establishment, mortality and morphological adjustment, potentially producing different habitat trajectories even under the same long-term mean sea-level trend. The selected harmonic constituents do not explicitly reproduce these seasonal, interannual or event-driven variations.
Nevertheless, the purpose of the representative forcing is to establish a consistent baseline for investigating long-term habitat changes under the principal astronomical tidal controls, rather than to reproduce every short-term fluctuation in observed water levels. The resulting predictions should therefore be interpreted in the context of this forcing assumption, with the potential influence of omitted seasonal, interannual and extreme-event variability recognised as a source of uncertainty.


3.3.4 Salinity representation and model limitations
Salinity is an important environmental control on mangrove establishment, growth and survival, particularly in the hyper-arid West Pilbara, where evaporation, limited freshwater input and restricted tidal exchange can produce hypersaline conditions. Field observations indicate that salinity is approximately 35–55 ppt near creek mouths, increases towards the landward intertidal zone and can exceed 140 ppt across salt-flat environments. These spatial gradients suggest that salinity may constrain mangrove colonisation even where inundation and elevation conditions become physically suitable.
During initial sensitivity testing, we encountered two difficulties when attempting to represent salinity in the modelling framework. First, stable simulations (short term runs) did not reproduce the high salinity concentrations observed in the landward intertidal and salt-flat environments, with modelled values generally remaining below approximately 55 ppt. Second, longer simulations exhibited numerical instability associated with wetting and drying transitions. In some runs, salinity increased sharply in cells undergoing wetting and drying, eventually reaching the model’s upper limit of 500 ppt. These extreme values (instability) subsequently spread across the computational domain, causing the simulation to crash.
These behaviours may be associated with the numerical treatment of salt during wetting and drying, including the handling of accumulated salt as cells become dry. However, the underlying cause was not investigated further, and the observed instability cannot be attributed conclusively to a particular numerical mechanism.
Consequently, salinity was excluded from the predictive framework. However, it is possible to indirectly represent the influence of salinity through other variables, such as the timing and duration of inundation events, the inundation fittness curve of the mangrove growth (see also Chapter 11 where we attempt to include the influence). It is noteworthy to mention that several existing studies have also omitted salinity in their approach e.g., Xie et al. (2022); Van Maanen et al. (2015); Willemsen et al. (2022); Dunlop et al. (2025). The omission reflects a modelling constraint rather than an assumption that salinity is ecologically unimportant.
This simplification has important implications for interpreting the predictions. Even with the indirect representation of salinity, the framework can identify locations where the modelled physical conditions are consistent with mangrove establishment, but it cannot independently determine whether salinity would permit successful establishment or sustained growth. Consequently, some locations predicted to be suitable may remain unsuitable under actual hypersaline conditions, particularly in the upper intertidal zone and on salt flats. The resulting predictions should therefore be interpreted as potential habitat distributions under the represented physical and ecological processes, rather than definitive forecasts of realised mangrove distribution.

title: 4  Model Overview and Evaluation
4  Model Overview and Evaluation
4  Model Overview and Evaluation
text:
4.3 Morphodynamic Module
Sediment transport and morphological evolution are simulated using the Delft3D-FM morphodynamic module (D-Morphology), accounting for both non-cohesive sand and cohesive sediment (mud) fractions. Suspended sediment transport is calculated using the advection–diffusion equation:
\[
\frac{\partial c}{\partial t}
+
\frac{\partial (uc)}{\partial x}
+
\frac{\partial (vc)}{\partial y}
+
\frac{\partial ((w-w_s)c)}{\partial z}
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}
\left(
\epsilon_{s,x}
\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}
\right)
+
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
\left(
\epsilon_{s,y}
\frac{\partial c}{\partial y}
\right)
+
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}
\left(
\epsilon_{s,z}
\frac{\partial c}{\partial z}
\right)
\tag{4.13}\]
where \(c\) is the sediment concentration, \(u\), \(v\), and \(w\) are the flow velocity components in the \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) directions, respectively, \(w_s\) is the sediment settling velocity, and \(\epsilon_{s,x}\), \(\epsilon_{s,y}\), and \(\epsilon_{s,z}\) are sediment diffusivities in each spatial direction.
For the present depth-averaged (2DH) model configuration, vertical transport terms are neglected. Boundary conditions at the free surface and bed define the exchange of suspended sediment between the water column and the seabed. At the free surface, the vertical diffusive flux is assumed to be zero:
\[
-w_s c - \varepsilon_{s,z}\frac{\partial c}{\partial z}=0,
\qquad
\text{at } z=\zeta \; (\text{free surface})
\tag{4.14}\]
The exchange of sediment between the bed and the water column is represented through erosion and deposition fluxes. The bed boundary condition is expressed as:
\[
-w_s c-\varepsilon_{s,z}\frac{\partial c}{\partial z}
=
D-E,
\qquad
\text{at } z=z_b \; (\text{bed level})
\tag{4.15}\]
where \(E\) and \(D\) represent the erosion and deposition fluxes, respectively. For cohesive sediments, erosion and deposition are calculated using the Partheniades–Krone formulations (Partheniades, 1965):
\[
E=
\begin{cases}
M
\left(
\frac{\tau_{b,\max}}{\tau_{cr,e}}-1
\right),
&
\text{when }
\tau_{b,\max}>\tau_{cr,e},
\\[8pt]
0,
&
\text{when }
\tau_{b,\max}\leq\tau_{cr,e},
\end{cases}
\tag{4.16}\]
\[
D=
\begin{cases}
w_s c
\left(
1-\frac{\tau_{b,\max}}{\tau_{cr,d}}
\right),
&
\text{when }
\tau_{b,\max}<\tau_{cr,d},
\\[8pt]
0,
&
\text{when }
\tau_{b,\max}\geq\tau_{cr,d}.
\end{cases}
\tag{4.17}\]
where \(M\) is the erosion parameter, \(\tau_{b,\max}\) is the maximum bed shear stress generated by currents and waves, \(\tau_{cr,e}\) is the critical bed shear stress for erosion, \(\tau_{cr,d}\) is the critical bed shear stress for deposition, \(w_s\) is the sediment settling velocity, and \(c\) is the depth-averaged suspended sediment concentration.

The coupled hydrodynamic, wave, and morphodynamic processes provide the physical framework required to simulate coastal ecosystem development, including feedback between vegetation establishment, flow modification, sediment dynamics, and morphological change.
Overall, the Delft3D-FM framework enables an integrated simulation of hydrodynamics, waves, sediment transport, and vegetation feedbacks, providing a robust tool for assessing coastal ecosystem dynamics under varying environmental conditions.

title: 4  Model Overview and Evaluation
text:
4.4 Mangrove Model

4.4.1 Colonisation
Mangrove establishment, growth, and mortality were explicitly coupled to local hydrodynamics through an inundation suitability framework. Colonisation is controlled jointly by inundation frequency (\(P\)) and hydrodynamic bed shear stress (\(\tau_{90}\)). These are optimised for each site specifically, however, for illustrative purposes, thresholds optimised for Giralia site is shown below.
Establishment can only occur within a bounded inundation window (\(P_{\min} \le P \le P_{\max}\), where \(P_{\min} = 0.05\) and \(P_{\max} = 0.60\)). Outside this range, establishment is not permitted, reflecting physiological limits on mangrove tolerance to submergence and desiccation. Within this window, colonisation is further constrained by bed shear stress:
\[
\tau_{90} \le \tau_{\text{thres}} \quad \text{where} \quad \tau_{\text{thres}} = 0.265 \text{ N m}^{-2}
\tag{4.18}\]
This adopted shear stress threshold falls within typical ranges reported in literature (Beselly et al., 2023; Willemsen et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022). Within this feasible hydrodynamic domain, the probability of establishment is directly proportional to an inundation suitability function, \(I(P)\). When shear stress exceeds the threshold (\(\tau_{90} > \tau_{\text{thres}}\)), colonisation is completely inhibited regardless of inundation suitability.


4.4.2 Inundation Suitability Framework
Similar to existing formulations (Berger & Hildenbrandt, 2000; Van Maanen et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2022), the inundation suitability function \(I(P)\) is defined as a quadratic response to inundation frequency \(P\):
\[
I(P) = \max \left( a_s P^2 + b_s P + c_s,\, 0 \right)
\tag{4.19}\]
where \(a_s = -13.22\), \(b_s = 8.59\), and \(c_s = -0.40\). The parameters \(a_s\), \(b_s\), \(c_s\), as well as \(\tau_{\text{thres}}\) and the inundation range, were optimised by conducting sensitivity simulations against LiDAR-derived vegetation boundaries and hydrodynamics simulated for the calibration period (January–December 2024).
This formulation yields a unimodal response with a maximum suitability (\(I(P) \approx 1.0\)) at intermediate inundation frequencies.


4.4.3 Vegetation Growth
Vegetation growth is modelled as a stem diameter increment rate \(\frac{dD}{dt}\), scaled jointly by inundation suitability \(I(P)\) and a space availability factor \(C_f\) (adapted from Xie et al., 2022):
\[
\frac{dD}{dt} = \frac{G \cdot D \left( 1 - \frac{D \cdot H}{D_{\max} \cdot H_{\max}} \right)}{274 + 3 b_2 D - 4 b_3 D^2} \cdot I(P) \cdot C_f
\tag{4.20}\]
where \(G = 4.39\) is a growth coefficient, \(D\) is stem diameter (\(\text{cm}\)), and tree height \(H\) (\(\text{cm}\)) is expressed as:
\[
H = 137 + b_2 D - b_3 D^2
\tag{4.21}\]
with growth coefficients \(b_2 = 21.3\) and \(b_3 = 0.2\) are optimised based on Giralia mangrove field data. The maximum structural dimensions (\(D_{\max} = 10 \text{ cm}\) and \(H_{\max} = 330 \text{ cm}\)) were established based on field observations and radiocarbon-dated chronology of arid Western Australian mangroves (Santini et al., 2013), while \(H_{\max}\) was further cross-referenced with regional \(98^{\text{th}}\) percentile LiDAR canopy height measurements. Growth parameters (\(G, b_2, b_3\)) were adjusted following Xie et al. (2022) to reflect growth responses under arid environmental conditions.
Growth is optimised within intermediate inundation frequencies where \(I(P)\) peaks. As trees approach maximum structural limits (\(D \to D_{\max}\)), the growth rate asymptotically approaches zero, representing the reduced growth increment characteristic of mature individuals.


4.4.4 Biomass and Spatial Footprint
To model cohort growth and evaluate total stand biomass within each grid cell, allometric relations based on stem diameter \(D\) (\(\text{m}\)) were implemented following Xie et al. (2022). Total standing biomass \(B_{\text{total}}\) (\(\text{kg}\)) per grid cell is calculated by summing aboveground and belowground biomass across all \(N\) cohorts present:
\[
B_{\text{total}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} n_i \left( \alpha_1 D_i^{\beta_1} + \alpha_2 D_i^{\beta_2} \right)
\tag{4.22}\]
where \(n_i\) and \(D_i\) are the stem density and stem diameter of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) cohort, respectively. Parameters \(\alpha_1, \beta_1\) represent aboveground biomass scaling, and \(\alpha_2, \beta_2\) represent belowground biomass scaling (Xie et al., 2022).
To quantify resource competition thresholds, a critical uncompeted stand capacity \(B_{\text{cap}}\) (\(\text{kg}\)) was derived using a “zone of influence” approach. This describes a fully stocked grid cell occupied by uninhibited mature mangroves (\(D = D_{\max}\)). The territorial footprint radius \(R_{\text{zoi}}\) (\(\text{m}\)) for a mature tree is defined as:
\[
R_{\text{zoi}} = 100 \cdot \left(\frac{D_{\max}}{2}\right)
\tag{4.23}\]
where \(100\) scales the stem radius to its zone of influence footprint. Assuming each mature tree occupies a square spatial footprint of side length \(2 R_{\text{zoi}}\), the maximum uncompeted biomass capacity for a cell area \(A_{\text{cell}}\) (\(\text{m}^2\)) is:
\[
B_{\text{cap}} = \left( \frac{A_{\text{cell}}}{(2 R_{\text{zoi}})^2} \right) \cdot B_{\text{single}}
\tag{4.24}\]
where \(B_{\text{single}}\) is the total individual biomass of a single mature tree (\(D = D_{\max}\)). \(B_{\text{cap}}\) serves as the baseline threshold for evaluating growth suppression and density-dependent mortality.


4.4.5 Intraspecific Competition
To account for spatial limits and resource constraints (e.g. light, space, and porewater nutrients) as vegetation matures, intraspecific competition is governed by a sigmoidal space/resource availability factor (\(C_f \in [0, 1]\)). It is computed as a function of total standing biomass \(B_{\text{total}}\):
\[
C_f = \frac{1}{1 + e^{d \cdot (B_{\text{total}} - B_{0.5})}}
\tag{4.25}\]
where \(B_{0.5}\) is the half-saturation biomass threshold at which resource stress reduces space availability to \(50\%\) (\(C_f = 0.5\)), and \(d\) is a scaling parameter controlling response steepness. Under low biomass conditions (\(B_{\text{total}} \ll B_{0.5}\)), \(C_f \to 1\), imposing negligible competitive inhibition. As biomass increases towards canopy closure (\(B_{\text{total}} \gg B_{0.5}\)), \(C_f \to 0\), representing maximal suppression.
Combined multi-factor environmental stress is evaluated as the product of inundation suitability and space availability (\(I(P) \cdot C_f\)). Intense competitive stress (\(C_f \to 0\)) depresses overall viability, slowing growth rates and initiating density-dependent self-thinning.


4.4.6 Mortality and Density Regulation
Vegetation mortality and density regulation follow a multi-factor, two-stage process driven by hydrodynamic stress, density-dependent competition, and desiccation. Total environmental stress is tracked via the combined viability product \(I(P) \cdot C_f\).
Sub-optimal conditions occur when total viability falls below a critical threshold (\(I(P) \cdot C_f < S_{\text{crit}}\)). For cells experiencing sub-optimal viability, a persistent stress counter \(T_{\text{stress}}\) is incremented sequentially at each time step; otherwise, \(T_{\text{stress}}\) resets to zero.

Complete Mortality: Triggered when a cell experiences sustained stress for five consecutive time steps (\(T_{\text{stress}} \ge 5\)) while simultaneously falling below a critical inundation threshold (\(I(P) < I_{\text{crit}}\)). Upon complete mortality, all structural vegetation attributes—stem density, stem diameter, canopy height, and root density—are reset to zero. Mature individuals are assumed to possess a maximum of \(1,000\) roots, with root counts updated following Van Maanen et al. (2015).
Self-Thinning: In cells subjected to stress (\(I(P) \cdot C_f < S_{\text{crit}}\)) that do not meet the full mortality criteria, self-thinning is applied by incrementally reducing stem density \(n_i\) by a fixed mortality rate factor \(m_{\text{rate}}\). Following self-thinning, \(B_{\text{total}}\) and \(C_f\) are dynamically re-evaluated to reflect the updated stand density.

Under low biomass conditions (\(B_{\text{total}} \ll B_{0.5}\)), \(C_f\) approaches zero, imposing negligible competitive limitations. As canopy closure and root crowding progress (\(B_{\text{total}} \gg B_{0.5}\)), \(C_f\) asymptotically approaches unity, reflecting maximum competition (acting as a proxy for light, space, and porewater nutrients). This competition factor directly modulates individual tree growth rates and exacerbates baseline environmental stress in densely populated grid cells.


4.4.7 Mortality and Self-Thinning
Vegetation mortality and density regulation were executed as a multi-factor, two-stage process influenced by hydrodynamic stress, density-dependent competition, and desiccation. Total environmental stress was computed as the joint product of inundation suitability (\(I(P)\)) and competition stress (\(C_f\)). Sub-optimal conditions were identified wherever total stress fell below a critical threshold:
\[
I(P) \times C_f \le 0.45
\tag{4.26}\]
For all grid cells outside suitable conditions, a persistent stress counter (\(\text{Mort}\)) was incremented sequentially; otherwise, the counter was reset to zero.

Complete Mortality: Triggered when a cell experiences sustained stress for five consecutive time steps (\(\text{Mort} \ge 5\), equivalent to 5 morphodynamic years) while simultaneously remaining below the critical threshold (\(I(P) \times C_f \le 0.45\)). Upon complete mortality, all structural vegetation attributes—including stem density, stem diameter, canopy height, and root density—were reset to zero.
Self-Thinning: In grid cells subjected to stress (\(I(P) \times C_f \le 0.45\)) that did not fulfill the complete mortality duration criteria, self-thinning was applied by incrementally reducing plant stem density by a fixed mortality rate factor (\(\text{Mort}_{\text{plant}}\)), after which \(C_f\) was dynamically re-evaluated to reflect the updated biomass density.

Similar to existing work (Xie et al., 2022), we assume a mature mangrove can have at most 1,000 roots. The number of roots is calculated following the approach of Van Maanen et al. (2015).

title: 5  Idealised modelling
text:
5.1 General
As the coupled flow, sediment transport, and vegetation modules involve numerous empirical coefficients, direct calibration within a complex, site-specific domain introduces significant ambiguity. It is often difficult to distinguish whether variations in model performance stem from underlying physical settings or from confounding domain characteristics such as irregular bathymetry.
To address this and support rigorous developmental purposes, exploratory models provide an effective framework for isolating and understanding these physical processes without site-specific noise. In this chapter, we use an idealised model configuration to systematically evaluate and optimise sediment transport formulations, boundary conditions, and vegetation settings through a three-stage approach.
First, we examine the effects of key environmental forcings on tidal-flat morphology using a simplified, constant-slope idealised domain to identify the hydrodynamic drivers most relevant for regional-scale representation. Next, we advance to a Giralia-based idealised model using site-derived boundary conditions to investigate the influence of sediment dynamics, with particular emphasis on sand–mud interactions, critical shear stress for mud erosion, and mud supply. Finally, following the framework described in Chapter 3 and Chapter 4, we integrate an idealised ecomorphodynamic model based on Giralia conditions to assess how variations in mangrove biological properties influence long-term tidal-creek morphological evolution and also mangrove model properties

title: 5  Idealised Hydromorphological modelling
text:
5.2 Model settings
The exploratory model was run by Delft3D Flexible Mesh, using the D-Flow and D-Morphology module to simulate hydrodynamics and sediment transport. The model was run in a two-dimensional (depth-averaged) domain \(2\times 20\ \mathrm{km}\) with an offshore open boundary, using a rectangular grid size of \(50 \times 50\ \mathrm{m}\). The offshore open boundary was driven by tidal constituents, e.g. M2 and M4, and the lateral and offshore boundaries were closed to ensure model stability. The model bathymetry was featured by alongshore uniform slope of 0.07%. An further mild slope of 0.035% on the high intertidal flat was applied to the model for initial bed profile sensitivity test. The initial bed level at the open boundary was set to-7m relative to mean sea level (MSL) to ensure that cross-shore tidal movement would not be obstructed by the landward boundary. Random perturbations of \(5\ \mathrm{cm}\) were superimposed on the bathymetry to initiate simulations.
Both sand and mud were considered in the idealised model. Sand transport followed the formulation of (Rijn, 1993), with the median grain size of 0.25mm. Mud transport was computed using the Partheniades’ equation (Sanford & Halka, 1993; Winterwerp J.C., 2007), with settling velocity of 0.25 mm/s and critical erosion shear stress of 0.1Pa. Bed friction was represented by a uniform Manning’s friction coefficient of 0.023 \(s\ m^{-1/3}\) . A constant mud supply was imposed at the open boundary. To accelerate morphological response to hydrodynamics, a morphological accelerator Morfac of 50 was used in this model.






Figure 5.1: Idealised model domain and cross section profile

title: 5  Idealised Hydromorphological modelling
text:
5.3 Scenarios design
The scenarios were designed to investigate morphological responses to variations in tidal range, tidal asymmetry, initial bed profile, sediment composition, and mud concentration. Runs 1–3 examined tidal ranges of 0.8, 1.5, and 3.0 m, representing microtidal, mesotidal, and macrotidal regimes, respectively. Because the study sites along the Pilbara coast of Western Australia are characterised by a mesotidal regime, a tidal range of 1.5 m was adopted for the subsequent scenarios.
Tidal asymmetry in Runs 4 and 5 was generated by combining the principal lunar semidiurnal constituent, M2, with its first overtide, M4. A relative phase difference of \(2\varphi_{M4} - \varphi_{M2}=90 ^\circ\) represented flood-dominant conditions, whereas a phase difference of \(270^\circ\) represented ebb-dominant condition. Here, \(\varphi_{M4}\) and \(\varphi_{M2}\) denote the phases of constituents M4 and M2, respectively. For simplicity, \(\varphi_{M2}=0^\circ\) in all scenarios
A gentle upper-intertidal slope of 0.035%, representing a convex-upward profile, was applied to the flood- and ebb-dominated conditions in Runs 6 and 7, respectively. The influence of sediment composition was examined in Runs 8 and 9, in which the mud fraction was increased to 20% and reduced to 0%, respectively. Run 9 therefore represented a purely sandy substrate. In Run 10, the suspended mud concentration at the boundary was increased from 5 to 10 mg L\(^{-1}\) to investigate the influence of sediment availability on tidal-flat morphology.

title: 5  Idealised Hydromorphological modelling
text:
5.4 Results

5.4.1 Morphology
Figure 5.2 presents the morphological changes after 200 years of simulation under different environmental forcing conditions. Panels (a)–(c) of Figure 5.2, together with Figure 5.3 a, illustrate the influence of tidal range on morphological evolution and the mean cross-sectional profile. As the tidal range increased, the accretion zone in the upper intertidal area, where the bed elevation was above 0 m, extended farther landward. Both the width and magnitude of deposition also increased with tidal range. In contrast, deposition in the subtidal and lower-intertidal zones, where the bed elevation was below 0 m, gradually diminished. Under a tidal range of 4 m, erosion became more pronounced and braided channels developed within these zones.
When tidal asymmetry was introduced, substantial morphological differences developed despite only minor changes in tidal range. Compared with the tidally symmetric case, flood-dominant conditions produced a broad depositional zone extending across the entire intertidal platform, between low- and high-water levels, and promoted the formation of two distinct channels. In contrast, ebb-dominant conditions caused pronounced erosion in the subtidal zone and generated a more complex, braided channel network. Changes in the mean cross-sectional profiles were also consistent with previous studies (Pritchard et al., 2002), which showed that flood dominance accelerates the landward progradation of tidal-flat profiles, whereas ebb dominance promotes their recession.
The initial bathymetry plays a crucial role on morphological evolution. Compared with morphological changes in Run 5, reducing slopes in the upper intertidal results in more significant channel-shoal patterns grown in ebb dominance. However, tidal channels under flood dominance do not become longer with increased depositional extent. This is because when the upper slope becomes milder, the intertidal storage becomes larger. With larger intertidal storage, the filing and draining of intertidal areas will slow the landward propagation of high tide relative to low tide. Low tide will partially catch up with high tide and the temporal transition from high to low water will be shortened, resulting in a quicker falling tide and a tendency towards ebb dominance over the flats. Consequently, channels under flood dominance are shortened while under ebb dominance are enhanced.
Increasing or decreasing the mud fraction of the sediment substrate did not substantially alter the extent of the depositional zone. However, a more mud-rich substrate resulted in slightly greater erosion in the subtidal and lower-intertidal zones. A similar response was observed when the mud supply from the open boundary was varied. Increasing the suspended mud supply produced a wider and more elevated depositional zone in the upper intertidal area, while morphological changes in the subtidal and lower-intertidal zones remained limited.






Figure 5.2: Morphological changes after 200-year simulation for idealised scenarios.









Figure 5.3: Bed profile after 200-year simulations when comparing (a) tidal range and (b) tidal asymmetry.





5.4.2 Sediment redistribution
Muddy zones, defined as areas with a mud fraction greater than 30%, developed primarily in the upper intertidal zone. The only exception was the microtidal case (Run 1), in which weaker tidal currents allowed suspended mud to settle at lower elevations. As tidal range increased, the muddy zones expanded and their mud content generally increased.
Tidal asymmetry strongly influenced sediment redistribution. Under flood-dominant conditions, extensive muddy deposits developed across the upper intertidal zone, and the channels also contained a higher proportion of mud. In contrast, ebb-dominant conditions produced only limited muddy deposits and a more extensive sandy area in the subtidal and lower intertidal zones. The channel–shoal patterns observed in Figure 5.2 e were primarily associated with sand erosion. When a gentler initial upper-intertidal slope was applied, mud was transported farther landward, resulting in a broader depositional zone under both flood- and ebb-dominant conditions. However, the gentler slope also enhanced ebb-directed flow. Under ebb-dominant conditions, this caused greater sand erosion and produced the wider and deeper channel networks shown in Figure 5.2 g.
Variations in the initial mud fraction of the sediment substrate produced similar muddy-zone distributions across the intertidal platform. This suggests that most of the deposited mud originated from the continuous suspended-sediment supply at the open boundary rather than from the initial bed composition. This interpretation is further supported by the comparison between Figure 5.4 b and Figure 5.4 j, in which doubling the mud concentration at the open boundary resulted in a substantially wider muddy zone.






Figure 5.4: Mud fraction after 200-year simulation for idealised scenarios.





5.4.3 Implications for regional hydromorphodynamic modelling
Our sensitivity tests using the schematised idealised model demonstrate that external environmental drivers play a dominant role in controlling morphological evolution and sediment redistribution. The results show that tidal range, tidal asymmetry, and the initial bed profile strongly influence morphological development and mud distribution, whereas the effects of initial substrate sediment composition and mud supply at the open boundary are comparatively limited. Therefore, when applying the morphodynamic model to tide-dominated real-world systems, accurate representation of local tidal conditions and bathymetry should be prioritised. Sediment composition and boundary mud supply can be considered secondary factors in model parameterisation. For further details on the selection and justification of morphodynamic model parameters, readers are referred to ?sec-appendix-c.
Friedrichs (2011) summarised the effects of different environmental drivers on tidal-flat profiles (Figure 5.5), showing that tide-dominated systems tend to develop convex-up profiles, whereas wave-dominated systems are more likely to exhibit concave-up profiles. Biological processes, such as bioturbation and bioadhesion, can further modify these profile shapes by either enhancing or reducing their convexity or concavity. As discussed previously, the Pilbara Coast is a well-sheltered, tide-dominated environment. Extensive mangrove forests occur along the fringing coast and tidal channels, where they act as natural buffers by reducing flow energy and stabilising channel banks. Therefore, biological processes, particularly the effects of mangrove vegetation, need to be properly represented in morphodynamic modelling of the Pilbara Coast.

title: 6  Model Application to Study Sites
text:
6.1 General
The sensitivity tests and idealised modelling presented in Chapter 5 demonstrated that local tidal forcing, ebb-dominant asymmetry, and initial bathymetric slope play a controlling role in governing morphodynamic evolution and habitat distribution across arid intertidal landscapes. To operationalise the insights gained from idealised modelling and address the broader research objectives, this study adopts a staged strategy focused on three targeted sites along the West Pilbara coast: Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston.
Each study site represents a distinct coastal environment and serves a specific role within the research design:
Giralia Domain: Serves as the primary baseline domain for detailed model development, calibration, and baseline physical process evaluation in a relatively well-studied setting.
Urala Domain: Provides a complex coastal setting with the proposed industrial footprint, serving as the core domain to investigate the hydrodynamic and ecological implications of coastal development.
Cape Preston Domain: Serves as a test case to evaluate the transferability and robustness of the established modelling framework across different environmental characteristics.
While these site-specific models accurately capture ambient tidal dynamics, local creek incision, and intertidal inundation under typical conditions, understanding the long term persistence of arid intertidal habitats also requires evaluating their response to severe coastal hazards. To fully understand the broader regional marine dynamics, extreme weather phenomena (such as tropical cyclones), and open ocean wave current interactions, a standalone Exmouth Gulf Regional Model was developed. Coupled directly with a wave generation and propagation module (SWAN), this broader regional domain encompasses both the Giralia and Urala domains, enabling the simulation of wind wave growth, wave setup, and storm surge dynamics across the Gulf during extreme events.

6.6 Regional Model: Exmouth Gulf

6.6.1 Model Setup & Domain
The Exmouth Gulf regional model was developed to capture large-scale hydrodynamic processes, regional-scale tidal propagation, and extreme weather events (such as storm surges) affecting both the Giralia and Urala model domains. Boundary conditions for the regional scale are driven by oceanographic and atmospheric reanalysis datasets. The model domain spans approximately 110 km in width and 150 km in length to encapsulate these broader regional oceanographic dynamics.
Figure 6.10 a provides an overview of the full model domain, while Figure 6.10 b presents a zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box, highlighting the refined grid spacing in critical shallow and coastal regions. The domain extent was similarly configured and verified under extreme Sea Level Rise (SLR) scenarios (+1.5 m) to ensure sufficient coverage for habitat migration predictions.






Figure 6.10: Delft3D Flexible Mesh grid layout for the Exmouth Gulf Domain showing: a) full domain overview, and b) zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box.





6.6.2 Bathymetry and Topography
The bathymetry and topography for the Exmouth Gulf domain were derived by integrating multiple high-resolution datasets:

LiDAR topography from surveys conducted by the University of Western Australia (UWA);
Multibeam creek bathymetry surveys dedicatedly conducted for the Exmouth Gulf region as part of this project;
Satellite-derived bathymetry for the Exmouth Gulf sourced from Geoscience Australia;
Digital Earth Australia (DEA) Intertidal Bathymetry, incorporated specifically to achieve a smooth, physically consistent transition between the terrestrial LiDAR topography and the satellite-derived bathymetry in the intertidal zones.

The integrated bathymetric map (Figure 6.11 a) and its detailed intertidal view (Figure 6.11 b) reflect iterative refinements against water level observations, particularly around creek entrances and intertidal mudflats, ensuring accurate numerical representation of wetting and drying dynamics.






Figure 6.11: Bathymetry and topography of the Exmouth Gulf Model Domain showing: a) full domain bathymetry, and b) zoomed-in view of intertidal regions and creek channels.

6.7 Site-Specific Hydrodynamic Models

6.7.1 Urala Domain Model

6.7.1.1 Mesh and Setup
The grid design for the Urala domain covers an area of approximately 44 km in length and 35 km in width. The grid consists entirely of triangular elements with variable resolutions, ranging from 250 m in open-water areas to 12 m near shorelines and critical locations such as creek mouths. This high-resolution approach ensures an accurate representation of hydrodynamic processes within the study area.
Figure 6.12 a provides an overview of the model domain, while Figure 6.12 b presents a zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box, demonstrating finer grid spacing in critical regions.
As the focus of this study is to predict habitat migration, optimizing the domain extent is a key consideration. To achieve this, an extreme Sea Level Rise (SLR) scenario of +1.5 m was arbitrarily simulated for one year. The outer domain extent was subsequently fixed based on these hydrodynamic inundation extents, ensuring appropriateness for long-term project objectives.






Figure 6.12: Delft3D Flexible Mesh grid layout for the Urala Domain showing: a) full domain overview, and b) zoomed-in view of variable resolution mesh.





6.7.1.2 Bathymetry and Topography
The bathymetry and topography incorporated into the model were derived from multiple high-quality sources:

LiDAR topography from surveys conducted by the University of Western Australia (UWA);
Creek bathymetry surveys conducted by UWA as part of Project A (existing data);
Satellite-derived bathymetry (from Geoscience Australia) for the Exmouth Gulf.

These combined datasets facilitated the development of a comprehensive, high-resolution bathymetric surface. Figure 6.13 a shows the bathymetry of the full domain, while Figure 6.13 b presents a zoomed-in view of the Urala North and South creeks along with the intertidal flats. Multiple iterations were performed, adjusting bathymetry based on comparisons with observed water level data to enhance model accuracy. Specific refinements were made at critical locations, such as the northern and southern mouths of Urala Creek, to better align simulated hydrodynamics with measured conditions.






Figure 6.13: Bathymetry and topography of the Urala Model Domain: a) full domain bathymetry, and b) zoomed-in view of Urala North and South creeks and intertidal flats.







6.7.2 Giralia Domain Model

6.7.2.1 Mesh and Setup
The grid design for the Giralia domain covers an area of approximately 44 km in length and 10 km in width. Similar to the Urala model, the grid consists entirely of triangular elements with variable resolutions, maintaining finer grid spacing near complex coastlines and creek systems to accurately resolve local hydrodynamic processes.
Figure 6.14 a provides an overview of the full model domain, while Figure 6.14 b presents a zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box, highlighting the refined grid spacing in critical intertidal regions. The domain extent was similarly configured and verified under extreme Sea Level Rise (SLR) scenarios (+1.5 m) to ensure sufficient coverage for habitat migration predictions.






Figure 6.14: Delft3D Flexible Mesh grid layout for the Giralia Domain showing: a) full domain overview, and b) zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box.





6.7.2.2 Bathymetry and Topography
The bathymetry and topography for the Giralia domain were derived by integrating multiple high-resolution datasets:

LiDAR topography from surveys conducted by the University of Western Australia (UWA);
Multibeam creek bathymetry surveys dedicatedly conducted for the Giralia domain as part of this project;
Satellite-derived bathymetry for the Exmouth Gulf sourced from Geoscience Australia;
Digital Earth Australia (DEA) Intertidal Bathymetry, incorporated specifically to achieve a smooth, physically consistent transition between the terrestrial LiDAR topography and the satellite-derived bathymetry in the intertidal zones.

The integrated bathymetric map (Figure 6.15 a) and its detailed intertidal view (Figure 6.15 b) reflect iterative refinements against water level observations, particularly around creek entrances and intertidal mudflats, ensuring accurate numerical representation of wetting and drying dynamics.






Figure 6.15: Bathymetry and topography of the Giralia Model Domain showing: a) full domain bathymetry, and b) zoomed-in view of intertidal regions and creek channels.







6.7.3 Cape Preston Domain Model

6.7.3.1 Mesh and Setup
The grid design for the Cape Preston domain covers an area of approximately 34 km in width and 58 km in length. Following the design principles of the Giralia and Urala models, the grid consists entirely of triangular elements with variable resolutions. Finer grid spacing is maintained near complex coastlines and intertidal creek systems to accurately resolve local hydrodynamic processes and boundary interactions.
Figure 6.16 a provides an overview of the full model domain, while Figure 6.16 b presents a zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box, showcasing the refined grid spacing across the nearshore and creek network. The domain extent was configured and verified under extreme Sea Level Rise (SLR) scenarios (+1.5 m) to ensure sufficient coverage for habitat migration predictions.






Figure 6.16: Delft3D Flexible Mesh grid layout for the Cape Preston Domain showing: a) full domain overview, and b) zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box.





6.7.3.2 Bathymetry and Topography
The bathymetry and topography for the Cape Preston domain were developed using a similar combination of spatial elevation and bathymetric datasets as the Giralia and Urala models to construct a seamless elevation surface.
Unlike the Giralia and Urala domains, no dedicated field creek bathymetry surveys were carried out for this site. Instead, the intertidal creek channels were manually carved into the digital elevation model. The spatial extents and widths of the creeks were derived from satellite imagery, while channel depths were assigned based on average cross-sectional profile conditions observed in the Giralia domain.
The resulting integrated bathymetric map (Figure 6.17 a) and its detailed view (Figure 6.17 b) reflect iterative refinements to ensure physically consistent transitions across the intertidal mudflats and accurately capture wetting and drying dynamics during tidal cycles.






Figure 6.17: Bathymetry and topography of the Cape Preston Model Domain showing: a) full domain bathymetry, and b) zoomed-in view of nearshore intertidal regions and creek channels.

6.8 Simulation Periods and Boundary Conditions

6.8.1 Simulation Period
The modelling period across all domains was established based on the availability of hydrodynamic validation data and satellite-derived habitat mapping. Field-collected data from a comprehensive monitoring campaign conducted between November 2023 and mid-April 2024 (Phase 1) were used for calibration and validation.
To establish a representative period for habitat predictive simulations, the complete calendar year of 2023 was selected. This period encompasses part of the calibration window and aligns with satellite-derived baseline habitat maps from Project A.

Simulation Period
Primary Objective




Calibration & Validation

6.8.2 Model Boundary Conditions & Environmental Forcings
An overview of the spatial domains and numerical model forcing datasets is illustrated in Figure 6.18.

Water Level & Tidal Forcing: Tidal boundaries were forced using measured water level data from the Onslow tide gauge station (Western Australia). Initial sensitivity evaluations demonstrated that local measured water levels outperformed regional/global tide models (TPXO global tide model and HYCOM sea surface height anomalies) by inherently capturing episodic, non-tidal extremes such as storm surges.
Atmospheric Forcing & Heat Flux: Surface meteorological forcing parameters—including air temperature, relative humidity, cloud cover, surface wind speed, and atmospheric pressure—were extracted from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset.
Evaporation Delft3D FM calculates surface heat dynamics and evaporation dynamically using a composite heat flux model. Latent heat exchange and evaporation rates are derived via bulk aerodynamic formulations based on atmospheric pressure, wind speed, and surface-to-air humidity gradients. Solar radiation fluxes are calculated internally as a function of geographical position, time of day, and cloud cover.
Rainfall Dynamics: Local measured rainfall data were included during the model calibration phase (November 2023 – April 2024) to account for flash-runoff events and localised salinity fluctuations. For predictive 2023 habitat simulations, only tidal and wind/atmospheric forces were applied.
Waves: Wave conditions across the target domains (Exmouth Gulf, Giralia, Cape Preston, and Urala) were incorporated using WHACS wave model outputs, complemented by local measured dataset observations in Exmouth Gulf for boundary validation.







Figure 6.18: Overview of the model boundary conditions, forcing datasets, and spatial model domains (Exmouth Gulf, Giralia, Cape Preston, and Urala).





6.8.3 Bed Roughness (Manning’s \(n\))
Flow resistance across diverse intertidal and benthic habitats was parameterised using mapped habitat distributions. For model calibration and validation purposes, spatially varying Manning’s roughness coefficients (\(n\)) were assigned according to habitat type based on existing literatures (Arefin et al., 2026; Kumbier et al., 2022; Medeiros, 2023; Rodríguez et al., 2017; Vulliet et al., 2023), as summarised in Table 6.3.

However, for predictive future simulations, spatial habitat distributions change dynamically over time. Consequently, a uniform baseline bed roughness of \(n = 0.023 \text{ s m}^{-1/3}\) was applied across the entire domain. Vegetation-induced hydrodynamic effects are instead introduced dynamically using the approach detailed in Section 4.4. Under this formulation (Baptist et al., 2007), flow resistance from evolving vegetation canopy is directly coupled to hydrodynamics by converting vegetation-induced drag into an equivalent increase in effective bed roughness.

6.9 Hydrodynamic Model Calibration & Validation
Hydrodynamics serve as the primary physical driver shaping intertidal habitats. Consequently, achieving accurate hydrodynamic predictions is crucial for assessing both baseline conditions and potential future environmental changes.
Hydrodynamic calibration was conducted by comparing simulated water surface elevations against field-measured water level time series across key monitoring stations representing diverse habitat zones.
The model was calibrated primarily by iteratively adjusting bottom roughness parameters (Manning’s \(n\) coefficients tailored to specific habitat types) and refining lateral boundary configurations: * Manning’s Roughness (\(n\)): Spatially varied to reflect vegetation cover and bed substrate resistance across different intertidal zones. * Lateral Boundary Conditions: Tested and refined using Neumann (flux/flow gradient) lateral boundaries, prescribed water level boundaries, and closed boundaries (implicit no-slip wall condition).

6.9.1 Urala Domain Calibration
Hydrodynamics serve as the primary physical driver governing intertidal habitat dynamics. Consequently, obtaining accurate hydrodynamic predictions is essential for assessing baseline conditions as well as forecasting future changes.
While salinity and temperature are important factors influencing habitat migration, the primary driver in this study is water level. Due to inherent uncertainties in simulated salinity and temperature data, habitat migration predictions are based solely on hydrodynamic conditions (i.e., inundation and flow parameters).
Model calibration was conducted by comparing simulated water surface elevations against field-measured water level time series across key monitoring locations representing diverse habitat zones, including: * Urala Creek North Mouth * Lower Creek * Mud Flat * Mid Mat (Lower Algal Mat) * Upper Mat (Upper Algal Mat)
Calibration was achieved by iteratively tuning bottom roughness parameters (spatially variable Manning’s \(n\) coefficients tailored to specific habitat bed types) and evaluating lateral boundary conditions (testing Neumann lateral boundaries vs. prescribed water level boundaries vs. closed wall boundaries). Other key calibration parameters typically adjusted during this process include turbulence/eddy viscosity, wind drag coefficients, bathymetric/bed smoothing, and wetting/drying depth thresholds.

6.9.1.1 Quantitative Performance Evaluation
The model achieved a strong overall agreement between measured and simulated water level time series:

Mouth & Lower Creek: The model exhibited excellent agreement with field measurements, achieving an RMSE of \(\approx 0.068\text{ m}\), a bias of \(-0.07\text{ m}\), a slope of \(0.99\), a scatter index of \(\approx 0.17\), and a correlation coefficient (\(R\)) of \(\approx 0.98\).
Lower & Upper Algal Mats / Mud Flats: Surface water levels showed moderate accuracy in amplitude; however, the model demonstrated robust performance when analyzing the amplitude and frequency of inundation—capturing approximately 70% of observed inundation events.
Spatial Inundation: Comparisons between simulated inundation extent and satellite-derived water coverage during representative high and low tides showed a strong spatial match, reinforcing confidence in the model’s ability to accurately simulate hydrodynamic processes and provide a reliable foundation for predicting future Habitat changes under Sea Level Rise (SLR) scenarios.



6.9.1.2 Dynamic Inundation Animation
The animation below illustrates the dynamic water depth variations, tidal propagation, and wetting/drying cycles across the specified monitoring locations within the Urala domain during the calibration period.








Figure 6.19: Dynamic hydrodynamic simulation of water depth across Urala intertidal habitat zones.






6.9.2 Giralia Domain Calibration
The hydrodynamic model for the Giralia domain was calibrated and validated against comprehensive field observations collected between November 2023 and February 2025, covering ambient, moderate, and storm event conditions. While the field campaign recorded pressure, temperature, water level, and salinity, water level was used as the principal variable for calibration and validation given its primary role in controlling mangrove habitat dynamics.
To account for hydrodynamic resistance in vegetated areas, existing mangrove vegetation was explicitly modeled using the Baptist vegetation formulation. Key physical parameters, including tree height and stem density, were derived from field LiDAR observations and applied across the vegetated domain.

6.9.2.1 Quantitative Performance Evaluation
Model performance was evaluated across multiple monitoring stations representing diverse habitat zones by comparing simulated water surface elevations against field measurements:

Overall Fit: The model demonstrated strong agreement across all monitoring locations and hydrodynamic conditions, consistently achieving high correlation coefficients (\(R > 0.90\)).
Slope & Bias: The regression slope exceeded \(0.90\) across nearly all locations (with a reasonable value of \(0.74\) at the Upper Mat site). Absolute bias remained exceptionally low (\(< 0.007\text{ m}\)).
Error Metrics: Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) values remained below \(0.20\text{ m}\) across all monitoring stations.

These statistical results confirm that the model accurately captures both temporal variability and peak magnitudes of water levels under varying hydrodynamic regimes. Because inundation frequency, duration, and depth are the principal controls on mangrove habitat suitability, this calibrated setup provides a robust foundation for predicting future habitat response under Sea Level Rise (SLR) scenarios.


6.9.2.2 Dynamic Inundation Animation
The animation below displays the spatial and temporal hydrodynamic calibration results across the Giralia domain monitoring stations:








Figure 6.20: Dynamic hydrodynamic simulation and water level time series comparison across monitoring stations in the Giralia domain.







6.9.3 Cape Preston Domain Application
Unlike the Urala and Giralia domains, a separate site-specific hydrodynamic calibration and validation was not carried out for Cape Preston. Instead, Cape Preston serves as a demonstrative site where the key hydrodynamic parameterizations, bed roughness settings, and vegetation flow resistance formulations calibrated and validated in the Urala and Giralia domains were directly applied.
By transferring these field-validated parameters to the Cape Preston domain, the model effectively simulates the baseline hydrodynamic processes including tidal propagation, inundation depth, and flow velocities providing a strong foundation for assessing habitat dynamics and predicting future coastal impacts under Sea Level Rise (SLR) scenarios.

title: 7  Overview
text:
7.1 Study Site: Giralia Bay
The study site is located in Giralia Bay, within the eastern portion of Exmouth Gulf, Western Australia (\(22.4^{\circ}\text{S}\), \(114.3^{\circ}\text{E}\)). Exmouth Gulf is a shallow, semi-enclosed embayment approximately \(75\text{ km}\) long and less than \(20\text{ m}\) deep, bordered by low-relief peninsulas to the west and south. The bay lies within the onshore portion of the Carnarvon Basin and is underlain by calcarenitic rock units covered by late Holocene deposits of shales and sandstones, which are overlain by unconsolidated Quaternary deposits. The coastal plain surrounding the bay is mantled by sequences of Holocene and late Pleistocene sediments, including relict beach ridges, coral reefs, aeolian sands, and supratidal sabkha flats with extensive evaporite crusts (Riera et al., 2023).
The region experiences a warm, hyper-arid climate, with a mean annual air temperature of \(25\,^{\circ}\text{C}\) (mean minimum \(17\,^{\circ}\text{C}\); mean maximum \(32\,^{\circ}\text{C}\)), and summer peaks reaching up to \(47\,^{\circ}\text{C}\). Mean annual rainfall is exceptionally low at \(250\text{ mm yr}^{-1}\). However, the region is periodically impacted by severe tropical cyclones every two to three years, bringing wind gusts exceeding \(300\text{ km h}^{-1}\) and extreme rainfall events exceeding \(600\text{ mm yr}^{-1}\) (Santini et al., 2013).
Recognising the high ecological significance and fragile environmental values of this arid coastal landscape, the Western Australian State Government established an Indigenous Land Use Agreement (ILUA) with the Nganhurra Thanardi Garrbu Aboriginal Corporation to create Giralia National Park and the adjoining Boologooro Nature Reserve under the Plan for Our Parks initiative.

title: 7  Overview
text:
Figure 7.1: Study site at Giralia Bay within the Exmouth Gulf, Northwestern Western Australia. (a) Regional setting. (b) Cross-shore intertidal zonation displaying mangroves, mudflats, cyanobacterial (algal) mats, and high-elevation salt flats.






7.1.1 Intertidal Habitat Zonation
Within Giralia Bay, intertidal habitats display a distinct, continuous cross-shore zonation dictated primarily by tidal inundation frequency and substrate elevation (Figure 7.1). Moving landward from the open water, the ecosystem transitions through four primary zones:

Seaward Mangrove Fringe: Predominantly composed of Avicennia marina, occupying the lower-to-mid intertidal zone where regular tidal flushing occurs.
Mudflats: Low-gradient unvegetated zones exposed during low tides.
Cyanobacterial (Algal) Mats: Expansive microbial communities covering the mid-to-high intertidal flat, thriving under episodic inundation.
High-Elevation Salt Flats: Supratidal sabkha environments characterized by hypersaline conditions and sparse or absent vegetation.

Hydrodynamics across this region are predominantly tidally driven, with wave forcing becoming significant primarily during cyclonic and severe storm events.

title: 7  Overview
text:
7.2 Eco-Geomorphic Modelling Approach
Predicting coastal habitat responses to accelerating sea-level rise (SLR) requires accounting for coupled bio-geomorphic feedbacks and physiological tidal inundation limits (Woodroffe et al., 2016). While mangroves exhibit inherent resilience (Gilman et al., 2008), landward restrictions combined with extreme hydrodynamic stress can induce “coastal squeeze,” leading to net habitat loss (Almeida et al., 2025).
To simulate these dynamics at a regional scale, we integrated a process-based hydrodynamic and morphodynamic engine with dynamic biological modules, see Chapter 4 for more details. Refer to Chapter 6 for model detailed model description.

Hydrodynamic & Morphodynamic Framework: We utilised Delft3D-Flexible Mesh (DFM) (Kernkamp et al., 2011) to model regional water levels, flow velocities, and bed shear stress across the complex grid geometry of Giralia Bay.
Mangrove Model: Coupled directly to DFM via NBSDynamics (Deltares, 2022), mangrove establishment, growth, and mortality (Avicennia marina) were dynamically evaluated based on inundation suitability and bed shear stress thresholds, as detailed in Section 4.4.
Cyanobacterial (Algal) Mat Prediction: Using the hydro-morphodynamic outputs generated by DFM combined with the dynamically predicted spatial boundaries of the mangrove forest, cyanobacterial (algal) mat distribution was subsequently mapped and predicted across the domain.

The calibration and validation of the hydrodynamic model, mangrove and algal mats are detailed in Section 6.5 and Section 8.1.2, respectively.

title: 7  Calibration and Validation
text:
7.1 Overview
In order to predict the future distribution and persistence of intertidal habitats under sea level rise and coastal development, the numerical modelling framework must first be calibrated and validated against present-day environmental conditions. Chapter 6 described the multi-scale model development, grid configurations, bathymetric synthesis, and environmental forcing datasets.
This chapter presents the comprehensive calibration and validation of the high-resolution Giralia domain model across three critical physical and ecological components:

title: 7  Calibration and Validation
text:
Hydrodynamic Calibration and Validation: Evaluating simulated water levels and inundation dynamics against continuous field gauge observations.
Mangrove Model Validation: Comparing modelled mangrove spatial extents and canopy parameters (stem diameter and height) against long-term historical satellite observations (2000–2023).
Cyanobacterial (Algal) Mat Validation: Using a data-driven approaches to calibrate and validate the persistent zone as outlined in Chapter 3.

title: 9  Sea Level Rise Scenarios
text:
9.1 Sea Level Rise (SLR) Forcing & Experimental Design
To evaluate the future response of mangrove ecosystems to accelerating environmental changes, we evaluated three Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (Calvin et al., 2023; O’Neill et al., 2016): SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585.
These scenarios encompass a broad spectrum of global emission trajectories and corresponding sea-level rise projections:
Implementing this three-tiered approach establishes a robust envelope of potential future outcomes—spanning conservative to pessimistic pathways—which is critical for identifying thresholds of mangrove vulnerability and potential ecosystem collapse (Figure 9.1).

title: 9  Sea Level Rise Scenarios
text:
SSP119 (Low SLR): Represents a low-emission, sustainability-focused pathway that limits global warming to approximately \(1.5^\circ\text{C}\), resulting in a projected reference SLR of \(\approx 0.5\text{ m}\) by year 2125.
SSP370 (Medium SLR): Models a medium-to-high emission future featuring regional rivalry and high radiative forcing, resulting in a reference SLR of \(\approx 0.95\text{ m}\) by year 2125.
SSP585 (High SLR): Projects a high-emission, fossil-fuel-intensive development strategy, resulting in a reference SLR of \(\approx 1.25\text{ m}\) by year 2125.








Figure 9.1: Sea level rise (SLR) projections based on Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios (SSP1-1.9, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5), representing low, medium, and high sea-level rise trajectories projected through 2125.

title: 8  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
8.1 Sea Level Rise Response
In this chapter, we present the response of mangroves to different sea-level-rise (SLR) scenarios at Giralia Bay. As described in Section 7.3, the predicted mangrove extent under present-day environmental conditions was used as the initial condition, and simulations were subsequently performed under a range of SLR scenarios representing low, medium, and high sea-level-rise conditions as discussed in Chapter 3. The SLR simulations were carried out over a 100-year projection period to assess the long-term response of the mangrove ecosystem to rising sea levels. The results were analysed to investigate changes in mangrove extent and biomass under each SLR scenario and to identify trends in mangrove migration, rates of habitat loss, and potential thresholds beyond which landward migration and ecosystem persistence are no longer possible.
Figure 8.1 shows the temporal evolution of mangrove canopy height (\(h\)) and bed elevation (\(z\)) across the Giralia Bay study site under three SLR scenarios: SSP119 (0.5 m SLR), SSP370 (0.9 m SLR), and SSP585 (1.25 m SLR) over the 100-year simulation period. The animation illustrates the dynamic interplay between rising sea levels, tidal inundation regimes, and mangrove growth, highlighting spatial and temporal patterns of mangrove expansion, dieback, and landward migration.
As SLR progresses, increased hydroperiod and depth along lower-elevation seaward fringes exceed physiological tolerances, triggering dieback and seaward edge drowning—most prominently under high SLR rates. Concurrently, newly inundated supratidal zones create favorable hydrodynamic conditions, facilitating landward encroachment and redistribution of mangroves across the intertidal gradient.
Mangrove biomass was calculated using the method described in Chapter 4. To examine spatial redistribution of biomass, longitudinal (northing) and transverse (easting) profiles were derived for Giralia Bay (Figure 8.2 and Figure 8.3). Figure 8.2 shows the temporal evolution of the longitudinal (northing) mangrove biomass profiles, normalised relative to initial conditions (\(\frac{B}{B_0}\)), at 25-year intervals over the 100-year projection period. Initial biomass has a unimodal spatial distribution centred within the mid-to-fringing intertidal zone.
Under the SSP119 scenario, the system undergoes a gradual transition characterised by a modest decline in seaward fringe biomass alongside a progressive landward migration driven by increased inundation frequency.
Conversely, the medium to higher-emission scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585) exhibit a two-phase response:
Beyond Year 50, extensive dieback is predicted to occur along the seaward fringe, accompanied by significant mangrove expansion into newly suitable landward high-intertidal habitats. Notably, by Year 100, landward biomass accumulation under SSP370 exceeds that of SSP585. This divergence indicates that the rate of SLR under SSP585 outpaces the maximum physiological or ecological colonisation rate of the mangroves, leading to net mangrove loss despite available inland migration space.
Figure 8.3 provides complementary transverse (easting) biomass profiles. Variability in these profiles is relatively small but increases with increasing SLR. Under both SSP119 and SSP585, biomass increases relative to the initial biomass in the central part of the domain. Under SSP370, the increase occurs at a slightly different transverse (easting) position.
The longitudinal (northing) biomass profiles in Figure 8.2 also indicate a landward shift in the location of peak biomass over time across all three scenarios. The magnitude of this shift differs between scenarios. Under SSP119 and SSP370, the landward displacement of the biomass peak is more pronounced. Under SSP585, the peak remains identifiable but is substantially lower, suggesting that biomass redistribution may not keep pace with the greater rate of SLR under this scenario.
Figure 8.4 shows the spatial distributions of mangroves for Year 50 and Year 100, highlighting the diverging long-term trajectory of mangrove extent across SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios. During the initial ~40 years of simulation across all climate projections, differences in predicted mangrove coverage remain relatively subtle, as SLR rates remain within thresholds that permit localised bed level equilibration and persistence along established intertidal zones.
Spatially, baseline mangrove distribution is heavily governed by tidal inundation limits and bed elevation, originally dominating the seaward and central channel networks. However, progressive SLR triggers a distinct landward transgression alongside substantial dieback along the seaward boundaries:

Figure 8.3: Biomass projections across different shared socioeconomic pathways (SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585) evaluated over the Giralia domain.






SSP119 (Low Emission): At Year 50 (Figure 8.4 a), the mangrove fringe maintains structural stability with negligible loss along the lower intertidal zone and initial establishment in the southern high-intertidal flats. By Year 100 (Figure 8.4 d), a modest landward expansion occurs into high-elevation flats characterised by shorter, newly established mangrove foliage (\(h < 1\text{ m}\)), while the core seaward forest retains canopy heights exceeding \(2\text{ m}\).
SSP370 (Intermediate Emission): By Year 50 (Figure 8.4 b), subtle fragmentation emerges along the seaward margin. By Year 100 (Figure 8.4 e), rapid landward migration dominates the southern boundary, where extensive, tall mangrove stands (\(h > 2\text{ m}\)) establish across newly inundated supratidal areas. Concurrent expansion also tracks along newly widened inner tidal channels.
SSP585 (High Emission): At Year 50 (Figure 8.4 c), shows a similar pattern to SSP370. However, by Year 100 (Figure 8.4 f), the system undergoes widespread coastal squeeze and seaward dieback. While mangroves colonise the far-southern landward fringe, the total footprint is diminished compared to SSP370. Higher inundation rates lead to channel drowning and permanent submergence of the seaward mudflats, causing significant loss of historical habitat without an equivalent gain in landward area.







NoteKey Findings: Non-Linear Tipping Points



Overall, the coupled eco-morphodynamic simulations highlight a non-linear tipping point past Year 50 under moderate-to-high SLR.
Landward expansion temporarily compensates for seaward loss; however, under extreme SLR (SSP585), the rate of sea-level rise outpaces landward colonisation capacity, resulting in net habitat contraction.








Figure 8.4: Modelled spatial evolution of bed elevation (\(z\)) and mangrove canopy height (\(h\)) across the study site at Year 50 (top row) and Year 100 (bottom row) under three climate projections: (a, d) SSP119, (b, e) SSP370, and (c, f) SSP585.





8.1.1 Morphological Response
To isolate and track the morphological response of the tidal network to SLR, the active creek network was extracted using the \(0.2\text{ m}\) bed elevation contour at 25-year intervals (Years 1, 25, 50, 75, and 100) in Figure 8.5. Across all scenarios, increased tidal prism volumes driven by rising sea levels induce pronounced bed scour, channel widening, and headward erosion. This forces the main tidal channels to extend progressively landward into previously supratidal salt flats over time.
The magnitude of this landward channel extension varies significantly across climate forcings:

SSP119: Primary tidal channels experience limited headward migration, extending southward by approximately \(0.5\text{ km}\) beyond their baseline position, with morphological changes mostly confined to localised lateral adjustments.
SSP370: Accelerated SLR drives substantial channel deepening and landward elongation, pushing the main creeks approximately \(2.5\text{ km}\) southward by Year 100 alongside extensive secondary branching.
SSP585: Massive headward erosion causes the main creeks to extend \(>4\text{ km}\) landward, accompanied by severe channel widening along the seaward reaches due to extreme estuarine drowning.







Figure 8.5: Spatiotemporal evolution of the tidal creek network over 100 years under (a) SSP119, (b) SSP370, and (c) SSP585 scenarios. Channels are delineated by extracting the \(0.2\text{ m}\) bed level contour at 25-year intervals (Years 1, 25, 50, 75, and 100).



To assess the systemic morphological and ecological adjustments to SLR, the normalised time series of total mangrove area and tidal creek planform footprint relative to initial conditions were evaluated (Figure 8.6).
During the first 40–50 years, both metrics exhibit a relative lag phase characterised by subtle, near-baseline fluctuations (normalised values fluctuating near \(1.0\)). This initial stability reflects a meta-stable equilibrium, where early hydrodynamic forcing and sea-level increments remain within ecological tolerance limits and thresholds for localised bed shear stress. Consequently, vertical accretion and minimal horizontal reconfiguration suffice to maintain system stability across all scenarios (SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585).
Beyond Year 50–60, clear non-linear divergence occurs across the projections, particularly governing channel footprint expansion (Figure 8.6 b):

SSP585 Channel Expansion: Under SSP585, the tidal creek expansion rate initially lags behind SSP370 up to approximately Year 60. Extreme early SLR in SSP585 increases the tidal prism volume and ebb-jet energy, causing channel responses to be dominated by vertical bed incision and cross-sectional deepening rather than rapid headward elongation.
Post-Year 60 Inflection: Past Year 60, an inflection point is reached as increased inundation frequency drowns intertidal margins, causing tidal shear stress to breach headward erosion thresholds. This initiates a sharp acceleration in landward channel extension and network branching through Year 100, reaching a relative footprint expansion \(>2.5\), compared to more moderate trajectories under SSP119 (\(<1.2\)).

Similarly, normalised mangrove surface area (Figure 8.6 a) shows complex non-monotonic behaviour driven by competing mechanisms of seaward edge drowning and landward opportunistic colonisation:

SSP585 Surge & Collapse: Under SSP585, mangrove footprint surges past Year 45, peaking at nearly \(1.4\times\) initial coverage around Year 60 due to rapid inland expansion across previously dry supratidal flats. However, between Years 70 and 80, catastrophic seaward fringe dieback and channel drowning cause a rapid decline back toward baseline values (\(1.0\)).
Spatial Displacement by Year 100: By Year 100, while net normalised mangrove area under SSP585 rebounds close to \(1.1\), a critical spatial displacement occurs: the historical low-intertidal forest is entirely lost to estuarine drowning, and survival is maintained solely because mangroves progressively climb the steeper, elevated terrain along the western margins of the basin.







Figure 8.6: Temporal evolution of normalised (a) total mangrove area and (b) tidal creek planform footprint relative to initial conditions over a 100-year simulation under SSP119 (black), SSP370 (red), and SSP585 (blue) scenarios.






8.1.2 Implications of Sea-Level Rise on the Present Mangrove Footprint
To evaluate the long-term viability of existing mangroves under different SLR scenarios, we restricted our analysis to the initial spatial footprint of mangroves and deliberately excluded landward migration. Figure 8.7 shows the temporal trajectory of total normalised biomass retained strictly within the initial mangrove extent over a 100-year simulation period (Figure 8.7 a) and the cumulative percentage of the initial mangrove footprint subjected to permanent inundation (Figure 8.7 b).
Permanent submergence is defined as continuous 14-day water depth exceeding site-specific tolerance thresholds:
\[z_{\text{submergence}} = \mu_{\text{threshold}} \pm 1\sigma\]
Across all three SLR scenarios, normalised biomass in original locations initially increases during the first two decades, reaching a peak near year 20 to 25 at approximately \(1.1\text{–}1.2\) times the initial baseline (Figure 8.7 a). This initial phase reflects early-stage canopy maturation and biomass accumulation in intertidal cells where water depth remains within tolerable physiological limits. During this same interval, permanent submergence remains low (Figure 8.7 b), staying below \(5\%\) across all scenarios.
Beyond year 25, a critical inflection point occurs as accelerating sea-level rise overwhelms intertidal elevations:








Scenario
Submergence Trajectory (Figure 8.7 b)
Biomass Retention Trajectory (Figure 8.7 a)




SSP119
Submergence reaches \(5\%\) at Year 50; terminates at \(\sim 15\%\) area loss by Year 100.
Normalised biomass stabilises around \(0.85\times\) toward end of century.


SSP370
Habitat loss accelerates after Year 60. Submergence reaches \(20\%\) at Year 75, rising to \(\sim 45\%\) by Year 100.
Normalised biomass declines steadily, dropping to \(0.45\times\) of initial value.


SSP585
Submergence reaches \(25\%\) at Year 50, \(60\%\) at Year 75, and exceeds \(85\%\) (upper bounds near \(95\%\)) by Year 100.
Rapid inundation triggers steep decline; total biomass drops to \(<0.1\times\) of initial levels.



We found a strong inverse relationship exists between the rate of permanent submergence (Figure 8.7) and the retention of localised biomass (Figure 8.7 a). The onset of rapid biomass decline across all scenarios directly mirrors the temporal acceleration of continuous drowning. While biomass loss exceeds the absolute percentage of drowned surface area, this could be due to environmental stress which reduces stem density and productivity prior to complete drowning. The relative divergence among climate scenarios follows an identical sequence in both metrics, with SSP585 showing severe degradation followed by moderate and partial degradation of SSP370 and SSP119.

Summary: Existing mangrove stands will experience widespread dieback and substantial standing biomass loss under moderate-to-high sea-level rise scenarios.







Figure 8.7: The temporal trajectory of total normalised biomass retained within the initial mangrove extent over a 100-year simulation period in panel a) and the cumulative percentage of the initial mangrove footprint subjected to permanent inundation exceeding specific thresholds ranging from \(0.2\text{--}0.8\text{ m}\) represented as \(\text{mean} \pm 1\text{ standard deviation}\)
