title: 8  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
8.2 Discussion
Our numerical modelling demonstrates that mangrove migration in response to sea-level rise (SLR) is an inherently non-linear process. Even under high SLR scenarios, mangroves within the fringing coast do not simply retreat uniformly; instead, they display spatial resilience, surviving and persisting within elevated coastal patches across the region. Crucially, this non-linear response can only be captured because our model incorporates the full, bi-directional coupling of hydro-morphodynamic and eco-vegetation feedbacks, allowing the landscape and vegetation to dynamically co-evolve rather than assuming passive inundation.
In this section, we discuss the broader implications of applying this fully coupled framework to sea-level rise predictions, compare its performance against traditional modelling paradigms, and evaluate the overall transferability of our Python-based workflow to other coastal systems. Finally, we address the key assumptions and limitations inherent to our modelling approach and outline critical future research directions to further refine regional-scale eco-morphodynamic forecasting.


8.2.1 Implications of Hydro-Morphodynamic and Vegetation Feedbacks for Sea-Level Rise Predictions
In this study, we present a fully coupled approach that explicitly resolves the three-way, non-linear feedbacks between hydrodynamics, morphodynamics, and vegetation dynamics. While previous research has successfully demonstrated the significance of three-way dynamic coupling, existing frameworks have largely been restricted to idealised laboratory domains or localised site-specific applications on the order of hundreds of meters. Here, we scale up this coupled numerical framework to regional coastal scales spanning hundreds of kilometers, allowing us to evaluate multi-decadal landscape evolution under sea-level rise (SLR).
Accounting for such a fully dynamic coupled system is paramount when predicting long-term coastal morphological response to SLR. Static or uncoupled models fail to capture the continuous bi-directional adjustments between fluid flow, sediment transport, bed level changes, and vegetation colonisation or mortality—feedbacks that fundamentally dictate channel network stability, sediment trapping, and inland marsh or mangrove migration pathways.
To demonstrate the critical necessity of this integrated framework, numerical simulations were executed under identical hydrodynamic forcing and initial topographic conditions across three distinct vegetation treatments:

No Vegetation: Unvegetated morphodynamics.
Static Vegetation: Spatially fixed, passive vegetation drag without temporal adaptation.
Dynamic Mangroves (SSP370): Explicit eco-morphodynamic feedback involving establishment, growth, and dieback.

Figure 8.8 highlights the long-term creek evolution across these three scenarios, where tidal creek channels were delineated by extracting contours corresponding to a bed elevation threshold of \(0.2\text{ m}\) relative to datum across a 100-year simulation timeline (Year 1 to Year 100).






Figure 8.8: Long-term creek evolution across no vegetation (panel a), static vegetation (panel b) and dynamic vegetation (panel c) for a similar sea level rise forcing with identical initial conditions.



The morphological progression of tidal creek networks exhibits fundamental differences across the three scenarios:

No Vegetation (Figure 8.8 a): In the absence of vegetation, unconstrained flow drives widespread channel widening, severe headward incision, and erratic, unanchored creek migration over time. Lacking root-induced soil cohesion and vegetative flow resistance, channels bifurcate and avulse unpredictably, creating an over-extended, highly unstable drainage network that rapidly erodes under rising water levels.
Static Vegetation (Figure 8.8 b): Incorporating non-adaptive, static drag element vegetation reduces local flow velocity, confining channel migration compared to the unvegetated case. However, because the vegetation cannot adaptively grow, die back, or recolonise in response to changing inundation regimes, channels become locked into fixed corridors. Sediment continuously accumulates within static drag fields without eco-morphodynamic relief, eventually forcing abrupt channel avulsions or localised drowning as the system fails to accommodate accelerating SLR.
Dynamic Mangroves (Figure 8.8 c): The fully coupled dynamic mangrove model reveals a significantly more cohesive, resilient, and focused channel network. Dynamic feedbacks allow mangroves to continuously adjust their density and spatial distribution based on inundation frequency and bed shear stress. As mangroves colonise newly suitable elevated mudflats, flow is selectively funnelled into major drainage corridors, stabilising channel banks while promoting landward network elongation. By Year 100, the dynamic framework predicts organised, highly continuous creek systems extending farther inland to maintain hydrological equilibrium—a trajectory completely uncaptured by static or uncoupled assumptions.







NoteSummary: Century-Scale Ecological Trajectories in Giralia Bay



Synthesising multi-decadal predictions from our coupled eco-morphodynamic model reveals critical distinctions in how Giralia Bay’s mangrove systems adapt to sea-level rise across emission pathways:


8.3 Scenario Profiles & Ecosystem Trajectories

SSP119 (Low SLR – 0.5 m): Dynamic Eco-morphodynamic Equilibrium

Ecosystem Regime: Stable and resilient.
Trajectory: Minimal seaward edge drown-out, paired with steady, localised landward expansion. Intertidal zonation and core canopy architecture remain largely intact throughout the 100-year window.

SSP370 (Intermediate SLR – 0.9 m): Non-linear Ecological Reorganisation

Ecosystem Regime: Spatial restructuring and regime shift past Year 50.
Trajectory: Seaward fringe drown-out is substantial, but active creek elongation allows rapid landward colonisation into newly flooded accommodation space, preserving high net biomass.

SSP585 (High SLR – 1.25 m): Threshold Exceedance & Habitat Collapse

Ecosystem Regime: Marine inundation outpaces ecological adaptation.
Trajectory: An initial inland expansion surge (Years 40–60) is quickly truncated by severe estuarine drowning. Over 85% of the original mangrove footprint is permanently submerged by Year 100, leaving survival restricted to a diminished landward fringe along elevated basin margins.




Insight: Giralia Bay mangroves demonstrate high capacity for landward adaptation under low-to-moderate SLR rates. However, under high-emission forcing (SSP585), the pace of sea-level rise exceeds maximum ecological migration rates, triggering severe net habitat contraction and coastal squeeze.

title: 9  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
9.1 Sea-Level Rise Response
In this chapter, we present the response of cyanobacterial mats to different sea-level-rise (SLR) scenarios across the Giralia Bay intertidal domain. As described in Section 7.4, cyanobacterial mat distributions were predicted using two complementary data-driven approaches: the Random Forest (RF) machine-learning classifier and the Threshold-Based Optimisation approach. The complete model architectures, parameterisation, and algorithmic implementations are detailed in Section 4.5.
Predictions were evaluated over a 100-year projection period at discrete intervals representing present-day baseline, Year 50, and Year 100 conditions to assess long-term structural and spatial adjustments to rising sea levels. Unlike the continuous biomass and canopy height metrics evaluated in the mangrove analysis (Chapter 8), cyanobacterial mat distributions are evaluated as a binary spatial classification (i.e. presence or absence), delineating critical shifts in habitat suitability across the supratidal salt flat gradient.
As highlighted in Section 7.4, the calibrated models were used to predict algal mat responses across the projected sea-level rise scenarios. For illustrative purposes, active creek network extensions extracted using the \(0.2\text{ m}\) bed elevation contour are overlaid on all projections to contextualise hydrodynamic changes relative to mat migration.
Both the Random Forest (RF) approach and the threshold-based optimisation approach reveal a clear landward migration of cyanobacterial mats over the 100-year projection period, closely tracking the inland elongation of the tidal creek network. However, the two modelling paradigms capture distinct facets of spatial reorganisation. The Random Forest model predicts broader, highly continuous spatial coverage with smooth, non-linear transitions across the supratidal gradient, showing extensive Year 50 (red) and Year 100 (black) mat persistence stretching deep into the southern domain across all scenarios. In contrast, the threshold-based optimisation approach enforces strict hydrodynamic boundaries including inundation frequency, 98th percentile water depth, and bed shear stress limits producing sharply delineated spatial bands that more explicitly highlight habitat compression and drowning thresholds.
Zonation remains coherent and well-defined during the first 50 years across all projections, but divergence between the climate scenarios becomes more pronounced by Year 100. Under the low-emissions SSP119 scenario, both models project extensive landward migration, with cyanobacterial mats establishing expansive cover across newly wetted supratidal flats in the southern sector. Under the moderate SSP370 scenario, migration remains progressive, though spatial continuity begins to fragment as tidal channels extend landward. However, under the high-emissions SSP585 scenario, the models reveal severe habitat degradation and divergence. While the RF model maintains moderate spatial persistence, the threshold-based model demonstrates a drastic contraction of the Year 100 mat footprint, where the rapid velocity of sea-level rise exceeds the landward migration capacity and inundation tolerance limits of the mats, resulting in severe coastal squeeze and permanent submergence of historical intertidal zones.
To further understand the evolution of the algal mat also in conjunction with the mangrove prediction, we combined the algal mat and mangrove predictions from both approaches. For illustrative purposes, we computed the alongshore average for the Giralia bay for algal mat (coverage fraction), and also the mangrove coverage fraction. We also did the alongshore mean of the bottom profile with plus or minus 1 std shown for each approach below.

9.2 Methodology

9.2.1 Persistent algal mats zone
The persistent algal-mat distribution used in this report was derived from the Project A output, which provides monthly averaged probabilities of algal-mat presence. We selected the period 2016–2020, during which algal mats were initially scarce in Giralia Bay (due to cyclone in 2015) and subsequently expanded before reaching a relatively stable distribution. To determine an appropriate probability threshold for identifying persistent algal mats, we randomly selected points across the domain and examined their probability time series. Figure 3 shows that locations with persistent algal mats generally exhibited increasing probabilities during the first two years, followed by relatively stable values with seasonal fluctuations over the subsequent three years. Based on this pattern, a probability threshold of 0.5 was adopted to identify algal-mat presence. The persistence of algal mats during 2018–2020 is shown in Figure 4. Areas shown in yellow represent locations where algal mats occurred consistently throughout the period, whereas red areas indicate locations with less frequent occurrence.



Figure 2. The probability of algal mats presence from 2016-2018





Figure 3. Monthly averaged time series of algal mats probability at selected points





Figure 4 Persistent zone of algal mats over 2018-2020.




9.2.2 Algal mats zone hydrodynamics: Single points
To understand the persistent zone hydrodynamics, we random selected points and analyzed the exceedance probability curve of water depth, bed shear stress and continuous exposure hours. Points located in the persistent zone (solid lines) are within a limited range of water depth at high exceedance, for example range between 0.15 to 0.3 m at 2.5% exceedance. The similar trend is observed in terms of bed shear stress and continuous exposure hours that range from 500 to 1000 hours at 5% exceedance. Points in the mangrove zone or bright salt zones (dashed lines) are either featured with too depth water or too long exposure hours. Therefore, we hypotheses that persistent algal mats favor shallow water inundation and moderate exposure hours.



Figure 5. Exceedance curves of (a) water depth (b) bed shear stress, and (c) continuous exposure hours




9.2.3 Algal mats zone hydrodynamics: Calibration over the whole domain
Based on the hypothesis of shallow water inundation is the primary control on the persistence of algal mats, we combined the inundation frequency (P), water depth (D) and continuous exposure hours (Exp) to calibrate the potential distribution of persistent algal mats. After several round of calibration, the following thresholds were adopted.

0<P<25%
0.03 <\(97.5^{th}\)D < 0.22m
\(97^{th}\)Exp<1000 hours

Figure 6 compares the simulated potential distribution of algal mats with satellite images, and persistent algal mats distribution, and dynamic algal mats distribution. The simulated distribution captures approximately 75.5% of the observed persistent algal-mat zone, although it tends to extend more broadly across the higher intertidal flat. Given that algal-mat occurrence is controlled not only by hydrodynamic conditions but also by spatial variability in mat composition and other environmental factors, this approach provides a reasonable first-order representation of the persistent algal-mat zone.

title: 9  Algal mats Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
9.3 Results

9.3.1 Prediction of habitats under future scenarios
Figures 7–9 show the present-day, 50-year, and 100-year distributions of mangrove forests and persistent algal mats under low, intermediate, and high sea-level-rise scenarios (SSP1-1.9, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5, respectively). As sea level rises, both mangroves and persistent algal mats migrate landward under all scenarios, although the magnitude and spatial pattern of migration differ among scenarios.
Under the low sea-level-rise scenario (\(50^{th}\) percentile SSP1-1.9; Figure 7), both mangroves and persistent algal mats shift landward and expand substantially after 50 years. Only limited mangrove loss occurs along the seaward fringe. After 100 years, mangroves continue to migrate landward and gain area, whereas persistent algal mats are displaced farther inland toward the margins of hills and cliffs, resulting in a reduction in their total area.
Under the intermediate sea-level-rise scenario (\(50^{th}\) percentile SSP3-7.0; Figure 8), both mangroves and persistent algal mats also migrate landward and expand during the first 50 years. Compared with SSP1-1.9, however, persistent algal mats migrate farther inland and reach the cliff boundary within 50 years, whereas this transition takes approximately 100 years under SSP1-1.9. After 100 years, substantial widening and landward extension of tidal channels lead to mangrove loss along the seaward fringe and compress the mangrove habitat toward the higher intertidal flat, where persistent algal mats were previously distributed. Consequently, persistent algal mats are increasingly constrained by both mangrove encroachment and sea-level rise and become largely restricted to areas near the cliff boundary.
Under the high sea-level-rise scenario (\(50^{th}\) percentile SSP5-8.5; Figure 9), mangroves migrate even farther landward after 50 years. Persistent algal mats also shift landward, but their expansion is more limited than under the low and intermediate sea-level-rise scenarios. After 100 years, extensive lengthening, widening, and deepening of tidal channels fragment the mangrove forest into more discrete patches and cause substantial retreat along the seaward fringe. Persistent algal mats are compressed against the cliff boundary, with only a limited area remaining.

title: 12  Overview of the Urala Study Site
text:
12.1 Sediment Characteristics and Particle Size Distributions
The Urala study site is located approximately \(40\text{ km}\) south-east of Onslow, positioned along the eastern shoreline near the mouth of Exmouth Gulf. Unlike Giralia Bay, the Urala study region does not exhibit a uniform intertidal zonation. While a distinct shore-normal zonation occurs across the southern area, the northern domain displays a complex morphology where the North Creek and South Creek systems converge and interconnect via a network of micro-creeks (Figure 12.1).
The site exhibits a subtle, extremely low-relief topographic gradient characteristic of arid, hypersaline coastal environments. Elevation increases gently landward from the open water and tidal creek boundaries across distinct ecological zones:
Sediment sampling across the Urala intertidal landscape reveals two distinct sedimentary regimes: open sandy habitats (representing general shoreface and channel substrate) and sheltered mudflats (Figure 12.2 and Figure 12.3).
The sedimentary signatures reflect contrasting hydro-geomorphic energy regimes:

title: 12  Overview of the Urala Study Site
text:
Figure 12.2: Particle size distribution (PSD) representative of general sandy substrate across Urala, showing a narrow, unimodal distribution dominated by medium-to-fine sand fractions (\(100\text{-}500\,\mu\text{m}\); \(\Phi = 1.0\text{-}2.5\)).









Figure 12.3: Particle size distribution (PSD) representative of mudflat environments across Urala, displaying a broad, polymodal distribution spanning fine silts and clays (\(< 10\,\mu\text{m}\)) through fine sand (\(100\,\mu\text{m}\)) to coarse biogenic fragments (\(800\text{-}1000\,\mu\text{m}\)).





General Sandy Substrate (Figure 12.2): Exhibits a highly sorted, well-defined unimodal distribution centered predominantly around fine-to-medium sand (\(150\text{-}300\,\mu\text{m}\), corresponding to Phi values \(\Phi = 1.0\text{-}2.5\), where \(\Phi = 1.5\text{-}2.0\) comprises over \(70\%\) of the sample volume). This narrow grain-size spectrum indicates an energetic, tide- and wave-dominated environment where fine silts and clays are continuously winnowed away, leaving a clean, well-sorted sandy substrate along channels and exposed flats.
Mudflat Substrate (Figure 12.3): Displays a broad, complex polymodal distribution characteristic of low-energy depositional settings. The primary peak resides within the fine-sand and coarse-silt boundary (\(\sim 80\text{-}100\,\mu\text{m}\)), accompanied by a significant fine-grained tail extending into fine silts and clays (\(< 10\,\mu\text{m}\); \(\Phi = 4.0\text{-}11.0\), contributing over \(45\%\) of total volume). Secondary coarse peaks (\(\sim 800\text{-}1000\,\mu\text{m}\); \(\Phi = -0.5\text{-}0.5\)) reflect the accumulation of coarse shell hash and biogenic material. This wide grain spectrum highlights calm, baffled hydraulic conditions within sheltered tidal creeks and mangrove interiors that facilitate fine-sediment settling.

title: 12  Overview of the Urala Study Site
text:
12.2 Site Characteristics and Environmental Drivers

Geomorphology & Dynamic Creeks: The site is defined by extensive barrier spit networks, dynamic creek mouths, and broad landward salt flats (sabkhas). The North and South Creek systems form interconnected drainage pathways that experience spatial adjustments during extreme discharge events.
Hydrodynamics & Tides: Hydrodynamics are governed by a macro-to-mesotidal regime with semi-diurnal tides. Strong tidal currents dominate the primary creek channels, driving bed shear stresses that maintain open, sandy channels while steering fine sediment into adjacent sheltered bays and mangrove fringes.
Metocean Stressors: Similar to Giralia Bay, Urala is subject to a hyper-arid climate with high evaporation rates and extremely variable annual rainfall. Periodic tropical cyclones deliver intense wave energy and catchment flooding, which temporarily override tidal forcing, reorganising barrier spits and driving episodic fine-sediment flux across the mudflats.
crumbs: 12  Overview of the Urala Study Site

title: 12  Overview of the Urala Study Site
text:
12.3 Existing Conditions and Baseline Modelling
To further understand the existing hydrodynamicconditions, we carried out a 1-year hydrodynamic run for an ENSO-neutral year (2018) and used that to represent mean habitats from the satellite-derived map Hickey et al. (2025). To characterise the physical environment governing these zones, the hydrodynamic parameters were evaluated using the 25th to 75th quantile of their distribution. The selected predictors included key inundation-related parameters such as:

inundation frequency,
percentage of submergence,
number of dry days,
number of consecutive dry days,
mean dry days,
total number of wet/dry events (based on hourly data),
depth-averaged mean and maximum currents, and
mean and maximum water depths.

These hydrodynamic parameters were chosen to provide a comprehensive representation of habitat exposure to tidal and submersion dynamics, which are known to be critical determinants for predicting habitat migration patterns under changing environmental conditions. Figure 12.4 shows the hydrodynamic parameters for different habitats across the Urala study site, highlighting the distinct environmental conditions experienced by each habitat type.






Figure 12.4: Habitat Classification Map for the 2018 ENSO Neutral Year Baseline




12.3.1 Hydrodynamic Regime Summary

Mangrove Zones: Experience frequent wetting cycles with near-100% inundation frequency and high submergence percentages (median ~40–50%). They occupy areas with the highest mean water depths (~0.1–0.2 m) and maximum water depths (reaching up to ~0.7–1.5 m), alongside higher maximum currents (~0.3–0.4 m/s) required to prevent extreme salinity build-up.
Cyanobacterial Mats & High Intertidal Flats: Share moderate submergence percentages (~30%) and shallow mean water depths (< 0.1 m). They endure frequent wetting-drying cycles with maximum dry event durations typically staying under 20–25 days, creating optimal moist, hypersaline windows.
Bright Salt Flats: Characterised by minimal submergence percentages (median < 10%), near-zero mean water depths, and prolonged dry periods exceeding 120–175 days, leading to intense evaporation and crust formation.
crumbs: 12  Overview of the Urala Study Site

title: 12  Overview of the Urala Study Site
text:
12.4 Prediction approach
Following the methodology established for Giralia Bay (Section 7.2), an integrated numerical model was developed for the Urala region. The hydrodynamic model was calibrated first to establish accurate flow and tidal dynamics. Subsequently, the mangrove vegetation module was coupled to simulate and calibrate baseline present-day mangrove distributions across the domain.
Once present-day mangrove boundaries were initialised, cyanobacterial (algal) mat distributions were calibrated using an offline (decoupled) predictive approach based on hydrodynamic and mangrove spatial outputs. The calibrated, coupled modelling framework was then applied to simulate future sea-level rise scenarios for both mangrove ecosystems and algal mats.
Detailed calibration and validation procedures for the hydrodynamic model, as well as the mangrove and algal mat modules, are provided in Section 7.5 and ?sec-urala-calibration, respectively.

title: 10  Calibration and Validation
text:
10.1 Hydrodynamic Calibration and Validation
This chapter presents a comprehensive calibration and validation of the high-resolution Urala domain model. The approach largely follows that adopted for Giralia in Chapter 7, with Urala-specific adjustments described below. Three physical and ecological components are evaluated:
As highlighted in Chapter 1, we focus our effort on the salt project development aspect of the constraints. Nevertheless, hydrodynamics serve as the primary physical driver shaping intertidal habitats in Urala, much like other study sites. Achieving accurate hydrodynamic predictions is crucial for assessing baseline conditions, potential future environmental changes, and developmental constraints.
Hydrodynamic calibration was conducted by comparing simulated water surface elevations against field-measured water level time series across key monitoring locations (readers are referred to Chapter 16 for more details about monitoring) representing diverse habitat zones, including:
Calibration involved adjusting bottom roughness using spatially variable Manning’s n coefficients assigned to the habitat bed types (Table 6.1). Other parameters and numerical settings examined included turbulence/eddy viscosity, wind drag coefficients, bathymetry/bed smoothing and wetting/drying depth thresholds.
The animation below illustrates the dynamic water depth variations, tidal propagation, and wetting/drying cycles across the specified monitoring locations within the Urala domain during the calibration period.
The model achieved a strong overall agreement between measured and simulated water level time series:

title: 10  Calibration and Validation
text:
10.3 Initial Model Transferability & Overprediction Issues
As a first attempt, we evaluated model transferability by applying the calibrated mangrove model coefficients directly from Giralia to Urala. However, this preliminary setup resulted in a spatial overprediction of mangrove extent, with the model predicting mangrove establishment across vast stretches of the high intertidal and supratidal salt flats where no mangroves exist.
This overprediction highlighted a key limitation: the initial model framework did not resolve substrate-level abiotic stressors specifically, groundwater and surface salinity dynamics. In hyper-arid systems like Urala, extreme evaporation across shallow salt flats that are infrequently inundated generates hypersaline conditions (\(> 60–80\text{ PSU}\)) that severely constrain mangrove seedling establishment and survival. Without an explicit salinity stress mechanism, the hydro-morphological suitability criteria alone proved insufficient to constrain mangrove boundaries.


10.3.1 Proxy Salinity Model Formulation
To address this limitation and improve spatial precision, we implemented a proxy salinity mass-balance module. This module dynamically tracks salinity accumulation, evaporation, and ocean flushing across each model cell based on inundation depth and tidal exchange frequency.

10.3.1.1 Water & Salt Mass Balance Equations
For each grid cell, the water depth \(h(t)\) determines the active wetting state based on a minimum depth threshold \(h_{\text{min}}\) (e.g., \(0.05\text{ m}\)).
When a dry cell becomes inundated (\(h(t) > h_{\text{min}}\) and \(h(t-\Delta t) \le h_{\text{min}}\)), the initial salt mass \(M(t)\) is calculated from incoming seawater at ambient concentration \(S_0\) (\(35\text{ PPT}\)), plus any residual salt mass \(M_{\text{res}}\) left behind from previous drying cycles:
\[
M(t) = h(t) \cdot S_0 + M_{\text{res}}
\tag{10.1}\]
For continuously wet cells (\(h(t) > h_{\text{min}}\) and \(h(t-\Delta t) > h_{\text{min}}\)), changes in water depth \(\Delta h = h(t) - h(t-\Delta t)\) dictate salt flux and evaporative concentration:

Rising Tide (\(\Delta h > 0\)): Additional marine water enters the cell, increasing salt mass: \[
M(t) = M(t-\Delta t) + \Delta h \cdot S_0
\tag{10.2}\]
Falling Tide (\(\Delta h \le 0\)): Total water loss equals \(-\Delta h\). Water loss is partitioned into evaporative loss (\(E_{\text{evap}}\)) driven by the pan evaporation rate \(E\), and physical drainage/outflow loss (\(L_{\text{drain}}\)): \[
E_{\text{evap}} = \min(E \cdot \Delta t, -\Delta h)
\tag{10.3}\]
\[
L_{\text{drain}} = -\Delta h - E_{\text{evap}}
\tag{10.4}\]
Drainage removes salt proportional to the instantaneous ambient concentration \(S_{\text{now}} = \frac{M(t-\Delta t)}{\max(h(t-\Delta t), h_{\text{min}})}\), while evaporation concentrates the remaining salt mass: \[
M(t) = M(t-\Delta t) - L_{\text{drain}} \cdot S_{\text{now}}
\tag{10.5}\]



10.3.1.2 Concentration Limits and Desiccation Accumulation
The instantaneous surface water salinity \(S(t)\) is computed from the remaining salt mass and bounded by a physical capping limit \(S_{\text{cap}}\) (\(250\text{ PSU}\)):
\[
S(t) = \min\left( \frac{M(t)}{\max(h(t), h_{\text{min}})}, S_{\text{cap}} \right)
\tag{10.6}\]
When a cell completely dries out (\(h(t) \le h_{\text{min}}\)), all remaining salt mass accumulates as residual deposit \(M_{\text{res}}\) to be dissolved upon the next wetting cycle:
\[
M_{\text{res}} \leftarrow M_{\text{res}} + M(t)
\tag{10.7}\]


10.3.1.3 Salinity Stress Function
The resulting 90th percentile salinity (\(S_{p90}\)) drives the non-dimensional vegetation stress coefficient \(S_{\text{sal}} \in [0, 1]\):
\[
S_{\text{sal}} = \operatorname{clip}\left( \frac{S_{p90} - S_{\text{thres}}}{S_{\text{lethal}} - S_{\text{thres}}}, 0, 1 \right)
\tag{10.8}\]
where \(S_{\text{thres}}\) is the salinity threshold above which stress begins to impact growth, and \(S_{\text{lethal}}\) is the upper lethal limit causing complete vegetation mortality.



10.3.2 Model Initialisation & Performance Evaluation
Figure 10.3 shows the modelled mangrove distribution across the Urala region under present environmental conditions. Because the objective was to reproduce the representative baseline mangrove extent, the model simulations were forced with dominant tidal constituents (M2, S2, K1 and O1; see Section 3.3) for the prediction of present-day conditions.
The spatial agreement between the modelled and observed mangrove extents was evaluated by categorising grid cells: * True Positives (Green): Correctly predicted mangrove areas. * False Negatives (Black): Observed mangrove areas missed by the model. * False Positives (Red): Areas predicted as mangrove where none were observed.
To quantitatively evaluate spatial performance within the core analysis domain, precision, recall, and the \(F_1\) score were computed:









Statistic
Definition
Formula
Model Performance




Precision
Proportion of modeled mangrove cells corresponding to true observed mangroves
\(\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\)
\(0.680\)


Recall
Proportion of observed mangrove cells correctly reproduced by the model
\(\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\)
\(0.534\)


\(F_1\) Score
Harmonic mean of precision and recall
\(F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\)
\(0.598\)



The model achieved precision of 0.680, recall of 0.534 and an F1 score of 0.598. Precision indicates that 68.0% of predicted mangrove cells corresponded to observed mangroves, while recall indicates that 53.4% of observed mangrove cells were reproduced. Missed areas include narrow fringing strips along smaller tidal channels; the extent to which these discrepancies reflect model resolution, elevation data or other process representations requires further evaluation.



10.3.3 Modelled Vegetation Structural Parameters
In addition to spatial extent, the model captures key structural attributes of the mangrove canopy across the Urala domain:

Stem Diameter (\(d\)): Predicted spatial distributions (Figure 10.3 b) range between \(0.03\text{ m}\) and \(0.07\text{ m}\). Larger diameters (\(>0.05\text{ m}\)) are concentrated within the well-established, sheltered tidal creek network, indicating that mature mangroves are forming in the true observed locations relatively well.
Stem Height (\(h\)): Corresponding spatial distributions (Figure 10.3 c) show heights ranging predominantly between \(1.8\text{ m}\) and \(2.6\text{ m}\), displaying a clear structural gradient: taller, mature trees occupy the sheltered, frequently inundated main creek channels, while smaller, shorter trees (\(<2.0\text{ m}\)) form along the landward transitions and peripheral fringes.

The predicted stem diameter and height distributions provide a model-based description of canopy structure. Their spatial correspondence with observed mangrove occurrence does not constitute quantitative validation of these attributes or of internal vegetation dynamics. Independent structural observations would be needed to evaluate those predictions.






Figure 10.3: Mangrove validation and vegetation structural parameter distributions across the Urala study area. (a) Spatial confusion map highlighting true positives, false negatives, and false positives alongside bounded performance metrics (\(F_1\) score, precision, recall). (b) Spatial distribution of modelled stem diameter (\(d\)). (c) Spatial distribution of modelled stem height (\(h\)).

title: 10  Calibration and Validation
text:
10.4 Algal Mat Calibration and Validation
Using the calibrated hydrodynamic and mangrove model outputs, the algal mat module was subsequently calibrated to predict present-day distributions across the Urala domain.
Algal mats are highly dynamic ecosystems that undergo rapid temporal fluctuations, even within single spring–neap tidal cycles. Algal spores are widely distributed throughout the intertidal zone; under favorable environmental conditions, they actively photosynthesize and expand, whereas under stress, they remain dormant. When suitable conditions persist for extended periods, they develop into thick, contiguous mats, as observed across several intertidal zones in Urala.
Due to this highly dynamic behaviour, implementing a fully mechanistic growth approach—similar to that used in the mangrove model—presents significant challenges. However, because this study focuses primarily on long-term spatial trajectories, we utilized satellite-derived probability maps from Hickey et al. (2025) to isolate persistent algal mat distributions. A threshold of annual probability \(> 25\%\) was applied across 2019 to define the baseline stable algal mat coverage (Figure 10.4).






Figure 10.4: Algal mat persistence map based on Hickey et al. (2025) for 2019.



Hydrodynamic simulations were conducted for the 2019 calibration period to evaluate the governing environmental drivers. By integrating key hydrodynamic indicators—namely maximum bed shear stress (\(\tau_{\text{max}}\)), inundation frequency, and the 98th percentile water depth (\(d_{98}\))—we established the following environmental suitability thresholds for algal mat persistence at Urala:

Maximum Bed Shear Stress: \(0.2 \le \tau_{\text{max}} \le 0.7\text{ N m}^{-2}\)
Inundation Frequency: \(0.0001 \le \text{Inundation Frequency} \le 0.95\)
98th Percentile Water Depth: \(0.01 \le d_{98} \le 0.55\text{ m}\)

To capture complex, non-linear environmental interactions, a Machine Learning framework using a Random Forest (RF) classifier was also implemented. The ML model was trained and evaluated using a 50/50 train-test split to ensure robust out-of-sample generalisation, and the resulting calibrations were further validated against independent hydrodynamic metrics from an alternate simulation year.
The spatial validation results comparing both approaches across the Urala domain are presented below:

Machine-Learning Approach (Random Forest)Threshold-Based Optimisation Approach








Figure 10.5: Spatial validation and error distribution for the Random Forest machine-learning model across the Urala domain (50/50 train-test split).











Figure 10.6: Spatial validation and error distribution for the threshold-based optimisation model across the Urala domain.

title: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
11.1 Sea Level Rise Response
In this section, we present the response of mangroves and creek morphology to different SLR scenarios for the Urala study site. Similar to the Giralia Bay simulations, we evaluated three distinct IPCC Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) SLR scenarios (refer to Section 3.4 for more details) representing low, medium and high SLR scenarios and consider over a 100-year projection period.
The predicted mangrove extent under present-day environmental conditions (Figure 10.3) was used as the initial condition for all runs. The simulations were executed to assess long-term mangrove migration patterns, dieback, and the co-evolution of tidal creek channels under changing hydrodynamics.
Figure 11.1 illustrates the spatial co-evolution of mangrove canopy height (\(h\)) and bed level elevation (\(z\)) across the Urala domain under the three SLR scenarios over the 100-year simulation period.
crumbs: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise

title: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
Figure 11.1: Spatial and temporal evolution of mangrove canopy height (\(h\), right colorbar) overlaid on bed level elevation (\(z\), left colorbar) across the Urala study site for three Sea Level Rise scenarios: SSP119 (0.5 m), SSP370 (0.9 m), and SSP585 (1.25 m) over a 100-year simulation period.




11.1.1 Mangrove Dynamics and Morphological Evolution
The simulations reveal a strong coupling between sea level rise, intertidal wetland encroachment, and tidal creek network extension across the Urala coastal plain:

Low-SLR Scenario (SSP119): Under SSP119, increases in the tidal prism remain modest because the rate of sea-level rise is relatively low. As a result, the main tidal creeks in SSP119 show minimal expansion or deep headward incision. The existing network geometry accommodates the minor increase in tidal volume without inducing substantial bed erosion or channel widening. Mangroves along the creek banks and within the main basin maintain dynamic equilibrium, experiencing subtle landward growth while keeping pace with water level changes without major dieback.
Moderate to High-SLR Scenarios (SSP370 & SSP585): As sea level rise accelerates in SSP370 and SSP585, larger volumes of water flood the expansive, low-lying supratidal flats behind the main coastal barrier during each tidal cycle. This dramatic increase in the tidal prism drives higher flow velocities within the main drainage arteries, initiating severe scour and progressive channel expansion.

Creek Evolution: The main tidal channels migrate landward, widening and deepening into the upper intertidal basin to handle the increased flood/ebb volumes.
Mangrove Migration & Dieback: Concurrently, higher baseline water levels drown out the lowermost seaward fringe of mangroves due to prolonged hydroperiod inundation. However, the newly formed tidal channels and headward creek extensions deliver tidal flushing deeper inland, creating favorable hydrodynamics that allow mangroves to colonise new landward accommodation space.








NoteKey Findings: Urala SLR Response Dynamics




SSP119 (+0.5 m): Mangrove extents remain stable, and tidal creeks show negligible expansion due to minimal change in the overall tidal prism.
SSP370 (+0.9 m): Moderate seaward fringe drown-out, compensated by landward channel extension and inland mangrove encroachment.
SSP585 (+1.25 m): Pronounced morphological restructuring. Enhanced tidal prism drives significant tidal creek widening and inland incision, accompanied by broad landward shift and redistribution of mangrove canopy height (\(h\)).



Figure 11.2 shows the spatial distributions of mangroves and tidal channel evolution for Year 50 and Year 100 across the Urala domain, highlighting the diverging long-term trajectory of mangrove extent and bed morphodynamics across SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios. Similar to the Giralia site, during the initial ~40–50 years of simulation across all climate projections, mangrove distributions remain relatively comparable, maintaining established populations along the lower intertidal margins and tidal creek networks.
Spatially, baseline mangrove distribution is heavily governed by tidal inundation and bed elevation. However, progressive SLR drives significant channel morphological changes alongside a distinct landward transgression and localised mangrove dieback:

SSP119 (Low Emission): At Year 50 (Figure 11.2 a), mangroves remain well-established throughout the central and southern intertidal flats with tall canopy structures (\(h > 2\text{ m}\)). By Year 100 (Figure 11.2 d), mangrove coverage undergoes localised thinning and slight dieback along the middle channels, while lower-canopy mangroves (\(h \approx 1\text{–}1.5\text{ m}\)) establish along the landward boundaries. Creek structures in SSP119 undergo minor expansion, preserving the overall channel geometry.
SSP370 (Intermediate Emission): By Year 50 (Figure 11.2 b), slight fragmentation and colonization are visible along the expanding creek channels. By Year 100 (Figure 11.2 e), tidal creeks evolve dramatically, deepening and incision-carving wide, branching channel networks deep into the landward supratidal flats. Mangroves dynamically track this channel incision, establishing dense, tall stands (\(h > 2\text{ m}\)) along the newly formed creek banks and migrating significantly inland into newly inundated tidal zones.
SSP585 (High Emission): At Year 50 (Figure 11.2 c), channel enlargement and mangrove establishment mirror the intermediate scenario. By Year 100 (Figure 11.2 f), extreme SLR leads to severe tidal creek incision, mouth widening, and extensive channel network propagation far landward. Mangroves colonise these newly formed, deeply incised creek margins and landward margins; however, rapid sea-level rise causes significant drowning and dieback of lower intertidal mangroves, limiting total net spatial coverage compared to SSP370.







NoteKey Findings: Tidal Creek Incision and Mangrove Relocation



Overall, spatial modelling for the Urala domain demonstrates that under moderate-to-high SLR (SSP370 and SSP585), dramatic tidal creek network expansion and incision serve as the primary pathways for landward mangrove migration.
While deeper, incised channels facilitate significant inland colonization along creek banks, extreme SLR under SSP585 outpaces lower-intertidal bed accretion, leading to seaward drowning and a restricted total habitat footprint.








Figure 11.2: Modelled spatial evolution of bed elevation (\(z\)) and mangrove canopy height (\(h\)) across the Urala study site at Year 50 (top row) and Year 100 (bottom row) under three climate projections: (a, d) SSP119, (b, e) SSP370, and (c, f) SSP585.






11.1.2 Morphological Response
To isolate and track the morphological response of the tidal network to sea-level rise (SLR), the active creek network across the Urala domain was extracted using the \(0.2\text{ m}\) bed elevation contour at 25-year intervals (Years 1, 25, 50, 75, and 100) in Figure 11.3. Driven by expanding tidal prism volumes under rising sea levels, severe channel scour, bed incision, and headward erosion push the primary tidal network landward into upper intertidal and supratidal flats over time.
The magnitude and planform complexity of headward channel propagation vary across the climate projections:

SSP119: Channel headward expansion is minor or near-trivial compared to moderate and extreme scenarios. Morphological alterations remain largely confined to minor widening of primary channels, with negligible headward extension into inland flats by Year 100.
SSP370: Driven by accelerated SLR, the creek network undergoes extensive landward extension. Primary and secondary tidal channels carve deep branching networks into the landward flats, extending \(>5\text{ km}\) inland along main tributaries by Year 100.
SSP585: Demonstrates a remarkably similar spatial response and planform network footprint to SSP370, showing only marginal differences in network geometry and reach. Under both moderate (SSP370) and extreme (SSP585) forcings, headward incision reaches a plateau, suggesting that channel extension in the Urala domain becomes topographically constrained once tidal networks fully incise through the inland salt flats.









Figure 11.3: Spatiotemporal evolution of the tidal creek network over 100 years under (a) SSP119, (b) SSP370, and (c) SSP585 scenarios. Channels are delineated by extracting the \(0.2\text{ m}\) bed level contour at 25-year intervals (Years 1, 25, 50, 75, and 100).



To evaluate the integrated hydro-morphodynamic and ecological trajectories of the Urala domain under SLR, the normalised time series of total mangrove surface area and tidal creek planform footprint relative to initial conditions were tracked (Figure 11.4).
During the initial 10-15 years of simulation, both mangrove extent and channel planform footprint exhibit relative stability, maintaining normalised values near baseline (\(1.0\)). Early rate-of-rise metrics remain within threshold tolerances for local bed shear stress, allowing localised bed accretion and canopy retention to buffer hydrodynamic shifts without broad structural reorganisation across SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585.
Beyond Year 50, non-linear hydro-morphodynamic bifurcation occurs across scenarios, driving coupled channel expansion (Figure 11.4 b) and ecological redistribution (Figure 11.4 a):

Creek Expansion under the Higher-Emissions SLR Scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585): Both SSP370 and SSP585 exhibit rapid, quasi-parallel acceleration in creek planform area past Year 50. Increasing tidal prism volume amplifies ebb-jet velocities which could be triggering widespread headward headcut erosion and lateral secondary branching. While SSP585 drives slightly greater initial incision depth, total planform network footprint expansion converges between SSP370 and SSP585 by Year 100, contrasting sharply with the stable, baseline-constrained trajectory of SSP119.
Eco-Morphodynamic Lag and Opportunistic Relocation: Normalised mangrove area highlights a strong eco-geomorphic coupling with channel network evolution. Under SSP370 and SSP585, early landward extension of incised creeks provides newly inundated, sheltered drainage corridors that facilitate a temporal surge in canopy colonisation between Years 50 and 80.
Seaward Mangrove Loss and Landward Migration: Under SSP585, increasing sea levels initially promote landward mangrove expansion as newly inundated areas become suitable for colonisation. This expansion is predicted to continue for approximately 50–60 years, resulting in an increase in total mangrove extent. However, this trend subsequently reverses as environmental conditions across parts of the model domain extend beyond the prescribed ranges for mangrove establishment and growth. Once these conditions exceed the modelled tolerance thresholds, the mortality rules are activated, resulting in vegetation loss and a decline in total mangrove area. Consequently, mangrove extent decreases after its initial peak, with greater losses under SSP585 than SSP370 by Year 100. This trajectory reflects the balance between initial landward establishment and subsequent mortality under increasingly unsuitable environmental conditions.







Figure 11.4: Temporal evolution of normalised (a) total mangrove area and (b) tidal creek planform footprint relative to initial conditions over a 100-year simulation under SSP119 (black), SSP370 (red), and SSP585 (blue) scenarios.





11.1.3 Total Biomass Dynamics Across SLR Scenarios
To quantify systemic ecological productivity under changing climate projections, total domain-wide mangrove biomass was calculated and normalised relative to initial baseline conditions (\(t = 0\)) over the 100-year simulation period (Figure 11.5).
Across all SLR scenarios, total normalised biomass exhibits an initial lag phase during the first 20–30 years, remaining close to baseline values (\(1.0\)). Following this initial lag, significant non-linear divergences occur:

SSP119 (Low Emission): Total biomass experiences a gentle expansion, peaking at approximately \(1.25\times\) baseline levels around Year 55–60. As sea-level rise rates stabilise, biomass gradually declines, returning close to initial levels (\(\approx 1.0\)) by Year 100.
SSP370 (Intermediate Emission): Biomass surges rapidly past Year 30, reaching a peak of approximately \(1.75\times\) initial biomass between Years 60 and 65. This rapid growth is driven by landward expansion along newly incised creek networks. However, after Year 65, increased submergence triggers a steep decline, settling closer to the baseline by Year 100.
SSP585 (High Emission): Total biomass tracks closely with SSP370 during the expansion phase, reaching a secondary peak of \(\approx 1.6\times\) baseline around Year 55–60. Beyond Year 60, extreme inundation outpaces accretion, initiating a sharp biomass contraction down to baseline levels (\(\approx 1.0\)) by Year 100.







Figure 11.5: Temporal evolution of normalised total mangrove biomass relative to initial conditions over a 100-year simulation across SSP119 (black), SSP370 (red), and SSP585 (blue) scenarios. Points indicate raw simulated output; solid curves denote smoothed trendlines.






11.1.4 SLR Implications on the Initial Mangrove Footprint
To isolate the vulnerability of established forests from opportunistic landward colonisation, the temporal decay of the initial mangrove footprint area and its corresponding biomass dynamics were tracked exclusively within the original baseline boundaries (Figure 11.6). Mangrove footprint area was quantified in hectares, while biomass was normalised relative to its initial value at timestep \(t = 0\).

11.1.4.1 Footprint Area Decay Dynamics
As shown in Figure 11.6 a, the initial mangrove footprint area (\(\approx 2200\text{ ha}\)) experiences progressive, stepwise losses across all scenarios as sea levels rise:

Lag Phase (Years 0–30): All scenarios retain approximately \(1950\)–\(2000\text{ ha}\) of their initial footprint, equivalent to around \(89\)–\(91\%\) of the baseline area. During this period, losses are relatively limited and occur primarily through localised reductions in the existing mangrove footprint.
Accelerated Loss (Years 30–70): Under SSP370 and SSP585, mangrove footprint losses become increasingly pronounced, consistent with greater exposure to inundation and the associated modelled mortality. By Year 70, the initial footprint has declined to approximately \(1350\text{ ha}\) under SSP370 and \(900\text{ ha}\) under SSP585. The SSP585 trajectory subsequently declines sharply, falling below \(500\text{ ha}\) at approximately Year 72–73.
Continued Decline and Scenario Divergence (Years 70–100): Losses continue under SSP370 and SSP585, with both scenarios approaching near-complete depletion of the initial footprint by Year 100. Under SSP585, less than \(100\text{ ha}\) remains, representing less than \(5\%\) of the original area. SSP370 retains approximately \(200\text{ ha}\) (around \(9\%\)), whereas SSP119 retains more than \(1250\text{ ha}\) (approximately \(58\%\)). The SSP119 trajectory therefore indicates a substantially slower decline in the original mangrove footprint compared with the higher sea-level rise scenarios.



11.1.4.2 Normalised Biomass Dynamics within Initial Boundaries
Normalised biomass within the initial footprint (Figure 11.6 b) closely tracks the spatial decay of forest coverage, revealing clear stress mechanisms:

Threshold Stress Past Year 35: Biomass remains stable (\(1.0\)) during the first 30 years. Beyond Year 35, hydrodynamic stress (increased hydroperiod and permanent inundation) impairs tree growth and triggers mortality.
Divergent Collapse Rates: Past Year 50, normalised biomass in SSP585 decays rapidly, dropping below \(0.1\) (\(10\%\) of initial biomass) by Year 80. SSP370 exhibits a similar steep decline, reaching \(\approx 0.08\) by Year 100. In contrast, SSP119 maintains over \(45\%\) of its initial biomass at Year 100.



11.1.4.3 Drivers of Initial Footprint Loss
Losses within the initial mangrove footprint occur as increasing inundation exceeds the modelled tolerance of established stands, particularly along the lower intertidal margin. This analysis tracks only the original footprint and excludes establishment in new landward areas. It therefore shows the vulnerability of existing stands, rather than demonstrating that landward migration is physically blocked. Persistence of mangroves across the wider domain depends strongly on successful establishment in newly suitable areas along the evolving creek network.






Figure 11.6: Temporal evolution of (a) remaining initial mangrove footprint area (ha) and (b) normalised biomass dynamics within the initial baseline footprint over 100 years across SSP119 (black), SSP370 (red), and SSP585 (blue) scenarios.






11.1.5 Comparative Transect and Localised Morphodynamics (SSP119 vs. SSP585)
To evaluate the fine-scale eco-geomorphic mechanisms governing mangrove survival and channel realignment, a high-resolution, zoomed-in dynamic comparison was conducted for a critical section within the Urala Creek South domain (Figure 11.7). This detailed focus isolates how opposing SLR extremes (SSP119 vs. SSP585) alter cross-sectional bed profile evolution, creek incision rates, and canopy height distribution over the 100-year simulation.
The bottom cross-sectional transects highlight fundamentally diverging trajectories between low and high emission scenarios:

SSP119 Hydro-Geomorphic Stability: Under SSP119 (Figure 11.7 a), tidal forcing remains well within ecological and morphodynamic threshold limits. Bed elevation profile shifts are minor, with localised vertical bed level equilibrium preventing channel drowning. Mangrove canopy heights along the cross-section remain stable, maintaining structural continuity without significant dieback or rapid migration.
SSP585 Non-Linear Scour and Landward Shift: Under SSP585 (Figure 11.7 b), accelerated SLR triggers severe bed scour along the primary channel floor, deepening the creek bed while eroding intertidal banks. Concurrently, lower-intertidal mangrove stands undergo progressive canopy collapse due to excessive inundation frequency. However, higher-elevation intertidal margins along the transect experience opportunistic colonisation, where juvenile trees (\(h \approx 1\text{-}1.5\text{ m}\)) establish as tidal boundaries retreat landward.





SSP119 Scenario (a)SSP585 Scenario (b)















Figure 11.7: Comparative spatiotemporal evolution of bed level (\(z\)) and mangrove canopy height (\(h\)) along a high-resolution zoomed transect in the Urala Creek South region under (a) SSP119 and (b) SSP585 scenarios.





11.1.6 Influence of Development Envelope
To assess how a physical barrier could affect mangrove migration under sea-level rise, simulations incorporated a hypothetical development footprint based on the original salt-pond proposal. Runs were conducted under the intermediate (SSP370) and high (SSP585) SLR scenarios. In Delft3D Flexible Mesh, the boundary was represented as a rigid, impermeable thin dam wall. This is an illustrative development scenario rather than a representation of an approved development.
The impermeable boundary prevents water and sediment from crossing into the development footprint, restricting tidal inundation and the landward extension of creeks within that area. It therefore provides an explicit physical constraint on potential mangrove migration under sea-level rise. Figure 11.8 shows the study site in Western Australia (Figure 11.8 a) and the boundary used for the hypothetical barrier scenario (Figure 11.8 b).






Figure 11.8: Location of the Urala study site in Western Australia (panel a), with a closer view of the hypothetical development footprint in panel b. The boundary, shown in red, is based on the original salt-pond proposal and is used here to investigate the effects of a barrier to landward migration.



To systematically evaluate the eco-geomorphic alterations induced by this physical barrier, the comparative analysis focuses on evaluating baseline (unconstrained) conditions against the development scenario under the high-emission forcing (SSP585), representing the most critical stress test for system resilience and spatial adaptation.
For illustrative purposes, we present the spatio-temporal evolution of mangrove height and bed morphodynamics under the SSP585 scenario with the hypothetical development boundary (Figure 11.9). Numerical results indicate that as sea-level rise accelerates, mangroves actively attempt to migrate landward into newly inundated intertidal zones. However, the rigid and impermeable bund walls intercept this natural landward retreat pathway. Mangrove stands initially colonise and cluster along the immediate seaward edges of the bund walls. As sea levels continue to rise throughout the 100-year projection, the physical barrier prevents any further landward migration, forcing the vegetation into prolonged inundation stress, acute coastal squeeze, and eventual canopy dieback.

To further isolate these eco-geomorphic alterations and evaluate the localised impact of the bund walls on mangrove height and channel profile evolution, we systematically compare the zoomed-in transect animations for the SSP585 scenario with and without the development footprint (Figure 11.10).

title: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
section: 11.2 Eco-Geomorphic Impacts of Development Bund Walls
text:
11.2 Eco-Geomorphic Impacts of Development Bund Walls
To evaluate the influence of coastal development infrastructure, the normalised temporal evolution of mangrove extent and tidal creek footprints under baseline climate scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585) was systematically compared against their development-constrained counterparts over a 100-year simulation period (Figure 11.11). Both metrics are normalised relative to initial conditions at Year 1.






Figure 11.11: Temporal evolution of (a) normalised mangrove area expansion and (b) normalised tidal creek footprint expansion over 100 years, comparing baseline climate scenarios (SSP370, SSP585) against development scenarios constrained by bund walls (DEV_SSP370, DEV_SSP585).



During the initial nine decades (Years 0–90), both baseline and development scenarios exhibit comparable growth patterns, expanding mangrove area up to 3.0–3.3 times the baseline footprint (Figure 11.11 a). Minor variance between years 50 and 75 reflects localised, transient hydro-period adjustments upstream of the bund walls.
Around Years 92-94, the development and no-development trajectories diverge sharply (Figure 11.11 a):

Baseline scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585): Mangrove area remains approximately 2.0-2.35 times its initial value by Year 100.
Hypothetical development scenarios (DEV_SSP370 and DEV_SSP585): The bund-wall barrier restricts landward migration and mangrove area falls to approximately 1.6 and 1.2 times its initial value, respectively, by Year 100.

This divergence represents a 32% to 41% net reduction in late-century mangrove habitat availability caused directly by the physical bund wall footprint.

11.2.1 Tidal Creek Evolution
The creek-footprint trajectories diverge earlier than the sharp late-century reduction in mangrove area (Figure 11.11 b):

Early alignment (Years 0-35): All scenarios follow similar trajectories, with creek footprints increasing by approximately 0.2-0.3%.
Divergence (from about Year 35): The hypothetical development scenarios begin to diverge from the baseline trajectories as bund walls restrict landward creek extension and branching.
Year 100 comparison: Baseline creek footprints reach approximately 1.019 times the initial value under SSP370 and 1.0205 under SSP585. With the hypothetical bund walls, the corresponding values are approximately 1.014 and 1.015.

The presence of bund walls inhibits natural channel branching, confining hydrodynamics within established pathways and preventing the formation of secondary tidal drainage networks.






NoteSummary: Ecological Trajectories and Infrastructure Impacts at Urala



The simulations show how sea-level rise could change mangrove distribution and tidal creeks at Urala, and how a hypothetical development barrier could restrict the habitats available for landward migration.

11.3 Mangrove and Tidal Creek Responses to Sea-Level Rise

SSP119 (Low SLR, 0.5 m): Smaller changes in tidal creeks. The volume of water entering and leaving the intertidal area with each tide changes relatively little, so creek expansion is limited. Some mangroves are lost from the original footprint while others establish in new landward areas. By Year 100, total mangrove area remains above its initial value, while total biomass is close to its initial value.
SSP370 (Intermediate SLR, 0.9 m): Landward expansion along tidal creeks. As more water enters and leaves the intertidal area with each tide, creeks extend inland and create areas suitable for mangrove establishment. Mangrove area and biomass initially increase, but some gains are subsequently lost as inundation increases.
SSP585 (high SLR, 1.25 m) Extensive losses from the original mangrove footprint. Mangroves establish along newly formed inland creeks, while prolonged inundation causes major losses from existing stands. By Year 100, less than 5% of the original footprint remains. Establishment in new landward areas allows mangroves to persist across the wider domain.



11.4 Effects of the Hypothetical Development Barrier

Restricted landward migration: The hypothetical bund walls block water and sediment exchange across the development boundary, limiting creek extension and access to areas where mangroves could otherwise establish as sea level rises.
Less mangrove habitat by Year 100: Under SSP370 and SSP585, total mangrove area is approximately 2.0-2.35 times its initial value without the barrier, compared with approximately 1.2-1.6 times its initial value with the hypothetical bund walls.
Difference between scenarios: The hypothetical development produces approximately 32-41% less mangrove area by Year 100 than the corresponding scenario without development. Creek expansion and branching are also reduced.


Management implication: Access to suitable landward areas helps mangroves persist as sea level rises in these simulations. The hypothetical bund-wall experiment shows how a barrier can restrict that adaptation and reduce future habitat. These results highlight the need to consider migration pathways when assessing coastal development.

title: 12  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
12.1 Projected Impact of Sea-Level Rise on Algal Mat Redistribution
Following the mangrove response to sea level rise predictions as described in Chapter 11, we carried out additional only hydrodynamic simulations with various discrete time steps representing the 50 and 100-Year for different sea level rise scenarios. In these simulations, the bed level changes and mangrove distributions were fixed to the predicted values at the corresponding time steps. The hydrodynamic outputs were then used to predict the potential distribution of persistent algal mats under future sea level rise scenarios.
To evaluate the long-term response of algal mats under climate change, numerical simulations were carried out across three IPCC Shared Socioeconomic Pathways: SSP119 (low emissions / low SLR), SSP370 (medium-to-high emissions / moderate SLR), and SSP585 (high emissions / extreme SLR). Figure 12.1 - Figure 12.3 shows the predicted algal mat response to different SLR scenarios using the threshold based approach. Similary, Figure 12.4 - Figure 12.6 shows the predicted algal mat response to different SLR scenarios using Random Forest (RF) approach.
The threshold based and RF approaches produced broadly similar trajectories of habitat change, including the progressive fragmentation and landward redistribution of algal mats under increasing SLR. Mangrove distributions were identical between the two approaches because mangrove suitability was determined using the same underlying hydrodynamic and elevation criteria. Differences between the approaches therefore reflect their respective representations of algal mat suitability. Both approaches predicted a significant loss of algal mat area for SSP370 and the worst SLR scenario tested (SSP585) by Year 100. SSP119 showed clear habitat migration as expected with mild SLR; the hydrodynamic suitability zones tend to shift, which is clearly reflected in this scenario. Furthermore, to illustrate the distributional changes of algal mats and mangroves across the three SLR scenarios, we present a comparative analysis of the predicted spatial extent at Year 0, Year 50, and Year 100 for each scenario. The following sections provide a detailed description of the predicted trends and ecological implications associated with each SLR pathway.

title: 12  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
12.2 Comparative Dynamics Across Scenarios
At Year 0 (present condition), spatial mapping reveals an extensive, contiguous algal mat complex occupying high-elevation salt flats landward of the coastal mangrove fringe (panel a across all spatial figures). Under baseline hydrodynamic conditions, these expansive intertidal flats maintain low hydrodynamic shear stress (\(\tau_{\text{max}} \le 0.7\text{ N m}^{-2}\)), suitable inundation frequencies, and shallow water depths during high tides (\(d_{98} \le 0.55\text{ m}\)), allowing stable algal mats to flourish.
The cross-shore transect profile at Year 0 (b) highlights distinct zonation between the two coastal ecosystems along the elevation gradient: * Mangrove Fringe (\(3,000\text{ m} \le x \le 8,000\text{ m}\)): Mangroves achieve their highest alongshore coverage fraction (\(\sim 0.40–0.50\)) on intertidal mudflats where mean bed elevation ranges between \(-1.0\text{ m}\) and \(0.5\text{ m}\). * Algal Mat Zone (\(6,000\text{ m} \le x \le 11,000\text{ m}\)): Algal mats dominate higher supratidal flats (\(0.5\text{ m} \le z \le 1.8\text{ m}\)), reaching peak alongshore coverage fractions exceeding \(0.60–0.70\).


12.2.1 SSP119 Projection

Year 50 (c): Under mild sea-level rise, the algal mat footprint experiences minor fragmentation along its lower seaward margin (\(x \sim 6,000–8,000\text{ m}\)). However, the cross-shore profile shows that high coverage fractions (\(\sim 0.40–0.60\)) persist across the broad central supratidal flat (\(10,000\text{ m} \le x \le 14,000\text{ m}\)), while the mangrove fringe maintains stable coverage fractions (\(\sim 0.20–0.30\)) around \(x = 4,000–8,000\text{ m}\).
Year 100 (d): Increased inundation drives localised seaward retreat along outer boundaries. Despite this, a substantial portion of the algal mat profile remains viable across higher-elevation flats (\(10,000\text{ m} \le x \le 16,000\text{ m}\)) where coverage fractions remain around \(0.20–0.40\). Mangrove distribution exhibits minimal cross-shore compression, holding steady low-density presence along channel edges.




12.2.2 SSP370 Projection

Year 50 (c): Moderate sea-level rise triggers drowning across low-lying algal mat habitat. The contiguous Year 0 mat fragments into isolated clusters near expanding tidal channels where inundation frequencies exceed tolerance limits (\(> 0.95\)). In the transect profile, the peak algal coverage fraction drops sharply from \(> 0.60\) down to \(\sim 0.30\), shifting landward toward \(x = 10,000–14,000\text{ m}\). Simultaneously, mangroves expand slightly inland along creek banks, raising mangrove coverage fractions up to \(\sim 0.35\) around \(x = 6,000–8,000\text{ m}\).
Year 100 (d): Significant loss of persistent algal mat coverage occurs across the central domain. As deeper tidal networks expand inland, water depth thresholds (\(d_{98} > 0.55\text{ m}\)) are exceeded, restricting viable mat habitat to narrow landward bands (\(x > 12,000\text{ m}\)) with low coverage fractions (\(< 0.15\)). While the mangrove distribution curve appears broadly distributed across the domain (\(2,000\text{ m} \le x \le 12,000\text{ m}\)), its alongshore coverage fraction remains low (\(\le 0.15–0.20\)). This indicates that rather than forming a dense forest, mangroves are restricted to narrow, highly dispersed bands along dissected channel networks.




12.2.3 SSP585 Projection

Year 50 (c): Accelerated sea-level rise triggers rapid ecological drowning across mid-to-high intertidal flats. The extensive northern mat complex collapses, causing the cross-shore algal coverage fraction to decline to \(< 0.25\) beyond \(x = 10,000\text{ m}\). Mangroves temporarily display an opportunistic inland pulse between \(x = 5,000\text{ m}\) and \(9,000\text{ m}\) (fractions reaching \(\sim 0.40\)) as higher water levels temporarily convert formerly hyper-saline salt flats into habitable intertidal zones.
Year 100 (d): Extreme sea-level rise drives near-complete collapse of persistent algal mats across the Urala domain. Channel network enlargement increases maximum bed shear stress (\(\tau_{\text{max}} > 0.7\text{ N m}^{-2}\)) and causes permanent inundation, virtually eliminating the environmental window required for algal mat stability (coverage fractions \(< 0.05\)). Although the mangrove distribution curve spans continuously from \(x = 2,000\text{ m}\) to \(x = 15,000\text{ m}\), the alongshore coverage fraction stays under \(0.15\) throughout. This demonstrates that mangroves do not form an expansive contiguous wetland, but rather survive as highly fragmented, low-density linear fringes fringing deep tidal creeks across an otherwise drowned landscape.







NoteManagement Implications & Strategic Recommendations



The findings of this numerical modelling study provide process-based insights for coastal managers, regional planners, and environmental impact assessors operating along the Urala coastline. Earlier site assessments (e.g., Seashore Engineering (2021)) relied primarily on empirical morphometric relationships to infer habitat responses under generic sea-level rise allowances (\(0.4\text{ m}\) by 2070 and \(0.9\text{ m}\) by 2110). While those studies identified tidal creek network expansion as a key driver of habitat reorganization and long-term habitat loss, our process-based Delft3D-FM simulations reveal specific hydrodynamic thresholds and spatial nuances across different climate pathways.

12.2.4 Habitat Migration Dynamics and Supratidal Buffer Corridors
Our results demonstrate that intertidal habitat response is highly scenario-dependent. Under lower emission pathways (SSP119), both mangrove and algal mat habitats demonstrate notable resilience, retaining spatial continuity through Year 100. Under moderate-to-high emission pathways (SSP370 and SSP585), both ecosystems attempt to migrate landward (\(x > 10,000\text{ m}\)), though algal mats experience significant landward compression compared to expanding channel-fringe mangroves.
Management Consideration: To accommodate natural landward migration and reduce the risk of coastal squeeze, coastal management frameworks could identify and designate supratidal buffer zones behind current high-elevation salt flats. Planning future coastal infrastructure (such as solar salt evaporation ponds, access roads, pipelines, bund walls, or pastoral fencing) with these migration pathways in mind (\(x = 10,000\text{ m}\) to \(18,000\text{ m}\)) would help preserve remaining intertidal accommodation space. Furthermore, proposed developments across the intertidal platform can directly obstruct or alter these migration trajectories, as detailed in Chapter 11.


12.2.5 Differentiating Spatial Extent from Ecosystem Quality and Density
Broad spatial mapping and remote sensing can obscure localized changes in habitat quality when evaluating coastal wetland response. Under SSP370 and SSP585 at Year 100, mangrove presence appears across a broad cross-shore zone (\(2,000\text{ m}\) to \(15,000\text{ m}\)), which might initially resemble habitat expansion. However, cross-shore profile analysis indicates that alongshore coverage fractions remain low (\(\le 0.15\)).
Management Consideration: Environmental monitoring programs could incorporate metrics for canopy closure, structural continuity, and biomass density alongside spatial boundaries. Low-density, linear fringe mangroves along dissected creeks offer different ecosystem function profiles—such as altered wave attenuation, shoreline stabilization, and blue carbon capacity—compared to dense, contiguous forests. Monitoring metrics that reflect habitat fragmentation provide a clearer picture of ecological state.


12.2.6 Recognition and Conservation of Cyanobacterial Algal Mats
In arid and semi-arid tropical environments like the Pilbara coast, cyanobacterial algal mats serve as primary producers and nitrogen fixers supporting intertidal food webs. Because they occupy high supratidal flats often categorized as salt flats, they are sometimes deprioritised in environmental evaluations relative to mangrove forests. Our results indicate that algal mats possess distinct hydrodynamic tolerance windows, experiencing structural fragmentation as maximum bed shear stress (\(\tau_{\text{max}} > 0.7\text{ N m}^{-2}\)) and inundation depths (\(d_{98} > 0.55\text{ m}\)) exceed physical suitability thresholds.
Management Consideration: Environmental assessments could explicitly evaluate persistent algal mat zones as sensitive intertidal habitats. Where coastal engineering works (such as channel dredging, culvert installations, or tidal barriers) are planned, evaluating their potential effects on shallow tidal inundation frequencies across supratidal flats would help mitigate premature disruption to these primary-producing communities.


12.2.7 Scenario-Based Adaptive Management Thresholds
Comparative analysis across climate pathways demonstrates that habitat survival and zonation rely heavily on the rate of sea-level rise. Under SSP119, intertidal zonation remains largely stable through Year 100, whereas higher pathways (SSP370/SSP585) lead to progressive habitat reorganization between Year 50 and Year 100 as tidal creek networks expand.
Management Consideration: Regional management frameworks could consider Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways (DAPP), linking planning thresholds to observed local sea-level rise rates and channel network expansion rather than fixed calendar years. Where monitoring indicates sea-level rise approaching intermediate thresholds (\(\sim 0.4\text{ m}\)), proactive options—such as localized sediment management or living shoreline strategies—could be evaluated to assist high-value intertidal zones before extensive channel enlargement occurs.
