title: 17  Appendix A: Field Campaign, Data and Processing
text:
17.3 Water Level Correction Methodology
To convert raw pressure recorded by submerged loggers into accurate water surface elevations, a three-stage correction pipeline was applied:

Barometric Correction
Density Correction
Datum Correction


17.3.1 Barometric Correction
Because non-vented pressure loggers were used, total recorded pressure required adjustment for atmospheric pressure fluctuations. Continuous barometric pressure was measured at both Giralia and Urala (Figure 17.5).
To fill missing data during periods when the Giralia barometric logger was offline, an empirical linear regression model was established using Urala barometric observations (Figure 17.6). All barometric pressure series were interpolated to a 15-minute interval prior to subtraction.






Figure 17.5: Recorded barometric pressure at Giralia and Urala.









Figure 17.6: Correlation between Giralia and Urala barometric pressure readings.




17.3.1.1 Rugged Troll Loggers
Rugged Troll loggers record total pressure (\(P_{\text{logger\_RT}}\)) with a factory-assigned constant barometric offset (\(P_{\text{constant\_offset}}\)). Absolute pressure (\(P_{\text{absolute}}\)) was calculated via:
\[P_{\text{absolute}} = P_{\text{logger\_RT}} + P_{\text{constant\_offset}}\]
Net water pressure (\(P_{\text{water\_RT}}\)) was subsequently isolated by subtracting interpolated barometric pressure (\(P_{\text{barometric}}\)):
\[P_{\text{water\_RT}} = P_{\text{absolute}} - P_{\text{barometric}}\]
An example of the Rugged Troll correction sequence is shown in Figure 17.7.






Figure 17.7: Example pressure correction sequence for a Rugged Troll logger (G-MID-CHANNEL).





17.3.1.2 AquaTroll Loggers
AquaTroll loggers (\(P_{\text{logger\_AT}}\)) do not store the static offset internally. Net water pressure (\(P_{\text{water\_AT}}\)) was derived relative to average barometric conditions (\(P_{\text{barometric\_average}}\)):
\[P_{\text{water\_AT}} = P_{\text{logger\_AT}} + (P_{\text{barometric}} - P_{\text{barometric\_average}})\]
Note: This formulation assumes initial logger baseline setup occurred near mean atmospheric pressure. An example correction is shown in Figure 17.8.






Figure 17.8: Example pressure correction sequence for an AquaTroll logger (G-MOUTH-CHANNEL-AT).







17.3.2 Density Correction
Corrected water pressure (\(P_{\text{corrected}}\) in bar) was converted to water depth (\(H_{\text{corrected}}\) in metres) using variable water density (\(\rho\) in \(\text{g/cm}^3\)). Density was calculated at 15-minute time steps as a function of salinity (\(S\), PSU) and water temperature (\(T\), °C):
\[\rho = 1000 + 0.75 \cdot S - 0.2 \cdot (T - 4)\]
While temperature was continuously recorded across all sites, missing salinity records were reconstructed using a hierarchical fallback sequence:

Mean salinity observed at the same SiteId.
Mean salinity from a assigned fallback site (Fallback_Salinity_SiteId, Table 17.3).
Mean salinity across the local geomorphic location category.
Mean regional salinity (Giralia vs. Urala).




Table 17.3: Fallback salinity site assignments for density calculations.





Target SiteId
Fallback Salinity SiteId




Fallback mappings
…












Figure 17.9: Distribution of salinity data sources resulting from the fallback hierarchy.



Calculated densities showed strong agreement (\(r^2 > 0.94\)) against sites equipped with direct density sensors (Figure 17.10 and Figure 17.11).






Figure 17.10: Calculated vs. observed water density across validation sites (\(r^2 > 0.94\)).









Figure 17.11: Calculated 15-minute water density time series across all monitoring sites.



Corrected water depth above the logger was calculated via:
\[H_{\text{corrected}} = \frac{P_{\text{corrected}} \cdot 10.1972}{\rho}\]
Linear regression between \(H_{\text{corrected}}\) and \(P_{\text{corrected}}\) yielded a correlation coefficient of \(0.996\) (Figure 17.12). Residual analysis comparing logger-reported depth versus density-corrected depth revealed a residual standard deviation of \(7.3\text{ cm}\) (Figure 17.13), which represents a notable magnitude in shallow intertidal systems.






Figure 17.12: Density-corrected depth vs. corrected pressure (\(r = 0.996\)).









Figure 17.13: Histogram of depth residuals (logger-reported depth vs. re-calculated density-corrected depth).






17.3.3 Datum Correction
Because initial logger sensor elevations were un-surveyed, elevations were referenced to Australian Height Datum (mAHD) using LiDAR ground elevation baselines (Table 17.1) and regional tide gauge calibrations.

Estuarine Mouth Calibration: Submerged loggers at the Giralia and Urala river mouths were calibrated against mAHD tidal observations from the Exmouth tide gauge by matching peak spring tide elevations (Figure 17.14 and Figure 17.15).







Figure 17.14: River mouth logger elevation calibration matching Exmouth tidal peaks (mAHD).









Figure 17.15: Scatter plot of monthly peak water levels at channel mouths vs. Exmouth tide gauge.




Upstream Hydraulic Calibration: Upstream loggers were sequentially adjusted to match monthly peak water levels along primary hydraulic conveyances (e.g., Mouth Channel \(\rightarrow\) Mid Channel \(\rightarrow\) Mid Creek \(\rightarrow\) Upper Channel \(\rightarrow\) Algal Mat). Peak correlations along connected flow paths are shown in Figure 17.16 and Figure 17.17.

title: 9  Sea Level Rise Scenarios
text:
9.2 Key Modelling Assumptions & Boundary Forcing
To evaluate long-term eco-geomorphic adaptation, two critical methodological assumptions were applied to the model setup:

9.2.1 Isolation of Sea Level Rise as a Single Driver
While climate change encompasses multiple interconnected environmental drivers—including shifting wind regimes, warming temperatures, varying atmospheric humidity, intensified storm frequency, and complex root-zone salinity dynamics—this study intentionally isolates sea level rise. Decoupling SLR from other confounding factors allows us to evaluate its direct physical and hydrodynamic impact on landward mangrove migration and survival.


9.2.2 Filtering Short-Term Noise via Harmonic Analysis
In northwestern Western Australia, short-term hydrodynamic variability on seasonal and interannual scales (1–5 years) is pronounced and heavily influenced by the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Shifting ENSO phases can temporarily amplify or mask local water levels.
To prevent transient climatic fluctuations from skewing long-term morphodynamic trends, we performed harmonic analysis on the boundary forcing. We extracted the primary astronomical tidal constituents: * \(M_2\) (Principal lunar semidiurnal) * \(S_2\) (Principal solar semidiurnal) * \(K_2\) (Lunisolar semidiurnal) * \(O_1\) (Lunar diurnal)
By superimposing projected SLR onto these fundamental tidal constituents, high-frequency interannual noise is filtered out, ensuring that the simulations isolate true long-term ecological and morphological adaptation trends.

title: 13  Calibration and Validation
text:
13.1 Overview
Cape Preston provides a demonstration of applying the framework to a slightly contrasting coastal setting, with different tidal conditions, shoreline morphology, and intertidal extent from Giralia and Urala. As a secondary focus of Projects A and C, it features a less comprehensive observational basis for model application. This allows the study to examine both the potential transferability of the framework and the practical consequences of applying it where supporting data are more limited.
Greater uncertainty in bathymetry (offshore and creek), and available in situ observations affects model inputs and limits independent evaluation. Consequently, model outputs should be interpreted as exploratory, scenario based assessments of potential habitat change. Unlike Giralia and Urala, a dedicated hydrodynamic calibration was not undertaken due to the lack of sufficient validation data; however, the availability of satellite derived habitat maps from Project C provides a valuable opportunity to calibrate and evaluate the habitat prediction components directly. The application also helps identify the additional observations needed to strengthen predictions at this site.
This chapter presents the application and evaluation of the framework at Cape Preston across the following key areas:

Figure 17.3: Particle size distribution (PSD) representative of mudflat environments across Urala, displaying a broad, polymodal distribution spanning fine silts and clays (\(< 10\,\mu\text{m}\)) through fine sand (\(100\,\mu\text{m}\)) to coarse biogenic fragments (\(800\text{-}1000\,\mu\text{m}\)).





General Sandy Substrate (Figure 17.2): Exhibits a highly sorted, well-defined unimodal distribution centered predominantly around fine-to-medium sand (\(150\text{-}300\,\mu\text{m}\), corresponding to Phi values \(\Phi = 1.0\text{-}2.5\), where \(\Phi = 1.5\text{-}2.0\) comprises over \(70\%\) of the sample volume). This narrow grain-size spectrum indicates an energetic, tide- and wave-dominated environment where fine silts and clays are continuously winnowed away, leaving a clean, well-sorted sandy substrate along channels and exposed flats.
Mudflat Substrate (Figure 17.3): Displays a broad, complex polymodal distribution characteristic of low-energy depositional settings. The primary peak resides within the fine-sand and coarse-silt boundary (\(\sim 80\text{-}100\,\mu\text{m}\)), accompanied by a significant fine-grained tail extending into fine silts and clays (\(< 10\,\mu\text{m}\); \(\Phi = 4.0\text{-}11.0\), contributing over \(45\%\) of total volume). Secondary coarse peaks (\(\sim 800\text{-}1000\,\mu\text{m}\); \(\Phi = -0.5\text{-}0.5\)) reflect the accumulation of coarse shell hash and biogenic material. This wide grain spectrum highlights calm, baffled hydraulic conditions within sheltered tidal creeks and mangrove interiors that facilitate fine-sediment settling.

title: 17  Study Site: Cape Preston
text:
17.2 Site Characteristics and Environmental Drivers

Geomorphology & Dynamic Creeks: The site is defined by extensive barrier spit networks, dynamic creek mouths, and broad landward salt flats (sabkhas). The North and South Creek systems form interconnected drainage pathways that experience spatial adjustments during extreme discharge events.
Hydrodynamics & Tides: Hydrodynamics are governed by a macro-to-mesotidal regime with semi-diurnal tides. Strong tidal currents dominate the primary creek channels, driving bed shear stresses that maintain open, sandy channels while steering fine sediment into adjacent sheltered bays and mangrove fringes.
Metocean Stressors: Similar to Giralia Bay, Urala is subject to a hyper-arid climate with high evaporation rates and extremely variable annual rainfall. Periodic tropical cyclones deliver intense wave energy and catchment flooding, which temporarily override tidal forcing, reorganising barrier spits and driving episodic fine-sediment flux across the mudflats.

title: 17  Study Site: Cape Preston
text:
17.3 Existing Conditions and Baseline Modelling
To further understand the existing hydrodynamicconditions, we carried out a 1-year hydrodynamic run for an ENSO-neutral year (2018) and used that to represent mean habitats from the satellite-derived map Hickey et al. (2025). To characterise the physical environment governing these zones, the hydrodynamic parameters were evaluated using the 25th to 75th quantile of their distribution. The selected predictors included key inundation-related parameters such as:

inundation frequency,
percentage of submergence,
number of dry days,
number of consecutive dry days,
mean dry days,
total number of wet/dry events (based on hourly data),
depth-averaged mean and maximum currents, and
mean and maximum water depths.

These hydrodynamic parameters were chosen to provide a comprehensive representation of habitat exposure to tidal and submersion dynamics, which are known to be critical determinants for predicting habitat migration patterns under changing environmental conditions. Figure 17.2 shows the hydrodynamic parameters for different habitats across the Urala study site, highlighting the distinct environmental conditions experienced by each habitat type.






Figure 17.2: Habitat Classification Map for the 2018 ENSO Neutral Year Baseline




17.3.1 Hydrodynamic Regime Summary

Mangrove Zones: Experience frequent wetting cycles with near-100% inundation frequency and high submergence percentages (median ~40–50%). They occupy areas with the highest mean water depths (~0.1–0.2 m) and maximum water depths (reaching up to ~0.7–1.5 m), alongside higher maximum currents (~0.3–0.4 m/s) required to prevent extreme salinity build-up.
Cyanobacterial Mats & High Intertidal Flats: Share moderate submergence percentages (~30%) and shallow mean water depths (< 0.1 m). They endure frequent wetting-drying cycles with maximum dry event durations typically staying under 20–25 days, creating optimal moist, hypersaline windows.
Bright Salt Flats: Characterised by minimal submergence percentages (median < 10%), near-zero mean water depths, and prolonged dry periods exceeding 120–175 days, leading to intense evaporation and crust formation.

title: 13  Overview
text:
13.2 Prediction approach
Following the methodology established for Giralia Bay (?sec-giralia-approach), an integrated numerical model was developed for the Cape Preston region. However, unlike Giralia and Urala, we did not carry out the same level of detailed calibration for the hydrodynamic model. The hydrodynamic model was initialised using the Giralia and Urala calibtrated settings and subsequently, the mangrove vegetation module was coupled. This is due to the limited availability of field data for Cape Preston, which constrained our ability to perform a comprehensive calibration. However, as the mangrove and algal mat mapping was carried out using the same methodology as Giralia and Urala, we were able to initialise the model with present-day mangrove boundaries derived from satellite imagery.
Once present-day mangrove boundaries were initialised, cyanobacterial (algal) mat distributions were calibrated using an offline (decoupled) predictive approach based on hydrodynamic and mangrove spatial outputs. The calibrated, coupled modelling framework was then applied to simulate future sea-level rise scenarios for both mangrove ecosystems and algal mats.
Detailed calibration and validation procedures for the mangrove and algal mat modules, are provided in ?sec-hydro-calibration and ?sec-urala-calibration, respectively.

title: 14  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
14.1 Sea Level Rise Response
In this chapter, we present the response of mangroves to different SLR scenarios at Cape Preston. As described in Section 13.3, the predicted mangrove extent under present-day environmental conditions was used as the initial baseline condition, and simulations were subsequently performed under a range of SLR scenarios representing low, medium, and high sea-level-rise conditions as discussed in Chapter 3. The SLR simulations were carried out over a 100-year projection period to assess the long-term response of the mangrove ecosystem to rising sea levels. The results were analysed to investigate changes in mangrove extent and biomass under each SLR scenario and to identify trends in mangrove migration, rates of habitat loss, and potential thresholds beyond which landward migration and ecosystem persistence are no longer possible.
Unlike the pronounced seaward edge drowning observed at Giralia and Urala, the response of mangroves at Cape Preston under SLR scenarios exhibits minimal drastic dieback along the seaward fringe. Instead, landward migration proceeds steadily and remains highly comparable across all three SLR scenarios (SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585).
Figure 14.4 illustrates this spatial evolution at Years 50 and 100 across the scenarios, highlighting the progressive, stable landward encroachment into supratidal zones without significant seaward collapse as we observed for other sites (Giralia and Urala).

section: 19.2 Eco-Geomorphic Impacts of Development Bund Walls
text:
19.2 Eco-Geomorphic Impacts of Development Bund Walls
To evaluate the structural influence of coastal infrastructure, the normalised temporal evolution of mangrove extent and tidal creek footprints under baseline climate scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585) was systematically compared against their development-constrained counterparts (DEV_SSP370 and DEV_SSP585) over a 100-year simulation period (Figure 19.12). Both metrics are normalised relative to initial conditions at Year 1.






Figure 19.12: Temporal evolution of (a) normalised mangrove area expansion and (b) normalised tidal creek footprint expansion over 100 years, comparing baseline climate scenarios (SSP370, SSP585) against development scenarios constrained by bund walls (DEV_SSP370, DEV_SSP585).



During the initial nine decades (Years 0–90), both baseline and development scenarios exhibit comparable growth patterns, expanding mangrove area up to 3.0–3.3 times the baseline footprint (Figure 19.12 a). Minor variance between years 50 and 75 reflects localised, transient hydro-period adjustments upstream of the bund walls.
However, a critical threshold is reached around Year 92–94, where the development bund walls impose a severe physical barrier to landward retreat: * Baseline Scenarios (SSP370 & SSP585): Endure late-stage sea-level stress but sustain a relative expansion factor between 2.05× and 2.35× by Year 100. * Development Scenarios (DEV_SSP370 & DEV_SSP585): Experience catastrophic canopy retreat and coastal squeeze, dropping sharply to 1.6× (DEV_SSP370) and 1.2× (DEV_SSP585) by Year 100.
This divergence represents a 32% to 41% net reduction in late-century mangrove habitat availability caused directly by the physical bund wall footprint.

19.2.1 Tidal Creek Evolution
Unlike mangrove area loss, which manifests rapidly near the end of the century, tidal creek footprint expansion shows an earlier and sustained restriction due to development infrastructure (Figure 19.12 b): * Early Alignment (Years 0–35): All scenarios follow nearly identical expansion curves, increasing channel network footprints by approximately 0.2% to 0.3%. * Divergence Point (~Year 35): Development curves begin steadily decoupling from baseline trajectories as bund walls restrict lateral channel migration and tidal headward incision. * Late-Century Contrast (Year 100): Baseline creek networks expand to 1.019× (SSP370) and 1.0205× (SSP585) relative to Year 1. In contrast, bund-constrained networks are restricted to 1.014× and 1.015×, respectively.
The presence of bund walls inhibits natural channel branching, confining hydrodynamics within established pathways and preventing the formation of secondary tidal drainage networks.

title: 15  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
15.1 Sea-Level Rise Response
Similar to Giralia, we carried out the hydrodynamic runs for discrete time intervals with the mangroves, bedlevels information from the mangrove projection runs and carried out the algal mat runs for static increase of water level at respective time steps. Using the hydrodynamic data, we project the algal mat response using two different data-driven approaches as described in Chapter 3.
Both modelling approaches predict changes in the distribution and spatial organisation of cyanobacterial mats across the Cape Preston intertidal domain over the 100 year projection period. However, the predicted spatial patterns differ considerably between the RF and threshold-based optimisation approaches.
The RF model predicts extensive and relatively continuous baseline coverage across the central intertidal flats. By Year 50 and Year 100, predicted future coverage is more spatially restricted, occurring predominantly along the southern margins and within western salt flat embayments. In contrast, the threshold-based optimisation model predicts a more dispersed distribution of future suitable areas, with patches extending towards the higher intertidal flats. These differences indicate that the two approaches represent the spatial redistribution of cyanobacterial mats differently under changing environmental conditions.
The influence of the SLR scenario also varies between the modelling approaches. Under the low emissions SSP119 scenario, both approaches predict changes in cyanobacterial mat distribution, including expansion into some areas of higher elevation. Under the moderate emissions SSP370 and high emissions SSP585 scenarios, the RF model predicts comparatively restricted future distributions, with much of the projected coverage concentrated along the margins of the existing mats. Conversely, the threshold-based optimisation model predicts a more dispersed pattern of potential future coverage across the intertidal domain. The differences between scenarios are particularly evident in the distribution of isolated patches and the extent of predicted expansion beyond the existing mat boundaries.
These projections reflect differences in the mathematical formulations and assumptions underlying the two approaches. The Random Forest classifier identifies statistical relationships between observed cyanobacterial mat distributions and environmental predictors, accounting for potentially complex and nonlinear interactions. In comparison, the threshold-based optimisation model determines suitable areas according to prescribed environmental thresholds, including inundation frequency and water depth limits. Consequently, its predictions are more directly influenced by the spatial distribution of hydrodynamic conditions and local topography.
The spatiotemporal projections reveal a marked response of cyanobacterial mats to sea-level rise across the Cape Preston intertidal domain. Under the low-emissions SSP119 scenario, algal mat coverage exhibits moderate resilience, experiencing a reduction of roughly 15% to 25% by Year 50 and up to 40% by Year 100 as wetting extends across the flats. Under moderate (SSP370) and high (SSP585) emissions scenarios, the rate of water level rise outpaces landward migration capacity, leading to severe habitat contraction with algal mat coverage reductions exceeding 65% by Year 50 and dropping by more than 85% to complete near-total submergence by Year 100.
Comparing the two modelling paradigms, the Random Forest (RF) classifier captures smooth, broader spatial persistence across supratidal zones by relying on non-linear probabilistic associations among hydrodynamic drivers. In contrast, the threshold-based optimisation approach enforces strict physical envelope boundaries, predicting more sharply delineated zonation bands that explicitly highlight coastal squeeze and acute drowning thresholds under high-forcing scenarios.
Regarding the mangrove communities evaluated alongside the algal dynamics, alongshore-averaged profiles show that mangrove fractions maintain a stable distribution across lower-to-middle intertidal elevations during the first 50 years, but experience compression and upward landward shifting by Year 100 as rising sea levels alter intertidal inundation frequencies and bed shear stress limits.

title: 15  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
15.2 Comparative Dynamics Across Scenarios
At Year 0 (present condition), spatial mapping reveals an extensive, contiguous algal mat complex occupying high-elevation salt flats landward of the coastal mangrove fringe (panel a across all spatial figures). Under baseline hydrodynamic conditions, these expansive intertidal flats maintain low hydrodynamic shear stress (\(\tau_{\text{max}} \le 0.7\text{ N m}^{-2}\)), suitable inundation frequencies, and shallow water depths during high tides (\(d_{98} \le 0.55\text{ m}\)), allowing stable algal mats to flourish.
The cross-shore transect profile at Year 0 (b) highlights distinct zonation between the two coastal ecosystems along the elevation gradient: * Mangrove Fringe (\(3,000\text{ m} \le x \le 8,000\text{ m}\)): Mangroves achieve their highest alongshore coverage fraction (\(\sim 0.40–0.50\)) on intertidal mudflats where mean bed elevation ranges between \(-1.0\text{ m}\) and \(0.5\text{ m}\). * Algal Mat Zone (\(6,000\text{ m} \le x \le 11,000\text{ m}\)): Algal mats dominate higher supratidal flats (\(0.5\text{ m} \le z \le 1.8\text{ m}\)), reaching peak alongshore coverage fractions exceeding \(0.60–0.70\).


15.2.1 SSP119 Projection

Year 50 (c): Under mild sea-level rise, the algal mat footprint experiences minor fragmentation along its lower seaward margin (\(x \sim 6,000–8,000\text{ m}\)). However, the cross-shore profile shows that high coverage fractions (\(\sim 0.40–0.60\)) persist across the broad central supratidal flat (\(10,000\text{ m} \le x \le 14,000\text{ m}\)), while the mangrove fringe maintains stable coverage fractions (\(\sim 0.20–0.30\)) around \(x = 4,000–8,000\text{ m}\).
Year 100 (d): Increased inundation drives localised seaward retreat along outer boundaries. Despite this, a substantial portion of the algal mat profile remains viable across higher-elevation flats (\(10,000\text{ m} \le x \le 16,000\text{ m}\)) where coverage fractions remain around \(0.20–0.40\). Mangrove distribution exhibits minimal cross-shore compression, holding steady low-density presence along channel edges.




15.2.2 SSP370 Projection

Year 50 (c): Moderate sea-level rise triggers drowning across low-lying algal mat habitat. The contiguous Year 0 mat fragments into isolated clusters near expanding tidal channels where inundation frequencies exceed tolerance limits (\(> 0.95\)). In the transect profile, the peak algal coverage fraction drops sharply from \(> 0.60\) down to \(\sim 0.30\), shifting landward toward \(x = 10,000–14,000\text{ m}\). Simultaneously, mangroves expand slightly inland along creek banks, raising mangrove coverage fractions up to \(\sim 0.35\) around \(x = 6,000–8,000\text{ m}\).
Year 100 (d): Significant loss of persistent algal mat coverage occurs across the central domain. As deeper tidal networks expand inland, water depth thresholds (\(d_{98} > 0.55\text{ m}\)) are exceeded, restricting viable mat habitat to narrow landward bands (\(x > 12,000\text{ m}\)) with low coverage fractions (\(< 0.15\)). While the mangrove distribution curve appears broadly distributed across the domain (\(2,000\text{ m} \le x \le 12,000\text{ m}\)), its alongshore coverage fraction remains low (\(\le 0.15–0.20\)). This indicates that rather than forming a dense forest, mangroves are restricted to narrow, highly dispersed bands along dissected channel networks.




15.2.3 SSP585 Projection

Year 50 (c): Accelerated sea-level rise triggers rapid ecological drowning across mid-to-high intertidal flats. The extensive northern mat complex collapses, causing the cross-shore algal coverage fraction to decline to \(< 0.25\) beyond \(x = 10,000\text{ m}\). Mangroves temporarily display an opportunistic inland pulse between \(x = 5,000\text{ m}\) and \(9,000\text{ m}\) (fractions reaching \(\sim 0.40\)) as higher water levels temporarily convert formerly hyper-saline salt flats into habitable intertidal zones.
Year 100 (d): Extreme sea-level rise drives near-complete collapse of persistent algal mats across the Urala domain. Channel network enlargement increases maximum bed shear stress (\(\tau_{\text{max}} > 0.7\text{ N m}^{-2}\)) and causes permanent inundation, virtually eliminating the environmental window required for algal mat stability (coverage fractions \(< 0.05\)). Although the mangrove distribution curve spans continuously from \(x = 2,000\text{ m}\) to \(x = 15,000\text{ m}\), the alongshore coverage fraction stays under \(0.15\) throughout. This demonstrates that mangroves do not form an expansive contiguous wetland, but rather survive as highly fragmented, low-density linear fringes fringing deep tidal creeks across an otherwise drowned landscape.







NoteManagement Implications & Strategic Recommendations



The findings of this numerical modelling study provide process-based insights for coastal managers, regional planners, and environmental impact assessors operating along the Urala coastline. Earlier site assessments (e.g., Seashore Engineering (2021)) relied primarily on empirical morphometric relationships to infer habitat responses under generic sea-level rise allowances (\(0.4\text{ m}\) by 2070 and \(0.9\text{ m}\) by 2110). While those studies identified tidal creek network expansion as a key driver of habitat reorganization and long-term habitat loss, our process-based Delft3D-FM simulations reveal specific hydrodynamic thresholds and spatial nuances across different climate pathways.

15.2.4 Habitat Migration Dynamics and Supratidal Buffer Corridors
Our results demonstrate that intertidal habitat response is highly scenario-dependent. Under lower emission pathways (SSP119), both mangrove and algal mat habitats demonstrate notable resilience, retaining spatial continuity through Year 100. Under moderate-to-high emission pathways (SSP370 and SSP585), both ecosystems attempt to migrate landward (\(x > 10,000\text{ m}\)), though algal mats experience significant landward compression compared to expanding channel-fringe mangroves.
Management Consideration: To accommodate natural landward migration and reduce the risk of coastal squeeze, coastal management frameworks could identify and designate supratidal buffer zones behind current high-elevation salt flats. Planning future coastal infrastructure (such as solar salt evaporation ponds, access roads, pipelines, bund walls, or pastoral fencing) with these migration pathways in mind (\(x = 10,000\text{ m}\) to \(18,000\text{ m}\)) would help preserve remaining intertidal accommodation space. Furthermore, proposed developments across the intertidal platform can directly obstruct or alter these migration trajectories, as detailed in Chapter 11.


15.2.5 Differentiating Spatial Extent from Ecosystem Quality and Density
Broad spatial mapping and remote sensing can obscure localized changes in habitat quality when evaluating coastal wetland response. Under SSP370 and SSP585 at Year 100, mangrove presence appears across a broad cross-shore zone (\(2,000\text{ m}\) to \(15,000\text{ m}\)), which might initially resemble habitat expansion. However, cross-shore profile analysis indicates that alongshore coverage fractions remain low (\(\le 0.15\)).
Management Consideration: Environmental monitoring programs could incorporate metrics for canopy closure, structural continuity, and biomass density alongside spatial boundaries. Low-density, linear fringe mangroves along dissected creeks offer different ecosystem function profiles—such as altered wave attenuation, shoreline stabilization, and blue carbon capacity—compared to dense, contiguous forests. Monitoring metrics that reflect habitat fragmentation provide a clearer picture of ecological state.


15.2.6 Recognition and Conservation of Cyanobacterial Algal Mats
In arid and semi-arid tropical environments like the Pilbara coast, cyanobacterial algal mats serve as primary producers and nitrogen fixers supporting intertidal food webs. Because they occupy high supratidal flats often categorized as salt flats, they are sometimes deprioritised in environmental evaluations relative to mangrove forests. Our results indicate that algal mats possess distinct hydrodynamic tolerance windows, experiencing structural fragmentation as maximum bed shear stress (\(\tau_{\text{max}} > 0.7\text{ N m}^{-2}\)) and inundation depths (\(d_{98} > 0.55\text{ m}\)) exceed physical suitability thresholds.
Management Consideration: Environmental assessments could explicitly evaluate persistent algal mat zones as sensitive intertidal habitats. Where coastal engineering works (such as channel dredging, culvert installations, or tidal barriers) are planned, evaluating their potential effects on shallow tidal inundation frequencies across supratidal flats would help mitigate premature disruption to these primary-producing communities.


15.2.7 Scenario-Based Adaptive Management Thresholds
Comparative analysis across climate pathways demonstrates that habitat survival and zonation rely heavily on the rate of sea-level rise. Under SSP119, intertidal zonation remains largely stable through Year 100, whereas higher pathways (SSP370/SSP585) lead to progressive habitat reorganization between Year 50 and Year 100 as tidal creek networks expand.
Management Consideration: Regional management frameworks could consider Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways (DAPP), linking planning thresholds to observed local sea-level rise rates and channel network expansion rather than fixed calendar years. Where monitoring indicates sea-level rise approaching intermediate thresholds (\(\sim 0.4\text{ m}\)), proactive options—such as localized sediment management or living shoreline strategies—could be evaluated to assist high-value intertidal zones before extensive channel enlargement occurs.

text:
Core Mangrove Stability: The dense, central intertidal stands display exceptional long-term stability (green), representing resilient core communities where tidal inundation frequency remains optimal[cite: 1].
Fringing Loss and Retreat: Localised dieback and landward/creek-bank retreat (red) are concentrated along upper intertidal boundaries and exposed tidal channel margins[cite: 1]. These retreat patterns reflect heightened stress during pronounced regional low water-level events (e.g., ENSO-driven sea-level drawdowns) and extreme heat events (Lovelock et al., 2017).
Channel Colonisation and Expansion: Dynamic gains and seaward expansion (black) occur primarily along tidal creek networks and lower intertidal mudflats, where local sediment accretion provides new suitable substrate for colonisation[cite: 1].

title: 14  Mangrove Response to SLR
text:
14.2 Model Initialisation & Performance Evaluation
The calibrated numerical model was forced with regional harmonic tidal constituents (MSKO) to simulate present-day hydrodynamics and predict equilibrium mangrove distribution across Cape Preston. Spatial agreement between the simulated model output and high-resolution ground truth observations was evaluated across the grid using a categorical spatial confusion matrix[cite: 2]:

True Positives (Green): Grid cells where both model and satellite observations confirm mangrove presence[cite: 2].
False Negatives (Yellow): Observed mangrove areas omitted by the model prediction[cite: 2].
False Positives (Red): Areas predicted as mangrove by the model where none were observed in reality[cite: 2].

To quantitatively evaluate spatial classification accuracy across the domain, precision, recall, and the \(F_1\) score were computed based on the cell counts (Figure 14.2)[cite: 2]:









Statistic
Definition
Formula
Model Performance




Precision
Proportion of modelled mangrove cells corresponding to true observed mangroves
\(\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\)
\(0.650\)


Recall
Proportion of observed mangrove cells correctly reproduced by the model
\(\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\)
\(0.520\)


\(F_1\) Score
Harmonic mean of precision and recall
\(F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\)
\(0.580\)



The statistical metrics confirm strong predictive capability and spatial fidelity across the primary intertidal zones (\(F_1 = 0.580\))[cite: 2]. The precision score of \(0.650\) indicates high reliability in positive predictions, demonstrating that simulated mangrove stands closely match real-world distributions[cite: 2]. The lower recall value (\(0.520\)) and associated false negatives (yellow patches) occur predominantly along sub-grid scale tidal channels and highly fragmented upper intertidal margins, where micro-topographic variations and sharp hydrodynamic gradients fall beneath the discrete numerical mesh resolution[cite: 2]. Overall, removing the salinity mass balance proxy successfully optimised model behaviour for Cape Preston’s unique hydrodynamic environment.






Figure 14.2: Spatial performance and validation of the calibrated mangrove model for the Cape Preston site. Spatial distribution of True Positives (green), False Negatives (yellow), and False Positives (red) mapped over high-resolution aerial imagery, alongside summary spatial classification metrics (Precision = 0.65, Recall = 0.52, \(F_1\) Score = 0.58).

title: About
text:
About the Mardie Project
The Mardie Marine and Intertidal Research Offset Program, which is led by the Western Australian Marine Science Institution, was established to develop an understanding of the West Pilbara’s intertidal habitats, with a focus on mangroves, cyanobacterial (algal) mats and, their ecological role and the changes these habitats may face in the future due to climate change and salt project developments. The program includes five major research components on the west Pilbara coast which are being delivered by more than 20 scientists from the WAMSI partnership.

title: 1  About
text:
About the Project
Environmental offsets are actions that provide environmental benefits which counterbalance the significant residual environmental impacts or risks of a project or activity.
WAMSI is leading an offset project on the Pilbara Coast to provide the science needed for the Western Australian Government to make more informed sustainable decisions on these projects.
Mardie Minerals Pty Ltd is developing the Mardie Project in the Pilbara Region of Western Australia and has been granted conditional approval for the construction and operation of a solar salt and sulphate of potash production facility and provided financial offsets for marine and intertidal research.
The overall aim of the Mardie Offset Marine and Intertidal Research Program includes three major research components:

To map the original and current extent of samphire and algal mat on the west Pilbara Coast,
To identify and quantify the potential effects of sea level rise on mangroves, samphire and algal mat on the west Pilbara Coast, and
To identify the ecological roles, values and functions of algal mat on the west Pilbara coast.

title: About
section: Quantifying the effects of climate change on intertidal habitats of the west Pilbara coast (Project B)
text:
Quantifying the effects of climate change on intertidal habitats of the west Pilbara coast (Project B)
The overall aim of this specific project is to develop a predictive understanding of how West Pilbara Benthic Communities and Habitats (BCH) are likely to change in the future due to climate change and salt project developments. Specific project aims include:

Undertake a synthesis of our current understanding and knowledge gaps through data review, and develop conceptual models of key coastal processes in the region.
Develop a modelling capability that will be applied to assess how intertidal BCH will respond to changes in sea level, flooding, extreme events, and coastal development.
Assess how different coastal processes determine the function and migration capacity of intertidal BCH.
Assess how future changes in sea level, extreme events and salt works may impact upon the intertidal BCH distributions and function.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
Figure 1.1: Conceptual eco-geomorphic cross-section of an arid coastal environment illustrating habitat zonation, salinity gradients, and hydro-evaporative feedback processes from subtidal seagrass beds to supratidal terrestrial dunes.









Subtidal to Lower Intertidal Zone: Subtidal seagrass meadows and macroalgal communities may occur adjacent to fringing mangrove forests along sheltered tidal channels and lower intertidal shorelines. Mangrove distribution is influenced by inundation frequency, substrate stability, and salinity, while tidal exchange can facilitate salt export and influence soil salinity (Cohen & Lara, 2003; Saintilan et al., 2018; Semeniuk, 1994).
Mid- to Upper Intertidal Zone: Landward of, or interspersed with, mangrove forests, saltmarsh and succulent halophyte communities, including Tecticornia spp., may occupy areas subject to less frequent tidal inundation and variable soil salinity. The distribution of these communities depends on local elevation, hydroperiod, substrate properties, and hydrological conditions (Saintilan et al., 2018; Yando et al., 2023).
Upper Intertidal to Supratidal Zone: Saltflats, including hypersaline flats sometimes described as sabkhas, and cyanobacterial mats commonly occur in upper-intertidal and supratidal environments. Infrequent inundation, high evaporation, and restricted drainage can promote salt accumulation, creating conditions that limit the establishment of vascular plants. These habitats may form mosaics or transitional zones between vegetated intertidal communities and terrestrial vegetation or coastal dunes (Figure 1.1) (Blanco-Sacristán et al., 2022; Eliot, 2013; Semeniuk, 1994).

title: 1  Introduction
section: 1.2 The Unique Case and Diversity of the Pilbara Setting
text:
1.2 The Unique Case and Diversity of the Pilbara Setting
The Pilbara region of Western Australia represents a globally rare hyper-arid coastal setting where extensive tidal creeks, hypersaline supratidal mudflats, and low-lying coastal landforms interact with a macro-tidal regime (Eliot, 2013; Semeniuk, 1994). Rainfall across the Pilbara is highly unpredictable and hyper-variable, primarily driven by episodic tropical cyclone events rather than seasonal river flow. Consequently, terrestrial sediment and nutrient delivery to the coast occur in intense, intermittent pulses.
Benthic Coastal Habitat (BCH) communities in the West Pilbara exhibit pronounced, hyper-salinity-driven zonation along the intertidal profile (Semeniuk, 1994). Intertidal mangrove forests (Avicennia marina, Rhizophora stylosa) line lower tidal creek channels, transitioning landward into dense succulent samphire marshes (Tecticornia spp.), expansive cyanobacterial algal mats, and hyper-saline saltflats (sabkhas) (Figure 1.1). Cyanobacterial algal mats and samphire communities experience intricate ecohydrological conditions governed by tidal inundation frequencies, extreme surface evaporation, and surface–groundwater interactions. These high-intertidal communities play a vital role in nutrient processing, sediment stabilization, and primary productivity, providing major ecosystem subsidies to adjacent marine and terrestrial food webs (Eliot, 2013).






Figure 1.2: Sites of interest within the Pilbara region, showing the study locations at Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston.




1.2.1 Regional Site Justification
To capture the physical, geomorphic, and ecological heterogeneity of the West Pilbara Coast, three representative study locations were selected (Figure 1.2): Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston. Each site represents a distinct coastal archetype and hydrodynamic setting across the regional spectrum:

Giralia (Exmouth Gulf): Represents an enclosed, macrotidal, low-energy estuarine gulf setting characterized by extensive landward saltflats and sheltered creek networks. Giralia offers an ideal setting to study hyper-saline groundwater dynamics, long-term sediment trapping, and landward marsh migration without exposed ocean wave forcing.
Urala (Onslow Coast / Deltaic Fringe): Represents an exposed, sediment-rich alluvial/deltaic coastal floodplain setting associated with intermittent river outflow (Ashburton River catchment). Urala is critical for examining how episodic cyclone-driven floods interact with sea-level variability to redistribute terrestrial sediments, flush root-zone salinity, and rebuild intertidal landforms.
Cape Preston: Represents a wave-exposed, bedrock-constrained rocky headland and island archipelago setting. Cape Preston provides a contrast in physical energy and geomorphology, where limited sediment supply and hard substrates constrain mangrove and samphire development to pocket beaches and structural creek fractures.

title: 1  Introduction
section: 1.3 Knowledge Gaps: Sea-Level Rise and Arid Coastal Dynamics
text:
1.3 Knowledge Gaps: Sea-Level Rise and Arid Coastal Dynamics
Despite the ecological and coastal protection value of these hyper-arid environments, major knowledge gaps remain regarding how sea-level rise (SLR) will alter arid intertidal dynamics.
First, while low-latitude tropical mangroves expand landward into high saltmarshes or saltflats in response to rising sea levels (Cohen & Lara, 2003), or colonize low mudflats where accommodation space is filled by sediment (Rogers et al., 2019; Cahoon2021?), the specific mechanisms governing mangrove-saltmarsh-algal mat interactions in arid environments remain poorly constrained (Bulleri2018?). Most empirical studies on mangrove-saltmarsh interactions are concentrated in transitional subtropical-temperate regions (e.g., 23 out of 29 global studies examine Avicennia germinans and Spartina alterniflora in the Gulf of Mexico) (Yando et al., 2023). These models cannot be directly applied to arid environments like the Pilbara, where succulent samphires (Tecticornia spp.) and hypersaline algal mats dominate high intertidal zones under extreme evaporative demand.
Second, climate change and SLR introduce non-linear response thresholds in arid systems. Minor sea-level anomalies (on the order of \(10\text{ cm}\)) during the 2015/16 El Niño event led to widespread, severe mangrove dieback across northern Australia (Lovelock et al., 2017). In hyper-arid regions where trees exist near their physiological salinity limits, elevated evaporation coupled with sea-level fluctuations can induce severe, sudden dieback (Dittmann et al., 2022). Such diebacks can rapidly invert eco-geomorphic trajectory: localized mangrove loss can shift intertidal areas into bare flats or create conditions suitable for pioneer saltmarsh species adapted to altered flooding regimes (Gomes2021?). Conversely, where saltmarshes facilitate mangrove establishment, expansion rates may accelerate relative to saltmarsh-free regions (Cohen et al., 2020; BlancoSacristan2022?). Empirical comparisons of mangrove expansion dynamics in arid regions with and without saltmarsh facilitation remain understudied.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Coastal Development and Anthropogenic Stressors
The eco-geomorphic resilience of the Pilbara coastline is increasingly challenged by human development superimposed onto climate change drivers (Guo et al., 2022). The West Pilbara is a critical economic corridor for global mineral and energy exports, driving coastal infrastructure development, port dredging, and industrial salt production.
Solar salt farm infrastructure, in particular, requires vast arrays of supratidal bund walls and evaporation ponds constructed directly across high-intertidal saltflats and algal mat zones. These physical barriers disrupt hydrological connectivity, alter surface-groundwater exchange, and block natural landward migration pathways for mangroves and samphires under sea-level rise. Furthermore, port dredging and industrial footprint alterations modify local tidal prisms and sediment budgets. Understanding how these localized anthropogenic perturbations interact with regional SLR, shifting cyclone frequencies, rising temperatures, and altered rainfall is crucial for regional environmental management.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Research Aims and Objectives
Addressing these critical knowledge gaps requires integrated predictive frameworks that account for the distinct physical and biological feedbacks of hyper-arid coastal environments.
The overall aim of this thesis is to quantify the eco-geomorphic sensitivity of hyper-arid intertidal habitats across the Pilbara Coast to the combined impacts of climate-driven sea-level rise and coastal development infrastructure. Specifically, this research aims to:

Characterize intertidal habitat zonation (mangroves, samphires, algal mats) and root-zone salinity dynamics across distinct Pilbara geomorphic settings (Giralia, Urala, Cape Preston).
Evaluate the role of samphire and algal mat communities in facilitating or constraining landward mangrove migration under rising sea levels.
Develop numerical and conceptual models to simulate hydro-evaporative, sediment transport, and vegetation feedbacks under future climate change scenarios and salt farm infrastructure footprints.
Provide predictive tools and baseline thresholds to assist environmental regulators and coastal managers in guiding conservation, risk assessment, and sustainable development along arid coastlines.
