title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 The Pilbara Setting

Regional Climate and Hydroclimatic Setting
The Exmouth–Pilbara region of Western Australia represents a distinctive arid coastal environment in which extensive tidal creeks, hypersaline supratidal mudflats, and low-lying coastal landforms interact with a macro-tidal regime (Eliot, 2013; Semeniuk, 1994). The regional climate is arid to semi-arid and tropical, characterised by high temperatures and low, highly variable rainfall. Summer maximum temperatures frequently exceed 32 °C along the coast and may surpass 45 °C inland, while winter coastal temperatures rarely fall below 10 °C (Sudmeyer, 2016). Mean annual precipitation is generally low, approximately 200–350 mm in parts of the region, and is strongly seasonal and spatially variable. Most rainfall occurs during the warmer months, particularly through episodic thunderstorms and tropical cyclone events. The Pilbara coast is also exposed to tropical cyclones, which can deliver substantial rainfall, generate extreme water levels, and drive episodic sediment transport (Bureau of Meteorology, 2009). In contrast, the cooler months are typically characterised by lower rainfall and high evaporation. Consequently, river discharge and terrestrial sediment delivery to the coast are highly episodic, with substantial inputs often associated with major rainfall and flood events (see Chapter 2 for a detailed assessment of hydroclimatic drivers).


Intertidal Geomorphology and Habitat Zonation
Intertidal benthic coastal habitat (BCH) communities across the West Pilbara exhibit pronounced spatial zonation associated with elevation, inundation frequency, salinity, and local geomorphological conditions (Hickey & Lovelock, 2022; Semeniuk, 1994). Along many sheltered tidal creeks and coastal embayments, mangrove forests, dominated by Avicennia marina, occupy lower intertidal margins. These may transition landward into succulent samphire communities, including Tecticornia spp., followed by extensive cyanobacterial mats and hypersaline saltflats, sometimes referred to as sabkhas (Hickey et al., 2025). Although this sequence is characteristic of many arid coastal settings, the distribution and continuity of individual habitats vary with local topography, hydrodynamics, sediment characteristics, drainage, and surface–groundwater interactions.
Mangroves in the region commonly fringe tidal creeks and occupy elevations subject to regular tidal inundation. In contrast, samphire communities and cyanobacterial mats may occupy higher intertidal and supratidal surfaces that experience less frequent inundation, high evaporative water loss, and variable soil salinity. Saltflats occur in areas where limited drainage and strong evaporation favour salt accumulation and restrict the establishment of vegetation. The resulting habitat mosaic reflects the interaction between tidal exchange, freshwater inputs, sediment dynamics, and groundwater processes. These intertidal communities contribute to sediment stabilisation, nutrient cycling, and primary production, supporting ecological connections between coastal, marine, and terrestrial food webs (Dee et al., 2026; Eliot, 2013; Hickey et al., 2023; Seashore Engineering, 2022).

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Knowledge Gaps
Despite the ecological value of these hyper-arid environments, major knowledge gaps remain regarding how sea-level rise (SLR) and/or any developmental activities will alter arid intertidal dynamics.
First, while low-latitude tropical mangroves expand landward into high saltmarshes or saltflats in response to rising sea levels (Cohen & Lara, 2003), or colonise low mudflats where accommodation space is filled by sediment (Rogers et al., 2019; Cahoon2021?), the specific mechanisms governing mangrove-saltmarsh-algal mat interactions in arid environments remain poorly constrained (Bulleri2018?). Most empirical studies on mangrove-saltmarsh interactions are concentrated in transitional subtropical-temperate regions (e.g., 23 out of 29 global studies examine Avicennia germinans and Spartina alterniflora in the Gulf of Mexico) (Yando et al., 2023). These models cannot be directly applied to arid environments like the Pilbara, where succulent samphires (Tecticornia spp.) and hypersaline algal mats dominate high intertidal zones under extreme evaporative demand.
Second, climate change and SLR introduce non-linear response thresholds in arid systems. Minor sea-level anomalies (on the order of \(10\text{ cm}\)) during the 2015/16 El Niño event led to widespread, severe mangrove dieback across northern Australia (Lovelock et al., 2017). In hyper-arid regions where trees exist near their physiological salinity limits, elevated evaporation coupled with sea-level fluctuations can induce severe, sudden dieback (Dittmann et al., 2022). Such diebacks can rapidly invert eco-geomorphic trajectory: localized mangrove loss can shift intertidal areas into bare flats or create conditions suitable for pioneer saltmarsh species adapted to altered flooding regimes (Gomes2021?). Conversely, where saltmarshes facilitate mangrove establishment, expansion rates may accelerate relative to saltmarsh-free regions (Cohen et al., 2020; BlancoSacristan2022?). Empirical comparisons of mangrove expansion dynamics in arid regions with and without saltmarsh facilitation remain understudied.

1.3.1 Regional Sites of Interest






Figure 1.2: Sites of interest within the Pilbara region, showing the focus study locations at Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston.



To address critical eco-geomorphic knowledge gaps and inform sustainable management, three primary sites of interest were identified across the West Pilbara Coast (Figure 1.2): Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston. These locations are of major scientific significance, representing distinct coastal archetypes across the regional environmental spectrum, while simultaneously serving as high-priority focus areas for commercial and industrial development plans (e.g., proposed solar salt production facilities and mining export infrastructure):

Giralia (Exmouth Gulf): Represents an enclosed, macrotidal, low-energy estuarine gulf setting dominated by extensive landward saltflats and sheltered creek networks. Scientific interest in Giralia stems from its status as one of the most comprehensively studied intertidal systems in the Pilbara setting (Reef et al., 2026; Riera et al., 2023; Santini et al., 2013), providing a vital historical benchmark for hyper-saline groundwater dynamics, long-term sediment trapping, and landward marsh migration without exposed ocean wave forcing.
Urala (Onslow Coast / Deltaic Fringe): Represents an exposed, sediment-rich alluvial/deltaic coastal floodplain setting associated with intermittent river outflow from the Ashburton River catchment. Scientifically, Urala provides a key setting for examining how episodic cyclone-driven flood pulses interact with sea-level variability to redistribute terrestrial sediments, flush root-zone salinities, and drive multi-decadal intertidal landform evolution.
Cape Preston: Represents a micro to meso tidal system, bedrock-constrained rocky headland and island archipelago setting. It holds scientific interest as a high-energy geomorphic contrast, where limited sediment supply and hard substrates constrain mangrove and samphire development to pocket beaches and structural creek fractures under heavy wave action.

title: Future of Intertidal Habitats in the Pilbara
text:
Project Motivation and Context
Much of the West Pilbara coastline has remained relatively undeveloped, but proposals for coastal and industrial development, including large-scale solar salt production, create potential pressures on its extensive intertidal habitats. These pressures coincide with climate change, particularly rising sea levels. Understanding how habitats may respond to these interacting changes is needed to assess future development proposals and inform coastal planning.
The long-term behaviour of these arid intertidal systems remains comparatively poorly understood. Much of the established understanding of coastal wetland responses comes from humid tropical mangroves, temperate wetlands and sediment-rich river deltas. The West Pilbara differs through its limited and episodic freshwater inputs, strong evaporation, variable salinity and extensive low-gradient intertidal landscapes. Research is therefore needed to establish how these conditions influence habitat responses and the feedbacks between vegetation, water movement, sediment transport and changing land elevations. Of particular importance is understanding the capacity and limits of habitats to adjust vertically or migrate landward as sea levels rise, and how future development could restrict migration pathways or alter tidal connectivity.
In response to these challenges, the Western Australian Marine Science Institution (WAMSI) initiated a collaborative research program to investigate the potential environmental implications of salt-farm development along the West Pilbara coast. The initiative brings together government regulators, environmental management agencies, research institutions, and industry stakeholders, including the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER), the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD), the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW), and BCI Minerals.
Within this program, the University of Western Australia undertook an integrated investigation of the physical and ecological processes governing intertidal habitats and their potential responses to environmental change and coastal development. The research combines field observations, analysis of environmental conditions and habitat distributions, and the development and application of predictive models. Together, these components improve understanding of an understudied coastal setting and provide a basis for assessing potential habitat change under future sea-level-rise scenarios and development-related constraints.

title: 1  Introduction
section: 1.3 Knowledge Gaps: Predicting Arid Intertidal Dynamics Under Sea-Level Rise and Coastal Development
text:
1.3 Knowledge Gaps: Predicting Arid Intertidal Dynamics Under Sea-Level Rise and Coastal Development
As relative sea level rises, changes in tidal inundation can alter the elevation range suitable for different habitats, while sediment accretion and erosion determine whether intertidal surfaces can maintain their position within the tidal frame. Although coastal wetlands can respond to these changes through vertical accretion, ecological adjustment, and landward migration, their capacity to persist depends on local geomorphology, sediment availability, hydrological connectivity, and the availability of suitable accommodation space (Krauss et al., 2014; Schuerch et al., 2018; Woodroffe et al., 2016). Where development restricts landward migration or modifies sediment and water flows, these processes may be insufficient to prevent habitat loss and redistribution (Day et al., 2024; Leo et al., 2019).
However, the processes governing these responses are not uniform across climatic settings. Much of the established understanding of coastal wetland responses to SLR is derived from research in temperate wetlands, humid tropical mangroves, and sediment-rich river deltas (Kirwan & Megonigal, 2013; Nienhuis et al., 2023; Saintilan et al., 2020; Schuerch et al., 2018; Woodroffe et al., 2016). Although this literature provides important insights into inundation stress, sediment accumulation, and coastal habitat migration, its direct application to hyper-arid coastlines requires caution. Arid intertidal environments are characterised by limited and episodic freshwater inputs, high evaporative demand, and strong spatial variation in sediment and salinity conditions. Groundwater discharge, infrequent rainfall events, and episodic catchment flows may exert disproportionate influences on local hydrology, while restricted freshwater replenishment and infrequent tidal flushing can promote hypersalinity in elevated intertidal areas. These conditions influence vegetation stature, ecosystem productivity, and the distribution of habitats across the tidal frame, potentially producing responses that differ from those observed in more humid environments (Adame et al., 2021; Woodroffe et al., 2016).
These characteristics introduce substantial uncertainty into projections of arid intertidal change under future SLR. Increasing inundation does not necessarily result in uniform landward migration or the expansion of mangrove forests. Depending on local elevation, tidal connectivity, sediment supply, and substrate stability, rising sea levels may create new habitat opportunities in some locations while increasing inundation stress, erosion, or habitat loss in others. The balance between these outcomes is particularly difficult to predict where sediment delivery is episodic and the capacity of intertidal surfaces to accrete vertically is poorly constrained. Furthermore, changes in inundation interact with salinity and freshwater availability, meaning that a location becoming more frequently inundated may not necessarily become more suitable for vegetation if other environmental constraints persist (Lovelock et al., 2015; Saintilan et al., 2020; Woodroffe et al., 2016). Consequently, projections based solely on changes in sea level or habitat elevation may overlook important constraints on ecosystem persistence in arid coastal settings.
Coastal development adds another dimension to this uncertainty. Infrastructure, land reclamation, industrial activities, and changes to drainage or sediment pathways can modify the physical conditions that sustain intertidal habitats. Development may also restrict the landward migration of habitats as sea level rises, creating coastal squeeze where suitable habitat is progressively lost between rising water levels and fixed landward barriers (Day et al., 2024; Leo et al., 2019). In arid regions, where suitable habitat may depend on specific combinations of elevation, salinity, freshwater availability, and sediment characteristics, such alterations can affect not only total habitat area but also the spatial arrangement and connectivity of different habitat types. Predicting future change therefore requires consideration of SLR and development together, rather than treating either pressure in isolation.
These knowledge gaps are particularly relevant to the hyper-arid coast of the West Pilbara, north-western Australia. The region supports extensive mangrove forests, cyanobacterial mats, salt flats, and other intertidal habitats across a coastline characterised by strong tidal forcing, high evaporative demand, and episodic freshwater and sediment inputs. Recent regional-scale mapping provides an important baseline for understanding the historical extent and dynamics of these habitats, but further work is needed to translate this understanding into forward-looking assessments of habitat persistence and redistribution under future environmental change (Hickey et al., 2025). In particular, there is a need to investigate how changes in tidal inundation and coastal development may alter the suitability and spatial availability of habitat, while accounting for the distinct environmental constraints experienced by different intertidal communities.
In this study, we focus primarily on mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats as two ecologically distinct but potentially interacting components of the West Pilbara intertidal landscape. By investigating their potential responses to SLR and coastal development, we aim to improve understanding of where these habitats may persist, expand, contract, or redistribute under future scenarios. This provides a basis for assessing the potential consequences of coastal change for arid intertidal ecosystems and for identifying the environmental constraints and spatial trade-offs that may shape their future distribution.

1.3.1 Predicting Mangrove Responses to Sea-Level Rise
Mangroves have been extensively studied in relation to sea-level rise (SLR) through satellite mapping, field observations, and numerical modelling. Satellite time series have been used to quantify changes in mangrove extent and distribution over decadal timescales, while comparisons with water-level and sea-level observations have helped investigate the environmental drivers of these changes (Lovelock et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018). Field measurements of surface-elevation change, sediment accumulation, and mangrove responses across different inundation and salinity conditions have further established that forest persistence depends on the balance between rising sea levels, sediment supply, and local ecological tolerances (Krauss et al., 2014; Lovelock et al., 2015; Woodroffe et al., 2016).
Numerous numerical modelling efforts have extended these observations towards future projections. Existing approaches include landscape-scale habitat-transition models, such as SLAMM, used to project future mangrove extent (Payo et al., 2016); global coastal-wetland models that assess the effects of SLR and sediment availability (Schuerch et al., 2018); and bio-morphodynamic models investigating vegetation–sediment feedbacks, coastal conditions, and mangrove vulnerability (Xie et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022). More recent developments, such as the Mangrove Lifecycle Ecosystem Analysis and Forecasting (LEAF) model, explicitly represent mangrove growth and mortality across different life stages and couple these processes with hydrodynamic and morphological modelling (Dunlop et al., 2025). Collectively, these approaches demonstrate that future mangrove distribution can be projected, but that the outcomes depend on model structure, environmental forcing, and the processes represented.
Predicting mangrove responses requires particular attention to climatic and geographical context. Mangroves in humid tropical environments may experience different freshwater availability, salinity regimes, and sediment conditions from those in hyper-arid coastlines. Consequently, model relationships and ecological parameters developed for one setting may not transfer directly to another. This is particularly important when projecting future changes in the West Pilbara, where episodic freshwater inputs, hypersalinity, and spatially variable sediment supply can constrain mangrove establishment and persistence.
A major challenge is representing the feedbacks between mangrove development and coastal morphology over long timescales. Sediment transport, erosion and accretion, tidal inundation, and vegetation establishment and mortality can interact to determine whether mangroves persist, migrate landward, or retreat. Explicitly representing these processes alongside the different stages of the mangrove life cycle can be computationally demanding and data-intensive. Some bio-morphodynamic studies have therefore used idealised domains to isolate key mechanisms (Xie et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022), while other developments, including LEAF, have focused on detailed modelling over shorter projection periods (Dunlop et al., 2025) and some focussed on relatively small sites (Beselly et al., 2023). For additional details, readers are referred to Section 3.2. These approaches provide important advances, but they do not yet establish a general capability for predicting mangrove redistribution across an entire, geomorphically heterogeneous coastline over centennial timescales.
Furthermore, the response predicted for one location cannot necessarily be transferred to another, even where the hydrodynamic conditions appear similar. Differences in coastal slope, sediment availability, substrate characteristics, freshwater supply, and the initial distribution of vegetation can produce different trajectories of habitat change. Coastal-scale predictions therefore require spatially explicit environmental conditions and sufficient representation of the processes governing mangrove establishment, persistence, and migration. Developing a modelling capability that can predict mangrove responses to future SLR across coastal-scale domains and centennial timescales, while representing the processes most relevant to habitat redistribution, is a key gap addressed by this project.


1.3.2 Cyanobacterial Mats: From Ecological Research to Future Habitat Prediction
Research on cyanobacterial mats has largely focused on their microbial ecology, physiological functioning, and biogeochemical roles. Nitrogen fixation has been a major research theme, with studies examining the organisms responsible, variations in nitrogenase activity, and the environmental controls on this process within microbial mats (Stal et al., 2010). These studies improve understanding of mat functioning but do not directly predict changes in the spatial extent of intertidal mats under future environmental conditions.
A separate body of research has investigated cyanobacterial growth and transport in rivers, using mathematical models that combine biological processes with hydraulic transport to predict the movement and development of planktonic cyanobacteria (Guven & Howard, 2006). In lakes and reservoirs, process-based and data-driven models have been developed to forecast cyanobacterial blooms from environmental variables such as water temperature, nutrient availability, and hydrological conditions (Rousso et al., 2020). Satellite remote sensing has also been widely used to detect and monitor aquatic cyanobacterial blooms, providing information about their occurrence, extent, and temporal variability (Shi et al., 2019). However, these studies generally concern planktonic or water-column blooms rather than benthic microbial mats attached to intertidal surfaces. Their methods and assumptions therefore cannot be directly transferred to predicting the migration of intertidal mats.
Research directly addressing cyanobacterial mats in arid intertidal environments has increasingly focused on habitat mapping and historical change. The Exmouth Gulf mapping study by Hickey et al. (2023) used satellite imagery and supervised classification to map cyanobacterial mats and associated salt-flat habitats, while subsequent multidecadal mapping has documented the dynamic distribution of intertidal habitat classes along the north-western Australian coastline (Hickey et al., 2023; Hickey et al., 2025). These studies provide essential baseline information on habitat extent and variability, but historical mapping alone does not establish how mat-covered surfaces will respond to future SLR or coastal development.
Based on the literature identified for this review, a predictive framework for long-term migration of arid intertidal cyanobacterial mats under future SLR and coastal development has not been established. In particular, there is no identified approach that can be directly applied to project their future spatial redistribution across the West Pilbara coastline. Unlike mangroves, for which several ecological and bio-morphodynamic modelling approaches already exist, cyanobacterial mats require the development of a habitat-specific predictive approach. Such an approach must establish how changes in inundation, surface elevation, salinity, and substrate conditions influence the persistence and spatial distribution of mat-covered surfaces, while accounting for the removal or modification of habitat by coastal development.


1.3.3 Modelling Gap and Project Objectives
The literature highlights different but related challenges for the two habitats considered in this study. For mangroves, the key challenge is extending existing modelling capabilities towards spatially explicit, coastal-scale projections over centennial timescales in hyper-arid environments. For cyanobacterial mats, the more fundamental challenge is developing a suitable predictive approach, because existing research is concentrated on microbial processes, aquatic blooms, and historical habitat mapping rather than long-term intertidal habitat migration.
This project addresses these gaps by developing and applying a modelling framework to investigate the potential redistribution of mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats along the West Pilbara coast under future SLR and coastal development scenarios. The aim is to predict where these habitats may persist, expand, contract, or be lost over centennial timescales, and to identify locations where development may constrain their potential migration. The framework is intended to support coastal-scale assessment of future habitat change while making explicit the processes represented, the assumptions required, and the limitations that remain.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Research Aims and Study-Site Strategy
The overall aim of this research is to improve understanding of intertidal habitats in hyper-arid coastal environments and to develop predictive tools for assessing how these habitats may change under future environmental conditions and coastal development. Achieving this aim requires an understanding of the environmental processes that regulate habitat distribution, as well as a modelling framework capable of translating these processes into projections of potential future change. However, predicting the long-term responses of arid intertidal ecosystems is challenging because habitat persistence and redistribution depend on interactions between sea-level variability, tidal inundation, climatic conditions, salinity, sediment dynamics, geomorphology, and biological processes. The environmental controls considered in this study, including sea-level variability and climatic drivers, are described in Chapter 2.






Figure 1.2: Sites of interest within the West Pilbara region, showing the study locations at Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston.



To address these challenges, the research adopts a staged approach based on three study sites along the West Pilbara coast: Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston (Figure 1.2). The sites represent slightly different coastal environments and have distinct roles within the research design. Giralia provides the primary domain for model development, Urala provides a setting in which to investigate the implications of coastal development, and Cape Preston serves as a demonstration of the approach’s potential transferability to a different coastal setting. This staged strategy allows the modelling approach to be developed and evaluated in a relatively well-studied environment before being applied to sites with different environmental characteristics and development constraints.

1.4.1 Giralia: Environmental Understanding and Model Development
Giralia Bay is located in the eastern portion of Exmouth Gulf, Western Australia (\(22.4^{\circ}\text{S}\), \(114.3^{\circ}\text{E}\)). Exmouth Gulf is a shallow, semi-enclosed embayment approximately \(75\text{ km}\) long and less than \(20\text{ m}\) deep, bordered by low-relief peninsulas to the west and south. The bay lies within the onshore portion of the Carnarvon Basin and is underlain by calcarenitic rock units and sedimentary deposits, overlain by unconsolidated Quaternary sediments. The surrounding coastal plain comprises Holocene and late Pleistocene deposits, including relict beach ridges, coral reefs, aeolian sands, and supratidal sabkha flats with extensive evaporite crusts (Riera et al., 2023).






Figure 1.3: Study site at Giralia Bay within Exmouth Gulf, north-western Western Australia. (a) Regional setting. (b) Cross-shore intertidal zonation, showing mangroves, mudflats, cyanobacterial mats, and high-elevation salt flats.



Giralia is the principal site for developing the modelling approach because the wider Exmouth Gulf region is one of the better-studied examples of arid intertidal ecosystems in north-western Australia. Previous research has investigated mangrove growth and wood properties (Santini et al., 2013), the ecological functioning and productivity of cyanobacterial mats (Dee et al., 2026; Lovelock et al., 2010), nutrient exchange between mats and inundating waters (Adame et al., 2012), and the influence of intense storms and associated freshwater and sediment inputs on mangrove nutrient status (Lovelock et al., 2011). Experimental studies have also examined the rapid reactivation of cyanobacterial mats following rehydration (Chennu et al., 2015), while remote-sensing research has documented the spatial and temporal variability of high-intertidal habitats across Exmouth Gulf (Hickey et al., 2023). Collectively, these studies provide an empirical foundation for investigating the environmental controls on habitat distribution, although translating this knowledge into quantitative predictions of long-term habitat change remains challenging.
The region experiences a warm, hyper-arid climate, with a mean annual air temperature of \(25,^{\circ}\text{C}\), a mean minimum temperature of \(17,^{\circ}\text{C}\), and a mean maximum temperature of \(32,^{\circ}\text{C}\). Summer temperatures can reach \(47,^{\circ}\text{C}\), while mean annual rainfall is approximately \(250\text{ mm yr}^{-1}\). Despite these dry conditions, the region is periodically affected by severe tropical cyclones, which can generate extreme winds and rainfall and deliver episodic freshwater and sediment inputs to the coastal environment (Santini et al., 2013). The interplay between persistent aridity, regular tidal forcing, and episodic climatic disturbances provides an important context for understanding the distribution and persistence of intertidal habitats.
The area is also of conservation significance. The Western Australian Government has pursued protection of the Exmouth Gulf region through the Plan for Our Parks initiative, including arrangements involving the Nganhurra Thanardi Garrbu Aboriginal Corporation and the establishment of Giralia National Park and the adjoining Boologooro Nature Reserve. This conservation context reinforces the importance of understanding how environmental change and coastal development may affect the region’s intertidal ecosystems.

1.4.1.1 Intertidal Habitat Zonation
Giralia Bay contains a cross-shore sequence of intertidal habitats associated with differences in surface elevation, tidal inundation frequency, and local environmental conditions (Figure 7.1). From the seaward margin towards the land, four principal habitat zones can be distinguished:

Seaward mangrove fringe: Predominantly composed of Avicennia marina, occupying the lower-to-middle intertidal zone, where regular tidal inundation and flushing occur.
Mudflats: Generally unvegetated, low-gradient intertidal surfaces that are exposed during low tide and provide a transition between the mangrove fringe and higher intertidal habitats.
Cyanobacterial mats: Microbial communities occupying parts of the middle-to-upper intertidal flats, where periodic inundation alternates with prolonged exposure and desiccation.
High-elevation salt flats: Supratidal sabkha environments characterised by high salinity, evaporite accumulation, and sparse or absent vegetation.

This spatial organisation, together with the broad intertidal flats and relatively distinct habitat zones, provides a useful basis for deriving an idealised representation of the system. By simplifying the landscape into characteristic cross-shore zones, the model-development process can focus on the fundamental relationships between environmental forcing, surface elevation, inundation, and habitat distribution before considering the additional complexity of individual sites. Giralia therefore serves not only as an ecologically informed study site but also as a conceptual basis for developing and testing the idealised model described in Chapter 5. The resulting framework can then support subsequent applications that incorporate more complex environmental conditions and development-related constraints.



1.4.2 Urala: Application Under Coastal Development Constraints
Urala, on the Onslow coast, is the second study site and provides an opportunity to apply the modelling approach developed at Giralia under different geomorphic conditions and with explicit representation of coastal development constraints. The area is of interest in the context of potential industrial development, including solar salt production. In this study, the focus is specifically on how development-related bund walls may modify hydrodynamic conditions and, consequently, influence the potential redistribution of intertidal habitats under future sea-level scenarios. Applying the framework at Urala therefore provides a means of examining how physical infrastructure interacts with environmental change to influence habitat persistence and spatial reorganisation.

1.4.2.1 Overview of the Urala Study Site
The Urala study site is located approximately \(40\text{ km}\) south-east of Onslow, along the eastern coast of the Pilbara region near the mouth of Exmouth Gulf. Unlike Giralia Bay, Urala does not exhibit a uniformly ordered cross-shore sequence of intertidal habitats. Although distinct shore-normal zonation occurs in the southern part of the study area, the northern domain has a more complex morphology, where North Creek and South Creek converge and interconnect through a network of smaller tidal channels (Figure 12.1).






Figure 1.4: Study site at Urala on the West Pilbara coast, north-western Western Australia. (a) Regional setting. (b) Morphological overview showing intertidal habitat distribution, interconnected tidal-creek systems, barrier spits, and extensive landward salt flats.



The site is characterised by subtle topographic gradients typical of low-relief, arid coastal environments. Elevation generally increases landward from the open water and tidal-creek margins, across a sequence of intertidal and supratidal environments:

Intertidal zone: Low-lying areas influenced by tidal inundation, including vegetated margins and surfaces dissected by tidal channels.
High-intertidal to supratidal zone: Broad, low-gradient platforms landward of the mangrove fringe, including salt flats and other sparsely vegetated surfaces.
Upper salt flats and dunes: Inland areas comprising relict salt pans, evaporite-rich surfaces, and terrestrial coastal vegetation and dune systems at higher elevations.

The combination of low relief, interconnected tidal channels, barrier spits, and extensive landward salt flats makes Urala a useful setting for examining how changes in hydrodynamic connectivity may affect habitat distribution. In particular, modifications to the pathways through which tides propagate across the landscape may alter inundation patterns and the spatial conditions under which intertidal habitats persist.


1.4.2.2 Sediment Characteristics and Particle-Size Distributions
Sediment samples from Urala represent two contrasting substrate types: relatively sandy environments associated with channels and more exposed coastal surfaces, and finer-grained sediments characteristic of sheltered mudflats (Figure 12.2 and Figure 12.3). These differences provide context for interpreting the site’s sedimentary environment and potential variation in sediment mobility across the intertidal landscape.






Figure 1.5: Particle-size distribution (PSD) representative of the general sandy substrate at Urala, showing a narrow, predominantly unimodal distribution dominated by medium-to-fine sand fractions (\(100\)–\(500,\mu\text{m}\); \(\Phi \approx 1.0\)–\(2.5\)).









Figure 1.6: Particle-size distribution (PSD) representative of Urala mudflat sediments, showing a broad, polymodal distribution extending from fine silts and clays (\(<10,\mu\text{m}\)) through fine sand (\(\sim100,\mu\text{m}\)) to coarse biogenic fragments (\(800\)–\(1000,\mu\text{m}\)).



The sandy substrate exhibits a relatively narrow, well-defined grain-size distribution, with much of the material concentrated in the fine-to-medium sand range (\(150\)–\(300,\mu\text{m}\)). This distribution is consistent with sediment sorting in environments where tidal currents and wave action can transport finer particles away from exposed surfaces and channels. In contrast, the mudflat samples exhibit a broader distribution, with a principal peak near the fine-sand and coarse-silt boundary (\(\sim80\)–\(100,\mu\text{m}\)), a fine-grained component extending into silts and clays (\(<10,\mu\text{m}\)), and secondary coarse fractions around \(800\)–\(1000,\mu\text{m}\) that may include shell fragments and other biogenic material.
These contrasting sediment distributions are consistent with spatial differences in depositional conditions, from relatively energetic sandy environments to more sheltered settings where fine particles can settle. They provide useful environmental context for interpreting the potential response of the coastal landscape to changes in hydrodynamic forcing. However, the sediment measurements are used here to characterise the study site; they should not be interpreted as direct validation of sediment transport or morphological change unless those processes are explicitly represented and evaluated in the model.


1.4.2.3 Geomorphology and Environmental Drivers
Urala’s geomorphology is defined by extensive barrier spits, dynamic creek mouths, interconnected tidal channels, and broad landward salt flats. The North Creek and South Creek systems provide important pathways for tidal exchange across the landscape, while their geometry and connectivity influence how water reaches adjacent intertidal surfaces. These features are particularly relevant when assessing the potential hydrodynamic consequences of infrastructure that intersects or constrains existing flow pathways.
Hydrodynamic conditions are influenced by the regional tidal regime, with semi-diurnal tides driving regular inundation and currents within the principal creek channels. Tidal currents (predominantly) anextreme events with wave action contribute to sediment redistribution, while the relative sheltering of adjacent mudflats and mangrove margins favours the retention of finer material. Tropical cyclones and other intense weather events can temporarily increase wave energy and freshwater discharge, potentially altering creek mouths, barrier spits, and sediment distribution. The importance of these episodic processes varies spatially and through time.
The region’s hyper-arid climate and high evaporative demand further distinguish Urala from more humid coastal environments. Rainfall is highly variable, and major rainfall events may produce short-lived freshwater and sediment inputs against a background of prolonged dry conditions. These climatic and hydrodynamic drivers provide the environmental context for interpreting potential habitat responses, as outlined in Chapter 2.


1.4.2.4 Application to Development Scenarios
Urala provides the next step in the staged modelling strategy by extending the framework developed at Giralia to a landscape with more complex tidal-channel connectivity and explicit development constraints. The modelling will examine how bund walls associated with potential coastal development may modify hydrodynamic pathways and inundation patterns, and how these changes may influence the potential distribution of mangroves and cyanobacterial mats under sea-level-rise scenarios.
The emphasis is on the physical effects of bund walls on hydrodynamics and the resulting habitat changes, rather than on industrial processes such as salt-brine discharge or their associated water-quality effects. By comparing scenarios with and without development-related barriers, the study can investigate the extent to which infrastructure-induced changes in water movement alter the spatial distribution of suitable intertidal habitat. The results will help distinguish potential changes associated with regional sea-level rise from those arising from the configuration of physical barriers within the coastal landscape.
Urala therefore provides an important application site for assessing the interaction between environmental change and development-related modifications to coastal connectivity. It also allows the modelling framework to be examined under geomorphic conditions that differ from those at Giralia, helping to identify which aspects of the approach may be transferable and which require site-specific representation.



1.4.3 Cape Preston: Demonstration and Transferability
Cape Preston is the third study site and provides an opportunity to demonstrate the application of the modelling framework beyond the initial model-development site at Giralia and the development-focused application at Urala. Its contrasting coastal morphology and tidal conditions provide a useful setting in which to examine the potential transferability of the approach to a different arid coastal environment. In particular, Cape Preston has a narrower intertidal zone and a more spatially variable shoreline than the extensive intertidal flats of Giralia and Urala. These differences provide an opportunity to explore how the framework represents habitat distribution under contrasting geomorphic and hydrodynamic conditions.

1.4.3.1 Study Site: Cape Preston
Cape Preston is located approximately \(55\text{ km}\) west-southwest of Karratha in the Pilbara region of Western Australia (Figure 16.1). A sandy beach coastline extends eastward from Cape Preston towards an intertidal sandbar connecting Great Sandy Island. Behind this sandbar, the shoreline comprises tidal creeks, mangrove habitats, and extensive cyanobacterial mats. The coastal landscape is subject to tropical cyclones and associated extreme water levels, wave action, and freshwater discharge, which can contribute to coastal geomorphic change (Stevens et al., 2025).






Figure 1.7: Map of the study region showing (a) regional context along the Western Australian coastline and (b) a detailed aerial overview of Cape Preston.





1.4.3.2 Hydrodynamic and Geomorphic Setting
Water levels along the Pilbara coast are dominated by semidiurnal lunisolar tides, although tidal range varies regionally with bathymetry and coastal configuration. The eastern Pilbara is slightly towards macrotidal, whereas parts of the western Pilbara are mesotidal. Cape Preston exhibits close to a macrotidal regime, with a Highest Astronomical Tide (HAT) of \(2.25\text{ m}\) relative to mean sea level (MSL), a mean spring tidal range exceeding \(3\text{ m}\), and a maximum astronomical tidal range of approximately \(4.5\text{ m}\) (See also Table Table 2.1). In comparison, Onslow exhibits a smaller tidal range, with a HAT of \(1.29\text{ m}\) MSL (Table 2.1). Regional tidal dynamics are influenced by local bathymetry, including Barrow Island and the shallow waters to its south, which affect the propagation of semidiurnal and diurnal tidal energy and contribute to spatial variability in tidal conditions.
The extent of the intertidal zone at Cape Preston also differs substantially from that at Giralia and Urala. At Cape Preston, intertidal flats extend approximately \(2.5\text{ km}\) on average from the high-water line, compared with approximately \(8\text{ km}\) at Giralia and between \(7\text{ km}\) and \(10\text{ km}\) at Urala, depending on the location within the northern and southern domains. These differences in intertidal width, together with the contrasting tidal regimes and shoreline morphology, are important when considering the spatial extent of habitat redistribution under sea-level rise. The relative availability of landward accommodation space and the arrangement of existing habitats may influence the potential pathways through which mangroves, samphires, and cyanobacterial mats could shift as inundation conditions change.


1.4.3.3 Demonstration and Transferability of the Modelling Framework
Cape Preston provides a demonstration site for applying the modelling tools developed through this research to a coastal environment that differs from the initial development and application sites. The framework will be used to explore potential habitat changes under sea-level-rise scenarios and, where represented in the model, development-related spatial constraints. This will help demonstrate how the approach can be used to investigate potential habitat redistribution in a landscape characterised by a narrower intertidal zone, different tidal conditions, and spatially variable geomorphology.
Unlike the Giralia model-development stage, the Cape Preston application is not intended to provide an independently hydrodynamically validated prediction. Its outputs should therefore be interpreted as scenario-based assessments of potential habitat change, conditional on the environmental data, boundary conditions, and processes represented in the model. The application can demonstrate the framework’s practical use while highlighting the additional site-specific observations and hydrodynamic validation that would be needed for more robust local predictions.
A further objective is to develop modelling tools that can be made openly available and adapted for use beyond the three study sites. Cape Preston therefore serves as a demonstration of the potential transferability of the approach to other arid and/or humid coastlines, while illustrating the importance of accounting for differences in geomorphology, tidal conditions, and habitat configuration when applying a common modelling framework across locations.



1.4.4 Integrated Research Objectives
The three sites form a staged research strategy that links environmental understanding, model development, application under development constraints, and demonstration of transferability. Across these sites, the research aims to:

Characterise environmental controls on intertidal habitat distribution and change, including sea-level variability, tidal inundation, climatic conditions, salinity, geomorphology, and sediment dynamics, as described in Chapter 2.
Develop a predictive modelling framework for investigating potential changes in the distribution of mangroves, samphires, and cyanobacterial mats under future environmental scenarios, using Giralia as the principal model-development site.
Assess potential development impacts by applying the framework at Urala to investigate how proposed infrastructure and associated spatial constraints may influence habitat persistence and redistribution under sea-level rise.
Demonstrate transferability and wider applicability by applying the approach at Cape Preston, while distinguishing scenario-based demonstrations from predictions supported by site-specific hydrodynamic validation.
Provide accessible modelling tools that can support future research and contribute to environmental assessment, coastal planning, and the evaluation of development scenarios in hyper-arid coastal environments.

Through this approach, the research seeks to establish a practical basis for assessing how environmental change and coastal development may jointly influence the future distribution of arid intertidal habitats. Rather than assuming that a single model configuration will represent every coastal setting equally well, the study uses the three sites to develop, apply, and demonstrate a framework whose assumptions, data requirements, and limitations can be made explicit.

title: 2  Controls on Coastal Ecosystems in Pilbara
text:
2.2 Sea-Level Variability and Water-Level Decomposition
To characterise sea-level variability along the Pilbara coast, water-level observations from the Exmouth and Onslow tide-gauge stations were analysed. The analysis follows the decomposition framework described by Lowe et al. (2021), which separates observed water levels into contributions operating over different temporal scales. Applying this framework to the two stations provides a regional basis for examining the relative importance of astronomical tides, seasonal and interannual fluctuations, and higher-frequency water-level anomalies.
Intertidal habitats experience water-level variability across a range of timescales, from individual tidal cycles and storm events to seasonal and interannual fluctuations and long-term sea-level change. Observed coastal water levels reflect the combined influence of several processes, including astronomical tides, changes in background sea level associated with oceanographic and climatic variability, and shorter-term anomalies driven by atmospheric forcing and coastal waves. Although these processes operate simultaneously, they differ in their characteristic timescales and influence the frequency, depth and duration of inundation, as well as the intervening periods of exposure. Separating these contributions provides a consistent framework for examining the water-level variability observed at Exmouth and Onslow, and for understanding how different sea-level processes shape inundation and exposure patterns across the region’s extensive intertidal environments.

2.2.1 Water-Level Decomposition Method
Following Lowe et al. (2021), the observed water-level time series, \(\eta(t)\), can be represented as the sum of a mean sea-level component, an astronomical tide, a seasonal contribution, an interannual contribution, and a higher-frequency residual:
\[
\eta(t) =
\eta_{\mathrm{MSL}}(t) +
\eta_{\mathrm{T}}(t) +
\eta_{\mathrm{A}}(t) +
\eta_{\mathrm{I}}(t) +
\eta_{\mathrm{SS}}(t)
\tag{2.1}\]
where \(\eta_{\mathrm{MSL}}(t)\) represents the long-term mean sea-level trend, \(\eta_{\mathrm{T}}(t)\) is the astronomical tide, \(\eta_{\mathrm{A}}(t)\) is the seasonal contribution, \(\eta_{\mathrm{I}}(t)\) represents interannual variability, and \(\eta_{\mathrm{SS}}(t)\) represents the remaining higher-frequency variability, which may include storm surges and other short-term processes. These components are estimated sequentially from the observed records.
First, the astronomical tide is estimated using harmonic tidal analysis, which represents the predictable tidal signal as a combination of constituents with known frequencies and estimated amplitudes and phases. The mean sea-level trend and predicted astronomical tide are then removed from the observed water levels to obtain the non-tidal residual (NTR), \(\eta_{\mathrm{NTR}}(t)\). The NTR represents water-level variability not explained by the fitted astronomical tide and mean sea-level trend.
The NTR is subsequently separated into seasonal and longer-term contributions. The seasonal signal is estimated by fitting annual and semiannual harmonic functions to the NTR time series. This approach captures the dominant annual cycle while allowing for an additional six-month component to represent departures from a purely sinusoidal annual pattern. The seasonal contribution is expressed as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\mathrm{A}}(t) ={}&
A_1 \cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{365.25}+\phi_1\right)\\
&+ A_2 \cos\left(\frac{4\pi t}{365.25}+\phi_2\right)+C
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.2}\]
where \(t\) is elapsed time in days, \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) are the annual and semiannual amplitudes, \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) are their respective phase offsets, and \(C\) is a constant offset. The parameters are estimated by fitting the harmonic function to the NTR observations using nonlinear least-squares optimisation. The resulting fitted series represents the seasonal contribution to non-tidal water-level variability.
After estimating the seasonal component, the remaining NTR is calculated by subtracting the fitted seasonal signal from the original NTR. To distinguish longer-term interannual fluctuations from shorter-term variability, the remaining series is then averaged monthly. This suppresses much of the daily-to-weekly variability and provides an estimate of the interannual component. The higher-frequency contribution is obtained from the remaining variability after accounting for the seasonal and interannual components. It is interpreted as a high-frequency residual rather than a direct measurement of storm surge alone, because it may also contain other short-period processes and errors associated with the decomposition.
The same decomposition framework is applied to the Exmouth and Onslow tide-gauge records to compare water-level variability across different temporal scales. The resulting components are examined to characterise seasonal fluctuations, interannual variability, long-term sea-level change, and higher-frequency water-level anomalies along the Pilbara coast. This provides a basis for understanding how variations in regional water levels may influence the frequency, depth, and duration of inundation across low-gradient intertidal habitats.
The decomposition for Onslow is illustrated in Figure 2.1. The figure brings together the observed water-level record, the estimated components of variability, tropical cyclone records, and the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI). This enables the different temporal contributions to be examined alongside potential climatic and meteorological influences.






Figure 2.1: Water-level decomposition for Onslow, Western Australia: (a) monthly maximum water levels (black), observed tidal range (blue); (b) estimated interannual water-level contribution (green) and long-term sea-level trend (red); (c) fitted seasonal contribution; (d) high-frequency residual and tropical cyclone events (green); (e) predicted astronomical tide; and (f) Southern Oscillation Index (SOI). Tropical cyclone records and SOI data are from the Australian Bureau of Meteorology and SOI monitoring page, respectively.



The decomposition distinguishes the recurring seasonal cycle from interannual fluctuations and longer-term sea-level change. The seasonal component (Figure 2.1 c) captures predictable annual and semiannual variations remaining after the fitted astronomical tide and long-term trend have been removed. The interannual component (Figure 2.1 b), in contrast, represents multi-year fluctuations that reflect large-scale oceanographic and atmospheric variability. Comparing this component with the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI; Figure 2.1 f) illustrates a strong link to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Positive SOI phases (La Niña conditions, shaded red, such as in 1999–2000, 2008, and 2010–2012) correspond to pronounced peaks in interannual water level (>0.2–0.3 m). Conversely, strong negative SOI phases (El Niño events, shaded blue, such as in 1997–1998 and 2015–2016) align with distinct drops in interannual baseline levels (reaching below -0.1 m).
The high-frequency residual (Figure 2.1 d) represents short-term water-level anomalies driven by atmospheric pressure drops, wind forcing, and storm surges. Comparing these surge anomalies against documented tropical cyclones (TCs; Figure 2.1 d) reveals major surge spikes corresponding directly to severe weather events, such as TC Vincent (~1990; storm surge peak exceeding 0.7 m) and TC Quang (~2015; storm surge peak ~0.6 m). However, the total water level experienced at the coastline depends on the additive combination and phase alignment of all components simultaneously.
The observed water level reflects the additive combination of the estimated components. When positive contributions coincide, they can reinforce one another and produce elevated total water levels; when contributions have opposing signs, they can partially offset one another. Consequently, the same astronomical tide can occur under different background water-level conditions, resulting in different maximum water levels and inundation extents. This is particularly relevant to the Pilbara’s extensive, low-gradient intertidal flats, where relatively small changes in water level may alter the areas reached by high tides and the duration of inundation near habitat elevation thresholds.
When positive contributions coincide, constructive alignment amplifies total water levels. For instance, during TC Elaine & Vance (1999), a moderate storm surge contribution (~0.31 m) coincided with a positive interannual sea-level anomaly (~0.18 m) driven by La Niña conditions (SOI > +1.0). Earlier around 1990 (TC Tina & Vincent), the highest individual storm surge peak in the record was observed (~0.72 m).
Conversely, when components have opposing signs or lack constructive alignment across all timescales, total water levels are moderated. During TC Frank & Jacob (1996), a substantial storm surge contribution (~0.52 m) coincided with a strong positive interannual anomaly (>0.20 m). However, because the seasonal contribution was essentially neutral and the storm occurred during a neap cycle, the resulting total water level in panel a did not exceed 1.6m. Similarly, during TC Quang (2015), although a major storm surge spike occurred (~0.60 m), it coincided with an El Niño-driven negative interannual anomaly and a lower phase of the seasonal cycle, which partially offset the surge contribution and prevented overall total water levels from reaching potential extremes.
For intertidal habitats, this decomposition helps distinguish the effects of regular tidal inundation, persistent shifts in background sea level and short-lived extreme events. It provides a basis for examining how different sea-level components influence habitat exposure over multiple timescales, and how their combined effects alter the frequency, depth and duration of inundation. Consequently, an astronomical tide or storm surge of the same magnitude can produce substantially different total water levels and inundation extents depending on the prevailing background sea-level conditions, including seasonal and interannual variability. This interaction is particularly important across the Pilbara’s low-gradient intertidal flats, where relatively small changes in background water level can substantially alter the spatial extent and duration of inundation, particularly near ecological elevation thresholds. Thus, the combined influence of these processes, rather than the magnitude of any individual component alone, is important for understanding water-level variability and its potential implications for intertidal ecosystems.

title: 2  Controls on Coastal Ecosystems in Pilbara
text:
2.8 Implications for Intertidal Habitats
The distribution and condition of intertidal habitats along the Pilbara coast reflect the combined influence of water-level variability, inundation and exposure, sediment dynamics, temperature, rainfall and wind. These drivers interact across different timescales: tides govern regular inundation cycles, seasonal and interannual fluctuations alter the background water level, and extreme weather events can produce short-lived departures from typical conditions. The resulting ecological effects depend on habitat elevation, local geomorphology, hydrological connectivity, substrate properties and the tolerance of individual organisms.

2.8.1 Mangroves
For mangroves, particularly Avicennia marina, tidal inundation determines the frequency, depth and duration of flooding, collectively described as the hydroperiod. Hydroperiod interacts with elevation, sediment conditions and drainage to influence mangrove establishment, growth and persistence (Krauss et al., 2014; Woodroffe et al., 2016). Changes in background sea level can alter the inundation experienced at a given elevation, while changes in sediment elevation and sediment supply affect the capacity of mangrove surfaces to keep pace with relative sea-level rise.
Seasonal and interannual water-level fluctuations can modify inundation even without a change in the elevation of the land surface. Periods of lower background water level may lengthen the exposure of upper-intertidal mangroves, while higher water levels can increase inundation frequency or extend flooding into areas that are only intermittently reached under typical conditions. The ecological outcome depends on the magnitude and duration of the change and on the availability of suitable landward accommodation space.
Temperature and rainfall influence the water and salt balance of mangrove environments. High temperatures and solar radiation increase evaporative demand, potentially increasing salinity in sediment porewater where freshwater inputs and tidal flushing are limited. Rainfall can temporarily dilute surface water and porewater salinity, although the effect depends on the amount and duration of rainfall, subsequent evaporation, drainage and the degree of connection with the sea. High temperature and hypersalinity can impose physiological stress, but mangrove responses should not be inferred from temperature or water level alone without considering local hydrological and substrate conditions.
Wind influences mangroves through several pathways. Sustained winds can modify coastal water levels, while wind-generated waves can increase sediment mobility and hydrodynamic stress along exposed shorelines. During extreme events, the combination of elevated water levels and wave action can contribute to erosion, sediment redistribution or damage to seedlings and vegetation. The magnitude of these effects depends on storm conditions, local exposure and the protection provided by shallow flats and coastal morphology.


2.8.2 Cyanobacterial Mats and Upper-Intertidal Flats
Cyanobacterial mats occupy intertidal and upper-intertidal surfaces where the balance between inundation and exposure differs from that of lower-elevation mangrove habitats. Their distribution and persistence are influenced by surface elevation, sediment characteristics, hydrological connectivity, salinity and the duration of wetting and drying. In arid settings, prolonged exposure and high evaporation can concentrate salts, while marine inundation and rainfall can temporarily alter surface-water and porewater conditions (Adame et al., 2012; Lovelock et al., 2010).
The timing and depth of tidal inundation determine how frequently mats are wetted and how often they exchange water and dissolved materials with adjacent environments. Seasonal and interannual water-level fluctuations can modify these wetting and drying intervals. Higher background water levels may increase the frequency or extent of inundation across some upper-intertidal surfaces, whereas lower water levels may prolong exposure. These changes do not necessarily produce the same response across all mat communities because local elevation, substrate permeability, drainage and salinity differ spatially.
Rainfall can provide a short-lived freshwater input, dilute accumulated salts and wet exposed mat surfaces. Under hot, dry conditions, however, evaporation can rapidly remove surface moisture and concentrate salts again. The ecological response therefore depends not only on total rainfall but also on event timing, rainfall intensity, the duration of subsequent exposure and the frequency of marine inundation. Temperature affects evaporation and the thermal conditions experienced by mat organisms; its effects on microbial activity and mat integrity depend on moisture availability and the temperature tolerance of the organisms present.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
section: 3.2 Advances and Limitations in Habitat Modelling Approaches
text:
3.2 Advances and Limitations in Habitat Modelling Approaches
Predicting long-term changes in intertidal habitats under sea-level rise (SLR) requires approaches that account for the interactions between biological processes, hydrodynamic forcing and coastal morphology. Previous studies have used a range of methods, from empirical relationships between vegetation distribution and tidal elevation to individual-based ecological models and coupled hydro-morphodynamic simulations. These approaches differ in their ability to represent habitat establishment, expansion, retreat and persistence, as well as their suitability for applications extending from individual sites to entire coastal landscapes. The following sections review these approaches for mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats, with particular attention to their ability to predict long-term spatial changes under evolving environmental conditions.

3.2.1 Mangrove forests
Mangrove forests are among the most extensively modelled intertidal ecosystems. Their response to sea-level rise (SLR) depends not only on changes in inundation frequency and duration, but also on sediment availability, surface elevation, salinity, propagule dispersal and the capacity of vegetation to establish and persist under changing environmental conditions. These interacting processes have motivated modelling approaches ranging from empirical habitat-distribution methods to individual-based ecological models and coupled eco-morphodynamic frameworks. A central distinction is whether models estimate potential habitat distribution from environmental relationships, simulate mangrove life-cycle processes explicitly, or represent feedbacks between vegetation, hydrodynamics and morphological evolution.
Elevation-based and statistical approaches relate the present-day distribution of mangroves to tidal elevation, hydroperiod or other environmental characteristics. These methods are computationally efficient and can provide first-order estimates of potential habitat redistribution under SLR. However, they generally provide limited representation of the processes that determine whether mangroves can colonise newly suitable areas, persist under changing environmental conditions or modify the physical environment through vegetation-mediated sediment trapping and surface-elevation change. Their predictions may therefore be sensitive to assumptions that present-day relationships between vegetation and the physical environment remain applicable under future conditions.
Recent applications have extended habitat-distribution modelling to incorporate both SLR and human constraints on landward migration. Ding et al. (2026), for example, used a multi-scenario framework based on the Sea Level Affecting Marsh Model (SLAMM), incorporating high-resolution elevation data, land-use dynamics and regional hydrological parameters to assess mangrove loss and migration under different climate and development scenarios (Ding et al., 2026). Their analysis considered barriers such as seawalls and restrictions associated with coastal development. This type of approach is particularly relevant to coastal planning because it can identify areas where potential landward migration is constrained by infrastructure or land use. However, scenario-based habitat-transition models do not necessarily resolve the detailed biological processes of mangrove establishment, growth and mortality or dynamically simulate the feedbacks between vegetation and sediment transport.
Individual-based models (IBMs) provide a more detailed representation of mangrove dynamics by simulating individual trees or cohorts and their responses to environmental conditions. Examples include MesoFON and its applications and extensions (Grueters et al., 2014; Grueters et al., 2019), modular modelling platforms such as MANGA and pyMANGA (Wimmler et al., 2024), and earlier frameworks including KiWi, FORMAN and MANGRO (Berger et al., 2008). Depending on their formulation, these models can represent growth, mortality, competition, forest structure and selected interactions between individual plants and their environment. Their principal advantage is the ability to resolve ecological processes that are difficult to capture using empirical vegetation–elevation relationships. However, their application across extensive coastal domains can be computationally demanding, and their predictions depend on appropriate ecological parameterisation and environmental forcing. An IBM does not necessarily simulate hydrodynamics or landscape evolution mechanistically unless it is coupled to a suitable physical model.
A related development is the mangrove Lifecycle Ecosystem Analysis and Forecasting (LEAF) model, developed by Dunlop, Felder and Glamore (2025) (Dunlop et al., 2025). LEAF represents mangrove dynamics across life stages, from seedlings to senescence, using relationships describing establishment, growth, stress, recovery and mortality. In its published application, LEAF was coupled with Delft3D Flexible Mesh to investigate how hydrodynamic and morphological conditions influence mangrove development and to assess forest attributes and responses to extreme events. This life-cycle representation helps distinguish the environmental requirements of recruitment and establishment from those of established trees. It also provides a framework for examining restoration trajectories and the potential effects of stressors on forest persistence. Nevertheless, predictions remain dependent on the ecological relationships and species characteristics used to parameterise the model, and the coupling of ecological and physical components adds implementation and calibration requirements. Furthermore, the approach is limited to idealised domains or small sites as not implemented for parallel computation across large coastal landscapes. Nevertherless, the LEAF model represents a significant advance in mechanistic mangrove modelling and provides a foundation for future development of coupled eco-morphodynamic frameworks.
Process-based hydrodynamic and morphodynamic models resolve physical processes controlling intertidal habitat conditions, including tidal propagation, water levels, currents, sediment transport and changes in bed elevation. Modelling systems such as Delft3D Flexible Mesh (DFM), MIKE and BASEMENT can be used to investigate how hydrodynamic forcing and sediment availability influence inundation and intertidal morphology (Fagherazzi et al., 2012; Lesser et al., 2004). However, a hydrodynamic model used on its own does not inherently predict mangrove presence or represent the biological processes governing establishment, growth and mortality. Ecological responses must be represented through additional model components or assessed using a separate predictive approach.
An alternative is to use the hydrodynamic model to characterise the physical environment and then apply a statistical or machine-learning model to estimate habitat occurrence. In the modelling workflow described in this report (Chapter 20), DFM is used as a standalone hydrodynamic tool, while a Random Forest classifier is used to predict the presence of mangroves and cyanobacterial mats from environmental predictors. This approach separates physical-process simulation from habitat classification rather than implementing a fully coupled vegetation–morphodynamic model. It provides a practical means of combining hydrodynamic information with observed habitat distributions, while allowing habitat prediction to be applied across the model domain. The Random Forest approach, predictor variables, training data and evaluation procedures are described in Appendix B {Chapter 20}. As with other statistical classifiers, predictions depend on the representativeness of the training data and the environmental conditions captured by the predictors; the workflow does not explicitly simulate mangrove demography or vegetation-driven morphological feedbacks.
Coupled eco-morphodynamic models seek to represent interactions between vegetation and the physical environment more explicitly. Xie et al. (2022) developed a bio-morphodynamic modelling approach to investigate how tidal range, small wind waves, sediment supply and coastal slope influence mangrove development and vulnerability under SLR (Xie et al., 2022). Their numerical experiments demonstrated that mangrove responses depend on the combined effects of coastal conditions and bio-morphodynamic feedbacks, rather than SLR alone. In particular, the interaction between sediment supply and the development of the coastal profile influenced the capacity of mangroves to maintain their position as sea level increased. This approach highlights the importance of considering site-specific hydrodynamics and sediment dynamics when evaluating mangrove vulnerability. Similar to the LEAF model, the Xie et al. (2022) framework was applied to idealised domains and required substantial further development to support studies across larger spatial and temporal scales.
Kumbier et al. (2022) developed a transferable eco-morphodynamic framework by dynamically coupling the depth-averaged TELEMAC-2D hydrodynamic model with an empirical wetland elevation model (Kumbier et al., 2022). The framework was applied to assess mangrove and saltmarsh distribution under SLR in a southeast Australian estuary. It represented spatial variations in tidal inundation and feedbacks between wetland surface-elevation change and estuarine hydrodynamics. Their results showed that the response of intertidal wetlands depended on SLR rates and assumptions about sediment accretion. The study also demonstrated that changes in wetland extent and substrate elevation can influence tidal dynamics, reinforcing the importance of representing interactions between physical processes and wetland development. However, the wetland elevation component was empirical, and the framework did not explicitly simulate all ecological processes governing individual mangrove life stages.
Beselly et al. (2023) developed DFMFON by coupling the individual-based MesoFON mangrove model with Delft3D-FM (Beselly et al., 2023). The framework represents mangrove life stages, propagule dispersal, salinity and other environmental forcing and feedbacks between vegetation and morphological development. Applied to a mangrove–mudflat system inspired by the Porong Delta, Indonesia, it demonstrated how coupled models can investigate forest expansion, retreat and colonisation under changing physical conditions. Compared with a workflow that uses hydrodynamic outputs as predictors in a separate habitat classifier, this type of model provides a more mechanistic representation of ecological and morphological feedbacks. Its framework is theoretically transferable to other environments; however, scaling it up to regional applications with parallel computation is challenging due to the complexity of the model and the Java-based implementation of MesoFON (which also limits its user-friendliness across HPCs).
Related developments in salt-marsh modelling also provide useful methodological insights, although their ecological formulations should not be assumed to apply directly to mangroves. Alizad et al. (2016) developed the Hydro-MEM model by coupling two-dimensional hydrodynamics with the Marsh Equilibrium Model to represent interactions between tidal inundation, Spartina alterniflora biomass, platform accretion and bottom friction (Alizad et al., 2016). The model demonstrated how biological feedbacks can alter the spatial distribution of marsh biomass and the evolution of the marsh platform under different sea-level rise (SLR) scenarios. The study also highlighted the importance of selecting an appropriate coupling time step: while a 50-year interval provided reasonable approximations of marsh productivity under low and approximately linear SLR, shorter intervals were necessary to achieve convergence under more rapid SLR, with a 5-year interval required for the high-SLR scenario. This indicates that long coupling intervals may overlook important feedbacks when environmental conditions change rapidly, although shorter intervals increase computational demands. Consequently, the coupling interval should be selected based on convergence testing and the rate of environmental change rather than adopting a fixed interval across scenarios. Furthermore, because the ecological component was developed for salt-marsh vegetation, direct application to mangrove forests would require an appropriate representation of mangrove-specific life stages, environmental tolerances and vegetation–sediment interactions.
Willemsen et al. (2022) similarly used a coupled hydrodynamic, morphodynamic and vegetation-growth framework to investigate salt-marsh development over several decades (Willemsen et al., 2022). Their results showed that wave forcing and sediment availability influence whether the marsh edge expands seaward or retreats landward. Although salt marshes differ from mangroves in vegetation structure and ecological requirements, these studies demonstrate the value of integrating hydrodynamic forcing, sediment dynamics and vegetation response when assessing long-term changes in intertidal habitat extent.
