3.2.2 Cyanobacterial mats
In contrast to mangrove forests, cyanobacterial mats have received comparatively limited attention in predictive modelling of long-term intertidal habitat change. These microbial communities commonly occur on upper intertidal and supratidal surfaces, including salt flats, mudflats and shallow depressions that experience intermittent tidal inundation, rainfall or local ponding. Their distribution is influenced by hydroperiod, salinity, surface elevation, temperature, light availability, sediment characteristics and hydrodynamic disturbance (Seashore Engineering, 2021, 2022; Taukulis et al., 2018).
An important distinction between cyanobacterial mats and mangrove forests is the timescale of their biological response. Whereas mangrove establishment and forest development generally involve recruitment and growth over longer periods, cyanobacterial mats can respond rapidly to changes in hydration, desiccation and salinity. Depending on the constituent organisms and their physiological adaptations, mat communities can persist through unfavourable conditions in dormant or metabolically reduced states and resume activity when moisture and other environmental conditions become favourable. Consequently, the presence of a mat at a particular location does not necessarily indicate that the location continuously provides optimal growth conditions. Instead, observed distributions may reflect repeated cycles of inundation, drying, salinity stress and reactivation.
These characteristics are particularly relevant to the semi-arid Pilbara, where upper intertidal surfaces are exceptionally flat, evaporation is high and inundation may be infrequent. Small differences in elevation and microtopography can produce substantial spatial variation in ponding, drainage and evaporative concentration. Local sediment ridges, swash lines and shallow depressions may therefore create contrasting conditions over short distances, influencing both the persistence of existing mats and the suitability of adjacent surfaces for colonisation. Changes in tidal inundation under SLR may alter these conditions, but the resulting habitat response will not necessarily follow a simple, linear shift in elevation.
Previous approaches to predicting cyanobacterial mat redistribution have relied largely on mapped habitat distributions and their relationships with tidal elevation or inundation conditions (Seashore Engineering, 2021). Such approaches can provide useful first-order estimates of potential changes in the area exposed to suitable hydroperiods. However, they do not necessarily resolve the effects of microtopography, local ponding, changing drainage pathways or the biological responses of mats to repeated wetting and drying. Nor do they explicitly account for feedbacks between mat development and sediment properties, including changes in surface stability and permeability.
The distinction between short-term biological responses and long-term spatial redistribution is therefore important. Rapid reactivation following favourable conditions does not, by itself, establish whether a mat will persist at a location over decades. Long-term predictions require an assessment of how frequently and for how long suitable environmental conditions occur, how those conditions change as sea level rises, and whether local surface morphology continues to support mat persistence. Compared with mangrove modelling, the literature reviewed here indicates a more limited development of dedicated, spatially explicit numerical approaches for predicting cyanobacterial mat growth, colonisation and migration with feedbacks to coastal morphology. This limitation should be interpreted as a gap in the modelling approaches reviewed rather than proof that no relevant process-based models exist.


3.2.3 Synthesis and implications for coastal-scale prediction
Previous modelling studies demonstrate the value of combining environmental forcing, ecological requirements and morphological change when predicting the long-term distribution of intertidal habitats. Empirical and threshold-based approaches are useful for identifying potential habitat limits, while individual-based and coupled models provide greater insight into ecological dynamics and physical–biological feedbacks. Salt-marsh modelling further illustrates how wave forcing and sediment availability can influence habitat development over decades.
However, the processes governing mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats differ substantially. Mangrove predictions benefit from representing recruitment, growth, mortality and, where possible, interactions with sediment dynamics. Cyanobacterial mat predictions must account for rapid and potentially reversible responses to inundation, desiccation and salinity, together with the spatial variability of upper-intertidal environments. For both habitats, simple elevation-based projections may be insufficient where local hydrodynamics, sediment redistribution and surface morphology change over time.
The central challenge is therefore to identify an approach that resolves the physical processes controlling habitat suitability across a coastal domain and over long timescales, while representing biological requirements at a level appropriate to each habitat. Machine-learning approaches and the relevant DFM modelling framework are discussed separately in Appendix B. The following section describes the modelling approach selected for this project.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
section: 3.2 Advances and Limitations in Habitat Modelling Approaches
text:
3.2 Advances and Limitations in Habitat Modelling Approaches
Predicting long-term changes in intertidal habitats under sea-level rise (SLR) requires approaches that account for the interactions between biological processes, hydrodynamic forcing and coastal morphology. Previous studies have used a range of methods, from empirical relationships between vegetation distribution and tidal elevation to individual-based ecological models and coupled hydro-morphodynamic simulations. These approaches differ in their ability to represent habitat establishment, expansion, retreat and persistence, as well as their suitability for applications extending from individual sites to entire coastal landscapes. The following sections review these approaches for mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats, with particular attention to their ability to predict long-term spatial changes under evolving environmental conditions.

3.2.1 Mangrove forests
Mangrove forests are among the most extensively modelled intertidal ecosystems. Their response to sea-level rise (SLR) depends not only on changes in inundation frequency and duration, but also on sediment availability, surface elevation, salinity, propagule dispersal and the capacity of vegetation to establish and persist under changing environmental conditions. These interacting processes have motivated modelling approaches ranging from empirical habitat-distribution methods to individual-based ecological models and coupled eco-morphodynamic frameworks. A central distinction is whether models correctly describe potential habitat distributions from environmental relationships, simulate mangrove life-cycle processes explicitly, or represent feedbacks between vegetation, hydrodynamics and morphological evolution.
Elevation-based and statistical approaches relate the present-day distribution of mangroves to tidal elevation, hydroperiod or other environmental characteristics. These methods are computationally efficient and can provide first-order estimates of potential habitat redistribution under SLR. However, they generally provide limited representation of the processes that determine whether mangroves can colonise newly suitable areas, persist under changing environmental conditions or modify the physical environment through vegetation-mediated sediment trapping and surface-elevation change. Their predictions may therefore be sensitive to assumptions that historical and present-day relationships between vegetation and the physical environment remain applicable under future conditions. Lifecycle threshold approaches provide a more detailed representation of the conditions required at different stages of mangrove development. Henderson & Glamore (2024) developed a multi-forcing threshold model for Avicennia marina that represents reproduction, propagule dispersal, seedling establishment and development, and mature-tree survival. Their application across eastern Australian estuaries demonstrates the value of distinguishing establishment requirements from the conditions tolerated by mature trees.
Recent applications have extended habitat-distribution modelling to incorporate both SLR and human constraints on landward migration. Ding et al. (2026), for example, used a multi-scenario framework based on the Sea Level Affecting Marsh Model (SLAMM), incorporating high-resolution elevation data, land-use dynamics and regional hydrological parameters to assess mangrove loss and migration under different climate and development scenarios (Ding et al., 2026). Their analysis considered barriers such as seawalls and restrictions associated with coastal development. This type of approach is particularly relevant to coastal planning because it can identify areas where potential landward migration is constrained by infrastructure or land use. However, scenario-based habitat-transition models do not necessarily resolve the detailed biological processes of mangrove establishment, growth and mortality or dynamically simulate the feedbacks between vegetation and sediment transport.
Individual-based models (IBMs) provide a more detailed representation of mangrove dynamics by simulating individual trees or cohorts and their responses to environmental conditions. Examples include MesoFON and its applications and extensions (Grueters et al., 2014; Grueters et al., 2019), modular modelling platforms such as MANGA and pyMANGA (Wimmler et al., 2024), and earlier frameworks including KiWi, FORMAN and MANGRO (Berger et al., 2008). Depending on their formulation, these models can represent growth, mortality, competition, forest structure and selected interactions between individual plants and their environment. Their principal advantage is the ability to resolve ecological processes that are difficult to capture using empirical vegetation–elevation relationships. However, their application across extensive coastal domains can be computationally demanding, and their predictions depend on appropriate ecological parameterisation and environmental forcing. An IBM does not necessarily simulate hydrodynamics or landscape evolution mechanistically unless it is coupled to a suitable physical model.
A related development is the mangrove Lifecycle Ecosystem Analysis and Forecasting (LEAF) model, developed by Dunlop et al. (2025). LEAF represents mangrove dynamics across life stages, from seedlings to senescence, using relationships describing establishment, growth, stress, recovery and mortality. In its published application, LEAF was coupled with Delft3D Flexible Mesh (DFM), a hydrodynamic-morphodynamic numerical model, to investigate how hydrodynamic and morphological conditions influence mangrove development and to assess forest attributes and responses to extreme events. This life-cycle representation helps distinguish the environmental requirements of recruitment and establishment from those of established trees. It also provides a framework for examining restoration trajectories and the potential effects of stressors on forest persistence. Nevertheless, predictions remain dependent on the ecological relationships and species characteristics used to parameterise the model, and the coupling of ecological and physical components adds implementation and calibration requirements. Furthermore, the approach is limited to idealised domains or small sites as not implemented for parallel computation across large coastal landscapes. Nevertherless, the LEAF model represents a significant advance in mechanistic mangrove modelling and provides a foundation for future development of coupled eco-morphodynamic frameworks.
Physical-process models linked to habitat prediction resolve physical processes controlling intertidal habitat conditions, including tidal propagation, water levels, currents, sediment transport and changes in bed elevation. Modelling systems such as Delft3D Flexible Mesh (DFM), MIKE and BASEMENT can be used to investigate how hydrodynamic forcing and sediment availability influence inundation and intertidal morphology (Fagherazzi et al., 2012; Lesser et al., 2004). However, a hydrodynamic model used on its own does not inherently predict mangrove presence or represent the biological processes governing establishment, growth and mortality. To predict habitat responses, these physical simulations must be linked to a habitat-suitability method or an ecological component. The two approaches adopted here illustrate this distinction.
One of the two approaches adopted in this study combines the DFM hydrodynamic model with a Random Forest classifier to estimate potential mangrove and cyanobacterial mat distributions from modelled environmental conditions (Chapter 19). In this workflow, DFM is used as a standalone hydrodynamic tool to characterise the physical environment, while the Random Forest classifier relates modelled environmental predictors to observed habitat occurrence (Breiman, 2001). This approach separates physical process simulation from habitat classification, allowing hydrodynamic information to be combined with observed habitat distributions to predict potential habitat occurrence across the model domain. The predictor variables, training data and evaluation procedures used in the classification are described in Chapter 19. As with other statistical classifiers, predictions depend on the representativeness of the training data and the range of environmental conditions captured by the predictors. Consequently, this approach does not explicitly simulate mangrove establishment, growth and mortality, or vegetation driven morphological and hydrodynamic feedbacks.
The second approach explicitly simulates mangrove dynamics and couples changes in vegetation properties back into the physical model, thereby representing interactions between vegetation development and hydro-morphodynamic processes, as described in Section 3.3. Unlike the statistical classification approach, this method represents dynamic vegetation responses and their feedbacks to the physical environment.
Coupled eco-morphodynamic models seek to represent interactions between vegetation and the physical environment more explicitly. Xie et al. (2022) developed a bio-morphodynamic modelling approach to investigate how tidal range, small wind waves, sediment supply and coastal slope influence mangrove development and vulnerability under SLR. Their numerical experiments demonstrated that mangrove responses depend on the combined effects of coastal conditions and bio-morphodynamic feedbacks, rather than SLR alone. In particular, the interaction between sediment supply and the development of the coastal profile influenced the capacity of mangroves to maintain their position as sea level increased. This approach highlights the importance of considering site-specific hydrodynamics and sediment dynamics when evaluating mangrove vulnerability. However, similar to the LEAF model, the Xie et al. (2022) framework was applied to idealised domains and required substantial further development to support studies across larger spatial and temporal scales.
Kumbier et al. (2022) developed a transferable eco-morphodynamic framework by dynamically coupling the depth-averaged TELEMAC-2D hydrodynamic model with an empirical wetland elevation model. The framework was applied to assess mangrove and saltmarsh distribution under SLR in a southeast Australian estuary. It represented spatial variations in tidal inundation and feedbacks between wetland surface-elevation change and estuarine hydrodynamics. Their results showed that the response of intertidal wetlands depended on SLR rates and assumptions about sediment accretion. The study also demonstrated that changes in wetland extent and substrate elevation can influence tidal dynamics, reinforcing the importance of representing interactions between physical processes and wetland development. However, the wetland elevation component was empirical, and the framework did not explicitly simulate all ecological processes governing individual mangrove life stages.
Beselly et al. (2023) developed DFMFON by coupling the individual-based MesoFON mangrove model with Delft3D-FM. The framework represents mangrove life stages, propagule dispersal, salinity and other environmental forcing and feedbacks between vegetation and morphological development. Applied to a mangrove–mudflat system inspired by the Porong Delta, Indonesia, it demonstrated how coupled models can investigate forest expansion, retreat and colonisation under changing physical conditions. Compared with a workflow that uses hydrodynamic outputs as predictors in a separate habitat classifier, this type of model provides a more mechanistic representation of ecological and morphological feedbacks. Its framework is theoretically transferable to other environments; however, scaling it up to regional applications with parallel computation is challenging due to the complexity of the model and the Java-based implementation of MesoFON (which also limits its user-friendliness across high-performance computing (HPC) systems).
Related developments in salt-marsh modelling also provide useful methodological insights, although their ecological formulations should not be assumed to apply directly to mangroves. Alizad et al. (2016) developed the Hydro-MEM model by coupling two-dimensional hydrodynamics with the Marsh Equilibrium Model to represent interactions between tidal inundation, Spartina alterniflora biomass, platform accretion and bottom friction. The model demonstrated how biological feedbacks can alter the spatial distribution of marsh biomass and the evolution of the marsh platform under different sea-level rise (SLR) scenarios. The study also highlighted the importance of selecting an appropriate coupling time step: while a 50-year interval provided reasonable approximations of marsh productivity under low and approximately linear SLR, shorter intervals were necessary to achieve convergence under more rapid SLR, with a 5-year interval required for the high-SLR scenario. This indicates that long coupling intervals may overlook important feedbacks when environmental conditions change rapidly, although shorter intervals increase computational demands. Consequently, the coupling interval should be selected based on convergence testing and the rate of environmental change rather than adopting a fixed interval across scenarios. Furthermore, because the ecological component was developed for salt-marsh vegetation, direct application to mangrove forests would require an appropriate representation of mangrove-specific life stages, environmental tolerances and vegetation–sediment interactions.
Willemsen et al. (2022) similarly used a coupled hydrodynamic, morphodynamic and vegetation-growth framework to investigate salt-marsh development over several decades. Their results showed that wave forcing and sediment availability can influence whether the marsh edge expands seaward or retreats landward. Although salt marshes differ from mangroves in vegetation structure and ecological requirements, these studies demonstrate the value of integrating hydrodynamic forcing, sediment dynamics and vegetation response when assessing long-term changes in intertidal habitat extent.

Developing and validating this capability for arid intertidal systems remains an important modelling gap.


3.2.3 Synthesis and implications for coastal-scale prediction
Previous modelling studies demonstrate the value of integrating environmental forcing, ecological requirements and morphological change when predicting the long-term distribution of intertidal habitats. Empirical and threshold-based approaches provide a basis for identifying potential habitat limits, while individual-based and coupled models offer ways to represent ecological dynamics and physical–biological feedbacks. As discussed in Section 1.3.3, important knowledge gaps remain in predicting the long-term redistribution of mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats across the hyper-arid West Pilbara coast. Addressing these gaps requires a modelling approach that can represent the physical processes controlling habitat suitability across a coastal domain and over long timescales, while accounting for relevant processes for each habitat. In particular, the approach should account for the coupled hydrodynamic, morphological and biological feedbacks that govern habitat dynamics and are essential for reliable long-term predictions of intertidal habitat change. The following section proposes the development of a modelling framework designed to address these knowledge gaps and support coastal-scale projections of future habitat change.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Research Aims and Study-Site Strategy
The overall aim of this research is to establish baseline understanding of the physical and ecological processes governing arid intertidal habitats and to develop predictive tools for assessing their potential responses to future environmental change and coastal development. Achieving this aim requires an understanding of the environmental processes that regulate habitat distribution, as well as a modelling framework capable of translating these processes into projections of potential future change. However, predicting the long-term responses of arid intertidal ecosystems is challenging because habitat persistence and redistribution depend on interactions between sea-level variability, tidal inundation, climatic conditions, salinity, sediment dynamics, geomorphology, and biological processes. The environmental controls considered in this study, including sea-level variability and climatic drivers, are described in Chapter 2.






Figure 1.4: Sites of interest within the West Pilbara region, showing the study locations at Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston.



To address these challenges, the research adopts a staged approach based on three study sites along the West Pilbara coast: Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston (Figure 1.4). The sites represent slightly different coastal environments and have distinct roles within the research design. Giralia provides the primary domain for model development, Urala provides a setting in which to investigate the implications of coastal development, and Cape Preston serves as a demonstration of the approach’s potential transferability to a different coastal setting. This staged strategy allows the modelling approach to be developed and evaluated in a relatively well-studied environment before being applied to sites with different environmental characteristics and development constraints.

1.4.1 Giralia: Environmental Understanding and Model Development
Giralia Bay is located in the eastern portion of Exmouth Gulf, Western Australia (\(22.4^{\circ}\text{S}\), \(114.3^{\circ}\text{E}\)). Exmouth Gulf is a shallow, semi-enclosed embayment approximately \(75\text{ km}\) long and less than \(20\text{ m}\) deep, bordered by low-relief peninsulas to the west and south. The bay lies within the onshore portion of the Carnarvon Basin and is underlain by calcarenitic rock units and sedimentary deposits, overlain by unconsolidated Quaternary sediments. The surrounding coastal plain comprises Holocene and late Pleistocene deposits, including relict beach ridges, coral reefs, aeolian sands, and supratidal sabkha flats with extensive evaporite crusts (Riera et al., 2023).






Figure 1.5: Study site at Giralia Bay within Exmouth Gulf, north-western Western Australia. (a) Regional setting. (b) Cross-shore intertidal zonation, showing mangroves, mudflats, cyanobacterial mats, and high-elevation salt flats.



Giralia is the principal site for developing the modelling approach because the wider Exmouth Gulf region is one of the better-studied examples of arid intertidal ecosystems in north-western Australia. Previous research has investigated mangrove growth and wood properties (Santini et al., 2013), the ecological functioning and productivity of cyanobacterial mats (Dee et al., 2026; Lovelock et al., 2010), nutrient exchange between mats and inundating waters (Adame et al., 2012), and the influence of intense storms and associated freshwater and sediment inputs on mangrove nutrient status (Lovelock et al., 2011). Experimental studies have also examined the rapid reactivation of cyanobacterial mats following rehydration (Chennu et al., 2015), while remote-sensing research has documented the spatial and temporal variability of high-intertidal habitats across Exmouth Gulf (Hickey et al., 2023). Collectively, these studies provide an empirical foundation for investigating the environmental controls on habitat distribution, although translating this knowledge into quantitative predictions of long-term habitat change remains challenging.
Giralia combines an arid climate, regular tidal forcing and episodic cyclone-driven freshwater and sediment inputs (Santini et al., 2013). The regional climatic setting is described in Section 1.2 and Chapter 2.
The area is also of conservation significance. The Western Australian Government has pursued protection of the Exmouth Gulf region through the Plan for Our Parks initiative, including arrangements involving the Nganhurra Thanardi Garrbu Aboriginal Corporation and the establishment of Giralia National Park and the adjoining Boologooro Nature Reserve. This conservation context reinforces the importance of understanding how environmental change and coastal development may affect the region’s intertidal ecosystems.

1.4.1.1 Intertidal Habitat Zonation
Giralia Bay contains a cross-shore sequence of intertidal habitats associated with differences in surface elevation, tidal inundation frequency, and local environmental conditions (Figure 1.5). From the seaward margin towards the land, four principal habitat zones can be distinguished:

Seaward mangrove fringe: Predominantly composed of Avicennia marina, occupying the lower-to-middle intertidal zone, where regular tidal inundation and flushing occur.
Mudflats: Generally unvegetated, low-gradient intertidal surfaces that are exposed during low tide and provide a transition between the mangrove fringe and higher intertidal habitats.
Cyanobacterial mats: Microbial communities occupying parts of the middle-to-upper intertidal flats, where periodic inundation alternates with prolonged exposure and desiccation.
High-elevation salt flats: Supratidal sabkha environments characterised by high salinity, evaporite accumulation, and sparse or absent vegetation.

This spatial organisation, together with the broad intertidal flats and relatively distinct habitat zones, provides a useful basis for deriving an idealised representation of the system. By simplifying the landscape into characteristic cross-shore zones, the model-development process can focus on the fundamental relationships between environmental forcing, surface elevation, inundation, and habitat distribution before considering the additional complexity of individual sites. Giralia therefore serves not only as an ecologically informed study site but also as a conceptual basis for developing and testing the idealised model described in Chapter 5. The resulting framework can then support subsequent applications that incorporate more complex environmental conditions and development-related constraints.



1.4.2 Urala: Application Under Coastal Development Constraints
Urala, on the Onslow coast, is the second study site and provides an opportunity to apply the modelling approach developed at Giralia under different geomorphic conditions and with explicit representation of coastal development constraints. The area is of interest in the context of potential industrial development, including solar salt production. In this study, the focus is specifically on how development-related bund walls may modify hydrodynamic conditions and, consequently, influence the potential redistribution of intertidal habitats under future sea-level scenarios. Applying the framework at Urala therefore provides a means of examining how physical infrastructure interacts with environmental change to influence habitat persistence and spatial reorganisation.

1.4.2.1 Overview of the Urala Study Site
The Urala study site is located approximately \(40\text{ km}\) south-east of Onslow, along the eastern coast of the Pilbara region near the mouth of Exmouth Gulf. Unlike Giralia Bay, Urala does not exhibit a uniformly ordered cross-shore sequence of intertidal habitats. Although distinct shore-normal zonation occurs in the southern part of the study area, the northern domain has a more complex morphology, where North Creek and South Creek converge and interconnect through a network of smaller tidal channels (Figure 1.6).






Figure 1.6: Study site at Urala on the West Pilbara coast, north-western Western Australia. (a) Regional setting. (b) Morphological overview showing intertidal habitat distribution, interconnected tidal-creek systems, barrier spits, and extensive landward salt flats.



The site is characterised by subtle topographic gradients typical of low-relief, arid coastal environments. Elevation generally increases landward from the open water and tidal-creek margins, across a sequence of coastal and supratidal environments:

Seaward coastal barriers and dunes: Locally developed coastal dune and barrier systems fronting the sea, which are prominent along the northern portion of the Urala domain but absent in the southern region[cite: 1].
Intertidal zone: Low-lying areas influenced by tidal inundation, including vegetated margins and surfaces dissected by tidal channels[cite: 1].
High-intertidal to supratidal zone: Broad, low-gradient platforms landward of the mangrove fringe, including salt flats and other sparsely vegetated surfaces[cite: 1].
Upper salt flats and inland dunes: Inland areas comprising relict salt pans, evaporite-rich surfaces, and terrestrial coastal vegetation and dune systems at higher elevations[cite: 1].

The combination of low relief, interconnected tidal channels, localised coastal barriers, and extensive landward salt flats makes Urala a useful setting for examining how changes in hydrodynamic connectivity may affect habitat distribution. In particular, modifications to the pathways through which tides propagate across the landscape may alter inundation patterns and the spatial conditions under which intertidal habitats persist.
The region’s hyper-arid climate and high evaporative demand further distinguish Urala from more humid coastal environments. Rainfall is highly variable, and major rainfall events may produce short-lived freshwater and sediment inputs against a background of prolonged dry conditions. These climatic and hydrodynamic drivers provide the environmental context for interpreting potential habitat responses, as outlined in Chapter 2.


1.4.2.2 Application to Development Scenarios
Urala provides a contrasting application setting in which potential coastal development could alter tidal connectivity and constrain future habitat redistribution. The study uses development-related bund-wall scenarios to investigate these physical effects under sea-level rise. This provides a case study of the interactions between infrastructure, hydrodynamics and habitat change, independent of the approval or implementation of a particular development proposal.
The emphasis is on the physical effects of bund walls on hydrodynamics and the resulting habitat changes, rather than on industrial processes such as salt-brine discharge or their associated water-quality effects. By comparing scenarios with and without development-related barriers, the study can investigate the extent to which infrastructure-induced changes in water movement alter the spatial distribution of suitable intertidal habitat. The results will help distinguish potential changes associated with regional sea-level rise from those arising from the configuration of physical barriers within the coastal landscape.



1.4.3 Cape Preston: Demonstration and Transferability
Cape Preston provides a demonstration of applying the framework to a contrasting coastal setting, with different tidal conditions, shoreline morphology and intertidal extent from Giralia and Urala. It was a secondary focus of Projects A and C and has a less comprehensive observational basis for model application. This allows the study to examine both the potential transferability of the framework and the practical consequences of applying it where supporting data are more limited.
Greater uncertainty in bathymetry, topography and available in situ observations affects model inputs and limits independent evaluation. The outputs should therefore be interpreted as exploratory, scenario-based assessments of potential habitat change. The application also helps identify the additional observations needed to strengthen predictions at this site.

1.4.3.1 Study Site: Cape Preston
Cape Preston is located approximately \(55\text{ km}\) west-southwest of Karratha in the Pilbara region of Western Australia (Figure 1.7). A sandy beach coastline extends eastward from Cape Preston towards an intertidal sandbar connecting Great Sandy Island. Behind this sandbar, the shoreline comprises tidal creeks, mangrove habitats, and extensive cyanobacterial mats. The coastal landscape is subject to tropical cyclones and associated extreme water levels, wave action, and freshwater discharge, which can contribute to coastal geomorphic change (Stevens et al., 2025).






Figure 1.7: Map of the study region showing (a) regional context along the Western Australian coastline and (b) a detailed aerial overview of Cape Preston.





1.4.3.2 Hydrodynamic and Geomorphic Setting
Water levels along the Pilbara coast are dominated by semidiurnal lunisolar tides, although tidal range varies regionally with bathymetry and coastal configuration. The eastern Pilbara is slightly towards macrotidal, whereas parts of the western Pilbara are mesotidal. Cape Preston exhibits close to a macrotidal regime, with a Highest Astronomical Tide (HAT) of \(2.25\text{ m}\) relative to mean sea level (MSL), a mean spring tidal range exceeding \(3\text{ m}\), and a maximum astronomical tidal range of approximately \(4.5\text{ m}\) (See also Table Table 2.1). In comparison, Onslow exhibits a smaller tidal range, with a HAT of \(1.29\text{ m}\) MSL (Table 2.1). Regional tidal dynamics are influenced by local bathymetry, including Barrow Island and the shallow waters to its south, which affect the propagation of semidiurnal and diurnal tidal energy and contribute to spatial variability in tidal conditions.
The extent of the intertidal zone at Cape Preston also differs substantially from that at Giralia and Urala. At Cape Preston, intertidal flats extend approximately \(2.5\text{ km}\) on average from the high-water line, compared with approximately \(8\text{ km}\) at Giralia and between \(7\text{ km}\) and \(10\text{ km}\) at Urala, depending on the location within the northern and southern domains. These differences in intertidal width, together with the contrasting tidal regimes and shoreline morphology, are important when considering the spatial extent of habitat redistribution under sea-level rise. The relative availability of landward accommodation space and the arrangement of existing habitats may influence the potential pathways through which mangroves, samphires, and cyanobacterial mats could shift as inundation conditions change.



1.4.4 Integrated Research Objectives
The three sites form a staged research strategy that links environmental understanding, model development, application under development constraints, and demonstration of transferability. Across these sites, the research aims to:

Characterise environmental controls on intertidal habitat distribution and change, including sea-level variability, tidal inundation, climatic conditions, salinity, geomorphology, and sediment dynamics, as described in Chapter 2.
Develop a predictive modelling framework for investigating potential changes in the distribution of mangroves, samphires, and cyanobacterial mats under future environmental scenarios, using Giralia as the principal model-development site.
Assess potential development impacts by applying the framework at Urala to investigate how proposed infrastructure and associated spatial constraints may influence habitat persistence and redistribution under sea-level rise.
Demonstrate transferability and wider applicability by applying the approach at Cape Preston, while distinguishing scenario-based demonstrations from predictions supported by site-specific hydrodynamic validation.
Provide accessible modelling tools that can support future research and contribute to environmental assessment, coastal planning, and the evaluation of development scenarios in hyper-arid coastal environments.

Through this approach, the research seeks to establish a practical basis for assessing how environmental change and coastal development may jointly influence the future distribution of arid intertidal habitats. Rather than assuming that a single model configuration will represent every coastal setting equally well, the study uses the three sites to develop, apply, and demonstrate a framework whose assumptions, data requirements, and limitations can be made explicit.

title: 4  Model Overview and Evaluation
text:
4.5 Cyanobacterial Mat Habitat-Suitability Modelling
To predict cyanobacterial mat distribution and account for methodological uncertainty in environmental management, we applied two complementary habitat-suitability modelling approaches: a data-driven Random Forest (RF) classifier and a Threshold-Based Optimisation approach. Using both methods allows managers to evaluate model sensitivity, contrast flexible nonlinear relationships against explicit physical envelopes, and make more robust conservation decisions.

4.5.1 Method 1: Random Forest Machine-Learning Approach
To predict cyanobacterial mat distribution without assuming predetermined parametric relationships, we used a data-driven machine-learning approach based on a Random Forest (RF) classifier. This approach was selected to identify complex, nonlinear relationships between observed mat occurrence and multiple hydrodynamic characteristics. RF methods are widely used for classification problems because they can represent high-order interactions among predictors and combine the predictions of multiple decision trees to produce a single robust classification (Breiman, 2001; Cutler et al., 2007).
A Random Forest is constructed by generating multiple decision trees from resampled training data. In a classification problem, each tree separates observations into groups according to their predictor values, seeking splits that distinguish the response classes. Random subsets of predictors are considered at each split, reducing the dependence between individual trees. The predictions from the resulting trees are then combined to produce the forest’s overall prediction.
In the present application, the response classes represent mesh locations classified either as persistent cyanobacterial mat or non-persistent mat. The model learns combinations of hydrodynamic conditions associated with the observed persistent-mat distribution, identifying nonlinear interactions among variables such as inundation frequency, exposure duration, and water depth that distinguish persistent locations.
The splitting process can be described using the Gini impurity, a measure of how mixed the two habitat classes are within a group of observations. For a tree node \(m\), Gini impurity is
\[
G_m = 1 - \sum_{k=0}^{1} p_{mk}^{2},
\tag{4.27}\]
where \(p_{mk}\) is the proportion of observations belonging to class \(k\) at node \(m\). A node containing only one habitat class has zero impurity, whereas a node containing a mixture of persistent and non-persistent locations has a higher value.
For a candidate split into two child nodes, the weighted impurity is
\[
G_{\mathrm{split}} =
\frac{n_L}{n_m}G_L +
\frac{n_R}{n_m}G_R,
\tag{4.28}\]
where \(n_m\) is the number of observations in the parent node, \(n_L\) and \(n_R\) are the numbers of observations in the left and right child nodes, and \(G_L\) and \(G_R\) are their respective Gini impurity values. The tree selects splits that reduce the weighted impurity of the resulting groups.
Each tree produces an estimate of the probability that a location belongs to the persistent-mat class. The Random Forest combines these estimates across its \(B\) trees:
\[
\hat{p}_i =
\frac{1}{B}
\sum_{b=1}^{B}
\hat{p}_{ib},
\tag{4.29}\]
where \(\hat{p}_i\) is the mean estimated probability of persistent mat occurrence at location \(i\), and \(\hat{p}_{ib}\) is the probability estimated by tree \(b\). The final classification is the class with the highest mean estimated probability:
\[
\hat{y}_i =
\underset{k \in \{0,1\}}{\operatorname{argmax}}
\ \hat{p}_{ik},
\tag{4.30}\]
where \(\hat{p}_{ik}\) is the forest’s estimated probability for class \(k\) at location \(i\).



4.5.2 Method 2: Threshold-Based Optimisation Approach
While machine-learning models capture complex nonlinear interactions, their black-box nature can introduce uncertainty when extrapolated across dynamic tidal environments. To complement the RF classifier and establish explicit physical parameter bounds, we implemented a threshold-based optimisation approach using Differential Evolution (DE) (Storn & Price, 1997).
This approach searches for optimal lower and upper bounds (\(L_j\) and \(U_j\)) for each hydrodynamic predictor \(x_{ij}\) (such as inundation frequency, 98th-percentile water depth, and mean water depth) to define a multi-dimensional physical habitat envelope. A mesh face \(i\) is classified as suitable habitat if its hydrodynamic metrics simultaneously fall within the acceptable bounds of all active predictors:
\[
S_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & L_j \leq x_{ij} \leq U_j \quad \text{for all active predictors } j, \\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\tag{4.31}\]
where \(S_i\) is the binary suitability prediction for mesh face \(i\).
To determine optimal parameter thresholds without manual calibration, the optimisation algorithm iteratively refines boundary values by maximising the F1-score against the observed persistent-mat binary mask (\(y_i\)), following the evaluation framework detailed in Section 4.6. The optimisation objective minimises the negative F1-score:
\[
\min_{L_j, U_j} (-F_1)
\tag{4.32}\]
Because hydrodynamic regimes, microtopography, and hydrodynamic forcing vary spatially across coastal settings, the optimised threshold ranges are site-dependent and adapt to local environmental constraints. Consequently, derived bounds reflect local calibration rather than universal physiological thresholds, capturing site-specific physical envelopes favourable for cyanobacterial mat persistence.
For the Threshold-Based Optimisation model, global optimisation via differential evolution determined precise bounding intervals for active physical drivers (such as inundation frequency, 98th-percentile depth, and mean depth).
By comparing the probabilistic flexibility of the Random Forest against explicit physical boundaries of the threshold optimisation model, environmental managers can cross-validate habitat predictions, quantify structural uncertainty, and make more resilient, evidence-based conservation decisions.



4.5.3 Observation Data and Definition of Persistent Mat
The observed cyanobacterial mat distribution was derived from monthly mean probability maps presented by (Hickey et al., 2023). These maps provide spatially explicit estimates of mat presence, rather than a simple binary classification of every pixel as present or absent.
Cyanobacterial mats can be dynamic, with visible distribution and activity responding to changes in inundation, exposure, and other environmental conditions. Consequently, a mat occurrence observed in an individual month may not represent a persistent habitat location. To focus modelling on locations with recurrent mapped occurrence (a stable region), we considered a persistent-mat mask derived from at least 12 months of monthly probability rasters to account for water level variations.
For each pixel \(i\), persistent occurrence was defined as
\[
M_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & q_{i,t} \geq 0.25 \quad \text{for all } t=1,\ldots,T, \\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\tag{4.33}\]
where \(q_{i,t}\) is the mapped probability of mat presence at pixel \(i\) in month \(t\), and \(T\) is the number of monthly rasters included in the analysis. A pixel was classified as persistent mat only when its mapped probability was at least 0.25 in every available monthly raster. Pixels failing this criterion were classified as non-persistent for model development.
Monthly rasters were reprojected to model coordinates using bilinear resampling before applying the persistence criterion. The resulting mask was spatially linked to the Delft3D-FM unstructured mesh. Persistent raster pixels were assigned to nearest mesh-face centres, providing a binary observed response for model training and evaluation.



4.5.4 Hydrodynamic Predictors and Model Integration
To relate the observed persistent-mat distribution to its physical environment, we conducted a hydrodynamic simulation for the corresponding period. Hydrodynamic metrics were extracted from this simulation to characterise inundation, exposure, and water-movement conditions.
Eight hydrodynamic metrics were considered as candidate predictors:

Maximum continuous exposure duration (hours);
Maximum bed shear stress;
Inundation frequency;
98th-percentile water depth;
Percentage submergence;
Maximum water depth;
Maximum current velocity; and
Mean water depth.

For each mesh face \(i\), these variables formed the predictor vector \(\mathbf{x}_i = [x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{i8}].\)
For the Random Forest model, the dataset was split into 80:20 training and test subsets with stratification. Model settings included 100 decision trees, maximum tree depth of 12, a minimum of 10 observations per internal split, and balanced class weights to prevent majority-class bias.
For the Threshold-Based Optimisation model, global optimisation via differential evolution determined precise bounding intervals for active physical drivers. By comparing probabilistic flexibility against explicit physical boundaries, environmental managers can cross-validate habitat predictions and quantify structural uncertainty.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
text:
3.4 Sea-Level Rise (SLR) Scenarios
To evaluate the future response of intertidal ecosystems to accelerating environmental change, we examine three Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (Calvin et al., 2023; Fox-Kemper et al., 2021; Garner et al., 2021; O’Neill et al., 2016): SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585.

3.4.1 Rationale and Objectives of the Three-Tiered Approach
Choosing a multi-tiered scenario approach rather than a single projection is critical for risk-informed coastal management. By bracketing future greenhouse gas emissions from aggressive mitigation to high-emission trajectories, these scenarios allow us to test the non-linear boundaries of habitat survival: - SSP119 (Low SLR, \(\approx 0.5\text{ m}\) by 2125): Represents a sustainability-focused, low-emission future (\(1.5^\circ\text{C}\) warming). This scenario intends to show whether intertidal habitats can comfortably keep pace with slow, predictable sedimentation and vertical accretion under minimal stress. - SSP370 (Medium SLR, \(\approx 0.95\text{ m}\) by 2125): Models a medium-to-high emission pathway featuring regional rivalry. This scenario tests transitional tipping points where landward migration pathways may begin to encounter physical or anthropogenic barriers (e.g., infrastructure or steep coastal topography). - SSP585 (High SLR, \(\approx 1.25\text{ m}\) by 2125): Projects a fossil-fuel-intensive development strategy. This scenario is designed to test extreme stress limits, identifying thresholds of severe coastal drowning, rapid habitat contraction, or total ecosystem collapse.
Implementing this spectrum establishes a robust envelope of potential future outcomes (Figure 3.2).






Figure 3.2: Sea level rise (SLR) projections based on Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios (SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585), representing low, medium, and high sea-level rise trajectories projected through 2125.



As detailed in the overarching methodology, these scenarios are incorporated into the regional hydrodynamic models by superimposing the scenario-specific SLR increments onto the baseline MSKO tidal constituents, forcing the offshore open boundaries with adjusted water-level time series.
While climate change encompasses multiple interconnected environmental drivers—including shifting wind regimes, warming temperatures, varying atmospheric humidity, intensified storm frequency, and complex root-zone salinity dynamics—this study intentionally isolates sea level rise. Other environmental and meteorological forcings are maintained at contemporary ambient conditions for the long-term simulations while salinity and storm conditions are not considered. Decoupling SLR from these confounding variables allows us to isolate and evaluate its direct physical and hydrodynamic impacts on intertidal inundation, bed-shear stress evolution, and landward mangrove and algal mat migration.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
section: 3.5 Summary of Model Application and Analysis Objectives
text:
3.5 Summary of Model Application and Analysis Objectives
By integrating the dynamically coupled bio-hydro-morphodynamic framework with the three-tiered SLR scenarios, we aim to analyse the following key aspects of intertidal habitat dynamics across the three study sites (Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston):

Habitat Trajectories and Extent: Quantifying spatial gains, losses, and net area changes for both mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats across centennial timescales.
Landward Migration and Constraints: Identifying the capacity of habitats to migrate upslope and pinpointing where natural or anthropogenic barriers impede migration.
Vulnerability and Thresholds: Evaluating the critical SLR thresholds (between SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585) that trigger habitat contraction, severe coastal drowning, or structural ecological collapse.
Site-Specific Responses: Comparing these ecological resilience metrics across the distinct geomorphic settings of Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston to inform risk-aware coastal management.

title: 4  Model Overview and Evaluation
text:
4.6 Evaluation
For both mangrove and algal-mat models, evaluation followed the same general framework, allowing classification performance to be assessed consistently across the two habitat-modelling approaches. The RF classifier was evaluated against the held-out test subset using the confusion matrix, precision, recall and F1-score.
Precision measures the proportion of locations predicted as persistent mat (or mangrove presence) that were also classified as persistent (or mangrove presence) in the observed mask:
\[
\mathrm{Precision} =
\frac{TP}{TP+FP},
\tag{4.34}\]
where \(TP\) and \(FP\) denote true positives and false positives, respectively.
Recall measures the proportion of observed mangroves (or algal-mat locations) correctly identified by the model:
\[
\mathrm{Recall} =
\frac{TP}{TP+FN},
\tag{4.35}\]
where \(FN\) denotes false negatives.
The F1-score provides a single measure that balances precision and recall:
\[
F_1 =
2 \frac{\mathrm{Precision}\times\mathrm{Recall}}
{\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}.
\tag{4.36}\]
A true positive is a location classified as presence in both the observed mask and model prediction. A false positive is predicted as presence but does not meet the observed criterion, while a false negative meets the observed criterion but is predicted as absence. Precision, recall and F1-score were considered together because they capture different aspects of classification performance.
The evaluation metrics reported for model validation should be calculated from the predictions for the held-out test subset. For the algal mat validation, although the classifier was subsequently refitted using all valid observations to produce the final spatial prediction, performance calculated from these same observations would represent in-sample performance rather than independent validation. In addition, because the training and test observations were divided randomly among mesh faces, spatial autocorrelation may cause the test metrics to overestimate performance when predicting spatially separate areas. Spatially blocked validation would provide a stronger test of spatial transferability. The resulting model should be interpreted as a data-driven classification of hydrodynamic conditions associated with persistent mapped cyanobacterial mat occurrence. It does not explicitly simulate mat growth, mortality, dispersal, physiological responses to salinity or temperature, or feedbacks between mats and sediment dynamics.

title: 5  Idealised modelling
text:
5.2 Idealised hydromorphodynamic model
Intertidal flats form the transition between the ocean and the land and are periodically exposed between the lowest and highest astronomical tides. Their morphology is shaped by interactions among coastal hydrodynamics, sedimentary processes, and biological activity. The morphological evolution of tidal flats can be characterised in terms of profile shape, bed slope, and sediment properties, which vary systematically with sediment supply, wave conditions, and tidal forcing (Friedrichs, 2011). When averaged over annual or longer timescales, tidal-flat morphology may approach a state of dynamic equilibrium with the prevailing external forcing. For example, tide-dominated environments generally favour convex-upward tidal-flat profiles, whereas wave-dominated environments tend to produce concave profiles (Friedrichs & Perry, 2001). Friedrichs (2011) summarised the effects of different environmental drivers Figure 5.1 on tidal-flat profiles, showing that increased tidal range, decreased wave height, increased sediment supply and faster flooding tides tend to develop convex-up profiles, whereas decreased tidal range, increased wave, decreased sediment supply and faster ebbing tides are more likely to exhibit concave-up profiles, vice versa .
The Pilbara coast of Western Australia is characterised by considerable spatial variability in tidal forcing, bed profiles, sediment composition, and sediment availability. To support the development and interpretation of regional morphodynamic models for sites along the Pilbara coast, including Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston, it is necessary to understand how tidal-flat morphology responds to these environmental drivers.
Understanding this morphological response is a crucial factor that requires careful model calibration. However, spatially varying sediment-related information along the region remains limited, despite the availability of localised point data at Giralia and Urala. Calibrating the morphodynamic model is therefore essential to ensure that simulated morphological responses to future sea-level rise can be trusted. To determine and justify these morphodynamic parameters on sound physical grounds, this study resorts to idealised modelling. Specifically, this chapter uses schematised bathymetry and tidal forcing to systematically investigate the morphological responses of tidal flats under different environmental conditions.






Figure 5.1: Conceptual diagram summaring the response of tidal flat shap and properties to a variety of independent forcings favoring either a convex-up or concave-up profile. Adopted from Friedrichs, 2012




5.2.1 Model settings
The exploratory model was run by Delft3D Flexible Mesh, using the D-Flow and D-Morphology module to simulate hydrodynamics and sediment transport. The model was run in a two-dimensional (depth-averaged) domain \(2\times 20\ \mathrm{km}\) with an offshore open boundary, using a rectangular grid size of \(50 \times 50\ \mathrm{m}\) Figure 5.2. The offshore open boundary was driven by tidal constituents, e.g. M2 and M4, and the lateral and offshore boundaries were closed to ensure model stability. The model bathymetry was featured by alongshore uniform slope of 0.07%. An further mild slope of 0.035% on the high intertidal flat was applied to the model for initial bed profile sensitivity test. The initial bed level at the open boundary was set to-7m relative to mean sea level (MSL) to ensure that cross-shore tidal movement would not be obstructed by the landward boundary. Random perturbations of \(5\ \mathrm{cm}\) were superimposed on the bathymetry to initiate simulations.
Both sand and mud were considered in the idealised model. Sand transport followed the formulation of (Rijn, 1993), with the median grain size of 0.25 mm. Mud transport was computed using the Partheniades’ equation (Sanford & Halka, 1993; Winterwerp J.C., 2007), with settling velocity of 0.25 mm/s and critical erosion shear stress of 0.1 Pa. Bed friction was represented by a uniform Manning’s friction coefficient of 0.023 \(\text{s}\,\text{m}^{-1/3}\) (default value). A constant mud supply was imposed at the open boundary. To accelerate morphological response to hydrodynamics, a morphological accelerator \(f_{\mathrm{mor}}\) of 50 was used in this model.






Figure 5.2: Idealised model domain and cross section profile





5.2.2 Scenarios design
The scenarios were designed to investigate morphological responses to variations in tidal range, tidal asymmetry, initial bed profile, sediment composition, and mud concentration. Runs 1–3 examined tidal ranges of 0.8, 1.5, and 3.0 m, representing microtidal, mesotidal, and macrotidal regimes, respectively. Because the study sites along the Pilbara coast of Western Australia are characterised by a mesotidal regime, a tidal range of 1.5 m was adopted for the subsequent scenarios.
Tidal asymmetry in Runs 4 and 5 was generated by combining the principal lunar semidiurnal constituent, M2, with its first overtide, M4. A relative phase difference of \(2\varphi_{M4} - \varphi_{M2}=90 ^\circ\) represented flood-dominant conditions, whereas a phase difference of \(270^\circ\) represented ebb-dominant condition. Here, \(\varphi_{M4}\) and \(\varphi_{M2}\) denote the phases of constituents M4 and M2, respectively. For simplicity, \(\varphi_{M2}=0^\circ\) in all scenarios
A gentle upper-intertidal slope of 0.035%, representing a convex-upward profile, was applied to the flood- and ebb-dominated conditions in Runs 6 and 7, respectively. The influence of sediment composition was examined in Runs 8 and 9, in which the mud fraction was increased to 20% and reduced to 0%, respectively. Run 9 therefore represented a purely sandy substrate. In Run 10, the suspended mud concentration at the boundary was increased from 5 to 10 mg L\(^{-1}\) to investigate the influence of sediment availability on tidal-flat morphology.

5.2.3 Results

5.2.3.1 Morphology
Figure 5.3 presents the morphological changes after 200 years of simulation under different environmental forcing conditions. Panels (a)–(c) of Figure 5.3, together with Figure 5.4 a, illustrate the influence of tidal range on morphological evolution and the mean cross-sectional profile. As the tidal range increased, the accretion zone in the upper intertidal area, where the bed elevation was above 0 m, extended farther landward. Both the width and magnitude of deposition also increased with tidal range. In contrast, deposition in the subtidal and lower-intertidal zones, where the bed elevation was below 0 m, gradually diminished. Under a tidal range of 4 m, erosion became more pronounced and braided channels developed within these zones.
When tidal asymmetry was introduced, substantial morphological differences developed despite only minor changes in tidal range. Compared with the tidally symmetric case, flood-dominant conditions produced a broad depositional zone extending across the entire intertidal platform, between low- and high-water levels, and promoted the formation of two distinct channels. In contrast, ebb-dominant conditions caused pronounced erosion in the subtidal zone and generated a more complex, braided channel network. Changes in the mean cross-sectional profiles were also consistent with previous studies (Pritchard et al., 2002), which showed that flood dominance accelerates the landward progradation of tidal-flat profiles, whereas ebb dominance promotes their recession.
The initial bathymetry plays a crucial role on morphological evolution. Compared with morphological changes in Run 5, reducing slopes in the upper intertidal results in more significant channel-shoal patterns grown in ebb dominance. However, tidal channels under flood dominance do not become longer with increased depositional extent. This is because when the upper slope becomes milder, the intertidal storage becomes larger. With larger intertidal storage, the filing and draining of intertidal areas will slow the landward propagation of high tide relative to low tide. Low tide will partially catch up with high tide and the temporal transition from high to low water will be shortened, resulting in a quicker falling tide and a tendency towards ebb dominance over the flats. Consequently, channels under flood dominance are shortened while under ebb dominance are enhanced.
Increasing or decreasing the mud fraction of the sediment substrate did not substantially alter the extent of the depositional zone. However, a more mud-rich substrate resulted in slightly greater erosion in the subtidal and lower-intertidal zones. A similar response was observed when the mud supply from the open boundary was varied. Increasing the suspended mud supply produced a wider and more elevated depositional zone in the upper intertidal area, while morphological changes in the subtidal and lower-intertidal zones remained limited.






Figure 5.3: Morphological changes after 200-year simulation for idealised scenarios.









Figure 5.4: Bed profile after 200-year simulations when comparing (a) tidal range and (b) tidal asymmetry.





5.2.3.2 Sediment redistribution
Muddy zones, defined as areas with a mud fraction greater than 30%, developed primarily in the upper intertidal zone. The only exception was the microtidal case (Run 1), in which weaker tidal currents allowed suspended mud to settle at lower elevations. As tidal range increased, the muddy zones expanded and their mud content generally increased.
Tidal asymmetry strongly influenced sediment redistribution. Under flood-dominant conditions, extensive muddy deposits developed across the upper intertidal zone, and the channels also contained a higher proportion of mud. In contrast, ebb-dominant conditions produced only limited muddy deposits and a more extensive sandy area in the subtidal and lower intertidal zones. The channel–shoal patterns observed in Figure 5.3 e were primarily associated with sand erosion. When a gentler initial upper-intertidal slope was applied, mud was transported farther landward, resulting in a broader depositional zone under both flood- and ebb-dominant conditions. However, the gentler slope also enhanced ebb-directed flow. Under ebb-dominant conditions, this caused greater sand erosion and produced the wider and deeper channel networks shown in Figure 5.3 g.
Variations in the initial mud fraction of the sediment substrate produced similar muddy-zone distributions across the intertidal platform. This suggests that most of the deposited mud originated from the continuous suspended-sediment supply at the open boundary rather than from the initial bed composition. This interpretation is further supported by the comparison between Figure 5.5 b and Figure 5.5 j, in which doubling the mud concentration at the open boundary resulted in a substantially wider muddy zone.






Figure 5.5: Mud fraction after 200-year simulation for idealised scenarios.






5.2.4 Implications for regional hydromorphodynamic modelling
Our sensitivity tests using the schematised idealised model demonstrate that external environmental drivers play a dominant role in controlling morphological evolution and sediment redistribution. The results show that tidal range, tidal asymmetry, and the initial bed profile strongly influence morphological development and mud distribution, whereas the effects of initial substrate sediment composition and mud supply at the open boundary are comparatively limited. Therefore, when applying the morphodynamic model to tide-dominated real-world systems, accurate representation of local tidal conditions and bathymetry should be prioritised. Sediment composition and boundary mud supply can be considered secondary factors in model parameterisation.
From Chapter 2, we know that the Pilbara Coast is a well-sheltered micro- to meso-tidal system, featured with ebb-dominated tides (stronger ebbing tide than flooding tide), and low sediment supply from the open boundary as well as relatively mild bathymetric slopes. These features are similar to settings in Run 7. For regional-scale morphodynamic models in Grialia, Urala and Cape Preston, we incorporated multiple tidal constituents, including M2, S2, O1, and K1, to represent an ebb-dominated tidal asymmetry and to reproduce spring–neap variability, thereby providing a more realistic representation of natural tidal conditions. Here, tidal asymmetry was induced by interaction between M2, O1 and K1 interaction (Song et al., 2011).
Biological processes, such as bioturbation and bioadhesion, can further modify these profile shapes by either enhancing or reducing their convexity or concavity. As discussed previously, the Pilbara Coast is a well-sheltered, tide-dominated environment. Extensive mangrove forests occur along the fringing coast and tidal channels, where they act as natural buffers by reducing flow energy and stabilising channel banks. Therefore, biological processes, particularly the effects of mangrove vegetation, need to be properly represented in morphodynamic modelling of the Pilbara Coast.

title: 5  Idealised modelling
text:
5.3 Giralia-based Idealised hydromorphological model

5.3.1 Introduction
The exploratory idealised model presented in the previous section provided insights into the roles of tidal range, tidal asymmetry, and initial bathymetry in shaping tidal-flat morphology. Building on these findings, we developed a more realistic idealised model based on measured bathymetry and tidal conditions from Giralia Bay. Because the spatial distribution of sediment properties is not well constrained, we conducted sensitivity analyses on key sediment parameters, including the critical shear stress for mud erosion and sand–mud interactions.


5.3.2 Model settings
To capture the extent of one of the main tidal creeks in the Giralia area, a rectangular computational grid is constructed with a length of 15 km (longshore) and a width of 1.5 km (cross-shore). The grid has a resolution of dx = dy = 15 meter, which ensures the main channel is represented by at least one cell (at the landward end) and more than 15 cells at the seaward end. The initial bathymetry is assumed alongshore uniform with a convex profile shape that is associated with muddy coastlines. The following function is used to describe the cross-shore bathymetry:
\[z(y)=a*e^{b-c*y}+d \tag{5.1}\]
here \(z(y)\) is the bed level at a certain distance y, and \(a=-0.730, b=0.0351, c=-1.65e^{-4}, d=3.50\) derived from Giralia Bay Bathymetry. In this model,the vertical datum of the bathymetry data is 1.45 meter above Mean Sea Level.






Figure 5.6: Convex cross-shore bathymetry profile for the idealised model domain (orange line) obtained by fitting the longshore-averaged GEBCO bathymetry of the selected area (blue line).




5.3.2.1 Boundary conditions
Tidal forcing is imposed on the seaward end of the domain, other boundaries are closed for model stability. Tidal components are obtained from the TPXO8 global tide database and can be found in the following table. The constituents with amplitude smaller than 0.1m are considered insignificant and therefore neglected, leaving M2, S2, O1, K1. The difference between the bathymetry datum and mean sea level (1.45m) is prescribed as an A0 component.

5.3.3 Scenarios design
The model is run for three hydrodynamic years and a morphological acceleration factor (\(f_{\mathrm{mor}}\)) of 50, resulting in 150 years of morphological development. With the aim of first attaining morphological equilibrium, no sea-level rise is imposed. We investigate the model sensitivity to erosion by first evaluating the effect of sand-mud erosion interaction (using \(\tau_e = 0.5 \,\text{N/m}^2\)). Thereafter, the critical bed shear stress for erosion of mud is varied between \(0.125\,\text{N/m}^2\) (easily eroded) and \(2.0\,\text{N/m}^2\)(consolidated mud).


5.3.4 Results

5.3.4.1 Effect of sand-mud erosion interaction (\(\tau_e=0.5 \,\text{N/m}^2\))
The morphological development without sand-mud erosion interaction is gradual in the simulated 150 morphological years. The width-averaged elevation shows erosion between +2 m (y ~ 4000 m) and 0 m (y ~ 10000 m) and accretion between 0 m (y~10000) and – 2.5 m (y~13000). One main channel has formed in the simulated period. Mud erodes only for \(\tau > \tau_e = 0.5 \,\text{N/m}^2\), conditions that do not occur often (see later, ). Therefore,mud fraction increases in the erosion zone as mud in the bed is immobile and sand is eroded, whereas mud fraction decreases in the deposition zone as sand is deposited and mud immobile, see Figure 5.9. This leads to a stabilization of the eroding zone as the higher mud-content increases the critical bed shear stress for erosion of sand. When channels start forming, higher flow velocities occur in the deeper parts and will exceed the erosion threshold for mud (occasionally). This does not occur on the shallower parts adjacent to the channels and mud accumulates there.






Figure 5.7: Width-averaged elevation vs seaward distance for t_mor = 0, 10, 20 ….. 150 years without erosion interaction.









Figure 5.8: Bed level for 0, 50, 100, 150 years without erosion interaction









Figure 5.9: The fraction mud in the active toplayer for 0, 50, 100, 150 years without erosion interaction



Significant increase in morphological development occurs when accounting for sand-mud erosion interaction. The erosion and deposition zones, while on similar location, are larger and show greater change compared to the simulation without interaction, see Figure 5.10. Large tidal channels have formed after 50 morphological years which develop until (and after) 150 morphological years, and are flanked by shallower shoals, see Figure 5.11. Significant bodies of sand are deposited towards the seaward end of the domain that raise the local bed level. The mud-content reflects the channel-shoal dynamics, with muddy zones (red in Figure 5.12) near the landward end and on the channel banks, where flow velocities are small. Furthermore, another muddy zone is at the offshore boundary where mud enters the domain and flow velocities are small. The mixture approach allows for erosion of both sand and mud, even when the critical erosion of (pure) mud \(\tau_e=0.5 \,\text{N/m}^2\) is not exceed. The result is a more dynamic channel-shoal system.






Figure 5.10: Width-averaged elevation vs seaward distance for 0, 10, 20 ….. 150 years with erosion interaction.









Figure 5.11: The bed level for 0, 50, 100, 150 years with erosion interaction.









Figure 5.12: The mud fraction in the active toplayer for 0, 50, 100, 150 years with erosion interaction





5.3.4.2 Sensitivity test on critical bed shear stress for mud erosion
In Colina Alonso et al. (2023), the sensitivity of channel-shoal patterns to the critical erosion of mud when applying sand-mud erosion interaction is shown. Due to the absence of waves and generally milder conditions (lower bed-shear stresses), less profound differences in channel-shoal patterns are found when varying the critical erosion of mud. Channel size and patterns are comparable for \(\tau_e = 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2\,\text{N/m}^2\) as transport is mainly non-cohesive. More easily erodible mud (\(\tau_e = 0.125, 0.25\,\text{N/m}^2\)) results in channels that reach less far landward (see Figure 5.13). The most erodible mud (\(\tau_e = 0.125\,\text{N/m}^2\)) stands out as the landward end is more distinctly muddy at a greater distance from the sea, and muddy shoals are of smaller size (see Figure 5.14). Without further investigation, the other cases seem to yield similar results, which can be attributed to the bed shear stresses in this domain not exceeding the respective erosion thresholds.






Figure 5.13: The bed level after 150 morphological years for \(\tau_e = 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2\,\text{N/m}^2\)









Figure 5.14: The mud fraction in the active top layer after 150 morphological years for \(\tau_e = 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2\,\text{N/m}^2\)






5.3.5 Implication for regional hydromorphodynamic modelling
In this Giralia-based idealised morphological model, we investigated how variations in sediment properties influence tidal-flat morphology. Sand–mud interactions produced a more dynamic channel–shoal system and promoted the development of additional channels across the tidal platform. The critical shear stress for mud erosion exerted a strong influence on mud redistribution, but had a comparatively smaller effect on the overall channel–shoal morphology. These results highlight the importance of appropriately representing sand–mud interactions and sediment erodibility in regional-scale morphodynamic models.

title: 5  Idealised modelling
text:
5.4 Giralia-based ecomorphological model

5.4.1 Introduction
Compared with those in tropical humid climates, mangroves in arid regions exhibit greater tolerance to climatic extremes (low precipitation and high temperature) but have shorter tree stature and lower diversity. Different from tall and dense mangrove forests in tropical humid climates, mangroves in arid climates like the Pilbara coast are usually sparse and lower, with small stem size, slow growth rate, and low reproduction rate (Adame et al., 2021; Santini et al., 2013). Operating near their physiological limits and lacking riverine sediment supply, arid mangrove forest were thought to be more sensitive to global warming and sea-level rise. Therefore, in this exploratory model, we systematically analysed different mangrove tree properties (stem diameter, growth rate and density) on morphological evolution using the frame work proposed in Chapter 3.


5.4.2 Model settings
The Idealised model domain was configured to represent a gently sloping tide-dominated mangrove system, applicable to Giralia Bay, Western Australia. The model was run in a two-dimensional domain with an offshore open boundary, using a gradually fining rectangular grid size, from 200*20 m to 20*20m. An alongshore uniform convex profile \(z=2.2-8.5e^{-0.165(y-8.19)}\) ,derived from the mean bed profile in Giralia Bay, was used as the initial profile with a funnel-shaped channel in the middle Figure 5.15. The funnel-shaped channel followed the bathymetric characteristics measured in Giralia Bay – channel width (mouth width \(B_0=0.6 \mathrm{km}\)) decreased exponentially towards landward and disappeared when it became smaller than the grid width (20 m). Channle thalweg elevation increased linearly from subtidal and remained constant on the platform. The open boundary conditions were based on primary constituents (M2, S2, O1, K1) extracted from TPXO10.
Both sand (90% in volume) and mud (10% in volume) were considered in the sediment substrate, and their transport was resolved by the formulation of (Rijn, 1993) and the equations of Partheniades and Krone (Partheniades, 1965), respectively. Following previous studies on dynamic mangrove modelling (Xie et al., 2022), the critical shear stress for mud erosion was set to \(0.2\,\text{N/m}^2\).






Figure 5.15: (a) Real domain of tidal flats with a channel in Giralia Bay, Western Australia, representative of tide-dominated mangrove systems in arid climates. (b) Schematised model domain with idealised bathymetry. (c) cross-shore profile of tidal flat platform and channel thalweg





5.4.3 Scenarios design
Scenarios started from bare tidal flats without any mangrove forest (Run 0). Different mangrove biological properties were listed in the following table. Parameters in Run 1 were adopted from (Xie et al., 2022), which represent relatively large, fast-growing, and dense mangrove forest. In Run 2, the maximum growth rate of stem diameter was decreased to 0.3 cm per year to understand the impact of growth rate. Later, the maximum tree stem diameter decreased to 10 cm in Run 3, with unchanged growth parameters (G, b2, and b3) and Run 4, with unchanged maximum rate. For Run 1 to Run 4, the inundation fitness curve was designed that mangrove growth quality reaches an optimal at inundation frequency P=0.25 and decrease on both sides.
