5.4.4 Results
The following figures show the spatial distributions of mangrove vegetation, morphological change, and mud redistribution after the system reached ecological equilibrium following 120 years of coupled simulation. Compared with the unvegetated case, all vegetated scenarios exhibited enhanced erosion within the central channel and greater sediment accretion across the tidal platform. Higher mud fractions were also observed along channel banks and the coastal fringe. In addition, the presence of mangroves promoted the development of a denser and more highly branched tidal-creek network. These results suggest that mangrove vegetation enhances channel incision, promotes tidal-creek formation and branching, and promotes sediment accumulation on the intertidal platform, consistent with findings reported in previous studies (D’Alpaos et al., 2006; Fagherazzi et al., 2012; Mariotti, 2018; Mariotti & Carr, 2014).
Comparisons between simulations with different tree growth rates (Run 1 vs. Run 2 and Run 3 vs. Run 4) show that the faster-growing cases (Runs 1 and 4) develop higher biomass throughout the upper intertidal zone (y > 0 km). This greater biomass is associated with a higher proportion of mud-dominated cells, larger cross-sectional channel areas, and greater channel depths along the cross-shore direction.
Comparisons between simulations with different stem diameters (Run 2 vs. Run 4) reveal a different response. Although the smaller-stem case (Run 4) exhibits lower biomass throughout the upper intertidal zone, it develops a greater proportion of muddy cells, a denser and more highly branched tidal-creek network, larger channel cross-sectional areas, and a deeper central channel.
This response can be attributed to the higher stem density associated with smaller individual stem diameters and the earlier attainment of mature vegetation densities. Despite the lower biomass, the increased stem density enhances the cumulative vegetation-induced drag exerted on the flow, thereby strengthening vegetation–flow interactions and promoting more pronounced patterns of channel erosion and platform sediment accretion.

Figure 5.17: Alongshore averaged platform elevation (a), thalweg line elevation of the central channel (b), and percentage of muddy cells (mud fraction > 30%) at ecological equilibrium after 120-year coupling (c).









Figure 5.18: Alongshore averaged biomass (a), number of channels (b), cross-sectional area below mean sea level (c), and central channel depth (d) after ecological equilibrium (120-year coupling).

The exploratory idealized model provides an efficient framework for investigating the long-term effects of different processes on tidal-creek morphological evolution. title: 4  Model Overview and Evaluation
text:
4.7 Optimising through Idealised Modelling
While the hydrodynamic, wave, morphodynamic, and ecological modules provide a comprehensive framework for simulating real-world coastal and estuarine dynamics, the sheer volume of empirical parameters across these interconnected systems introduces significant calibration challenges. Directly tuning these parameters in a complex, site-specific domain makes it difficult to isolate whether changes in model performance stem from underlying physical settings or confounding site-specific characteristics like irregular bathymetry.
To address this and ensure rigorous model development, we carry out a series of exploratory simulations using an idealised model configuration. This controlled approach allows us to systematically evaluate and optimise sediment transport formulations, boundary conditions, and vegetation settings without the noise of complex domain geometries.
For a detailed breakdown of this framework, experimental design, and initial parameter optimisations, see Chapter 5.

title: 5  Idealised modelling
section: 5.5 Summary of idealised models and key findings
text:
5.5 Summary of idealised models and key findings
The exploratory idealised models provide an efficient framework for isolating and understanding the long-term effects of key environmental drivers on tidal-flat morphological evolution. By systematically testing variables in a controlled environment without site-specific bathymetric noise, these simulations offer critical insight into evolutionary responses and establish a practical physical basis for parameterisation in site specific models.

5.5.1 Findings

Tidal Forcing: Increased tidal range extends the upper-intertidal accretion zone landward, while macro-tidal regimes (\(4\text{ m}\)) trigger greater subtidal erosion and braided channel formation.
Tidal Asymmetry: Flood-dominant conditions promote broad intertidal deposition and channel formation, whereas ebb-dominant conditions drive pronounced subtidal erosion and deeper, complex channel networks.
Sediment Dynamics & Sand-Mud Interactions: Accounting for sand-mud erosion interactions creates a significantly more dynamic channel-shoal system compared to non-interactive runs. While the critical shear stress for mud erosion strongly influences mud redistribution, it has a secondary effect on overall channel-shoal morphology.
Mangrove Vegetation: Incorporating mangrove forests acts as a natural buffer, enhancing platform sediment accretion while intensifying central-channel incision and tidal-creek branching. Variations in biological traits (such as stem diameter and growth rate) exert a smaller overall influence than the presence or absence of vegetation itself, though smaller stem diameters enhance channel incision through higher cumulative drag.



5.5.2 Implications for Regional-Scale Modelling
Our sensitivity tests demonstrate that external environmental drivers—specifically local tidal range, ebb-dominant asymmetry, and initial mild bathymetric slopes—play a dominant role in controlling morphological evolution. For regional-scale morphodynamic models along the Pilbara coast (including Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston), these insights justify: 1. Multi-Constituent Tidal Forcing: Incorporating primary constituents (\(M_2, S_2, O_1, K_1\)) to capture ebb-dominant asymmetry and spring-neap variability (following Song et al. (2011)). 2. Vegetation Representation: Adopting arid-adapted mangrove parameterisations (such as Run 4 settings, featuring relatively small stem diameters and slow growth rates) to accurately simulate mangrove properties, sediment retention and creek incision. 3. Parameter Prioritisation: Prioritising accurate representation of local tidal conditions and bathymetry over secondary factors like initial substrate sediment composition or open-boundary mud supply.
We show the site-specific model development and calibrations in ?sec-hydro-overview.

title: 1  Introduction
section: 1.3 Knowledge Gaps in Predicting Intertidal Habitat Change in the Pilbara
text:
1.3 Knowledge Gaps in Predicting Intertidal Habitat Change in the Pilbara
As relative sea level rises, changes in tidal inundation can alter the elevation range suitable for different habitats, while sediment accretion and erosion determine whether intertidal surfaces can maintain their position within the tidal frame. Although coastal wetlands can respond to these changes through vertical accretion, ecological adjustment, and landward migration, their capacity to persist depends on local geomorphology, sediment availability, hydrological connectivity, and the availability of suitable accommodation space (Krauss et al., 2014; Schuerch et al., 2018; Woodroffe et al., 2016). Where development restricts landward migration or modifies sediment and water flows, these processes may be insufficient to prevent habitat loss and redistribution (Day et al., 2024; Leo et al., 2019).
However, the processes governing these responses are not uniform across climatic settings. Much of the established understanding of coastal wetland responses to SLR is derived from research in temperate wetlands, humid tropical mangroves, and sediment-rich river deltas (Kirwan & Megonigal, 2013; Nienhuis et al., 2023; Saintilan et al., 2020; Schuerch et al., 2018; Woodroffe et al., 2016). Although this literature provides important insights into inundation stress, sediment accumulation, and coastal habitat migration, its direct application to hyper-arid coastlines requires caution. Arid intertidal environments are characterised by limited and episodic freshwater inputs, high evaporative demand, and strong spatial variation in sediment and salinity conditions. Groundwater discharge, infrequent rainfall events, and episodic catchment flows may exert disproportionate influences on local hydrology, while restricted freshwater replenishment and infrequent tidal flushing can promote hypersalinity in elevated intertidal areas. These conditions influence vegetation stature, ecosystem productivity, and the distribution of habitats across the tidal frame, potentially producing responses that differ from those observed in more humid environments (Adame et al., 2021; Woodroffe et al., 2016).
These characteristics introduce substantial uncertainty into projections of arid intertidal change under future SLR. Increasing inundation does not necessarily result in uniform landward migration or the expansion of mangrove forests. Depending on local elevation, tidal connectivity, sediment supply, and substrate stability, rising sea levels may create new habitat opportunities in some locations while increasing inundation stress, erosion, or habitat loss in others. The balance between these outcomes is particularly difficult to predict where sediment delivery is episodic and the capacity of intertidal surfaces to accrete vertically is poorly constrained. Furthermore, changes in inundation interact with salinity and freshwater availability, meaning that a location becoming more frequently inundated may not necessarily become more suitable for vegetation if other environmental constraints persist (Lovelock et al., 2015; Saintilan et al., 2020; Woodroffe et al., 2016). Consequently, projections based solely on changes in sea level or habitat elevation may overlook important constraints on ecosystem persistence in arid coastal settings.
Coastal development adds another dimension to this uncertainty. Infrastructure, land reclamation, industrial activities, and changes to drainage or sediment pathways can modify the physical conditions that sustain intertidal habitats. Development may also restrict the landward migration of habitats as sea level rises, creating coastal squeeze where suitable habitat is progressively lost between rising water levels and fixed landward barriers (Day et al., 2024; Leo et al., 2019). In arid regions, where suitable habitat may depend on specific combinations of elevation, salinity, freshwater availability, and sediment characteristics, such alterations can affect not only total habitat area but also the spatial arrangement and connectivity of different habitat types. Predicting future change therefore requires consideration of sea level rise and development together, rather than treating either pressure in isolation.
The northwestern coast of Western Australia has attracted growing interest in the development of large scale solar salt farms. This intense industrial interest is driven by the region’s extensive natural salt flats, high evaporative demand, and substantial tidal range, which together provide optimal environmental conditions for solar salt extraction. Along this coastline, industrial production has expanded progressively over several decades. Historical project timelines illustrate a trajectory from early facility constructions in the late 1960s such as the Leslie and Dampier salt operations through to continuous operational increases, modern plant optimisations, and recent project milestones like the cancellation of the Ashburton project and the approval of the Optimised Mardie Project Figure 1.2.






Figure 1.2: Timeline of several salt projects within the northwestern region of Western Australia from 1966 to 2026.



The spatial footprint and current regulatory status of these developments vary significantly across the region, ranging from long standing active operations and pending assessments such as Eramurra to projects rejected or situated near ecologically sensitive areas, including the marine protected environments around Giralia Bay Figure 1.3. Because these industrial footprints intersect directly with hyper arid intertidal habitats, including mangrove fringes, salt flats, and cyanobacterial mats, mapping their spatial distribution and operational status is critical for assessing cumulative pressures, managing coastal squeeze, and evaluating habitat connectivity under future environmental change.






Figure 1.3: Spatial distribution, operational status, and key regional locations of solar salt projects across the Pilbara and Gascoyne coasts as at October 2026.



These knowledge gaps have direct implications for managing the West Pilbara coast. The relatively limited historical study of its arid intertidal systems constrains understanding of their natural variability, governing processes and capacity to respond to disturbance. Recent habitat mapping (Hickey et al., 2025) provides an important baseline, but management also requires an understanding of how habitats may respond to future climate change and coastal development. These pressures may produce inundation, connectivity and habitat conditions substantially different from those represented in present-day observations or the recent past. Developing process understanding and predictive tools is therefore needed to reduce uncertainty about potential habitat change and support environmental assessment and coastal planning.
In this study, we focus primarily on mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats as two ecologically distinct but potentially interacting components of the West Pilbara intertidal landscape. By investigating their potential responses to sea level rise and coastal development, we aim to improve understanding of where these habitats may persist, expand, contract, or redistribute under future scenarios. This provides a basis for assessing the potential consequences of coastal change for arid intertidal ecosystems and for identifying the environmental constraints and spatial trade offs that may shape their future distribution.

1.3.1 Predicting Mangrove Responses to Sea-Level Rise
Mangroves have been extensively studied, particularly in humid tropical and temperate settings, in relation to sea-level rise (SLR) through satellite mapping, field observations, and numerical modelling. Satellite time series have been used to quantify changes in mangrove extent and distribution over decadal timescales, while comparisons with water-level and sea-level observations have helped investigate the environmental drivers of these changes (Lovelock et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018). Field measurements of surface-elevation change, sediment accumulation, and mangrove responses across different inundation and salinity conditions have further established that forest persistence depends on the balance between rising sea levels, sediment supply, and local ecological tolerances (Krauss et al., 2014; Lovelock et al., 2015; Woodroffe et al., 2016).
Existing approaches to projecting mangrove change differ substantially in their representation of physical and ecological processes. Habitat-transition models, such as SLAMM (Payo et al., 2016), project changes between habitat classes, while other approaches relate wetland extent to SLR and sediment availability (Schuerch et al., 2018). More mechanistic models explicitly represent selected interactions between mangrove development, hydrodynamics and sediment dynamics, including the studies by Xie et al. (2020) and Xie et al. (2022), and the LEAF framework of Dunlop et al. (2025). These developments provide important capabilities, but their spatial scales, projection periods, ecological formulations and computational requirements differ. They therefore represent a range of approaches rather than a single, routinely transferable capability for predicting arid intertidal habitat change.
Predicting mangrove responses requires particular attention to climatic and geographical context. Mangroves in humid tropical environments may experience different freshwater availability, salinity regimes, and sediment conditions from those in hyper-arid coastlines. Consequently, model relationships and ecological parameters developed for one setting may not transfer directly to another. This is particularly important when projecting future changes in the West Pilbara, where episodic freshwater inputs, hypersalinity, and spatially variable sediment supply can constrain mangrove establishment and persistence.
A major challenge is representing the feedbacks between mangrove development and coastal morphology over long timescales. Sediment transport, erosion and accretion, tidal inundation, and vegetation establishment and mortality can interact to determine whether mangroves persist, migrate landward, or retreat. Explicitly representing these processes alongside the different stages of the mangrove life cycle can be computationally demanding and data-intensive. For example, some bio-morphodynamic studies have therefore used idealised domains to isolate key mechanisms (Xie et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022), while other developments, including LEAF, have focused on detailed modelling over shorter projection periods (Dunlop et al., 2025) and some focussed on relatively small sites (Beselly et al., 2023). For additional details, readers are referred to Section 3.2. These approaches provide important advances, but they do not yet establish a general capability for predicting mangrove redistribution across an entire, geomorphically heterogeneous coastline over centennial timescales.
Furthermore, the response predicted for one location cannot necessarily be transferred to another, even where the hydrodynamic conditions appear similar. Differences in coastal slope, sediment availability, substrate characteristics, freshwater supply, and the initial distribution of vegetation can produce different trajectories of habitat change. Coastal-scale predictions therefore require spatially explicit environmental conditions and sufficient representation of the processes governing mangrove establishment, persistence, and migration. Developing a process-based modelling capability that can predict mangrove responses to future SLR across coastal-scale domains and centennial timescales, while representing the processes most relevant to habitat redistribution, is a key gap addressed by this project.


1.3.2 Cyanobacterial Mats: From Ecological Research to Future Habitat Prediction
Research on cyanobacterial mats has largely focused on their microbial ecology, physiological functioning, and biogeochemical roles. Nitrogen fixation has been a major research theme, with studies examining the organisms responsible, variations in nitrogenase activity, and the environmental controls on this process within microbial mats (Stal et al., 2010). However, cyanobacterial mats differ significantly in community composition and salinity responses, including among tidal zones within the same coastal system. Relationships established for freshwater communities, planktonic blooms, or other mat types therefore need to be evaluated before being applied to arid intertidal mats. Predicting their distribution requires information relevant to the specific salinity, inundation, and exposure conditions experienced by the communities being modelled (Abed et al., 2007; Abed et al., 2008). While these physiological and ecological studies improve our understanding of mat functioning, they do not directly predict changes in the spatial extent of intertidal mats under future environmental conditions.
A separate body of research has investigated cyanobacterial growth and transport in rivers, using mathematical models that combine biological processes with hydraulic transport to predict the movement and development of planktonic cyanobacteria (Guven & Howard, 2006). In lakes and reservoirs, process-based and data-driven models have been developed to forecast cyanobacterial blooms from environmental variables such as water temperature, nutrient availability, and hydrological conditions (Rousso et al., 2020). Satellite remote sensing has also been widely used to detect and monitor aquatic cyanobacterial blooms, providing information about their occurrence, extent, and temporal variability (Shi et al., 2019). However, these studies generally concern planktonic or water-column blooms rather than benthic microbial mats attached to intertidal surfaces. Their methods and assumptions therefore cannot be directly transferred to predicting the migration of intertidal mats.
Research directly addressing cyanobacterial mats in arid intertidal environments has increasingly focused on habitat mapping and historical change. The Exmouth Gulf mapping study by Hickey et al. (2023) used satellite imagery and supervised classification to map cyanobacterial mats and associated salt-flat habitats, while subsequent multidecadal mapping has documented the dynamic distribution of intertidal habitat classes along the north-western Australian coastline (Hickey et al., 2023; Hickey et al., 2025). These studies provide essential baseline information on habitat extent and variability, but historical mapping alone does not establish how mat-covered surfaces will respond to future SLR or coastal development.
Based on the literature identified for this review, a predictive framework for the long-term migration of arid intertidal cyanobacterial mats under future sea-level rise (SLR) and coastal development has not yet been established. Developing this predictive capability is critical to reduce uncertainty regarding future habitat persistence and redistribution, and to provide a stronger scientific basis for management decisions under ongoing climate change and development pressures. In particular, there is no identified approach that can be directly applied to project their future spatial redistribution across the West Pilbara coastline. Unlike mangroves, for which several ecological and bio-morphodynamic modelling approaches already exist, cyanobacterial mats require the development of a habitat-specific predictive approach. Such an approach must establish how changes in inundation, surface elevation, salinity, and substrate conditions influence the persistence and spatial distribution of mat-covered surfaces, while accounting for the removal or modification of habitat by coastal development.


1.3.3 Modelling Gap and Project Objectives
The literature highlights different but related challenges for the two habitats considered in this study. For mangroves, the key challenge is extending existing modelling capabilities towards spatially explicit, coastal-scale projections over centennial timescales in hyper-arid environments. For cyanobacterial mats, the more fundamental challenge is developing a suitable predictive approach, because existing research is concentrated on microbial processes, aquatic blooms, and historical habitat mapping rather than long-term intertidal habitat migration.
This project addresses these gaps by developing and applying a modelling framework to investigate the potential redistribution of mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats along the West Pilbara coast under future SLR and coastal development scenarios. The aim is to predict where these habitats may persist, expand, contract, or be lost over centennial timescales, and to identify locations where development may constrain their potential migration. The framework is intended to support coastal-scale assessment of future habitat change while making explicit the processes represented, the assumptions required, and the limitations that remain.

title: 6  Model Application to Study Sites
text:
7.1 Introduction and Staged Strategy
The sensitivity tests and idealised modelling presented in Chapter 5 demonstrated that local tidal forcing, ebb-dominant asymmetry, and initial bathymetric slope play a controlling role in governing morphodynamic evolution and habitat distribution across arid intertidal landscapes. To operationalise these insights and address the broader research objectives, this study adopts a staged strategy focused on three targeted sites along the West Pilbara coast: Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston.
Each study site represents a distinct coastal environment and serves a specific role within the research design: * Giralia Domain: Serves as the primary baseline domain for detailed model development, calibration, and baseline physical process evaluation in a relatively pristine, well-studied setting. * Urala Domain: Provides a complex coastal setting with an existing and proposed industrial footprint, serving as the core domain to investigate the hydrodynamic and ecological implications of coastal development. * Cape Preston Domain: Serves as a test case to evaluate the transferability and robustness of the established modelling framework across different environmental characteristics and development constraints.
By progressing from a calibrated baseline site (Giralia) to a site undergoing active environmental assessment (Urala) and finally to a distinct regional context (Cape Preston), this staged strategy allows the modelling approach to be systematically evaluated before being applied across varied coastal settings.
To resolve coastal and intertidal hydrodynamic processes across these domains and underpin subsequent habitat migration predictions, a multi-scale numerical modelling framework was established using Delft3D Flexible Mesh (Delft3D FM). In total, four distinct numerical models were developed: three high-resolution Site-Specific Models (Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston) to capture local ambient tidal dynamics and intertidal inundation, and a standalone Exmouth Gulf Regional Model coupled with wave modules to evaluate extreme metocean conditions, wave growth, and storm surges across the broader Gulf.

title: 6  Model Application to Study Sites
text:
6.2 Model Setup
The numerical grids were generated using the SMS grid generator and subsequently converted to the Delft3D Flexible Mesh unstructured grid format, following the UGRID convention. The resulting meshes use triangular elements with spatially variable resolution to balance computational efficiency against the need to resolve narrow tidal creeks, creek junctions, intertidal flats and complex shorelines.
Grid resolution was selected according to the spatial scales of the dominant hydrodynamic processes and the quality of the available elevation data. Coarser elements were used in open water, where water level variations generally occur over larger spatial scales. Finer elements were introduced in shallow coastal areas, creek networks and habitat transition zones, where small changes in bed elevation and channel geometry can alter flow pathways and inundation patterns.
The grid design also considered the expected future distribution of intertidal habitats under sea level rise. Areas that could become suitable for future mangrove or cyanobacterial mat development were included within the model domains, with finer resolution allocated where necessary to resolve potential migration pathways and changes in inundation. This reduces the risk of excluding potential future habitat areas from the computational domain or representing important habitat boundaries too coarsely.
The model extent was assessed against a sea level rise scenario of +1.25 m to check whether the domains included the areas potentially exposed to future inundation and habitat migration. This assessment was used to inform the domain extent and grid design. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that the model can predict future habitat migration accurately, because the reliability of those predictions also depends on the bathymetry, ecological parameterisation and future boundary conditions.

6.2.1 Giralia Domain Model

6.2.1.1 Mesh and Setup
The grid design for the Giralia domain covers an area of approximately 44 km in length and 10 km in width. The grid consists entirely of triangular elements with variable resolutions, maintaining finer grid spacing near complex coastlines and creek systems to accurately resolve local hydrodynamic processes. Giralia is the principal model development site because of the extensive studies conducted in the area. The available high resolution topography, dedicated creek bathymetry and field observations provide a comparatively strong basis for evaluating the representation of local hydrodynamics.
Figure 6.1 a provides an overview of the full model domain, while Figure 6.1 b presents a zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box, highlighting the refined grid spacing in critical intertidal regions.






Figure 6.1: Delft3D Flexible Mesh grid layout for the Giralia Domain showing: a) full domain overview, and b) zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box.







6.2.2 Urala Domain Model

6.2.2.1 Mesh and Setup
The Urala domain covers approximately 44 km in length and 35 km in width. The triangular mesh uses variable resolution, ranging from approximately 250 m in open water to 12 m near shorelines and important features such as creek mouths.
The finer resolution is required to represent the local creek network, intertidal topography and areas where proposed coastal development could change flow connectivity or restrict tidal exchange. The broader domain also provides sufficient spatial coverage to represent the local hydrodynamic response to water levels imposed at the model boundaries.
Figure 6.2 a provides an overview of the model domain, while Figure 6.2 b presents a zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box, demonstrating finer grid spacing in critical regions.






Figure 6.2: Delft3D Flexible Mesh grid layout for the Urala Domain showing: a) full domain overview, and b) zoomed-in view of variable resolution mesh.







6.2.3 Cape Preston Domain Model

6.2.3.1 Mesh and Setup
The Cape Preston domain covers approximately 34 km in width and 58 km in length. As at Giralia and Urala, the grid consists of triangular elements with variable resolution. Finer elements are used around the nearshore environment, creek networks and intertidal regions where local topography influences tidal connectivity.
The principal limitation at Cape Preston is the lack of dedicated creek bathymetric survey data comparable to the Giralia survey. The channel geometry therefore cannot be constrained directly using equivalent field measurements. Instead, the creek bathymetry was idealised using the average creek width and depth derived from the Giralia bathymetric data. Satellite imagery was used to guide the representation of creek planform geometry.
This approach provides a consistent and physically informed initial representation of the creek network. However, it does not establish that the idealised channels reproduce the actual depths, cross sections or hydraulic conveyance of Cape Preston creeks. The resulting hydrodynamic and habitat predictions must therefore be interpreted in light of this uncertainty.
Figure 6.3 a provides an overview of the full model domain, while Figure 6.3 b presents a zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box, showcasing the refined grid spacing across the nearshore and creek network.






Figure 6.3: Delft3D Flexible Mesh grid layout for the Cape Preston Domain showing: a) full domain overview, and b) zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box.







6.2.4 Exmouth Gulf Regional Model

6.2.4.1 Mesh and Setup
The Exmouth Gulf regional model was developed to capture large-scale hydrodynamic processes, regional-scale tidal propagation, and extreme weather events (such as tropical cyclones and storm surges) affecting the broader regional footprint. Unlike the site-specific models focused on ambient intertidal dynamics, this regional domain spans approximately 110 km in width and 150 km in length, incorporating coupled wind-wave-current interaction modules.
The regional model’s full coupled wave and hydrodynamic assessment is outside the detailed site specific calibration and future habitat prediction results presented in this report. The setup is documented here to clarify its role in the overall modelling framework.
Figure 6.4 a provides an overview of the full model domain, while Figure 6.4 b presents a zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box, highlighting the refined grid spacing in shallow coastal regions.






Figure 6.4: Delft3D Flexible Mesh grid layout for the Exmouth Gulf Domain showing: a) full domain overview, and b) zoomed-in view of the variable-resolution mesh within the highlighted red box.

title: 6  Model Application to Study Sites
text:
6.3 Data Requirements and Model Forcings
Reliable hydrodynamic and habitat predictions require suitable input data, appropriate physical parameterisation and boundary forcing that represents the conditions experienced by each model domain. This is especially important in the West Pilbara, where the intertidal landscape contains shallow channels, extensive exposed flats, hypersaline environments and relatively small elevation differences between habitat zones.
The principal data requirements are:

Continuous and spatially consistent bathymetry and topography to define the geometry of the computational domain.
Appropriate grid resolution to represent tidal creeks, intertidal surfaces and potential future habitat areas.
Time varying water level and meteorological forcing to reproduce the hydrodynamic conditions acting on each domain.
Bed roughness and vegetation properties to represent the resistance exerted by the seabed and vegetation on tidal flows.
Field observations to evaluate model performance and identify uncertainty in the simulated water levels and inundation patterns.

The following sections describe the data sources, explain why they were selected, and distinguish between directly measured information and model assumptions.

6.3.1 Bathymetry and Topography
Bathymetry and topography across all domains were derived by integrating multiple spatial elevation datasets to ensure a smooth, physically consistent transition between terrestrial elevations and marine environments:

LiDAR Topography: High-resolution elevation surveys for all sites were conducted by the University of Western Australia (UWA).
Creek Bathymetry Surveys: Multibeam and single-beam bathymetry surveys dedicatedly conducted for the Giralia domains, alongside existing UWA survey data for Urala. Where dedicated surveys were unavailable (Cape Preston), creek bathymetry was idealised using planform geometry derived from satellite imagery and cross-sectional profiles scaled from the Giralia domain.
Satellite-Derived Bathymetry (SDB): 30m resolution satellite-derived bathymetry from the Blake (2020) model was incorporated to provide additional coverage in areas where LiDAR and creek bathymetry were unavailable or incomplete.
Digital Earth Australia (DEA) Intertidal Bathymetry: Satellite derived intertidal datasets (Bishop-Taylor et al. (2019);Bishop-Taylor et al. (2024)) were incorporated to bridge terrestrial LiDAR and SDB within intertidal zones.

Integrated bathymetric surfaces for each domain are presented in Figure 6.5, Figure 6.6, Figure 6.7, and Figure 6.8.

Figure 6.6: Bathymetry and topography of the Urala Model Domain: a) full domain bathymetry, and b) zoomed-in view of Urala North and South creeks and intertidal flats.

The datasets differ in spatial resolution, acquisition method and the physical environments they represent. Their integration therefore requires attention to horizontal reference systems, vertical datums, elevation sign conventions, spatial coverage and the treatment of overlapping cells. A continuous gridded surface does not necessarily imply that all elevations have the same accuracy.
The fine resolution LiDAR and creek bathymetric data provide the principal constraints on local terrain and channel geometry. The coarser satellite derived datasets extend coverage into areas where equivalent high resolution survey data are unavailable. Where datasets overlap, their relative reliability and suitability for the local environment should guide the merging procedure.
The Cape Preston bathymetry introduces additional uncertainty because its creek dimensions are based on an analogue from Giralia rather than direct survey measurements. Differences in sediment composition, tidal range, creek evolution and channel morphology may result in different hydraulic behaviour at Cape Preston. The model therefore provides a scenario based application of the framework rather than a fully survey constrained representation of the local creek network.
The elevation datasets also have implications for future habitat prediction. Where the predicted migration of mangroves or cyanobacterial mats depends on subtle elevation differences, uncertainty in the merged surface can affect the simulated timing and spatial extent of habitat establishment. These limitations should be considered alongside the uncertainty associated with future water levels, roughness and vegetation representation.


6.3.2 Model Forcings and Boundary Conditions
Hydrodynamic model performance depends on both the representation of the underlying bed and the forcing conditions imposed on the model. The forcing must reproduce the relevant variations in water level and atmospheric conditions over the simulation period. It is important to highlight that a detailed elevation model cannot compensate for inappropriate boundary conditions, while accurate forcing cannot compensate for unresolved creek geometry or incorrect habitat resistance.
The forcing strategy distinguishes between regional forcing, which establishes the large scale hydrodynamic conditions, and local forcing, which is used to represent the conditions acting on individual site models. The selection of each forcing dataset was guided by its ability to represent the relevant physical process, its temporal coverage and its suitability for the spatial scale of the model.
To accurately drive regional and local hydrodynamics, several physical boundary conditions and forcing parameters were incorporated.

6.3.2.1 Water level and tidal forcing
Water level forcing was treated differently for historical model calibration and future predictions. During the historical modelling period, measured water levels were used to force the model and to evaluate its performance against observations. The measured water level records were compared with simulated water levels at multiple locations within the Giralia and Urala domains. This approach allowed the model to be assessed against the observed tidal signal and its temporal variability across each domain, rather than relying solely on agreement at a single boundary location. The measurement locations and associated field data are described in Chapter 16, while the calibration and validation procedures and results are presented for each sites separately from Chapter 7 to Chapter 15 respectively.
Measured water levels were particularly important for establishing confidence in the model’s representation of local hydrodynamics. Unlike astronomical tide predictions alone, observed water levels can incorporate the combined effects of astronomical tides and non tidal variations present during the measurement period, including those associated with atmospheric pressure and wind. Using measured water levels during calibration therefore provided a basis for assessing whether the model could reproduce observed water level variations under the conditions represented by the field record.
Alternative water level products were also considered during the assessment of boundary forcing. These included the TPXO global ocean tide model and sea surface height (SSH) data from the Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM). TPXO provides harmonic tidal constituents derived through inverse modelling and assimilation of observational data (Egbert & Erofeeva (2002)). It is therefore useful for estimating the astronomical tidal signal where local observations are unavailable. However, its predicted astronomical tides do not, by themselves, reproduce the full non tidal water level variability recorded during individual weather events.
HYCOM provides modelled sea surface elevation as part of a broader ocean modelling system (Chassignet et al. (2009)). The SSH variable was considered as an alternative representation of time varying offshore water levels. Depending on the product and configuration, HYCOM SSH can represent ocean variability beyond the astronomical tide, but its spatial resolution, coastal representation and temporal characteristics may limit its ability to reproduce water levels within shallow, complex intertidal environments. TPXO and HYCOM SSH were therefore evaluated as alternative sources of water level information, rather than assumed to provide an equivalent representation of the local observed water levels.
The historical sensitivity evaluations indicated that measured water levels provided a better representation of the observed conditions than the tested TPXO and HYCOM SSH products. The measured records (Exmouth tide gauge data and Onslow tide gauge data) were consequently used to support historical calibration and model performance assessment. This comparison informed the selection of forcing for the historical simulations but did not mean that measured water levels were available or appropriate for future prediction periods.
For future predictions, the models were forced using the MSKO tidal constituent configuration described in Chapter 3.


6.3.2.2 Atmospheric forcing
Atmospheric forcing was derived from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset described by Hersbach et al. (2020). The meteorological variables used in the model include spatially varying wind speed and direction (represented as x and y direction), spatially uniform air temperature, relative humidity, and cloud cover, while for the regional model we also considered the atmospheric pressure.


6.3.2.3 Heat flux and evaporation
Heat exchange was represented using the meteorological variables supplied to the Delft3D Flexible Mesh heat flux formulation. Air temperature, relative humidity, cloud cover, atmospheric pressure and wind speed influence the exchange of heat and moisture between the water surface and the atmosphere.
Evaporation was calculated dynamically using bulk aerodynamic relationships (Deltares (2024)) within the selected heat flux configuration. This approach allows evaporation to vary with the atmospheric conditions rather than prescribing a single constant rate throughout the simulation.
This treatment is relevant to the hyper arid West Pilbara environment, where high temperatures, strong solar heating and low humidity can contribute to substantial evaporative water loss which can influence the percentage of submergence and inundation frequencies that are used for habitat prediction purposes.
It is important to note that the use of a heat flux formulation does not mean that groundwater discharge, subsurface salt transport or hypersaline porewater dynamics are explicitly represented. Those processes require additional data and model components. The current setup should therefore not be interpreted as a complete simulation of the subsurface hydrological processes that may affect mangrove establishment on hypersaline salt flats.


6.3.2.4 Rainfall
Measured daily rainfall data from the learmonth airport and Onslow airport were incorporated during the calibration period.


6.3.2.5 Wave forcing
Wave conditions were represented using outputs from WHACS wave modelling (Smith et al. (2025)), with local wave observations in Exmouth Gulf used where available. As highlighted in Chapter 3, we did not consider waves for the habitat future predictions however, included for extreme event case studies where waves can influence nearshore circulation and coastal water levels through wave driven setup, while wave generated bed stresses may affect sediment transport and intertidal morphology.
Wave forcing is therefore relevant to the regional model’s assessment of extreme coastal conditions. It also provides a basis for investigating how wave conditions interact with the tidal signal across the coastal domain.
An overview of the spatial domains and numerical model forcing datasets is illustrated in Figure 6.9.






Figure 6.9: Overview of the model boundary conditions, forcing datasets, and spatial model domains (Exmouth Gulf, Giralia, Cape Preston, and Urala).






6.3.3 Field Data Collection Campaign
Field collected hydrodynamic data—primarily continuous water level time series—were utilised for model calibration and validation. A comprehensive monitoring campaign was conducted across the study regions from November 2023 to February 2025, capturing ambient, spring-neap, and extreme event dynamics. For detailed information regarding field campaign design, sensor specifications, deployment locations, and data processing methodologies, readers are referred to Chapter 16.


6.3.4 Bed Roughness and Vegetation Parameterisation
Flow resistance across diverse intertidal and benthic habitats was parameterised using baseline habitat mapping derived from Project A (Hickey et al., 2025). Habitat maps do not directly provide Manning’s roughness coefficients. The mapped habitat classes must therefore be translated into numerical roughness classes that can be assigned to the hydrodynamic mesh. This translation is a model parameterisation step and involves assumptions about the hydraulic resistance associated with each habitat type. For calibration simulations, spatially varying Manning’s roughness coefficients (\(n\)) assigned by habitat type based on existing literatures (Arefin et al., 2026; Kumbier et al., 2022; Medeiros, 2023; Rodríguez et al., 2017; Vulliet et al., 2023), as summarised in Table 6.1.

For predictive future habitat simulations where habitat distributions evolve over time, a uniform baseline bed roughness of \(n = 0.023 \text{ s m}^{-1/3}\) was applied across domains, with vegetation-induced flow resistance introduced dynamically via Baptist canopy formulations.
In addition to habitat mapping derived roughness, LiDAR derived vegetation properties were used to represent vegetation influences in the model. The vegetation data provide spatial information that can be used to characterise the structure of vegetated areas more explicitly than a habitat label alone. The relevant properties and processing procedures are documented in Chapter 16.

title: 7  Calibration and Validation
text:
7.2 Hydrodynamic Calibration and Validation
Hydrodynamics govern tidal inundation, water movement and bed shear stress across the intertidal landscape. Inundation characteristics can also provide indirect information about salinity-related habitat constraints, although salinity itself is not explicitly simulated in the predictive framework (Section 3.3.4). Accurate simulation of water levels and inundation timing is therefore essential for evaluating habitat dynamics.
The Giralia hydrodynamic model was calibrated and validated using field observations collected between November 2023 and February 2025. The monitoring network captured a wide range of hydrodynamic conditions, including spring–neap tidal cycles, seasonal water level fluctuations, and episodic atmospheric disturbances. For detailed descriptions of sensor specifications, station coordinates, quality control, and data processing workflows, readers are referred to Chapter 16.
Model calibration involved iterative adjustment of physical parameters related to bottom roughness and vegetation drag, together with numerical settings and boundary conditions:

Bottom Roughness: Transitioned from a uniform bed roughness to spatially variable Manning’s roughness coefficients (\(n\)) assigned across benthic habitat classes (see also Chapter 6 for more details) to account for momentum dissipation across channels, mudflats, and vegetated zones.
Vegetation Drag: Inundation resistance within mangrove stands was explicitly parameterised using the Baptist canopy formulation (Baptist et al., 2007), incorporating field-measured tree heights and stem densities.
Time Step and CFL Sensitivity: Various computational time steps (\(dt\)) ranging from 15 s to 300 s (specifically tested at 15, 30, 60, 120, 150, and 300 s) and Courant numbers (CFL between 0.7 and 0.9) were evaluated. Based on calibration performance, a time step of 60 s combined with a maximum CFL of 0.7 was selected to ensure computational efficiency without compromising accuracy.
Minimum Water Depth: The threshold water depth for computation and wet/dry cell handling was set to \(0.01\text{ m}\).
Process Inclusions and Exclusions: The calibration testing process evaluated model sensitivity by excluding sediment transport and salinity dynamics, while incorporating the composite heat flux model to accurately capture thermodynamic and meteorological forcings.
Boundary Adjustments: Lateral boundary configurations were evaluated testing Neumann conditions versus omitting explicitly defined boundary conditions (treated as closed walls). Based on these sensitivity tests, omitting explicit lateral boundary constraints (with open boundary forcing driven purely by water level time series) yielded the most stable and physically consistent results.


7.2.1 Quantitative Performance Evaluation
Model accuracy was evaluated by comparing simulated water surface elevations directly against pressure sensor derived water level observations across key monitoring stations representing distinct intertidal zones (creek mouth, lower creek, mid-intertidal flat, and upper algal mat, see Figure 7.1).
Performance across the monitoring network demonstrated strong statistical agreement:

Correlation (\(R\)): Consistently high across all stations, exceeding \(R > 0.90\), indicating excellent reproduction of water levels.
Regression Slope and Bias: Regression slopes exceeded \(0.90\) at nearly all stations (with a slope of \(0.74\) retained at the upper intertidal boundary due to extreme shallow wetting–drying dynamics). Absolute water level bias remained minimal across the domain (\(< 0.007 \text{ m}\)).
Error Metrics: Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) values remained below \(0.20 \text{ m}\) across all monitoring locations under both spring and neap regimes.

These metrics indicate that the model reproduces spatial variability in water levels, peak water levels and drying thresholds across the intertidal gradient.
The spatial and temporal progression of the simulated water surface across Giralia Bay is illustrated in Figure 7.1. The model accurately reproduces the asymmetric tidal wave propagation, characterised by prolonged ebb drainage within the intertidal creek network and rapid wetting during flood spring tides. We have also tested the model for various conditions e.g., typical conditions and storm conditions which all predicted with similar statistical metrics as above providing condifdence in the approach.








Figure 7.1: Dynamic hydrodynamic simulation and water level time series comparison across monitoring stations in the Giralia domain.

title: 7  Calibration and Validation
text:
7.3 Mangrove Model Validation

7.3.1 Historical Mangrove Observations (2000–2023)
To establish a baseline for assessing future changes in mangrove ecosystems in the Giralia region, it is crucial to understand observed mangrove dynamics under present environmental conditions and to evaluate the model’s ability to reproduce the current mangrove extent.
We utilised monthly mangrove maps derived from Landsat imagery by Hickey et al. (2025) (part of Project A of the WAMSI Mardie Marine and Intertidal Research Offset Program) to examine temporal variability in mangrove distribution. Although the Landsat-derived dataset provides monthly observations over the available satellite record, the mangrove extents in 2000 and 2023 are compared in Figure 7.2 to illustrate any longer-term shifts in the mangrove distribution alongside corresponding water level variability recorded at the Exmouth tide station over the same period.
Overall, the Landsat observations indicate that mangrove extent in the Giralia region has remained relatively stable over the past two decades, with only minor changes in spatial distribution. Seasonal variations in water level did not result in substantial changes in mapped mangrove extent. However, a closer examination reveals that prolonged interannual environmental variations can produce more pronounced localised changes. For instance, mangrove dieback is evident in parts of the upper intertidal region during extended El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) periods (Lovelock et al., 2017), suggesting that prolonged periods of lower inundation relative to typical hydrodynamic conditions can adversely influence mangrove survival.
Despite these episodic changes, the overall mangrove extent has remained broadly consistent over the approximately 20-year observation period. This relative stability provides a suitable present-day baseline against which future changes under altered environmental conditions can be assessed.






Figure 7.2: Water level observations and historical mangrove extent in the Giralia region. (a) Water level recorded at the Exmouth tide station (WA Data Catalogue) displaying monthly range and monthly mean. (b) Comparison of Landsat-derived mangrove extents between 2000 and 2023 (Hickey et al., 2025).






7.3.2 Model Initialisation & Performance Evaluation
Figure 7.3 shows the mangrove distribution simulated under representative present-day tidal conditions. These simulations used water-level forcing reconstructed from four dominant astronomical tidal constituents (M2, S2, K1 and O1), with amplitudes and phases derived by harmonic analysis of tide-gauge observations. This provides a consistent tidal baseline for evaluating present-day mangrove extent. Chapter 3 describes the derivation of this forcing, and Table 3.2 lists the constituent parameters.
The spatial agreement between modelled and observed mangrove extents was evaluated using the approach described in Chapter 4 by categorising grid cells:

True Positives (Green): Correctly predicted mangrove areas.
False Negatives (Black): Observed mangrove areas missed by the model.
False Positives (Red): Areas predicted as mangrove where none were observed.

To quantitatively evaluate spatial performance, precision, recall, and the \(F_1\) score were computed and shown in Table 7.1:

The spatial comparison shows moderate agreement between modelled and observed mangrove distributions. The model reproduces broad features of the present-day extent, but also misses some observed mangrove areas and predicts mangroves in some areas where they were not observed.
In addition to spatial extent, the model predicts key structural attributes of the mangrove canopy:

Stem Diameter (\(d\)): Predicted spatial distributions (Figure 7.3 b) indicate relatively mature mangroves within the stable core of the mangrove distribution, characterised by larger stem diameters.
Stem Height (\(h\)): Corresponding spatial distributions (Figure 7.3 c) reflect taller individuals within core zones and smaller, shorter individuals transitioning toward the margins of the habitat.

The predicted gradients in stem diameter and height are qualitatively consistent with the expected transition from established mangrove stands to marginal habitat. However, these canopy attributes have not been quantitatively validated against independent observations, so their ecological plausibility does not establish the accuracy of the predicted canopy structure.

title: 7  Calibration and Validation
text:
7.5 Summary of Giralia Model Reliability
Reliable hydrodynamic predictions also depend on accurate representation of bathymetry and topography. Creek geometry and intertidal elevations influence tidal propagation, drainage, flow pathways and the timing and duration of inundation. Errors in these inputs can therefore affect both simulated water levels and the habitat conditions inferred from them. Uncertainty in the elevation data and their representation on the model grid should be considered when interpreting the calibration results and subsequent habitat projections.The combined hydrodynamic, mangrove, and cyanobacterial mat calibration results demonstrate that the Giralia domain model reproduces the present-day physical and biological dynamics of the hyper-arid intertidal ecosystem with a reasonable accuracy. With verified hydrodynamic forcing, low water level errors (\(RMSE < 0.20 \text{ m}\)), and validated spatial extents for key habitats, this calibrated model provides confidence in the approach for predicting intertidal habitat migration and response under future Sea Level Rise (SLR). Chapter 8 and Chapter 9 shows the mangrove and algal mat responses to the future sea level rise.

title: 4  Model Overview and Evaluation
text:
4.6 Evaluation
For both mangrove and algal-mat models, evaluation followed the same general framework, allowing classification performance to be assessed consistently across the two habitat-modelling approaches. The RF classifier was evaluated against the held-out test subset using the confusion matrix, precision, recall and F1-score.
Precision measures the proportion of locations predicted as persistent mat (or mangrove presence) that were also classified as persistent (or mangrove presence) in the observed mask:
\[
\mathrm{Precision} =
\frac{TP}{TP+FP},
\tag{4.34}\]
where \(TP\) and \(FP\) denote true positives and false positives, respectively.
Recall measures the proportion of observed mangroves (or algal-mat locations) correctly identified by the model:
\[
\mathrm{Recall} =
\frac{TP}{TP+FN},
\tag{4.35}\]
where \(FN\) denotes false negatives.
The F1-score provides a single measure that balances precision and recall:
\[
F_1 =
2 \frac{\mathrm{Precision}\times\mathrm{Recall}}
{\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}.
\tag{4.36}\]
A true positive is a location classified as presence in both the observed mask and model prediction. A false positive is predicted as presence but does not meet the observed criterion, while a false negative meets the observed criterion but is predicted as absence. Precision, recall and F1-score were considered together because they capture different aspects of classification performance.
The evaluation metrics reported for model validation should be calculated from the predictions for the held-out test subset. For the algal mat validation, although the classifier was subsequently refitted using all valid observations to produce the final spatial prediction, performance calculated from these same observations would represent in-sample performance rather than independent validation. In addition, because the training and test observations were divided randomly among mesh faces, spatial autocorrelation may cause the test metrics to overestimate performance when predicting spatially separate areas. Spatially blocked validation would provide a stronger test of spatial transferability. The resulting model should be interpreted as a data-driven classification of hydrodynamic conditions associated with persistent mapped cyanobacterial mat occurrence. It does not explicitly simulate mat growth, mortality, dispersal, physiological responses to salinity or temperature, or feedbacks between mats and sediment dynamics.

title: 9  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
9.2 Results and Comparative Analysis
Both the Random Forest (RF) classifier[cite: 1] and the threshold-based optimisation approach[cite: 2] reveal a clear landward migration of cyanobacterial mats over the 100-year projection period, closely tracking the inland elongation of the tidal creek network. However, the two modelling paradigms capture distinct facets of spatial reorganisation. The Random Forest model predicts broader, highly continuous spatial coverage with smooth, non-linear transitions across the supratidal gradient, showing extensive Year 50 (red) and Year 100 (black) mat persistence stretching deep into the southern domain across all scenarios[cite: 1]. In contrast, the threshold-based optimisation approach enforces strict hydrodynamic boundaries—including inundation frequency, 98th percentile water depth, and mean depth limits—producing sharply delineated spatial bands that more explicitly highlight habitat compression and drowning thresholds[cite: 2].
Zonation remains coherent and well-defined during the first 50 years across all projections, but structural divergence between the climate scenarios becomes stark by Year 100. Under the low-emissions SSP119 scenario, both models project successful and extensive landward migration, with cyanobacterial mats establishing expansive cover across newly wetted supratidal flats in the southern sector. Under the moderate SSP370 scenario, migration remains progressive, though spatial continuity begins to fragment as tidal channels extend landward. However, under the high-emissions SSP585 scenario, the models reveal severe habitat degradation and divergence. While the RF model maintains moderate spatial persistence[cite: 1], the threshold-based model demonstrates a drastic contraction of the Year 100 mat footprint[cite: 2], where the rapid velocity of sea-level rise exceeds the landward migration capacity and inundation tolerance limits of the mats, resulting in severe coastal squeeze and permanent submergence of historical intertidal zones.

title: 8  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
8.3 Scenario Profiles & Ecosystem Trajectories

SSP119 (Low SLR – 0.5 m): Dynamic Eco-morphodynamic Equilibrium

Ecosystem Regime: Stable and resilient.
Trajectory: Minimal seaward edge drown-out, paired with steady, localised landward expansion. Intertidal zonation and core canopy architecture remain largely intact throughout the 100-year window.

SSP370 (Intermediate SLR – 0.9 m): Non-linear Ecological Reorganisation

Ecosystem Regime: Spatial restructuring and regime shift past Year 50.
Trajectory: Seaward fringe drown-out is substantial, but active creek elongation allows rapid landward colonisation into newly flooded accommodation space, preserving high net biomass.

SSP585 (High SLR – 1.25 m): Threshold Exceedance & Habitat Collapse

Ecosystem Regime: Marine inundation outpaces ecological adaptation.
Trajectory: An initial inland expansion surge (Years 40–60) is quickly truncated by severe estuarine drowning. Over 85% of the original mangrove footprint is permanently submerged by Year 100, leaving survival restricted to a diminished landward fringe along elevated basin margins.




Insight: Giralia Bay mangroves demonstrate high capacity for landward adaptation under low-to-moderate SLR rates. However, under high-emission forcing (SSP585), the pace of sea-level rise exceeds maximum ecological migration rates, triggering severe net habitat contraction and coastal squeeze.

title: 9  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
section: 9.2 Comparison Between Machine Learning (RF) and Threshold-Based Approaches
text:
9.2 Comparison Between Machine Learning (RF) and Threshold-Based Approaches
Both modelling approaches demonstrate a primary general trend: cyanobacterial mats migrate landward over the 100-year simulation window, tracking the inland extension of tidal creeks and rising intertidal wetting fronts. However, significant differences emerge in how each framework handles spatial continuity and physical boundaries.
The Random Forest (RF) approach captures broader, more persistent spatial coverage with smoother non-linear transitions. Because it is a data-driven machine learning classifier trained on hydrodynamic features, it predicts the persistence of algal mats even under moderate-to-high stress conditions. Conversely, the threshold-based optimisation approach enforces strict physical limits (such as precise inundation frequency, maximum depth thresholds, and bed shear stress boundaries). This causes the threshold-based model to produce sharper spatial zoning bands that are highly sensitive to rapid elevation changes and water-depth increases. As such, we noticed a significant decline in presistent algal mats for moderate-to-high stress scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585) compared to SSP119.
crumbs: 9  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise

title: 9  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
9.3 Scenario-Wise Comparison
Evaluating performance across emission scenarios reveals diverging trajectories regarding long-term survival.

SSP119 and SSP370: Under low (SSP119) and moderate (SSP370) emissions, both approaches indicate successful landward migration. Algal mats maintain high coverage fractions as they shift into newly created supratidal accommodation space.
SSP585 (High Emissions): Under the high-emissions SSP585 scenario by Year 100, the models show starkly contrasting outcomes regarding mat survival. The threshold-based model projects complete or near-complete mortality (drowning) of the algal mat communities across the domain. This total die-back occurs because the rapid rate of sea-level rise under SSP585 exceeds the maximum vertical accretion capacity and physiological inundation tolerance limits enforced by the threshold parameters. Consequently, the intertidal zone experiences severe coastal squeeze, permanently submerging historical flats below the viable depth threshold. While the RF approach also shows substantial contraction under SSP585, its probabilistic classification allows for residual patches to persist in isolated high-intertidal niches.

An important methodological note is that simulations were executed independently for mangroves and algal mats without two-way biological competition feedback. As a result, overlaying the independent predictions reveals noticeable spatial overlaps instances where both mangroves and cyanobacterial mats occupy the same computational grid cell. In reality, mature mangrove expansion often induces shading, sediment modification, and root competition that can inhibit cyanobacterial mat development. Addressing these overlapping zones in future coupled iterations will help refine intertidal niche partitioning and competitive exclusion dynamics in eco-morphodynamic models.






NoteSummary: Trajectories of Algal Mats in Giralia Bay



Synthesising multi-decadal predictions from our data-driven frameworks (Random Forest vs. Threshold-Based Optimisation) reveals critical distinctions in how Giralia Bay’s cyanobacterial mat communities adapt to sea-level rise across emission pathways:


9.4 Scenario Profiles & Ecosystem Trajectories

SSP119 (Low SLR – 0.5 m): Expansive Supratidal Migration

Ecosystem Regime: Stable and expansive.
Trajectory: Cyanobacterial mats steadily migrate landward onto newly wetted supratidal salt flats, closely tracking the inland elongation of active tidal creeks. High spatial continuity and overall habitat footprint are preserved across both modelling approaches throughout the 100-year period.

SSP370 (Intermediate SLR – 0.9 m): Progressive Relocation & Spatial Fragmentation

Ecosystem Regime: High mobility accompanied by structural restructuring.
Trajectory: Progressive landward shift into upper accommodation space maintains significant mat coverage. However, expanding tidal channels begin to fragment continuous mat sheets into localized supratidal patches, introducing minor divergence between machine learning persistence and hydro-dynamic threshold bounds.

SSP585 (High SLR – 1.25 m): Threshold Exceedance & Habitat Collapse

Ecosystem Regime: Severe coastal squeeze and catastrophic drowning.
Trajectory: An initial landward migration phase (Years 1–50) is abruptly halted as the rapid velocity of sea-level rise exceeds the physiological inundation tolerances and landward accommodation limits of the mats. Under the threshold-based model, near-total mortality occurs by Year 100 as historical flats are permanently submerged below viable water-depth limits.




Insight: Cyanobacterial mats exhibit high landward migration potential under low-to-moderate SLR rates (SSP119 and SSP370) by capitalising on expanding supratidal wetting zones. However, under high-emission forcing (SSP585), rapid water-depth increases trigger widespread drowning and severe habitat contraction, highlighting critical physiological boundaries across the supratidal gradient.

Mouth & Lower Creek: The model exhibited excellent agreement with field measurements, achieving an RMSE of \(\approx 0.068\text{ m}\), a bias of \(-0.07\text{ m}\), a slope of \(0.99\), a scatter index of \(\approx 0.17\), and a correlation coefficient (\(R\)) of \(\approx 0.98\).

title: 10  Calibration and Validation
text:
10.2 Mangrove Model Validation
To establish a baseline for present environmental conditions and evaluate future mangrove redistribution, we assessed the performance of the mangrove dynamic model across the Urala region. Following the approach used for the Giralia calibration and validation, our primary focus is on long-term changes; thus, we considered only the dominant tidal constituents (M2, S2, K1 and O1; see Section 3.3) for predicting both present-day conditions and future sea-level rise (SLR) scenarios.

10.2.1 Historical Mangrove Observations (2000–2023)
To examine the temporal variability in mangrove distribution across the Urala domain, monthly mangrove maps derived from Landsat imagery by Hickey et al. (2025) were analysed. The mangrove extents between 2000 and 2023 are compared in Figure 10.2 to illustrate multi-decadal dynamics alongside long-term water-level variability recorded at the Onslow tide station—the closest operational tide gauge to the Urala domain.
While historical satellite observations reveal a overall stable mangrove footprint similar to the Giralia region over recent decades, key localised structural differences emerge upon spatial inspection (Figure 10.2 b). Unlike the core interior stability seen in Giralia, Urala displays more active dynamic shifts along its complex creek network and seaward fringes:

Fringing Loss and Retreat: Notable localised mangrove dieback and retreat (indicated in red) are concentrated along the narrow, highly exposed tidal channels and seaward creek boundaries. This localised dieback aligns with regional observations of upper intertidal stress triggered during extended El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) low water-level anomalies (Lovelock et al., 2017).
Seaward Expansion and Colonisation: Concurrently, minor localised seaward expansion and gain (indicated in black) occur in sheltered intertidal zones, indicating ongoing localized geomorphic adjustments and dynamic colonisation.

Despite these minor spatial fluctuations along the fringe boundaries, the core mangrove extent in Urala has remained largely resilient over the ~23-year observation window. This consistent baseline provides a reliable present-day benchmark against which future hydrodynamic modifications and climate-driven sea-level shifts can be evaluated.






Figure 10.2: Water level observations and historical mangrove extent in the Urala region. (a) Water level recorded at the Onslow tide station (WA Data Catalogue) displaying monthly range and monthly mean. (b) Comparison of Landsat-derived mangrove extents between 2000 and 2023 (Hickey et al., 2025), highlighting areas of stability (no change), loss, and gain.

title: 10  Calibration and Validation
text:
10.5 Chapter Summary
The calibration and validation provide a basis for evaluating present-day conditions at Urala, with performance differing among the hydrodynamic and habitat components.

Hydrodynamics: Agreement was strongest at the creek mouth and lower creek, with correlation of approximately 0.98. Water-level amplitudes were less accurately reproduced on the intertidal flats and mat habitats, where the model captured approximately 70% of observed inundation events. These differences remain relevant when interpreting habitat predictions.
Mangroves: Transferring the Giralia mangrove parameterisation to Urala initially resulted in an overprediction of mangrove extent. To address this, a proxy salinity mass-balance module was introduced to represent the additional constraint imposed by hypersalinity on mangrove establishment across infrequently inundated salt flats. This modification improved the spatial representation of mangrove extent, achieving a precision of \(0.680\), recall of \(0.534\) and an F1 score of \(0.598\). These results indicate a better balance between the identification of existing mangrove areas and the limitation of overpredicted extent. However, independent validation of predicted vegetation structural attributes, including stem diameter and height, is not reported here.

Cyanobacterial Mat Multi-Approach Performance: Threshold optimisation and Random Forest classification were evaluated as separate approaches for predicting persistent mat distributions from modelled bed shear stress, inundation frequency and water depth.

Implications for model application: The Urala results show why transfer between sites requires evaluation against local observations and consideration of site-specific habitat controls. The introduction of the salinity proxy addresses a limitation of using hydro-morphological suitability alone. Present-day agreement supports using the framework to explore future responses, while the projections remain conditional on the elevation data, boundary forcing, salinity representation and ecological parameterisation. Agreement in present-day habitat extent does not independently validate future habitat migration or vegetation structural dynamics.
Building upon this validated framework, the long-term responses and future trajectories of these intertidal ecosystems under various climate-driven sea-level rise (SLR) scenarios are presented in Chapter 11 and Chapter 12.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
text:
3.4 Sea-Level Rise (SLR) Scenarios
To evaluate the future response of intertidal ecosystems to accelerating environmental change, we examine three Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (Calvin et al., 2023; Fox-Kemper et al., 2021; Garner et al., 2021; O’Neill et al., 2016): SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585.

3.4.1 Rationale and Objectives of the Three-Tiered Approach
Choosing a multi-tiered scenario approach rather than a single projection is critical for risk-informed coastal management. By bracketing future greenhouse gas emissions from aggressive mitigation to high-emission trajectories, these scenarios allow us to test the non-linear boundaries of habitat survival: - SSP119 (Low SLR, \(\approx 0.5\text{ m}\) by 2125): Represents a sustainability-focused, low-emission future (\(1.5^\circ\text{C}\) warming). This scenario intends to show whether intertidal habitats can comfortably keep pace with slow, predictable sedimentation and vertical accretion under minimal stress. - SSP370 (Medium SLR, \(\approx 0.95\text{ m}\) by 2125): Models a medium-to-high emission pathway featuring regional rivalry. This scenario tests transitional tipping points where landward migration pathways may begin to encounter physical or anthropogenic barriers (e.g., infrastructure or steep coastal topography). - SSP585 (High SLR, \(\approx 1.25\text{ m}\) by 2125): Projects a fossil-fuel-intensive development strategy. This scenario is designed to test extreme stress limits, identifying thresholds of severe coastal drowning, rapid habitat contraction, or total ecosystem collapse.
Implementing this spectrum establishes a robust envelope of potential future outcomes (Figure 3.2).






Figure 3.2: Sea level rise (SLR) projections based on Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios (SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585), representing low, medium, and high sea-level rise trajectories projected through 2125.



For each scenario, the prescribed sea-level-rise increment was added to the water-level signal reconstructed from the selected tidal constituents. The resulting time series was applied at the offshore open boundaries of the regional hydrodynamic models.
While climate change encompasses multiple interconnected environmental drivers—including shifting wind regimes, warming temperatures, varying atmospheric humidity, intensified storm frequency, and complex root-zone salinity dynamics—this study intentionally isolates sea level rise. Other environmental and meteorological forcings are maintained at contemporary ambient conditions for the long-term simulations while salinity and storm conditions are not considered. Decoupling SLR from these confounding variables allows us to isolate and evaluate its direct physical and hydrodynamic impacts on intertidal inundation, bed-shear stress evolution, and landward mangrove and algal mat migration.

title: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
11.3 Scenario Profiles & Natural Ecosystem Responses

SSP119 (Low SLR – 0.5 m): Eco-Morphodynamic Stability

Ecosystem Regime: Stable and resilient.
Trajectory: Minimal seaward edge drowning. Tidal prism increases are small, resulting in minor creek expansion and steady, in-situ canopy retention. Intertidal zonation remains largely balanced throughout the 100-year window.

SSP370 (Intermediate SLR – 0.9 m): Headward Incision & Inland Colonisation

Ecosystem Regime: Dynamic creek-mediated relocation.
Trajectory: Accelerated SLR increases tidal prism volumes, driving deep headward creek incision (\(>5\text{ km}\) inland). These newly incised channels serve as vital corridors, facilitating rapid landward mangrove colonisation and a temporary surge in total biomass.

SSP585 (High SLR – 1.25 m): Severe Seaward Drowning & Coastal Squeeze

Ecosystem Regime: Extreme spatial restructuring and initial footprint collapse.
Trajectory: While channel networks fully expand, extreme inundation outpaces bed accretion at the lower-intertidal boundary. The original baseline footprint suffers terminal collapse (\(<5\%\) remaining by Year 100), forcing survival to rely entirely on landward migration along newly formed creek banks.
crumbs: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise

title: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
11.4 Impact of Coastal Development (Bund Walls)

Impassable Barrier to Migration: Natural mangrove survival under moderate-to-high SLR depends entirely on uninhibited landward migration. The proposed rigid bund walls intercept this natural retreat pathway, trapping vegetation against the infrastructure.
Quantified Habitat Loss: While unconstrained baseline scenarios (SSP370/SSP585) sustain a relative spatial expansion factor of 2.0× to 2.35× by Year 100, development-constrained scenarios (DEV_SSP370/DEV_SSP585) experience dramatic canopy retreat, dropping to 1.2× to 1.6×.
Net Reduction: This restriction results in a severe 32% to 41% net reduction in late-century mangrove habitat availability, alongside a permanent suppression of secondary tidal creek branching.


Insight: Under natural conditions, Urala mangroves survive moderate-to-high SLR by migrating inland via newly incised creek networks. However, the introduction of impermeable bund walls blocks this landward escape route, triggering acute coastal squeeze and severe long-term habitat loss.
