title: 12  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
section: 12.2 Comparative Dynamics Across Scenarios and Modelling Approaches
text:
12.2 Comparative Dynamics Across Scenarios and Modelling Approaches

12.2.1 Overview of Spatial and Cross-Shore Patterns
Spatial distribution maps and cross-shore transects were used to assess projected changes in mangrove and persistent algal mat distributions under three SLR scenarios (SSP119, SSP370 and SSP585). Spatial maps Figure 12.3 - Figure 12.8 (Panel a) show the predicted distributions at Year 100, with algal mats and mangroves overlaid on bed elevation. A representative seaward-to-landward transect is indicated by a chartreuse line. Alongshore-averaged cross-shore profiles Figure 12.3 - Figure 12.8 (Panels b–d) summarise habitat coverage at Present (Year 0), Year 50 and Year 100, respectively. These profiles express the fraction of locations occupied by each habitat along the cross-shore distance, thereby integrating spatial variability across the modelled coastline.
The threshold-based and Random Forest (RF) approaches produced broadly similar trajectories of habitat change, including the progressive fragmentation and landward redistribution of algal mats under increasing SLR. Mangrove distributions were identical between the two approaches because mangrove suitability was determined using the same underlying hydrodynamic and elevation criteria. Differences between the approaches therefore reflect their respective representations of algal mat suitability.






Figure 12.9: Direct comparison of predicted algal mat coverage fractions between the threshold based approach (solid lines) and the Random Forest model (dashed lines) across three sea level rise scenarios: (a) SSP119, (b) SSP370, and (c) SSP585[cite: 1]. Profiles illustrate temporal trajectories at Present (Year 0; black), Year 50 (green), and Year 100 (red) along a seaward to landward cross shore distance of 0 to 18,000 m.





12.2.2 Threshold-Based versus Random Forest Approaches

12.2.2.1 Baseline Habitat Distribution
At Present (Year 0; black curves in Figure 12.9), the threshold-based approach (solid line) predicted a relatively broad, continuous distribution of algal mats between approximately 6,000 and 11,000 m along the cross-shore profile, with peak coverage fractions exceeding 0.60–0.70. In comparison, the Random Forest (RF) approach (dashed line) predicted a narrower distribution, concentrated between approximately 5,000 and 9,500 m, with peak coverage of approximately 0.60–0.65.
These differences reflect the contrasting representations of habitat suitability in the two approaches. The threshold-based model classifies locations according to predefined environmental criteria, whereas the RF model estimates habitat occurrence from relationships among environmental predictors and observed distributions. The differences in predicted extent and peak coverage indicate that the representation of algal mat suitability influences the estimated baseline distribution, particularly near habitat boundaries.


12.2.2.2 Responses to Increasing Sea-Level Rise
Differences between the approaches become more apparent in their projections for Year 50 (green curves) and Year 100 (red curves; Figure 12.9). The threshold-based model (solid lines) generally produces sharper transitions in algal mat coverage, reflecting the discrete classification of locations according to predefined suitability criteria. As environmental conditions move beyond these criteria, locations become unsuitable, resulting in abrupt reductions in predicted coverage.
In contrast, the RF model (dashed lines) produces more gradual spatial transitions and retains low predicted coverage in some landward areas beyond 12,000 m under moderate-to-high SLR (Panels b and c in Figure 12.9). This broader distribution of residual habitat reflects differences in how the two approaches represent environmental suitability. However, the persistence of predicted algal mat occurrence does not necessarily indicate the presence of viable ecological refugia, which would require further validation against environmental conditions and observed habitat distributions.
Despite these differences, both approaches project a progressive decline in algal mat coverage as SLR intensifies. Their agreement in the overall direction of change indicates that the predicted loss of algal mat habitat is consistent across modelling approaches, although the spatial extent and continuity of the remaining habitat differ.



12.2.3 Scenario-Specific Projections

12.2.3.1 SSP119: Low Emissions and Lower Sea-Level Rise
Present (Year 0). Both approaches predict distinct spatial zonation between mangroves and algal mats (black curves in Panel a of Figure 12.9). Mangroves predominantly occupy the lower intertidal zone, between approximately 3,000 and 8,000 m along the cross-shore profile, whereas algal mats occur farther landward across the higher supratidal flats, where elevations range from approximately 0.5 to 1.8 m.
Year 50. Changes in algal mat distribution remain relatively limited (green curves in Panel a of Figure 12.9), although some fragmentation develops near the seaward margin between approximately 6,000 and 8,000 m. Coverage fractions remain relatively high, at approximately 0.40–0.60, across the central and landward flats between 10,000 and 14,000 m in both models.
Year 100. Under SSP119, both approaches project the persistence of substantial algal mat coverage across the higher intertidal and supratidal flats (red curves in Panel a of Figure 12.9). Coverage fractions of approximately 0.20–0.40 remain between 10,000 and 16,000 m, indicating that considerable portions of the existing distribution persist over the simulation period. Mangrove distributions also remain comparatively stable along tidal channels and their margins.
Overall, SSP119 produces the smallest changes in habitat distribution among the three scenarios. The persistence of algal mats across the higher flats indicates comparatively limited losses of predicted habitat under lower SLR, although the precise extent of persistence varies with the suitability-modelling approach.


12.2.3.2 SSP370: Intermediate-to-High Emissions and Moderate Sea-Level Rise
Year 50. Under SSP370, algal mat coverage becomes increasingly fragmented, particularly near expanding tidal channels and lower-lying areas (green curves in Panel b of Figure 12.9). Peak coverage decreases from baseline values exceeding 0.60 to approximately 0.30–0.50, while the principal coverage band shifts towards the landward portion of the profile, between approximately 10,000 and 14,000 m. Mangrove coverage increases locally along creek margins, indicating a redistribution of predicted mangrove occurrence within the intertidal zone.
Year 100. By Year 100, both approaches predict substantial reductions in algal mat coverage (red curves in Panel b of Figure 12.9). The threshold-based model (solid line) restricts the remaining distribution to small, fragmented landward patches, predominantly beyond 12,000 m, with coverage fractions below 0.10. In contrast, the RF model (dashed line) retains a more spatially continuous distribution of low coverage between approximately 6,000 and 16,000 m, with fractions generally around 0.10–0.15.
These differences demonstrate that the estimated extent of residual algal mat habitat under SSP370 is sensitive to the modelling approach. The threshold-based model predicts a more restricted distribution once environmental criteria are no longer satisfied, whereas the RF model retains low predicted occurrence across a broader section of the profile. Nevertheless, both approaches indicate substantial habitat loss relative to the baseline distribution.
Mangroves occupy a broader cross-shore range, extending approximately from 2,000 to 12,000 m, although coverage fractions generally remain below 0.15–0.20. This pattern indicates a dispersed distribution of mangroves across the profile rather than the development of extensive, continuous forest cover.
Overall, SSP370 represents an intermediate trajectory of habitat change, characterised by substantial fragmentation and contraction of algal mats alongside a broader but relatively low-coverage distribution of mangroves.


12.2.3.3 SSP585: High Emissions and Rapid Sea-Level Rise
Year 50. SSP585 produces the most pronounced changes in habitat distribution by Year 50 (green curves in Panel c of Figure 12.9). Both approaches predict substantial reductions in algal mat coverage across the existing intertidal and supratidal flats, with peak coverage falling below 0.50 and the principal distribution shifting towards 10,000–14,000 m. At the same time, mangrove coverage increases temporarily across parts of the inland profile, particularly between 5,000 and 9,000 m, where fractions reach approximately 0.40.
This temporary increase suggests that rising water levels may create conditions favourable for mangrove occurrence in some locations that are currently less frequently inundated. However, the predicted increase in coverage should be interpreted as a change in modelled distribution rather than direct evidence of successful colonisation or long-term establishment.
Year 100. By Year 100, both approaches predict a near-complete loss of persistent algal mat habitat across the modelled profile (red curves in Panel c of Figure 12.9). The threshold-based model (solid line) predicts coverage fractions below 0.05 across almost the entire transect. The RF model (dashed line) produces a similarly pronounced decline but retains small residual peaks of approximately 0.10–0.15 near the landward margin, between approximately 11,000 and 17,000 m.
The persistence of these small residual areas highlights an important difference between the approaches under extreme SLR. Although the RF model predicts a broader distribution of residual algal mat occurrence, the ecological significance and long-term persistence of these areas remain uncertain. The agreement between the models on the overall decline, despite differences in residual coverage, indicates that the projected loss of algal mat habitat is robust to the choice of suitability-modelling approach at the broad spatial scale.
Mangrove coverage extends across a wide cross-shore range, approximately 2,000–15,000 m, but remains below 0.15 across most of the profile. This combination of broad spatial extent and low coverage suggests a dispersed distribution along portions of the intertidal landscape rather than the formation of extensive, contiguous mangrove forest.
Overall, SSP585 produces the greatest reduction in persistent algal mat coverage and the most substantial reorganisation of the modelled habitat distribution. Although both approaches project a pronounced decline, their differences in residual habitat extent indicate that uncertainty in the spatial distribution of remaining algal mats increases under the most severe SLR scenario.

12.3 Development Scenario

12.3.1 Synthesis of Scenario and Model Responses
Across all three SLR scenarios, the models project a consistent progression from relatively extensive algal mat distributions under SSP119 to increasingly fragmented habitat under SSP370 and near-complete loss of persistent algal mat coverage under SSP585. The magnitude of these changes increases with the severity of the SLR scenario.
The threshold-based and RF approaches agree on the broad direction of algal mat change but differ in the spatial extent and continuity of the remaining habitat. The threshold-based model tends to produce sharper spatial boundaries and more restricted residual distributions, whereas the RF model retains low levels of predicted occurrence across some additional landward areas. These differences are most apparent under SSP370 and SSP585, when environmental conditions depart more substantially from the baseline.
Mangrove projections remain identical between the approaches by design. Their response is characterised by shifts in spatial distribution and, under some scenarios, temporary increases in coverage, followed by a dispersed distribution across the tidal-channel network. These patterns should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalent changes in forest biomass, structural complexity or ecological function, which are not directly represented by coverage fractions alone.
Taken together, the projections indicate that future SLR may substantially reorganise the distribution of intertidal habitats in the study area. While the overall decline in persistent algal mat habitat is consistent across modelling approaches, uncertainty remains regarding the persistence of small landward patches and the extent to which changes in modelled suitability translate into realised habitat persistence. These uncertainties are particularly relevant under high-emissions conditions and should be considered when interpreting the projected capacity of intertidal habitats to persist or redistribute under future sea-level rise.

12.2.1 Threshold-Based versus Random Forest Approaches

12.2.1.1 Baseline Habitat Distribution
At Present (Year 0; black curves in Figure 12.13), the threshold-based approach (solid line) predicted a relatively broad, continuous distribution of algal mats between approximately 6,000 and 11,000 m along the cross-shore profile, with peak coverage fractions exceeding 0.60–0.70. In comparison, the Random Forest (RF) approach (dashed line) predicted a slighly narrower distribution, concentrated between approximately 5,000 and 9,500 m, with peak coverage of approximately 0.60–0.65.
These differences reflect a slighly different representations of habitat suitability in the two approaches. The threshold-based model classifies locations according to predefined environmental criteria, whereas the RF model estimates habitat occurrence from relationships among environmental predictors and observed distributions. The differences in predicted extent and peak coverage indicate that the representation of algal mat suitability influences the estimated baseline distribution, particularly near habitat boundaries.


12.2.1.2 Responses to Increasing Sea-Level Rise
Differences between the approaches become more apparent in their projections for Year 50 (green curves) and Year 100 (red curves; Figure 12.13). The threshold-based model (solid lines) generally produces sharper transitions in algal mat coverage, reflecting the discrete classification of locations according to predefined suitability criteria. As environmental conditions move beyond these criteria, locations become unsuitable, resulting in abrupt reductions in predicted coverage.
In contrast, the RF model (dashed lines) produces more gradual spatial transitions and retains low predicted coverage in some landward areas beyond 12,000 m under moderate-to-high SLR (Panels b and c in Figure 12.13). This broader distribution of residual habitat reflects differences in how the two approaches represent environmental suitability. However, the persistence of predicted algal mat occurrence does not necessarily indicate the presence of viable ecological refugia, which would require further validation against environmental conditions and observed habitat distributions.
Despite these differences, both approaches project a progressive decline in algal mat coverage as SLR intensifies. Their agreement in the overall direction of change indicates that the predicted loss of algal mat habitat is consistent across modelling approaches, although the spatial extent and continuity of the remaining habitat differ.



12.2.2 Scenario-Specific Projections

12.2.2.1 SSP119
Present (Year 0). Both approaches predict distinct habitat zonation (black curves in Panel a of Figure 12.13), with mangroves occupying the lower intertidal zone (3,000–8,000 m) and algal mats distributed farther landward across supratidal flats at elevations of approximately 0.5–1.8 m.
Year 50. Algal mat distributions remain relatively stable, although some fragmentation occurs near the seaward margin (6,000–8,000 m). Coverage remains approximately 0.40–0.60 across the central and landward flats (10,000–14,000 m; green curves in Panel a).
Year 100. Both approaches predict persistent algal mat coverage of approximately 0.20–0.40 between 10,000 and 16,000 m, while mangrove distributions remain comparatively stable along tidal channels and their margins (red curves in Panel a).


12.2.2.2 SSP370
Year 50. Algal mats become increasingly fragmented near tidal channels and lower-lying areas, with peak coverage declining from baseline values above 0.60 to approximately 0.30–0.50. The main coverage band shifts landward towards 10,000–14,000 m (green curves in Panel b). Mangrove coverage increases locally along creek margins.
Year 100. Algal mat coverage declines substantially in both models (red curves in Panel b). The threshold-based approach predicts small, fragmented patches predominantly beyond 12,000 m, with coverage below 0.10. In contrast, the RF approach retains a more continuous, low-coverage distribution between approximately 6,000 and 16,000 m, with fractions of 0.10–0.15.
Mangroves extend across a broader cross-shore range (2,000–12,000 m), but coverage generally remains below 0.15–0.20, indicating a dispersed distribution rather than extensive, continuous forest cover.


12.2.2.3 SSP585
Year 50. Both approaches predict substantial reductions in algal mat coverage across the intertidal and supratidal flats, with peak coverage falling below 0.50 and the main distribution shifting towards 10,000–14,000 m (green curves in Panel c). Mangrove coverage temporarily increases between approximately 5,000 and 9,000 m, reaching around 0.40. This pattern suggests a potential expansion of suitable inundation conditions, although increased modelled coverage does not establish successful mangrove colonisation.
Year 100. Persistent algal mat habitat approaches complete loss across the profile (red curves in Panel c). The threshold-based model predicts coverage below 0.05 across almost the entire transect, whereas the RF model retains small residual peaks of approximately 0.10–0.15 between 11,000 and 17,000 m.
Mangroves extend across approximately 2,000–15,000 m but remain below 0.15 coverage across most of the profile, indicating a dispersed distribution rather than extensive forest development.



12.2.3 Synthesis Across Sea-Level Rise Scenarios
The projected changes in habitat distribution become progressively more pronounced from SSP119 to SSP585. Under SSP119, substantial algal mat coverage persists across the higher flats, whereas SSP370 produces greater fragmentation and contraction. Under SSP585, both approaches predict near-complete loss of persistent algal mat habitat by Year 100. Mangroves exhibit temporary increases in coverage in some areas but remain relatively sparse under the more severe scenarios.
The two modelling approaches agree on the overall direction of change but differ in the predicted extent of residual algal mat habitat. The threshold-based model generally produces more restricted distributions with sharper spatial boundaries, while the RF model retains low coverage across a broader range of locations. These differences are most evident under SSP370 and SSP585, highlighting uncertainty in the spatial distribution of remaining habitat under increasing SLR. Overall, the results indicate substantial scenario-dependent restructuring of coastal wetland habitats, with the greatest losses of persistent algal mats under high SLR scenarios.

12.3.1 Algal Mat Responses Under Development Scenarios
The inclusion of developmental bund walls imposes a profound constraint on algal mat distribution, primarily by blocking tidal flows and altering inundation frequencies within the project footprint (spanning approximately 10,000 to 16,000 m along the cross-shore profile).

SSP119 Without bund walls, SSP119 maintains a robust and widespread band of algal mats across the higher supratidal flats. However, with the bund walls in place, algal mat coverage within the impoundment zone experiences a substantial reduction, losing an estimated 30% to 50% of its prospective high elevation habitat area as direct tidal connectivity is restricted.
SSP370 The combined pressure of moderate SLR and hydrodynamic blockage leads to severe fragmentation. Algal mat coverage is largely restricted to narrow exterior fringes outside the bund walls, accelerating habitat loss compared to the unconstrained baseline.
SSP585 Under extreme SLR, both the non development and development simulations show severe declines, resulting in a near complete collapse of persistent algal mats by Year 100. Consequently, SSP585 exhibits the most similar trajectory between with and without bund wall conditions, as extreme sea level rise and inundation overwhelm both natural and modified hydrodynamic niches.



12.3.2 Influence of Bund Walls on Mangrove Distributions
Mangrove distributions exhibit distinct shifts due to the modified hydrodynamic regime imposed by the bund walls. Because mangroves rely heavily on tidal channel networks and intertidal inundation (typically occupying the lower to mid intertidal zone between 2,000 and 9,000 m), the physical obstruction of flow paths by the bund walls restricts their inland expansion potential. While unconstrained scenarios show temporary landward migration of mangroves under rising sea levels, the bund walls impede lateral tidal propagation, forcing mangroves to concentrate more densely along unblocked seaward channels and creek margins. This results in a more constrained and compartmentalised mangrove distribution with lower overall cross-shore dispersion compared to the unconstrained SLR projections.
For comparative purposes, Figure 12.26 and Figure 12.27 illustrate the direct scenario-wise cross shore profile comparisons between unconstrained (without development, solid lines) and bund wall constrained (with development, dashed lines) model runs across Present, Year 50, and Year 100 timeframes.

The comparative profiles reveal that the magnitude of deviation caused by the developmental bund walls varies distinctly across SLR scenarios as well as different modelling approaches:

SSP119: The most prominent divergence occurs across the central plateau (7,000 to 11,000 m). Without development, unconstrained hydrodynamic conditions allow robust algal mat coverage fractions to reach 0.50 to 0.65. With development, the restricted tidal exchange within the impoundment zone suppresses coverage fractions, creating a noticeable gap between solid and dashed curves during Year 50 and Year 100.
SSP370: Moderate SLR combined with structural blockage induces pronounced vertical and spatial compression. The threshold based approach exhibits sharper drop offs in suitability boundaries, whereas the RF model displays more gradual tapering, yet both models highlight a marked reduction in peak coverage within the mid profile region.
SSP585: Under extreme SLR, the difference between development and non development profiles narrows significantly. Because extreme sea level rise inundates and overwhelms the low lying coastal margins regardless of local bund structures, both modelling approaches project near identical, severely depressed coverage trajectories by Year 100.







NoteSummary: Trajectories of Algal Mats in Urala Under SLR and Development Scenarios



Synthesising multi-decadal predictions from our data driven frameworks (Random Forest vs. Threshold Based Optimisation) under the Salt Project development scenario reveals critical insights into how structural bund walls and modified hydrodynamics alter cyanobacterial mat communities across emission pathways:


12.4 Scenario Profiles & Ecosystem Trajectories

SSP119 (Low SLR – 0.5 m): Impoundment Suppression & Restricted Supratidal Extent

Ecosystem Regime: Constrained and compartmentalised.
Trajectory: Unlike the unconstrained baseline where algal mats expand freely across higher supratidal flats, the presence of developmental bund walls restricts direct tidal connectivity. Algal mat coverage within the impoundment zone experiences a substantial reduction, losing an estimated 30% to 50% of its prospective high elevation habitat area as internal wetting is impeded.

SSP370 (Intermediate SLR – 0.9 m): Structural Fragmentation & Marginal Restriction

Ecosystem Regime: High structural stress and severe spatial fragmentation.
Trajectory: The combined pressures of moderate sea level rise and hydrodynamic blockage accelerate habitat loss. Continuous mat sheets are heavily broken up, with survival restricted largely to narrow exterior fringes outside the bund walls as inundation patterns are fundamentally altered.

SSP585 (High SLR – 1.25 m): Severe Drowning & Convergence with Baseline

Ecosystem Regime: Catastrophic habitat collapse.
Trajectory: Extreme sea level rise and rapid inundation overwhelm both natural and modified hydrodynamic niches. By Year 100, both development and non development simulations show near total collapse and severe contraction of persistent algal mats, resulting in highly similar trajectories between constrained and unconstrained runs.




Insight: Developmental bund walls fundamentally reshape local hydrodynamics, imposing severe constraints on algal mat persistence within the project footprint by restricting tidal exchange. While low to moderate scenarios (SSP119 and SSP370) exhibit pronounced divergence from unconstrained baselines due to structural blockage, extreme sea level rise (SSP585) overrides these engineering constraints as widespread drowning overwhelms the entire coastal system.

Trajectory: Extreme sea level rise and rapid inundation overwhelm both natural and modified hydrodynamic niches. By Year 100, both development and non development simulations show near total collapse and severe contraction of persistent algal mats, resulting in highly similar trajectories between constrained and unconstrained runs.




Insight: Developmental bund walls fundamentally reshape local hydrodynamics, imposing severe constraints on algal mat persistence within the project footprint by restricting tidal exchange. While low to moderate scenarios (SSP119 and SSP370) exhibit pronounced divergence from unconstrained baselines due to structural blockage, extreme sea level rise (SSP585) overrides these engineering constraints as widespread drowning overwhelms the entire coastal system.

13.3 Mangrove Model Validation

13.3.1 Historical Mangrove Observations (2000–2023)
Similar to the approach followed in other regional study areas (Giralia and Urala), we first examined the baseline mangrove dynamics at the Cape Preston site. We utilised monthly mangrove maps derived from Landsat imagery by Hickey et al. (2025) (part of Project A of this Mardie Marine and Intertidal Research Offset Program) to analyse temporal variability in mangrove distribution. Although the dataset provides continuous monthly observations over the satellite record, mangrove extents from 2000 and 2023 are compared in Figure 13.2 to illustrate long-term distribution shifts alongside corresponding water level variability recorded at the Onslow tide gauge over the same period.
The historical observation data demonstrates that mangrove extents in the Cape Preston region have remained remarkably stable over the past two decades, exhibiting minimal net change despite localised inter-annual fluctuations.






Figure 13.2: Water level observations and historical mangrove extent changes in the Cape Preston region. (a) Water level recorded at the Onslow tide gauge (WA Data Catalogue) displaying monthly range and monthly mean. (b) Comparison of Landsat-derived mangrove extents between 2000 and 2023 (Hickey et al., 2025), highlighting areas of no change, loss, and gain.



We achieved a reasonable prediction evaluation using the hydrodynamic model setup for Cape Preston. Unlike the Urala site where we applied a proxy salt balance function to mimic the hyper-saline salinity regime the Cape Preston site features a distinctly different inundation pattern. Due to these differences in hydrodynamic and topographical characteristics, the proxy salinity mass balance function did not perform or work as expected. Consequently, to minimise uncertainties stemming from a calibration function with lower confidence, we decided to drop the proxy salinity functions entirely for the Cape Preston simulations.
The performance of the resulting spatial mangrove prediction and calibration is summarised in Figure 13.3, yielding a quantitative evaluation score of Precision: 0.65, Recall: 0.52, and an F1 Score: 0.58.

(a) Spatial confusion map highlighting true positives (green), false negatives (yellow), and false positives (red) alongside quantitative performance metrics (\(F_1\) score = 0.58, precision = 0.65, recall = 0.52).

The machine-learning (Random Forest) approach achieves a substantially higher recall (0.9059) than the threshold-based optimisation approach (0.5316), indicating a greater ability to capture true habitat extents and reduce underprediction across complex intertidal zones. 14.2 Ecosystem Biomass Dynamics and Initial Footprint Analysis
To quantify the broader ecological impact of these changing conditions, ecosystem performance was evaluated through domain-wide total biomass and localised dynamics restricted to the initial mangrove footprint.








Figure 14.5: Normalised total biomass dynamics over the 100-year simulation period for Cape Preston: (a) Total biomass across the entire domain, and (b) Biomass restricted strictly to the initial mangrove footprint under SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios.



As shown in Figure 14.5 (a), the normalised total biomass across the entire domain increases steadily over the first 60 to 70 years across all scenarios as new intertidal zones become available through landward migration, eventually stabilising or showing minor divergence depending on the severity of the SLR rate.
Conversely, examining the initial footprint biomass (Figure 14.5 b) isolates the performance of the pre-existing mangrove stands. Under the low SLR scenario (SSP119), the initial footprint experiences sustained growth, peaking at roughly 1.2 times its original baseline before stabilising. However, under medium (SSP370) and high (SSP585) SLR rates, the biomass within the initial footprint experiences a noticeable decline after year 60—dropping to approximately 0.93 (SSP370) and 0.86 (SSP585) of initial levels by Year 100. This indicates that while the overall ecosystem compensates via landward expansion, established stands under higher emission pathways undergo progressive submergence stress over multi-decadal timescales.

14.3 Morphological Dynamics and Sediment Redistribution
To understand the physical drivers governing the stability of the Cape Preston mangrove ecosystem under varying SLR scenarios, long-term morphological adjustments were evaluated.
Examining the creek network trajectory across the simulation period (Figure 14.6) reveals that channel migration and bank erosion are marginal and highly constrained across all three scenarios (SSP119, SSP370, and SSP585). Unlike environments prone to severe channel widening, Cape Preston exhibits a slightly stable tidal creek morphology, with minor shifts restricted primarily to active main-stem channels.

The surface sediment composition specifically the distribution of the top-layer mud fraction plays a critical role in determining substrate suitability and nutrient availability for mangrove colonisation and landward migration.

As illustrated by the mud fraction projections across the scenarios (Figure 14.7, Figure 14.8, Figure 14.9), fine sediment deposition progressively accumulates within newly inundated supratidal flats and upper intertidal transition zones over the 100-year timeframe.
Crucially, this sediment trapping creates favorable muddy substrate conditions in areas newly reached by tidal wetting. This matches the observed ecological response: rather than undergoing widespread fringe collapse, the combination of stable creek configurations, adequate fine-sediment accretion, and gentle topographic gradients allows mangroves at Cape Preston to steadily colonise the rising water levels, facilitating successful landward encroachment across all emission pathways.

title: 14  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
section: 14.4 Comparative Site Sensitivity and Hydrodynamic Controls
text:
14.4 Comparative Site Sensitivity and Hydrodynamic Controls
The differences in mangrove responses across sea level rise (SLR) scenarios at Cape Preston are less pronounced than those predicted for the Giralia and Urala study sites. This contrast suggests that mangrove sensitivity to SLR is strongly influenced by the prevailing tidal regime, local topography and the relationship between water level changes and the distribution of suitable elevations for mangrove establishment and persistence.
A key factor is the difference in tidal range between the study sites. Giralia and Urala experience tidal ranges of approximately 0.8 to 2.25 m, whereas Cape Preston is characterised by a substantially larger tidal range of approximately 1.5 to 4.2 m. At Cape Preston, the additional SLR increments considered in this study (0.5, 0.9 and 1.25 m) represent a smaller proportion of the overall tidal range than at the other sites. Consequently, although SLR raises mean water levels and modifies inundation frequency and duration, its relative influence on the existing tidal water level envelope may be less pronounced. This could contribute to the more similar mangrove responses predicted across the SLR scenarios at Cape Preston. However, tidal range alone does not determine mangrove sensitivity, as changes in inundation frequency, hydroperiod and exposure duration can still substantially alter the suitability of intertidal areas for mangrove establishment and persistence, even within a macrotidal system.
Topographic morphology provides a further explanation for the contrasting responses. Giralia and Urala contain extensive, low gradient upper intertidal surfaces, where relatively small changes in water level can produce substantial horizontal shifts in the inundation boundary. These surfaces can therefore amplify the spatial consequences of SLR, particularly where broad areas of terrain lie close to the elevation thresholds governing mangrove establishment and persistence. In contrast, the comparatively restricted high intertidal area at Cape Preston may limit the extent to which changes in water level translate into large horizontal expansions of suitable mangrove habitat. Where the available intertidal terrain is constrained by steeper elevation gradients or the configuration of existing landforms, similar vertical changes in water level may produce smaller changes in the area available for mangrove colonisation.
Together, these hydrodynamic and geomorphological characteristics provide a plausible explanation for the relatively consistent landward migration patterns predicted across the SLR scenarios at Cape Preston. The results indicate that mangrove responses depend not only on the magnitude of projected SLR, but also on the local elevation distribution, tidal inundation regime and availability of suitable land for colonisation. Nevertheless, the apparent similarity between scenarios should not be interpreted as evidence that Cape Preston is inherently less vulnerable to SLR. Mangrove responses may also depend on local elevation thresholds, sediment dynamics, establishment constraints and the potential for coastal infrastructure or other geomorphological barriers to restrict landward migration. These factors warrant consideration when interpreting the modelled projections and comparing mangrove sensitivity among sites.






NoteSummary: Century-Scale Ecological Trajectories at Cape Preston



Synthesising century scale eco-morphodynamic simulations reveals that mangrove responses across emission pathways at Cape Preston are remarkably uniform compared to other regional sites (Giralia and Urala). We think the local macro tidal environment features an immense tidal range spanning approximately 1.5 to 4.2 metres alongside a more restricted high intertidal area, additional sea level rise increments exert a proportionally smaller influence on overall habitat dynamics. Consequently, despite varying emission trajectories, Cape Preston demonstrates steady and highly comparable landward migration trends with minimal scenario divergence through to Year 100.

crumbs: 15  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise

title: 15  Cyanobacterial mat Response to Sea Level Rise
text:
15.2 Spatial Projections and Inter-Model Comparisons
The spatiotemporal projections reveal a marked response of cyanobacterial mats to sea-level rise across the Cape Preston intertidal domain. Under the low-emissions SSP119 scenario, algal mat coverage exhibits moderate resilience, experiencing a reduction of roughly 15% to 25% by Year 50 and up to 40% by Year 100 as wetting extends across the flats. Under moderate (SSP370) and high (SSP585) emissions scenarios, the rate of water level rise outpaces landward migration capacity, leading to severe habitat contraction with algal mat coverage reductions exceeding 65% by Year 50 and dropping by more than 85% to complete near-total submergence by Year 100.
Comparing the two modelling paradigms, the Random Forest (RF) classifier captures smooth, broader spatial persistence across supratidal zones by relying on non-linear probabilistic associations among hydrodynamic drivers. In contrast, the threshold-based optimisation approach enforces strict physical envelope boundaries, predicting more sharply delineated zonation bands that explicitly highlight coastal squeeze and acute drowning thresholds under high-forcing scenarios.
Regarding the mangrove communities evaluated alongside the algal dynamics, alongshore-averaged profiles show that mangrove fractions maintain a stable distribution across lower-to-middle intertidal elevations during the first 50 years, but experience compression and upward landward shifting by Year 100 as rising sea levels alter intertidal inundation frequencies and bed shear stress limits.

title: 13  Calibration and Validation
text:
13.5 Summary and Framework Transferability
Although formal hydrodynamic calibration was constrained by the absence of independent in-situ water level loggers, the successful calibration and validation of both the mangrove and cyanobacterial mat models demonstrate the practical transferability of the modelling framework. By relying on satellite-derived habitat maps from Project A (Hickey et al., 2025) to directly calibrate ecological responses, the framework successfully adapted to Cape Preston’s distinct geomorphology, narrower intertidal zone, and differing tidal regime without requiring a fully tuned hydrodynamic baseline.
As highlighted in the Chapter 1, Cape Preston was not intended to provide an independently hydrodynamically validated prediction, but rather to serve as an exploratory test bed. The reasonable agreement achieved for present-day baseline conditions particularly through the Random Forest classifier (\(F_1 = 0.6094\)) proves that data-driven habitat mapping components can robustly translate across diverse arid coastlines. This successfully illustrates the broader transferability of the tools developed through this research, providing an adaptable framework that can be reliably applied to other coastal environments where in-situ hydrodynamic data are limited. Chapter 14 and Chapter 15 shows the mangrove and algal mat’s response to the future SLR.
