title: 16  Synthesis and Integration
text:
16.1 Overarching Objectives
This research programme addresses a critical knowledge gap in coastal geomorphology and ecology: understanding how hyper arid intertidal ecosystems, particularly mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats, respond to accelerating sea level rise (SLR) and coastal development. Previous coastal wetland research has predominantly focused on humid tropical mangroves, temperate marshes and sediment rich river deltas, while the dynamics of arid, macrotidal and episodically inundated systems such as those along the West Pilbara coast remain less well understood. By integrating field observations, high resolution spatial datasets and a dynamically coupled biohydromorphodynamic modelling framework, this study evaluated the long term resilience, vulnerability and spatial redistribution of intertidal ecosystems across three distinct study domains: Giralia Bay, Urala and Cape Preston. The modelling framework combines Delft3D Flexible Mesh hydrodynamics with ecological modules and data driven habitat classification approaches. This synthesis brings together the principal findings to establish an integrated understanding of coastal ecosystem responses under low, intermediate and high greenhouse gas emission pathways.

title: 16  Synthesis and Integration
text:
16.2 Methodological Advancements and Paradigm Comparisons
Projecting coastal wetland trajectories over decadal to centennial timescales requires modelling frameworks capable of representing interactions between hydrodynamic forcing, sediment dynamics, morphological evolution and biological processes. Traditional assessments of SLR impacts have often relied on static bathtub models or simplified approaches in which hydrodynamic, morphological and ecological processes are represented separately. Bathtub models estimate inundation from water levels and static topography, without explicitly representing sediment transport, morphological adjustment or biological adaptation. Consequently, they may misrepresent future mangrove migration pathways where steep topography, sediment limitations or other physical constraints restrict landward expansion. Conversely, such approaches cannot adequately represent the potential for vegetation to modify flow resistance, influence sediment deposition and contribute to changes in bed elevation. Similarly, sequentially coupled or offline models may not fully capture the feedbacks between hydrodynamics, morphology and vegetation when these processes are updated independently or at relatively coarse time intervals.
To address these limitations, this study developed and applied a coupled biohydromorphodynamic modelling framework in which hydrodynamic conditions and vegetation related flow resistance interact dynamically. This approach provides a process based representation of the coevolution of intertidal landscapes and vegetation across spatial scales of several kilometres. The framework was complemented by two approaches for representing cyanobacterial mat distributions: Random Forest machine learning classification and threshold based optimisation using differential evolution. These methods account for the distinct characteristics of cyanobacterial mats, whose distribution and persistence are strongly influenced by inundation, hydration and desiccation conditions rather than the slower growth and establishment processes characteristic of woody vegetation. Together, these modelling approaches provide complementary means of evaluating potential habitat suitability, spatial continuity and fragmentation across heterogeneous arid coastal environments.

title: 18  Synthesis and Integration
section: 18.3 Overarching Ecosystem Trajectories Across Emission Pathways
text:
18.3 Overarching Ecosystem Trajectories Across Emission Pathways
The multi decadal projections across the three Shared Socioeconomic Pathway scenarios reveal substantial differences in the predicted responses of West Pilbara intertidal ecosystems to SLR. Under the low emissions pathway SSP119, representing approximately 0.5 m of SLR by 2125 in the scenarios considered, mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats generally exhibit greater persistence and more gradual spatial redistribution. At Giralia Bay and Urala, intertidal zonation remains comparatively stable over the 100 year projection period, although localised landward migration occurs as rising water levels increase inundation across previously higher elevation salt flats. Cyanobacterial mats also redistribute along and around tidal creek networks, with their persistence and spatial continuity influenced by local topography, inundation conditions and the availability of suitable substrate.
Under the intermediate and high emissions pathways, SSP370 and SSP585, the projected ecological responses become increasingly pronounced. These scenarios represent approximately 0.95 m and 1.25 m of SLR, respectively, by 2125. Increasing water levels initially create additional inundated areas and potential opportunities for landward expansion. At Urala, for example, increased tidal penetration under elevated sea levels promotes substantial headward extension of tidal creeks, with modelled incision extending more than five kilometres inland. Such changes may temporarily facilitate the redistribution of mangroves and cyanobacterial mats by connecting previously less frequently inundated areas to the tidal network. However, this initial expansion does not necessarily translate into long term persistence. Where rates of SLR exceed the capacity of vegetation to track suitable elevations, or where suitable landward areas become unavailable, the modelled distributions become increasingly restricted. Under SSP585, the projections indicate substantial losses of existing mangrove and cyanobacterial mat areas by Year 100, with more than 85% of the original mapped extent becoming submerged in the unconstrained settings considered. Remaining areas become concentrated along elevated basin margins and other locations where local elevation and inundation conditions continue to support persistence. These patterns highlight the potential for substantial coastal squeeze and ecosystem reorganisation under high SLR.
Regional geomorphology and tidal regime further influence the differences in projected responses among the three study sites. Giralia Bay and Urala contain extensive, low gradient upper intertidal flats, where relatively small vertical changes in water level can translate into substantial horizontal shifts in inundation boundaries. These topographic characteristics can facilitate landward redistribution but may also expose large areas to changing inundation regimes as sea levels rise. Cape Preston, by comparison, experiences a larger macrotidal range of approximately 1.5 to 4.2 m and has a more restricted high intertidal area. The SLR increments therefore represent a smaller proportion of its overall tidal range, potentially contributing to the comparatively consistent landward migration patterns predicted for mangroves across the scenarios. Nevertheless, the magnitude of the tidal range alone does not determine ecological sensitivity. Local elevation distributions, inundation frequency, substrate conditions and the availability of suitable land remain important controls on mangrove establishment and persistence. The projected redistribution of cyanobacterial mats at Cape Preston also varies between modelling approaches, demonstrating that the representation of ecological suitability can influence the spatial patterns and extent of future mat distributions.
Coastal development introduces an additional constraint on these natural redistribution processes. At Urala, the implementation of rigid, impermeable salt bund walls restricts the landward migration of mangroves under intermediate and high SLR scenarios. In the unconstrained simulations, the modelled mangrove extent increases to approximately 2.0 to 2.35 times the baseline extent by Year 100. In contrast, development constrained simulations produce substantial canopy retreat, resulting in a net reduction of approximately 32% to 41% in late century mangrove extent relative to the baseline. The bund walls also restrict the development of secondary tidal creek branches, potentially reducing the connectivity between tidal channels and landward areas. These results demonstrate how coastal infrastructure can alter hydrodynamic pathways and limit the capacity of intertidal ecosystems to respond to rising sea levels, even where suitable elevations may otherwise be available.

title: 16  Synthesis and Integration
text:
16.4 Key Assumptions and Model Limitations
Although the modelling framework provides process based insights into arid intertidal ecosystem dynamics, several assumptions and limitations should be considered when interpreting the projections. First, spatial and temporal variations in surface salinity and subsurface porewater dynamics were not fully represented in the primary dynamic vegetation framework. In hyper arid coastal environments, root zone salinity can exert a strong physiological influence on mangrove establishment, growth and survival. Preliminary implementation of a proxy salinity mass balance approach reduced spatial overprediction in some areas, including Urala. However, numerical instabilities associated with wetting and drying under extreme hypersaline conditions, on the order of 100 parts per thousand, limited the implementation of explicit salinity stress feedbacks across the modelling domains. Consequently, the predicted suitable areas primarily reflect physical inundation conditions and specified ecological criteria, rather than a comprehensive assessment of physiological tolerance to hypersaline sabkha soils. In particular, the model may overestimate the potential for landward mangrove migration where saline groundwater, subsurface brine accumulation or restricted tidal flushing creates additional barriers to establishment.
Second, the hydrodynamic simulations were driven by tidal forcing without explicitly incorporating wind waves, storm surges or cyclone related meteorological events. The projections therefore do not represent wave induced erosion along vegetation margins, extreme bed shear stresses or the disturbance and recovery processes associated with major storm events. These processes may substantially influence sediment redistribution, channel evolution and vegetation persistence in exposed coastal environments.
Third, the hydrodynamic models were implemented in two dimensional, depth averaged mode. Although this approach is computationally practical for regional domains spanning hundreds of square kilometres, it does not explicitly resolve vertical stratification or three dimensional circulation processes within deeper tidal channels. These processes may affect local sediment transport, mixing and the distribution of suitable ecological conditions.
Fourth, vegetation colonisation is governed primarily by local environmental suitability criteria and the assumed availability of propagules. Explicit propagule transport, dispersal times, seed viability and establishment probabilities are not fully represented. As a result, the model may predict colonisation in areas that are physically suitable but not necessarily accessible to propagules within the simulated timeframe. Similarly, the ecological modules do not fully represent all processes governing vegetation mortality, recovery and resprouting.
Finally, the representation of sediment accretion is focused on inorganic surface sediment processes, without explicitly resolving organic matter accumulation through peat formation, root production and turnover, or subsurface subsidence. These processes can influence net surface elevation change and the capacity of intertidal ecosystems to maintain their position relative to rising sea levels. Their omission introduces uncertainty into long term projections, particularly in areas where sediment supply is limited or organic matter accumulation makes a substantial contribution to surface elevation.
Taken together, these limitations indicate that the projections should be interpreted as conditional assessments of ecosystem responses under specified physical and ecological assumptions, rather than deterministic forecasts. The results are most informative when used to compare relative responses among SLR scenarios, study sites and development configurations, while recognising that additional physical and biological processes may alter the timing and extent of future changes.

title: 18  Synthesis and Integration
section: 18.5 Strategic Management Implications and Adaptive Pathways
text:
18.5 Strategic Management Implications and Adaptive Pathways
The findings provide a basis for informing coastal planning, environmental assessment and infrastructure development along the Pilbara coastline. The potential for substantial mangrove and cyanobacterial mat redistribution under intermediate and high SLR scenarios highlights the importance of maintaining landward accommodation space. Coastal management should therefore consider protecting supratidal buffer areas and migration corridors, particularly where low gradient terrain provides opportunities for ecosystems to shift inland as inundation regimes change. Future infrastructure, including evaporation ponds, access roads and pastoral fencing, should be assessed in relation to projected tidal creek expansion and potential ecosystem migration pathways. Where the model identifies critical landward areas, avoiding or minimising new barriers to tidal connectivity may help retain opportunities for ecological adjustment.
Management assessments should also distinguish between changes in total mapped extent and changes in ecological condition. An apparent persistence or expansion of mangrove area does not necessarily indicate that ecosystem structure and function are being maintained. Under intermediate and high SLR, mangroves may become concentrated along narrow margins or newly incised channels, resulting in fragmented distributions and reduced spatial continuity. Monitoring should therefore consider not only vegetation extent but also canopy density, biomass, fragmentation, connectivity and changes in the elevation and inundation conditions of occupied areas. Similarly, cyanobacterial mats should be recognised as ecologically important primary producers within arid intertidal systems, and their changing distribution and spatial continuity should be incorporated into assessments of ecosystem response.
The substantial scenario divergence projected beyond Year 50 further supports the use of adaptive management approaches. Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways provide a useful framework for linking management decisions to observed environmental changes rather than relying solely on fixed planning horizons. Potential triggers could include measured rates of local sea level rise, changes in tidal creek extent, progressive loss of suitable elevation zones, declining mangrove continuity and increasing restrictions on landward migration. Regular monitoring and periodic model reassessment would allow these triggers to be updated as new observations become available. This approach would also help identify where additional field measurements, improved salinity characterisation or more detailed hydrodynamic modelling are required to reduce uncertainty.
Overall, this research demonstrates that the future of arid intertidal ecosystems along the West Pilbara coast will depend on the interaction between sea level rise, tidal hydrodynamics, local geomorphology, ecological processes and coastal development. The coupled modelling framework provides a means of examining these interactions and identifying areas where ecosystem redistribution or loss may be most pronounced. Its application across Giralia Bay, Urala and Cape Preston also demonstrates that responses cannot be inferred from sea level rise magnitude alone, because local topography, tidal regimes and development constraints produce distinct spatial outcomes. Incorporating these site specific controls into coastal planning, while addressing the identified model limitations through targeted monitoring and further model development, will be important for improving assessments of long term coastal ecosystem resilience and informing adaptive management across the Pilbara region.

title: 16  Synthesis and Integration
section: 16.3 Ecosystem Trajectories Across Sea Level Rise Scenarios
text:
16.3 Ecosystem Trajectories Across Sea Level Rise Scenarios
The multi decadal projections across the three Shared Socioeconomic Pathway scenarios reveal substantial differences in the predicted responses of West Pilbara intertidal ecosystems to SLR. Under the low emissions pathway SSP119, representing approximately 0.5 m of SLR by 2125 in the scenarios considered, mangrove forests and cyanobacterial mats generally exhibit greater persistence and more gradual spatial redistribution. At Giralia Bay and Urala, intertidal zonation remains comparatively stable over the 100 year projection period, although localised landward migration occurs as rising water levels increase inundation across previously higher elevation salt flats. Cyanobacterial mats also redistribute along and around tidal creek networks, with their persistence and spatial continuity influenced by local topography, inundation conditions and the availability of suitable substrate.
Under the intermediate and high emissions pathways, SSP370 and SSP585, the projected ecological responses become increasingly pronounced. These scenarios represent approximately 0.95 m and 1.25 m of SLR, respectively, by 2125. Increasing water levels initially create additional inundated areas and potential opportunities for landward expansion. At Urala, for example, increased tidal penetration under elevated sea levels promotes substantial headward extension of tidal creeks, with modelled incision extending more than five kilometres inland. Such changes may temporarily facilitate the redistribution of mangroves and cyanobacterial mats by connecting previously less frequently inundated areas to the tidal network. However, this initial expansion does not necessarily translate into long term persistence. Where rates of SLR exceed the capacity of vegetation to track suitable elevations, or where suitable landward areas become unavailable, the modelled distributions become increasingly restricted. Under SSP585, the projections indicate substantial losses of existing mangrove and cyanobacterial mat areas by Year 100, with more than 85% of the original mapped extent becoming submerged in the unconstrained settings considered. Remaining areas become concentrated along elevated basin margins and other locations where local elevation and inundation conditions continue to support persistence. These patterns highlight the potential for substantial coastal squeeze and ecosystem reorganisation under high SLR.
Regional geomorphology and tidal regime further influence the differences in projected responses among the three study sites. Giralia Bay and Urala contain extensive, low gradient upper intertidal flats, where relatively small vertical changes in water level can translate into substantial horizontal shifts in inundation boundaries. These topographic characteristics can facilitate landward redistribution but may also expose large areas to changing inundation regimes as sea levels rise. Cape Preston, by comparison, experiences a larger macrotidal range of approximately 1.5 to 4.2 m and has a more restricted high intertidal area. The SLR increments therefore represent a smaller proportion of its overall tidal range, potentially contributing to the comparatively consistent landward migration patterns predicted for mangroves across the scenarios. Nevertheless, the magnitude of the tidal range alone does not determine ecological sensitivity. Local elevation distributions, inundation frequency, substrate conditions and the availability of suitable land remain important controls on mangrove establishment and persistence. The projected redistribution of cyanobacterial mats at Cape Preston also varies between modelling approaches, demonstrating that the representation of ecological suitability can influence the spatial patterns and extent of future mat distributions.
Coastal development introduces an additional constraint on these natural redistribution processes. At Urala, the implementation of rigid, impermeable salt bund walls restricts the landward migration of mangroves under intermediate and high SLR scenarios. In the unconstrained simulations, the modelled mangrove extent increases to approximately 2.0 to 2.35 times the baseline extent by Year 100. In contrast, development constrained simulations produce substantial canopy retreat, resulting in a net reduction of approximately 32% to 41% in late century mangrove extent relative to the baseline. The bund walls also restrict the development of secondary tidal creek branches, potentially reducing the connectivity between tidal channels and landward areas. These results demonstrate how coastal infrastructure can alter hydrodynamic pathways and limit the capacity of intertidal ecosystems to respond to rising sea levels, even where suitable elevations may otherwise be available.

title: 16  Synthesis and Integration
text:
16.5 Management Implications and Adaptive Pathways
The findings provide a basis for informing coastal planning, environmental assessment and infrastructure development along the Pilbara coastline. The potential for substantial mangrove and cyanobacterial mat redistribution under intermediate and high SLR scenarios highlights the importance of maintaining landward accommodation space. Coastal management should therefore consider protecting supratidal buffer areas and migration corridors, particularly where low gradient terrain provides opportunities for ecosystems to shift inland as inundation regimes change. Future infrastructure, including evaporation ponds, access roads and pastoral fencing, should be assessed in relation to projected tidal creek expansion and potential ecosystem migration pathways. Where the model identifies critical landward areas, avoiding or minimising new barriers to tidal connectivity may help retain opportunities for ecological adjustment.
Management assessments should also distinguish between changes in total mapped extent and changes in ecological condition. An apparent persistence or expansion of mangrove area does not necessarily indicate that ecosystem structure and function are being maintained. Under intermediate and high SLR, mangroves may become concentrated along narrow margins or newly incised channels, resulting in fragmented distributions and reduced spatial continuity. Monitoring should therefore consider not only vegetation extent but also canopy density, biomass, fragmentation, connectivity and changes in the elevation and inundation conditions of occupied areas. Similarly, cyanobacterial mats should be recognised as ecologically important primary producers within arid intertidal systems, and their changing distribution and spatial continuity should be incorporated into assessments of ecosystem response.
The substantial scenario divergence projected beyond Year 50 further supports the use of adaptive management approaches. Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways provide a useful framework for linking management decisions to observed environmental changes rather than relying solely on fixed planning horizons. Potential triggers could include measured rates of local sea level rise, changes in tidal creek extent, progressive loss of suitable elevation zones, declining mangrove continuity and increasing restrictions on landward migration. Regular monitoring and periodic model reassessment would allow these triggers to be updated as new observations become available. This approach would also help identify where additional field measurements, improved salinity characterisation or more detailed hydrodynamic modelling are required to reduce uncertainty.
Overall, this research demonstrates that the future of arid intertidal ecosystems along the West Pilbara coast will depend on the interaction between sea level rise, tidal hydrodynamics, local geomorphology, ecological processes and coastal development. The coupled modelling framework provides a means of examining these interactions and identifying areas where ecosystem redistribution or loss may be most pronounced. Its application across Giralia Bay, Urala and Cape Preston also demonstrates that responses cannot be inferred from sea level rise magnitude alone, because local topography, tidal regimes and development constraints produce distinct spatial outcomes. Incorporating these site specific controls into coastal planning, while addressing the identified model limitations through targeted monitoring and further model development, will be important for improving assessments of long term coastal ecosystem resilience and informing adaptive management across the Pilbara region.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
Figure 1.1: Conceptual eco-geomorphic cross-section of an arid coastal environment illustrating habitat zonation, salinity gradients, and hydro-evaporative feedback processes from subtidal seagrass beds to supratidal terrestrial dunes.









Subtidal to Lower Intertidal Zone: Subtidal seagrass meadows and macroalgal communities may occur adjacent to fringing mangrove forests along sheltered tidal channels and lower intertidal shorelines. Mangrove distribution is influenced by inundation frequency, substrate stability, and salinity, while tidal exchange can facilitate salt export and influence soil salinity (Cohen & Lara, 2003; Saintilan et al., 2018; Semeniuk, 1994).
Mid- to Upper Intertidal Zone: Landward of, or interspersed with, mangrove forests, saltmarsh and succulent halophyte communities, including Tecticornia spp., may occupy areas subject to less frequent tidal inundation and variable soil salinity. The distribution of these communities depends on local elevation, hydroperiod, substrate properties, and hydrological conditions (Saintilan et al., 2018; Yando et al., 2023).
Upper Intertidal to Supratidal Zone: Saltflats, including hypersaline flats sometimes described as sabkhas, and cyanobacterial mats commonly occur in upper-intertidal and supratidal environments. Infrequent inundation, high evaporation, and restricted drainage can promote salt accumulation, creating conditions that limit the establishment of vascular plants. These habitats may form mosaics or transitional zones between vegetated intertidal communities and terrestrial vegetation or coastal dunes (Figure 1.1) (Blanco-Sacristán et al., 2022; Eliot, 2013; Semeniuk, 1994).

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 The Pilbara Setting

Regional Climate and Hydroclimatic Setting
The Exmouth–Pilbara region of Western Australia represents a distinctive arid coastal environment in which extensive tidal creeks, hypersaline supratidal mudflats, and low-lying coastal landforms interact with a macro-tidal regime (Eliot, 2013; Semeniuk, 1994). The regional climate is arid to semi-arid and tropical, characterised by high temperatures and low, highly variable rainfall. Summer maximum temperatures frequently exceed 32 °C along the coast and may surpass 45 °C inland, while winter coastal temperatures rarely fall below 10 °C (Sudmeyer, 2016). Mean annual precipitation (\(P\)) is generally low, approximately 200–350 mm in parts of the region, and is strongly seasonal and spatially variable. This limited rainfall, combined with high potential evapotranspiration (\(\text{PET}\)) exceeding 2,500 mm annually, yields a low annual \(P/\text{PET}\) aridity index ratio of approximately \(0.05\) to \(0.20\) across the coastal zone, placing the system firmly within the arid to hyper-arid classification (Zomer et al., 2022b). Most rainfall occurs during the warmer months, particularly through episodic thunderstorms and tropical cyclone events. The Pilbara coast is also exposed to tropical cyclones, which can deliver substantial rainfall, generate extreme water levels, and drive episodic sediment transport (Bureau of Meteorology, 2009). In contrast, the cooler months are typically characterised by lower rainfall and high evaporation. Consequently, river discharge and terrestrial sediment delivery to the coast are highly episodic, with substantial inputs often associated with major rainfall and flood events (see Chapter 2 for a detailed assessment of hydroclimatic drivers).


Intertidal Geomorphology and Habitat Zonation
Intertidal benthic coastal habitat (BCH) communities across the West Pilbara exhibit pronounced spatial zonation associated with elevation, inundation frequency, salinity, and local geomorphological conditions (Hickey & Lovelock, 2022; Semeniuk, 1994). Along many sheltered tidal creeks and coastal embayments, mangrove forests, dominated by Avicennia marina, occupy lower intertidal margins. These may transition landward into succulent samphire communities, including Tecticornia spp., followed by extensive cyanobacterial mats and hypersaline saltflats, sometimes referred to as sabkhas (Hickey et al., 2025). Although this sequence is characteristic of many arid coastal settings, the distribution and continuity of individual habitats vary with local topography, hydrodynamics, sediment characteristics, drainage, and surface–groundwater interactions.
Mangroves in the region commonly fringe tidal creeks and occupy elevations subject to regular tidal inundation. In contrast, samphire communities and cyanobacterial mats may occupy higher intertidal and supratidal surfaces that experience less frequent inundation, high evaporative water loss, and variable soil salinity. Saltflats occur in areas where limited drainage and strong evaporation favour salt accumulation and restrict the establishment of vegetation. The resulting habitat mosaic reflects the interaction between tidal exchange, freshwater inputs, sediment dynamics, and groundwater processes. These intertidal communities contribute to sediment stabilisation, nutrient cycling, and primary production, supporting ecological connections between coastal, marine, and terrestrial food webs (Dee et al., 2026; Eliot, 2013; Hickey et al., 2023; Seashore Engineering, 2022).

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
section: 3.3 Modelling Approaches Adopted in This Study
text:
3.3 Modelling Approaches Adopted in This Study
This study adopted two approaches to predicting habitat change: physical modelling followed by statistical habitat prediction, and process-based mangrove modelling with two-way feedbacks to hydro-morphodynamics. DFM provides the physical modelling component in both approaches. The following sections describe the physical modelling configuration and the implementation of the coupled mangrove framework. Delft3D Flexible Mesh was selected as the core hydrodynamic–morphodynamic model for this study as it is an established, open-source (for academic) modelling platform for simulating coastal hydrodynamics, sediment transport and morphological evolution (Kernkamp et al., 2011). DFM has also been adopted in several studies coupling vegetation dynamics with hydrodynamic and morphological processes, including the frameworks developed by Xie et al. (2022); Willemsen et al. (2022); Beselly et al. (2023); Dunlop et al. (2025). These developments provided a methodological basis for selecting DFM as the physical modelling component of the framework developed here.
In the process-based approach, we developed a dynamically coupled bio-hydro-morphodynamic modelling framework integrating DFM with a vegetation module based on NBSDynamics (Nature-Based Solutions Dynamics) (Deltares, 2022), incorporating ecological parameterisation strategies adapted from Xie et al. (2022), Berger & Hildenbrandt (2000) and Van Maanen et al. (2015). A custom Python coupling interface manages information exchange between the hydro-morphodynamic model and the vegetation module, enabling the framework to run on high-performance computing (HPC) clusters and support spatially extensive simulations.

3.3.1 Model integration and information exchange
As illustrated in Figure 3.1, the framework represents interactions between hydrodynamic conditions, vegetation dynamics and morphological evolution through a two-way coupling process. DFM resolves hydrodynamics and sediment transport, while the vegetation module evaluates mangrove establishment, growth and mortality in response to environmental conditions. The resulting changes in vegetation properties are then returned to DFM to update spatially varying flow resistance and bed roughness.
The coupling operates through the following sequence at defined coupling intervals:

Hydrodynamic and morphodynamic simulation: DFM concurrently simulates hydrodynamics and sediment transport, calculating spatially distributed water levels, flow velocities, bed shear stresses, and bed level changes across the intertidal domain. These variables define the physical and morphological environment experienced by the vegetation.
Environmental output transfer: The Python coupling interface extracts and transfers the integrated hydrodynamic and morphodynamic outputs (water levels, bed shear stresses, and updated bed elevations) to the vegetation module.
Vegetation response and updates: At designated vegetation time steps, the vegetation module evaluates mangrove colonisation, growth, and mortality based on the updated environmental conditions and ecological thresholds. It then updates spatially distributed vegetation properties, including stem height, stem diameter, and stem density.
Feedback to hydro-morphodynamics: Updated vegetation parameters are converted into spatially varying flow resistance and drag parameters within DFM. This allows the evolving canopy and root structures to alter flow patterns and sediment transport in subsequent coupling steps.

This iterative exchange enables the framework to represent feedbacks between hydrodynamics, sediment transport, morphological evolution and mangrove development. Rather than prescribing vegetation as a static source of flow resistance, the framework allows vegetation properties and the physical environment to evolve in response to one another.
Unlike the mangrove component, cyanobacterial mats are represented using decoupled, data-driven habitat-suitability approaches. Although developing a mechanistic model of cyanobacterial mat dynamics coupled to hydrodynamics and sediment transport is technically feasible, such an approach would require substantial development, calibration, and validation. In particular, reliable numerical representation of mat dynamics requires a more comprehensive understanding of their responses to environmental forcing, including light availability, temperature, salinity, and hydrodynamic conditions, as well as sufficient observational data to parameterise and validate these relationships. Developing and validating such a model would extend beyond the timeframe of this project.
We therefore adopted two complementary data-driven approaches Section 4.5 that use the outcomes of the mangrove modelling framework to inform the hydrodynamic simulations from which potential cyanobacterial mat habitats are assessed. Specifically, the mangrove predictions provide the evolving vegetation distribution used to update the hydrodynamic representation, while cyanobacterial mat suitability is evaluated separately using the resulting hydrodynamic conditions.
To account for methodological uncertainty and evaluate different response characteristics, we implemented both a Random Forest (RF) machine-learning classifier with full model details and algorithmic implementation described in Section 4.5 and a threshold-based optimisation approach. These methods use eco-hydrodynamic thresholds and multi-dimensional envelopes derived from present-day satellite-based mat distributions to identify areas with physical conditions consistent with observed mat habitats (Hickey et al., 2025). This dual-method framework enables the potential redistribution of cyanobacterial mats to be assessed under changing physical conditions without explicitly simulating microbial growth, mat biomass, or mat-driven morphological feedbacks. The comprehensive data-driven methods and their implementations are detailed in Section 4.5.






Figure 3.1: Schematic representation of the dynamically coupled bio-hydro-morphodynamic modelling framework. Delft3D Flexible Mesh (DFM) simulates hydrodynamics, sediment transport and morphological change, while the vegetation module represents mangrove colonisation, growth and mortality. A Python coupling interface exchanges physical forcing and updated vegetation properties between the two components. Cyanobacterial mat suitability is assessed separately using hydrodynamic outputs.





3.3.2 Accelerating long-term simulations
The primary objective of the framework is to investigate intertidal habitat changes over centennial timescales across coastal-scale domains. Explicitly simulating every hydrodynamic and morphodynamic process over hundreds of years, while repeatedly updating vegetation, would impose substantial computational demands. We therefore employed the morphological acceleration factor (\(f_{\mathrm{mor}}\)) in DFM to accelerate bed-level evolution relative to the simulated hydrodynamic time.
A morphological acceleration factor of \(f_{\mathrm{mor}} = 50\) was adopted, such that approximately two years of hydrodynamic simulation could represent 100 years of morphological evolution under the accelerated-morphology assumption. This approach reduces the computational burden of long-term simulations while retaining spatially explicit hydrodynamic and sediment-transport calculations. Existing studies have also employed a similar morphological acceleration in coupled vegetation and morphodynamic studies, including those by Willemsen et al. (2022); Xie et al. (2022); Beselly et al. (2023); Dunlop et al. (2025).
However, accelerating morphological evolution does not automatically ensure that ecological processes remain consistent with the accelerated simulation timescale. Vegetation growth, establishment and mortality must be treated consistently with the temporal scaling applied to the physical processes; otherwise, the relative rates of vegetation development and morphological adjustment may become unrealistic. The coupling configuration and temporal treatment of the model components are described in more detail in Chapter 4.
Morphological acceleration also has implications for the interpretation of environmental forcing. In particular, transient water-level events, such as storm surges, should not necessarily be treated as representative of the long-term conditions experienced over the accelerated morphological timescale. The selection of hydrodynamic forcing therefore required consideration of the dominant tidal constituents and the broader water-level variability characteristic of the West Pilbara coast.


3.3.3 Derivation of representative tidal forcing
As discussed in Chapter 2, the West Pilbara coast experiences substantial water-level variability arising from astronomical tides, seasonal and interannual fluctuations, tropical cyclones and other meteorological processes. These variations influence inundation frequency and duration, sediment transport and the environmental conditions experienced by intertidal vegetation. Although such variability can affect long-term habitat trajectories, directly imposing the complete observed water-level record within a morphologically accelerated simulation may disproportionately amplify transient events relative to the timescale of morphological evolution.
To establish a representative tidal forcing for the long-term simulations, we therefore performed harmonic analysis of water-level observations from the Exmouth and Onslow tide gauges. The analysis was conducted using the Python implementation of UTide (Codiga, 2011), which estimates the amplitudes and phases of astronomical tidal constituents from observed water-level time series. The extracted constituents were ranked according to their contribution to the reconstructed tidal signal, and the four dominant constituents were selected to represent the principal tidal variability.
The four selected constituents were M2, S2, K1 and O1. Together, they account for approximately 100% of the tidal energy represented by the four selected constituents at both analysis sites. Their frequencies, amplitudes, phases and percentage energy contributions are summarised in Table 3.2.

The analysis of both tide gauges provided a basis for characterising the tidal regime across the study region. For simplicity, however, a single representative water-level forcing was applied across all study sites, as described in Table 3.2 and Section 1.4. This provides a consistent basis for comparing habitat responses between sites, although it does not capture all local differences in tidal amplitude, phase and water-level variability.
It it important to highlight that the use of the four dominant constituents also represents a deliberate simplification of the observed water-level regime. Seasonal and interannual variability, including variations associated with the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), can influence inundation patterns and sediment dynamics. The duration and timing of these variations may affect vegetation establishment, mortality and morphological adjustment, potentially producing different habitat trajectories even under the same long-term mean sea-level trend. The selected harmonic constituents do not explicitly reproduce these seasonal, interannual or event-driven variations.
Nevertheless, the purpose of the representative forcing is to establish a consistent baseline for investigating long-term habitat changes under the principal astronomical tidal controls, rather than to reproduce every short-term fluctuation in observed water levels. The resulting predictions should therefore be interpreted in the context of this forcing assumption, with the potential influence of omitted seasonal, interannual and extreme-event variability recognised as a source of uncertainty.


3.3.4 Salinity representation and model limitations
Salinity is an important environmental control on mangrove establishment, growth and survival, particularly in the hyper-arid West Pilbara, where evaporation, limited freshwater input and restricted tidal exchange can produce hypersaline conditions. Field observations indicate that salinity is approximately 35–55 ppt near creek mouths, increases towards the landward intertidal zone and can exceed 140 ppt across salt-flat environments. These spatial gradients suggest that salinity may constrain mangrove colonisation even where inundation and elevation conditions become physically suitable.
During initial sensitivity testing, we encountered two difficulties when attempting to represent salinity in the modelling framework. First, stable simulations (short term runs) did not reproduce the high salinity concentrations observed in the landward intertidal and salt-flat environments, with modelled values generally remaining below approximately 55 ppt. Second, longer simulations exhibited numerical instability associated with wetting and drying transitions. In some runs, salinity increased sharply in cells undergoing wetting and drying, eventually reaching the model’s upper limit of 500 ppt. These extreme values (instability) subsequently spread across the computational domain, causing the simulation to crash.
These behaviours may be associated with the numerical treatment of salt during wetting and drying, including the handling of accumulated salt as cells become dry. However, the underlying cause was not investigated further, and the observed instability cannot be attributed conclusively to a particular numerical mechanism.
Salinity was not simulated explicitly in the final predictive framework. The inundation fitness relationship used for mangrove growth was intended to account indirectly for some salinity-related limitations, through associations between inundation, flushing and habitat conditions. However, this relationship does not predict salinity directly or resolve the salt balance. Actual salinity also depends on evaporation, rainfall, tidal exchange and groundwater contributions, so similar inundation conditions may occur under different salinity regimes. It is noteworthy to mention that several existing studies have also omitted salinity in their approach e.g., Xie et al. (2022); Van Maanen et al. (2015); Willemsen et al. (2022); Dunlop et al. (2025). The omission reflects a modelling constraint rather than an assumption that salinity is ecologically unimportant.
This simplification has important implications for interpreting the predictions. Even with the indirect representation of salinity, the framework can identify locations where the modelled physical conditions are consistent with mangrove establishment, but it cannot independently determine whether salinity would permit successful establishment or sustained growth. Consequently, some locations predicted to be suitable may remain unsuitable under actual hypersaline conditions, particularly in the upper intertidal zone and on salt flats. The resulting predictions should therefore be interpreted as potential habitat distributions under the represented physical and ecological processes, rather than definitive forecasts of realised mangrove distribution.

title: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
section: 11.3 Mangrove and Tidal Creek Responses to Sea-Level Rise
text:
11.3 Mangrove and Tidal Creek Responses to Sea-Level Rise

SSP119 (Low SLR, 0.5 m): Smaller changes in tidal creeks. The volume of water entering and leaving the intertidal area with each tide changes relatively little, so creek expansion is limited. Some mangroves are lost from the original footprint while others establish in new landward areas. By Year 100, total mangrove area remains above its initial value, while total biomass is close to its initial value.
SSP370 (Intermediate SLR, 0.9 m): Landward expansion along tidal creeks. As more water enters and leaves the intertidal area with each tide, creeks extend inland and create areas suitable for mangrove establishment. Mangrove area and biomass initially increase, but some gains are subsequently lost as inundation increases.
SSP585 (high SLR, 1.25 m) Extensive losses from the original mangrove footprint. Mangroves establish along newly formed inland creeks, while prolonged inundation causes major losses from existing stands. By Year 100, less than 5% of the original footprint remains. Establishment in new landward areas allows mangroves to persist across the wider domain.

title: 11  Mangrove Response to Sea Level Rise
section: 11.4 Effects of the Hypothetical Development Barrier
text:
11.4 Effects of the Hypothetical Development Barrier

Restricted landward migration: The hypothetical bund walls block water and sediment exchange across the development boundary, limiting creek extension and access to areas where mangroves could otherwise establish as sea level rises.
Less mangrove habitat by Year 100: Under SSP370 and SSP585, total mangrove area is approximately 2.0-2.35 times its initial value without the barrier, compared with approximately 1.2-1.6 times its initial value with the hypothetical bund walls.
Difference between scenarios: The hypothetical development produces approximately 32-41% less mangrove area by Year 100 than the corresponding scenario without development. Creek expansion and branching are also reduced.


Management implication: Access to suitable landward areas helps mangroves persist as sea level rises in these simulations. The hypothetical bund-wall experiment shows how a barrier can restrict that adaptation and reduce future habitat. These results highlight the need to consider migration pathways when assessing coastal development.
